passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Protein T is a small, single-domain enzyme whose folded structure is rich in alpha helices. A biochemist compared four forms of the protein by thermal denaturation: wild-type (WT); a variant in which a buried leucine was replaced with alanine (L to A); a variant in which a surface lysine was replaced with glutamate (K to E); and a variant in which two residues on neighboring helices were each replaced with cysteine so that a disulfide bond could form (S-S). Each sample was held in identical buffer while the temperature was raised, and the circular dichroism (CD) signal at 222 nm, which reports on helical content, was converted to the fraction of protein folded. The melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature at which half of the protein is folded. Tm values are listed in Table 1, and the melting curves for WT and the S-S variant are shown in Figure 1.
Mass spectrometry confirmed that all four proteins had the expected masses, and the S-S variant was purified under oxidizing conditions so that its new disulfide bond was intact.

qs.q: According to Table 1, which variant would be mostly unfolded at 50 °C?
o: The L to A variant, because its Tm of 49 °C is below 50 °C
Correct: Tm is the temperature at which half the protein is folded, so above 49 °C the L to A variant is more than half unfolded.
The WT protein, because it has the lowest Tm of the four forms
WT has a Tm of 58 °C, which is higher than that of L to A, so it is still mostly folded at 50 °C.
The K to E variant, because any charge reversal destabilizes a protein
K to E has a Tm of 57 °C, essentially unchanged; a surface charge swap is not automatically destabilizing.
The S-S variant, because covalent crosslinks make proteins rigid and prone to unfolding
The S-S variant has the highest Tm (67 °C); the crosslink stabilizes the fold.
qs.x: Tm is the temperature at which half the protein is folded, so above 49 °C the L to A variant is more than half unfolded. Trap: Picking the variant with the lowest Tm without noticing that the lowest value in the table belongs to the L to A variant, not WT.

qs.q: The higher Tm of the S-S variant is best explained by the disulfide bond:
o: restricting the conformations available to the unfolded chain, which raises the free-energy cost of unfolding
Correct: A covalent crosslink lowers the entropy gained on unfolding, so more thermal energy is required to unfold the protein.
adding a hydrophobic side chain to the core, which increases the entropy of the folded state
Cysteines forming a disulfide are not new core hydrophobic contacts, and a more ordered folded state would not be favored by higher entropy.
neutralizing the net charge of the protein so repulsion is removed
Cysteine substitutions at neutral pH do not change net charge in a way that explains a 9 °C rise in Tm.
converting alpha helices into beta sheets, which resist heat
The crosslink does not alter the type of secondary structure; the CD signal still reports helical content.
qs.x: A covalent crosslink lowers the entropy gained on unfolding, so more thermal energy is required to unfold the protein. Trap: Assuming that a stronger bond within the folded state alone explains stabilization, forgetting the entropy effect on the unfolded state.

qs.q: Replacing the surface lysine with glutamate changed Tm by only 1 °C, whereas replacing the buried leucine with alanine lowered it by 9 °C. Which explanation is most consistent with these results?
o: Surface residues never contribute to stability of any protein
This overgeneralizes; surface residues can form salt bridges or hydrogen bonds, but this particular swap was minor.
Leucine is polar and forms hydrogen bonds with water in the folded state
Leucine is nonpolar and aliphatic; it does not hydrogen bond with water.
The buried leucine contributes to hydrophobic packing in the core, which the smaller alanine side chain cannot fully provide
Correct: Buried nonpolar residues make van der Waals and hydrophobic contacts; leucine to alanine leaves a cavity and weakens packing.
Alanine is charged at physiological pH and is therefore poorly tolerated in the interior
Alanine has a nonpolar methyl side chain and is uncharged at physiological pH.
qs.x: Buried nonpolar residues make van der Waals and hydrophobic contacts; leucine to alanine leaves a cavity and weakens packing. Trap: Treating all substitutions as equivalent regardless of whether the residue is buried or exposed.

qs.q: A loss of CD signal at 222 nm as the sample is heated mainly reflects loss of which structural feature?
o: Quaternary structure, through subunit dissociation
Protein T is a single-domain protein and has no subunit interface to lose.
Peptide bonds, through thermal hydrolysis
Peptide bonds do not hydrolyze at these temperatures; mass spectrometry would show fragments.
The amino acid sequence, through racemization
Primary structure is not changed by this brief heating and CD at 222 nm does not report on it.
Alpha-helical secondary structure
Correct: Ellipticity near 222 nm is characteristic of helical backbone hydrogen-bonding patterns, which melt during denaturation.
qs.x: Ellipticity near 222 nm is characteristic of helical backbone hydrogen-bonding patterns, which melt during denaturation. Trap: Confusing denaturation (loss of higher-order structure) with breakage of covalent bonds in the primary structure.

qs.q: Figure 1 shows that at 60 °C about 0.30 of WT and about 0.85 of the S-S variant are folded. The ratio of folded WT to folded S-S protein at 60 °C is closest to:
o: WT has less folded protein than S-S at 60 °C, so the ratio must be below 1.
Correct: 0.30 divided by 0.85 is about 0.35, which is about 1 to 3.
This would require a folded WT fraction of about 0.085.
This inverts the ratio; the S-S variant has more folded protein at 60 °C.
qs.x: 0.30 divided by 0.85 is about 0.35, which is about 1 to 3. Trap: Dividing in the wrong order and reporting the inverse ratio.

graph.title: Figure 1. Fraction of protein T folded versus temperature

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Three tripeptides were synthesized, each with a free amino terminus and a free carboxyl terminus: peptide 1 (Ala-Glu-Gly), peptide 2 (Lys-Ala-Gly), and peptide 3 (His-Ala-Ala). A researcher wanted to separate the peptides by charge. The isoelectric point (pI) of a peptide is the pH at which its net charge is zero. Approximate pKa values for the ionizable groups in short peptides are given in Table 1; assume that each group ionizes independently.

The peptides were first compared by paper electrophoresis in a buffer of pH 8.0. In a second experiment, a mixture of the three peptides was applied at pH 5.0 to a cation-exchange column, whose resin carries fixed negatively charged sulfonate groups. The column was washed with the starting buffer, and bound peptides were then eluted with a gradient of increasing NaCl concentration. Fractions were analyzed for peptide content by their absorbance after reaction with a reagent that detects free amino groups.

qs.q: The pI of peptide 1 is closest to:
o: This would average the amino terminus and Glu pKa values, but the amino terminus is still protonated near the pI.
Correct: The charge goes +1, 0, -1 as the carboxyl terminus (3.1) and then the Glu side chain (4.3) deprotonate; the zero-charge form lies between them, pI = (3.1 + 4.3)/2 = 3.7.
This averages the amino terminus (8.0) with the carboxyl terminus (3.1) and ignores the Glu side chain.
This is the pKa of the amino terminus, which is not the group that sets the neutral point of an acidic peptide.
qs.x: The charge goes +1, 0, -1 as the carboxyl terminus (3.1) and then the Glu side chain (4.3) deprotonate; the zero-charge form lies between them, pI = (3.1 + 4.3)/2 = 3.7. Trap: Using only the two terminal groups to compute pI and ignoring the acidic Glu side chain.

qs.q: At pH 7.0, the net charge of peptide 2 is closest to:
o: This would require the amino terminus and Lys side chain to both be deprotonated at pH 7.0.
Correct: Lys side chain is +1, the carboxyl terminus is -1, and the amino terminus (pKa 8.0) is about 90% protonated, giving a net charge near +1.
This would require the Lys and amino groups to be neutral, which happens only far above pH 10.
This ignores the negative charge on the ionized carboxyl terminus.
qs.x: Lys side chain is +1, the carboxyl terminus is -1, and the amino terminus (pKa 8.0) is about 90% protonated, giving a net charge near +1. Trap: Counting the two positive groups and forgetting to subtract the carboxylate.

qs.q: In paper electrophoresis at pH 8.0, peptide 3 (pI 7.0) will most likely:
o: migrate toward the anode, because pH 8.0 is above its pI and it carries a net negative charge
Correct: Above its pI a peptide carries net negative charge and moves toward the positive electrode.
remain at the origin, because any pH above 7 gives zero net charge
Zero net charge occurs only at the pI of 7.0, not at all higher pH values.
migrate toward the cathode, because pH 8.0 is above its pI
Above the pI the net charge is negative, so migration is toward the anode, not the cathode.
migrate toward the cathode, because its His side chain is protonated at pH 8.0
His (pKa 6.0) is mostly deprotonated at pH 8.0, so it does not supply a net positive charge.
qs.x: Above its pI a peptide carries net negative charge and moves toward the positive electrode. Trap: Mixing up the direction of migration relative to the pI, sending an anionic peptide to the cathode.

qs.q: In the cation-exchange experiment at pH 5.0, which peptide will pass through the column without binding?
o: Peptide 1
Correct: At pH 5.0 peptide 1 has net charge near -1 (Glu and carboxyl deprotonated, amino terminus protonated), so it is repelled by the negative resin.
All three peptides bind, because the resin binds every polypeptide at any pH
Binding depends on net charge; a net negative peptide is not retained.
Peptide 3
Peptide 3 is positively charged (about +1) at pH 5.0 because the amino terminus and mostly protonated His outweigh the carboxylate.
Peptide 2
Peptide 2 is positively charged (+1) at pH 5.0 and binds the sulfonate resin.
qs.x: At pH 5.0 peptide 1 has net charge near -1 (Glu and carboxyl deprotonated, amino terminus protonated), so it is repelled by the negative resin. Trap: Forgetting that a cation exchanger retains positively charged molecules, not negatively charged ones.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: Two membrane receptors, R1 and R2, bind the same soluble ligand L. The extracellular domain of each receptor was immobilized on a sensor chip, and ligand at several concentrations was passed over the surface in a surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiment. Binding was followed in real time to obtain the association rate constant (kon) and the dissociation rate constant (koff) for each receptor, and the fraction of receptor sites occupied at equilibrium (Y) was recorded at each ligand concentration. For simple one-to-one binding, the dissociation constant is Kd = koff/kon, and Y = [L]/(Kd + [L]).

Selected values are given in Table 1, and the full equilibrium binding curves are plotted in Figure 1. The ligand concentration range used in the experiment was chosen to span the Kd values of both receptors. After equilibrium measurements, buffer without ligand was flowed over the chip so that the decay of the bound signal could be followed.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the two receptors is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
o: R2 binds L with higher affinity, because it requires more ligand to saturate
Needing more ligand to bind indicates lower, not higher, affinity.
The receptors have equal affinity, because kon is identical
Affinity depends on the ratio koff/kon, and koff differs tenfold.
R2 binds L with higher affinity, because its koff is larger
A larger koff means faster release, which lowers affinity.
R1 binds L with higher affinity, because it reaches half-saturation at a lower ligand concentration
Correct: R1 reaches Y = 0.50 at 10 nM, R2 at 100 nM; the lower Kd means higher affinity.
qs.x: R1 reaches Y = 0.50 at 10 nM, R2 at 100 nM; the lower Kd means higher affinity. Trap: Equating a larger koff or a need for more ligand with tighter binding.

qs.q: What is the Kd of receptor R2 for ligand L?
o: 100 nM
Correct: Kd = koff/kon = 0.10 s⁻¹ / 1 × 10⁶ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 1 × 10⁻⁷ M = 100 nM.
0.1 nM
This would result from inverting the ratio and mis-scaling the exponent.
1 µM
This would need a koff of 1.0 s⁻¹.
10 nM
This is the Kd of R1 (0.010 / 1 × 10⁶).
qs.x: Kd = koff/kon = 0.10 s⁻¹ / 1 × 10⁶ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 1 × 10⁻⁷ M = 100 nM. Trap: Using kon/koff instead of koff/kon, or slipping a power of ten when converting to nM.

qs.q: The difference in affinity between R1 and R2 is primarily due to a difference in:
o: the molecular mass of the ligand bound
The ligand is the same for both receptors.
how rapidly ligand and receptor associate
kon is identical for the two receptors.
the total number of receptor sites on the chip
Y is a fractional occupancy and is independent of how many sites are present.
the rate of complex dissociation
Correct: kon is the same, so the tenfold difference in Kd comes entirely from the tenfold difference in koff.
qs.x: kon is the same, so the tenfold difference in Kd comes entirely from the tenfold difference in koff. Trap: Assuming that tighter binding must come from faster association rather than slower dissociation.

qs.q: Assuming first-order dissociation, the half-life of the R1-L complex after ligand removal is closest to:
o: Correct: t1/2 = ln 2 / koff = 0.693 / 0.010 s⁻¹ = about 69 s.
This is 1/koff, the mean lifetime, not the half-life.
This would correspond to koff = 0.10 s⁻¹, the value for R2.
This results from mis-scaling the exponent when dividing.
qs.x: t1/2 = ln 2 / koff = 0.693 / 0.010 s⁻¹ = about 69 s. Trap: Reporting 1/koff (100 s) instead of ln 2/koff for the half-life.

qs.q: At 10 nM ligand, the fraction of R1 sites occupied compared with the fraction of R2 sites occupied is about:
o: 5 times higher
Correct: 0.50 / 0.09 is about 5.5, so R1 is occupied about five times as much as R2.
10 times higher
The tenfold difference is in Kd, but occupancy at 10 nM is not simply proportional to Kd because R1 is near saturation.
the same
The two receptors have different Kd values and therefore different occupancy.
2 times lower
R1 has the lower Kd and is more occupied, not less.
qs.x: 0.50 / 0.09 is about 5.5, so R1 is occupied about five times as much as R2. Trap: Assuming occupancy differs by exactly the ratio of the Kd values.

graph.title: Figure 1. Fractional saturation versus ligand concentration

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Plasmid pTX is a circular, double-stranded DNA molecule of 6.0 kb that carries an ampicillin-resistance gene. A student digested samples of pTX with the restriction enzymes EcoRI, BamHI, and HindIII, alone and in combination, and separated the products by agarose gel electrophoresis. Fragment sizes were estimated by comparison with a DNA size ladder; they are listed in Table 1. EcoRI recognizes the palindromic sequence GAATTC and cuts between G and A on each strand, leaving single-stranded 5' overhangs.

The student then purified a 1.2 kb DNA fragment that had EcoRI-cut ends and no internal EcoRI site. The fragment was mixed with EcoRI-linearized pTX in the presence of DNA ligase and ATP, and the mixture was used to transform E. coli, which were plated on medium containing ampicillin. Colonies were picked, plasmid DNA was prepared, and each preparation was digested with EcoRI to confirm the presence of the insert. The digestion products were then compared with the pattern expected for the original plasmid on the same gel.

qs.q: How many HindIII recognition sites are present in pTX?
o: One
One cut in a circular plasmid yields a single linear 6.0 kb fragment, as seen with EcoRI.
Four
Four sites would give four fragments; the plasmid is circular, so sites equal fragment number.
Two
Correct: A circular molecule cut at n sites yields n fragments; HindIII gives two fragments, so there are two sites.
Three
Three sites would give three fragments.
qs.x: A circular molecule cut at n sites yields n fragments; HindIII gives two fragments, so there are two sites. Trap: Applying the rule for linear DNA (fragments = sites + 1) to a circular plasmid.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 indicate that the EcoRI site lies:
o: within the 1.5 kb BamHI fragment and the 4.0 kb HindIII fragment
The 1.5 kb BamHI fragment and the 4.0 kb HindIII fragment remain intact in the double digests, so EcoRI does not cut them.
within the 1.5 kb BamHI fragment and the 2.0 kb HindIII fragment
The 1.5 kb BamHI fragment appears unchanged in the EcoRI + BamHI digest.
in the 4.5 kb BamHI and 2.0 kb HindIII fragments
Correct: EcoRI converts 4.5 kb to 3.5 + 1.0 (BamHI 1.5 kb fragment unchanged) and 2.0 kb to 1.5 + 0.5 (HindIII 4.0 kb fragment unchanged).
exactly at one of the two BamHI recognition sites in the plasmid
A cut at a BamHI site would not produce the 3.5 and 1.0 kb fragments and the 4.5 kb fragment would be unchanged.
qs.x: EcoRI converts 4.5 kb to 3.5 + 1.0 (BamHI 1.5 kb fragment unchanged) and 2.0 kb to 1.5 + 0.5 (HindIII 4.0 kb fragment unchanged). Trap: Choosing the fragment that grew smaller instead of the one that was actually split by the second enzyme.

qs.q: Digestion of a recombinant plasmid containing one copy of the 1.2 kb insert with EcoRI is expected to yield:
o: a single linear fragment of 7.2 kb
This would occur only if the junction sites were no longer recognized by EcoRI.
fragments of 6.0 kb and 1.2 kb, regardless of the orientation of the insert
Correct: Both junctions regenerate EcoRI sites, so cutting there releases the vector (6.0 kb) and the insert (1.2 kb).
fragments of 4.8 kb and 1.2 kb
The vector is 6.0 kb, so subtracting the insert size is not appropriate.
fragments of 6.0 kb and 1.2 kb only if the insert is in a single orientation
Both orientations regenerate the same EcoRI sites, so the digest does not depend on orientation.
qs.x: Both junctions regenerate EcoRI sites, so cutting there releases the vector (6.0 kb) and the insert (1.2 kb). Trap: Adding the sizes and expecting one 7.2 kb fragment, forgetting that the junctions are recut by EcoRI.

qs.q: In the EcoRI + BamHI digest, which fragment will migrate farthest through the gel toward the positive electrode?
o: The 1.5 kb fragment
This fragment is larger than 1.0 kb and so travels a shorter distance.
All fragments move equally, because charge per base is constant
Charge-to-mass is similar, but the gel sieves by length, so migration differs.
The 1.0 kb fragment
Correct: DNA is negatively charged, and shorter fragments pass through the agarose matrix more easily and migrate farther.
The 3.5 kb fragment
Larger fragments are retarded by the matrix and migrate the least distance.
qs.x: DNA is negatively charged, and shorter fragments pass through the agarose matrix more easily and migrate farther. Trap: Thinking that equal charge per base means equal mobility.

qs.q: Digesting both the insert and the vector with EcoRI before adding ligase is useful because:
o: EcoRI methylates the ends, so the two DNAs recombine without ligase
EcoRI is a nuclease that cuts DNA; it does not make covalent joins.
EcoRI converts both fragments to single-stranded DNA
EcoRI leaves double-stranded DNA with short overhangs, not fully single-stranded molecules.
the complementary single-stranded overhangs on the two molecules can base-pair, and ligase then seals the sugar-phosphate backbone
Correct: Compatible sticky ends anneal, positioning the 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate for ligase to form phosphodiester bonds.
EcoRI removes the origin of replication from both fragments
Cutting at a single site does not remove the origin, and the recombinant plasmid needs it to replicate.
qs.x: Compatible sticky ends anneal, positioning the 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate for ligase to form phosphodiester bonds. Trap: Believing the restriction enzyme itself joins the pieces rather than creating compatible ends for ligase.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Researchers treated cultured cells with compound C, which activates a transcription factor, and measured changes in the abundance of two messenger RNAs by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Total RNA was extracted after 8 hours of treatment with compound C or with vehicle alone, equal amounts of RNA were converted to complementary DNA, and gene G, gene H, and a reference gene were each amplified. The cycle threshold (Ct) is the PCR cycle at which fluorescence first exceeds a set threshold; a lower Ct means more starting template. The reference gene is expressed at a constant level in these cells. Assuming that each amplification doubles the product every cycle, relative expression is calculated as 2 raised to the power of minus the difference between the treated and vehicle values of (Ct target minus Ct reference).
Results at 8 hours are shown in Table 1. In a separate time course, the fold change in gene G mRNA relative to time zero was measured (Figure 1).

qs.q: Based on Table 1, treatment with compound C changed the abundance of gene G mRNA by:
o: an 8-fold decrease
A lower Ct indicates more template, so the mRNA increased.
a 3-fold increase
3 is the difference in Ct, but each cycle is a doubling, so the fold change is 2³.
a 6-fold increase
This adds the ΔCt values (3 + 3) rather than raising 2 to the power of the difference.
an 8-fold increase
Correct: The target Ct fell by 3 cycles with no change in the reference, so abundance rose 2³ = 8-fold.
qs.x: The target Ct fell by 3 cycles with no change in the reference, so abundance rose 2³ = 8-fold. Trap: Reporting the Ct difference directly as the fold change instead of using 2 raised to that difference.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, the relative expression of gene H after compound C treatment is:
o: unchanged, because the reference gene Ct did not change
The target Ct increased from 26 to 29 while the reference stayed at 18, so expression changed.
0.33 of the vehicle level
This takes 1/3 from the Ct difference rather than 2 to the minus 3.
1/8 of the vehicle level
Correct: The target Ct rose by 3 cycles, so template fell 2³ = 8-fold, giving a relative expression of 1/8 = 0.125.
8 times the vehicle level
A higher Ct means less template, so expression decreased.
qs.x: The target Ct rose by 3 cycles, so template fell 2³ = 8-fold, giving a relative expression of 1/8 = 0.125. Trap: Misreading a higher Ct as higher expression.

qs.q: The reference gene is included in each RT-qPCR reaction primarily to:
o: amplify the target gene to a higher final yield
The reference gene is amplified separately and does not boost the target signal.
confirm that compound C enters the cells
A constant reference gene reports nothing about drug uptake.
correct for differences in the amount of RNA and the efficiency of cDNA synthesis among samples
Correct: Normalizing to a constitutively expressed gene accounts for loading and reaction efficiency differences so changes in the target are real.
act as a primer for reverse transcriptase
Primers are short oligonucleotides, and the reference gene is a measured target, not a primer.
qs.x: Normalizing to a constitutively expressed gene accounts for loading and reaction efficiency differences so changes in the target are real. Trap: Thinking the reference serves as a positive treatment control instead of a normalizer.

qs.q: RNA is first converted to cDNA in this procedure because:
o: PCR polymerase needs a DNA template
Correct: Reverse transcriptase uses the mRNA as template to make DNA, which can then be amplified by DNA polymerase.
mRNA cannot be quantified by fluorescence of any kind
Fluorescent detection works on DNA product; the issue is the template requirement, not detection of RNA per se.
DNA polymerase cannot function above 37 °C unless RNA is removed
The polymerase used in PCR is thermostable and RNA is not what limits it.
RNA does not contain the genetic information of the gene
mRNA carries the sequence information of the gene and is the starting point for this assay.
qs.x: Reverse transcriptase uses the mRNA as template to make DNA, which can then be amplified by DNA polymerase. Trap: Assuming RNA cannot be amplified because it lacks sequence information.

qs.q: The plateau in gene G mRNA between 8 and 24 hours (Figure 1) is most consistent with:
o: transcription of gene G having stopped completely at 8 hours
If transcription stopped, mRNA would decline as it degraded rather than remain constant.
degradation of gene G mRNA having stopped at 8 hours
If degradation stopped while synthesis continued, the level would keep rising.
compound C having been fully metabolized by 8 hours
Loss of the drug would lower the mRNA level over time, not hold it constant at 8-fold.
synthesis and degradation having balanced
Correct: A steady state arises when production and decay balance, leaving the level constant even though both processes continue.
qs.x: A steady state arises when production and decay balance, leaving the level constant even though both processes continue. Trap: Interpreting a flat curve as meaning that all production has stopped rather than balance of two opposing rates.

graph.title: Figure 1. Gene G mRNA fold change after compound C

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: To dissect the regulation of a human gene, PRM1, researchers cloned its upstream region into a plasmid placed in front of a firefly luciferase reporter gene. The full-length construct contained a TATA box located 30 bp upstream of the transcription start site and an enhancer element located 1,200 bp upstream. Additional constructs lacked the enhancer, lacked the TATA box, carried the enhancer in the reverse orientation, or carried the enhancer relocated 3 kb downstream of the reporter gene. Each plasmid was transfected into cultured cells together with a second plasmid that constitutively expresses Renilla luciferase. After 24 hours, firefly luciferase activity was divided by Renilla luciferase activity, and the ratio for the full-length construct was set to 100. Results are shown in Table 1.

The enhancer sequence was found to bind an activating transcription factor that is present in the transfected cell type. Cells were grown under identical conditions, and every construct was tested in triplicate on the same day.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the drop in activity from 100 to 12 when the enhancer is deleted?
o: The enhancer encodes part of the luciferase protein
Enhancers are regulatory DNA sequences and do not provide coding sequence for the reporter.
The enhancer contributes positively to transcription of the reporter gene
Correct: Removing a sequence that binds an activator lowers expression, showing that the element normally boosts transcription.
The enhancer represses transcription by binding a repressor
Removing a repressor-binding element would raise expression, not lower it.
The enhancer is an essential part of the core promoter that RNA polymerase II requires to start
Residual activity of 12 shows that transcription can occur without it; essential core elements like the TATA box abolish activity.
qs.x: Removing a sequence that binds an activator lowers expression, showing that the element normally boosts transcription. Trap: Confusing an enhancer, which increases transcription, with a core promoter element, which is required for any transcription.

qs.q: The results for the reverse-orientation and relocated enhancer constructs show that, in this system, the enhancer:
o: is converted to a promoter when moved
Moving it does not provide a TATA box; activity stays about the same, not as a new promoter.
works in any orientation or place
Correct: Activity stays near 90-95 after inversion and relocation, a hallmark of enhancer elements.
works only when positioned upstream and in the forward orientation
Activity is retained at 95 and 90 in the other configurations, so this is contradicted.
must be adjacent to the TATA box to function
The enhancer works from 1,200 bp upstream and even from 3 kb downstream.
qs.x: Activity stays near 90-95 after inversion and relocation, a hallmark of enhancer elements. Trap: Applying the strict position and orientation rules of a promoter to an enhancer.

qs.q: The near-complete loss of activity when the TATA box is deleted indicates that the TATA box is needed for:
o: assembly of the general transcription factors, including TBP, that position RNA polymerase II at the start site
Correct: The TATA box is bound by TBP in TFIID, nucleating the preinitiation complex; without it basal transcription fails.
splicing of the reporter transcript
Splicing is a post-transcriptional process and would not reduce transcript production this much.
binding of the activating transcription factor at the enhancer
The enhancer, not the TATA box, binds the activator, and enhancer deletion only lowered activity to 12.
translation of luciferase mRNA by ribosomes
The TATA box is a DNA element and not part of the mRNA recognized by ribosomes in this way.
qs.x: The TATA box is bound by TBP in TFIID, nucleating the preinitiation complex; without it basal transcription fails. Trap: Assigning the TATA box a role in post-transcriptional steps rather than initiation.

qs.q: Co-transfection with the Renilla luciferase plasmid is used to:
o: identify the transcription factor bound to the enhancer
The Renilla plasmid carries no information about transcription factor binding.
correct for transfection differences
Correct: Dividing by an internal constitutive control normalizes for how much plasmid entered the cells and for cell viability.
increase the expression of firefly luciferase
Renilla luciferase is a separate reporter and does not increase firefly expression.
measure the rate of mRNA degradation of the reporter
The ratio reports relative activity, not decay of mRNA.
qs.x: Dividing by an internal constitutive control normalizes for how much plasmid entered the cells and for cell viability. Trap: Assuming a second reporter measures the biology under study rather than serving as a normalization control.

r: Enhancer moved 3 kb downstream of reporter

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: A laboratory colony of 500 flour beetles was used to study the evolution of resistance to an insecticide. Resistance is controlled by a single autosomal locus: allele R is completely dominant to allele r, so RR and Rr beetles survive exposure and rr beetles are susceptible. Beetles in generation 0 were genotyped before any exposure, and the counts are shown in Table 1. The colony mated randomly. In every generation, adult beetles were exposed to the insecticide, and 100% of RR, 100% of Rr, and 20% of rr beetles survived to reproduce. The survivors were then allowed to mate at random to produce the next generation, which was again exposed. The calculated frequency of allele R at the start of each generation is plotted in Figure 1.
Assume that the population is large, that there is no mutation or migration, and that selection is the only factor changing allele frequencies.

qs.q: What is the frequency of allele R in generation 0?
o: This is the fraction of beetles that carry at least one R allele, 180/500.
This is the frequency of RR homozygotes, 20/500.
Correct: Allele R copies = 2(20) + 160 = 200 of 1,000 total alleles, so p = 0.20.
This is the frequency of heterozygotes, 160/500, not the allele frequency.
qs.x: Allele R copies = 2(20) + 160 = 200 of 1,000 total alleles, so p = 0.20. Trap: Using the fraction of beetles with the dominant phenotype or the heterozygote frequency as the allele frequency.

qs.q: After the first exposure, the frequency of allele R among the surviving parents is closest to:
o: This is the proportion of beetles carrying R before selection, not the allele frequency among survivors.
This would require roughly equal numbers of R and r alleles among survivors, which the counts do not give.
This is the frequency before selection.
Correct: Survivors: 20 RR, 160 Rr, 64 rr (20% of 320); R copies = 2(20) + 160 = 200 of 2(244) = 488 alleles, giving 0.41.
qs.x: Survivors: 20 RR, 160 Rr, 64 rr (20% of 320); R copies = 2(20) + 160 = 200 of 2(244) = 488 alleles, giving 0.41. Trap: Forgetting to recompute total alleles after the susceptible beetles are removed.

qs.q: In Figure 1, the increase in the frequency of R per generation becomes smaller as R becomes common. The best explanation is that:
o: mutation from R to r increasingly offsets the effect of selection
The problem states there is no mutation.
as allele r becomes rare, most r copies reside in Rr beetles that survive, so selection removes fewer r alleles each generation
Correct: Selection acts only on rr phenotypes, and when r is rare nearly all copies are shielded in heterozygotes, so response slows.
genetic drift is strongest when an allele is common in a large population
Drift is weak in large populations, and the question assumes it is absent.
the insecticide becomes less toxic to rr beetles as generations pass
The survival of rr beetles was fixed at 20% in every generation.
qs.x: Selection acts only on rr phenotypes, and when r is rare nearly all copies are shielded in heterozygotes, so response slows. Trap: Expecting a constant per-generation increase and attributing the slowdown to forces that the passage rules out.

qs.q: Which mode of natural selection is operating on the resistance trait in this experiment?
o: Directional selection, favoring one extreme
Correct: Allele frequency moves steadily in one direction as the resistant phenotype is favored.
Sexual selection, because beetles choose mates by phenotype
Mating was random, and survival rather than mate choice drives the change.
Stabilizing selection, because intermediate genotypes are favored
The heterozygote is not favored over RR; the resistant phenotypes are equally fit.
Disruptive selection, because both extremes are favored
Only one extreme, resistance, has an advantage.
qs.x: Allele frequency moves steadily in one direction as the resistant phenotype is favored. Trap: Choosing stabilizing selection because the heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype.

qs.q: Suppose the insecticide is withdrawn after generation 6, and R carriers have lower fertility than rr beetles. The frequency of R is most likely to:
o: decline over subsequent generations, because carriers of R now have lower reproductive fitness
Correct: Without the benefit of resistance, the fitness cost of R becomes the dominant selective force and R frequency falls.
drop to zero in a single generation
The R allele persists in heterozygotes and selection is not so strong as to eliminate it at once.
increase further, because dominant alleles always increase in frequency
Dominance does not by itself determine the direction of selection.
remain at 0.81, because allele frequencies at Hardy-Weinberg proportions never change under any conditions
Hardy-Weinberg stability requires no selection, and the fertility cost is selection.
qs.x: Without the benefit of resistance, the fitness cost of R becomes the dominant selective force and R frequency falls. Trap: Assuming dominant alleles are favored automatically and ignoring fitness costs.

graph.title: Figure 1. Frequency of allele R across generations of insecticide exposure

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: In maize, kernel color is controlled by a gene with alleles P (purple, dominant) and p (yellow), and kernel starch type is controlled by a gene with alleles W (starchy, dominant) and w (waxy). A plant that was heterozygous at both genes was crossed to a plant that was homozygous recessive at both genes (a testcross). The heterozygous parent was the progeny of a cross between a purple, starchy line and a yellow, waxy line. A total of 1,000 kernels from the testcross were scored for color and starch type, and the results are listed in Table 1.

A geneticist who also wished to place a third gene, X, on the same chromosome carried out similar testcrosses and found that recombinant kernels between X and the color gene made up 5% of progeny, whereas recombinant kernels between X and the starch gene made up 17% of progeny. Both genes studied here are on the same chromosome pair, and no double crossovers were detected.

qs.q: The testcross results are most consistent with which conclusion?
o: The genes assort independently, because all four phenotypes appear
Appearance of all classes happens with linkage as well; independent assortment requires equal numbers.
The yellow and waxy alleles are dominant, because the testcross parent was homozygous recessive
The homozygous recessive parent shows that its alleles are recessive; it does not make them dominant.
The color and starch genes are linked, because the parental phenotypes are far more frequent than the recombinant phenotypes
Correct: Independent assortment predicts four equal classes (1:1:1:1); a large excess of two parental classes indicates linkage.
The genes are on different chromosomes, because recombinants are observed
Recombinants occur for linked genes too, through crossing over.
qs.x: Independent assortment predicts four equal classes (1:1:1:1); a large excess of two parental classes indicates linkage. Trap: Interpreting the presence of all four phenotype classes as evidence of independent assortment.

qs.q: What is the map distance between the color gene and the starch gene?
o: 50 map units
This is the maximum recombination frequency, seen for unlinked genes.
88 map units
This is the percentage of parental kernels (880/1,000).
6 map units
This uses only one recombinant class (60/1,000).
12 map units
Correct: Recombinants are 60 + 60 = 120 of 1,000 kernels, or 12%, which corresponds to 12 map units.
qs.x: Recombinants are 60 + 60 = 120 of 1,000 kernels, or 12%, which corresponds to 12 map units. Trap: Counting only one of the two recombinant classes, or reporting the parental percentage.

qs.q: Which genotype arrangement did the heterozygous parent carry?
o: P w on one chromosome and p W on the homologous chromosome
This arrangement would make purple waxy and yellow starchy the most frequent classes.
P W on both chromosomes
The parent was heterozygous at both genes.
p w on both chromosomes
A parent with this genotype would show only the yellow, waxy phenotype and would not be heterozygous.
P W on one chromosome and p w on the homologous chromosome
Correct: The most common classes (purple starchy and yellow waxy) are parental, so P travels with W and p with w.
qs.x: The most common classes (purple starchy and yellow waxy) are parental, so P travels with W and p with w. Trap: Reading the arrangement from the recombinant classes instead of the parental classes.

qs.q: Recombinant kernels arise from crossing over, which occurs:
o: between sister chromatids during prophase of mitosis
Exchange between sister chromatids does not produce new allele combinations, and mitosis is not the source of gametes.
between nonhomologous chromosomes during anaphase I
Homologs separate in anaphase I; exchange occurs earlier, between homologs.
during prophase I of meiosis
Correct: Synapsis of homologs in prophase I forms tetrads in which nonsister chromatids exchange segments.
between the two strands of DNA during S phase
Replication copies DNA but does not exchange alleles between homologs.
qs.x: Synapsis of homologs in prophase I forms tetrads in which nonsister chromatids exchange segments. Trap: Placing crossing over in mitosis or during chromosome separation rather than in homolog pairing.

qs.q: Given the recombination frequencies for gene X, the most likely order of the three genes is:
o: color gene, X, starch gene
This would place X between the other two and give X distances that add to 12, not 5 and 17.
color gene, starch gene, X
This would make X to starch the smaller distance, but X is farther from the starch gene.
X, starch gene, color gene
Distances would then be X to starch 5 and X to color 17, the reverse of the data.
X, color gene, starch gene
Correct: X is 5 units from the color gene and 17 from the starch gene; because 5 + 12 = 17, the color gene lies between X and the starch gene.
qs.x: X is 5 units from the color gene and 17 from the starch gene; because 5 + 12 = 17, the color gene lies between X and the starch gene. Trap: Ignoring that map distances are additive when ordering three linked genes.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: A biochemist examined how cells drive thermodynamically unfavorable phosphorylation reactions by coupling them to reactions that release free energy. Standard free-energy changes at pH 7 (ΔG°') for several reactions are listed in Table 1. In the cell, reaction directions are determined by the actual free-energy change, ΔG = ΔG°' + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient. For these calculations the temperature is 310 K, and RT is about 2.6 kJ/mol. The biochemist also measured the concentrations of ATP, ADP, and inorganic phosphate (Pi) in a resting muscle cell and found that the ratio [ATP]/([ADP][Pi]) is maintained far above the value at equilibrium for ATP hydrolysis.

Glucose phosphorylation by hexokinase can be written as the sum of glucose + Pi giving glucose 6-phosphate (G6P) + H2O, and ATP hydrolysis. Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) transfers its phosphoryl group to ADP in the final step of glycolysis, a reaction that generates ATP even though no oxygen is consumed directly in the step.

qs.q: What is the ΔG°' of the hexokinase reaction, glucose + ATP → G6P + ADP?
o: -44.3 kJ/mol
This adds the magnitudes of both values and treats the phosphorylation as favorable.
+13.8 kJ/mol
This ignores the contribution of ATP hydrolysis, which is what drives the reaction.
+44.3 kJ/mol
This subtracts the ATP hydrolysis value instead of adding it.
-16.7 kJ/mol
Correct: Adding the two coupled reactions gives +13.8 + (-30.5) = -16.7 kJ/mol.
qs.x: Adding the two coupled reactions gives +13.8 + (-30.5) = -16.7 kJ/mol. Trap: Using the phosphorylation value alone instead of summing it with the ATP hydrolysis value.

qs.q: Why is the actual free energy released by ATP hydrolysis in the cell more negative than the standard value?
o: Because enzymes lower ΔG°' for ATP hydrolysis
Enzymes change rates, not the free-energy change of a reaction.
Because ATP is converted to a more stable molecule before hydrolysis
No such conversion occurs; the difference arises from concentrations in ΔG.
Because the cell raises the temperature to about 310 K
The standard value already refers to a reference state, and a modest temperature does not shift it greatly.
Because the ratio [ATP]/([ADP][Pi]) is maintained far above its equilibrium value, the reaction quotient Q for hydrolysis is small
Correct: ΔG = ΔG°' + RT ln Q; the cell keeps ATP high relative to products, making Q small and ln Q very negative.
qs.x: ΔG = ΔG°' + RT ln Q; the cell keeps ATP high relative to products, making Q small and ln Q very negative. Trap: Believing that an enzyme can change the thermodynamics of a reaction instead of only its rate.

qs.q: PEP can drive the formation of ATP from ADP because:
o: PEP and ATP have identical ΔG°' values, so the reaction is at equilibrium
The values differ by about 31 kJ/mol.
hydrolysis of PEP releases more free energy than ATP hydrolysis, giving PEP a higher phosphoryl transfer potential
Correct: PEP's ΔG°' of -61.9 is more negative than that of ATP (-30.5), so transfer of its phosphoryl group to ADP is favorable (net -31.4).
the reaction is driven by loss of pyruvate to the extracellular space
Nothing in the data suggests pyruvate leaves the cell, and energetics rely on the group transfer values.
ATP has a higher phosphoryl transfer potential than PEP
The data show the opposite; transfer from ATP to PEP is unfavorable.
qs.x: PEP's ΔG°' of -61.9 is more negative than that of ATP (-30.5), so transfer of its phosphoryl group to ADP is favorable (net -31.4). Trap: Assuming the energy currency (ATP) must always have the highest phosphoryl transfer potential.

qs.q: At 310 K, the equilibrium constant for the isomerization G6P to F6P is closest to:
o: This would correspond to ΔG°' of about +7.8 kJ/mol.
This would use exp(+0.65) and misses the sign: a positive ΔG°' favors reactant.
Correct: Keq = exp(-ΔG°'/RT) = exp(-1.7/2.6) = exp(-0.65), about 0.5.
This would correspond to ΔG°' of about -4.2 kJ/mol.
qs.x: Keq = exp(-ΔG°'/RT) = exp(-1.7/2.6) = exp(-0.65), about 0.5. Trap: Dropping the minus sign in Keq = exp(-ΔG°'/RT) and so predicting that products are favored.

passages.title: Mini01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Ten endurance-trained and ten untrained adults performed a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer. Intensity was increased stepwise and is expressed as a percentage of each person's maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max). Blood lactate concentration was measured at the end of each stage; mean values are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. The lactate threshold is the intensity above which blood lactate begins to rise steeply. In a separate analysis, muscle biopsies were taken from the thigh at rest, and the activity of citrate synthase, a mitochondrial matrix enzyme of the citric acid cycle that is used as an indicator of mitochondrial content, was measured. Mean citrate synthase activity was 42 µmol/min per gram of tissue in trained subjects and 20 µmol/min per gram in untrained subjects.

During intense exercise, muscle releases lactate into the blood. The liver takes up lactate from the blood. All subjects fasted overnight, avoided strenuous exercise for 48 hours beforehand, and were tested at the same time of day.

qs.q: At 70% VO2max, the blood lactate concentration in untrained subjects compared with trained subjects is about:
o: 2 times lower
Untrained subjects have the higher lactate, so the ratio is greater than 1.
the same
The two groups differ at 70% VO2max, with 2.8 mM versus 1.3 mM.
4 times higher
This would require untrained values near 5.2 mM.
2 times higher
Correct: 2.8 mM divided by 1.3 mM is about 2.2, so untrained subjects have roughly twice the lactate.
qs.x: 2.8 mM divided by 1.3 mM is about 2.2, so untrained subjects have roughly twice the lactate. Trap: Reading the lactate difference as a subtraction (1.5 mM) and then misapplying it as a ratio.

qs.q: The conversion of pyruvate to lactate during intense exercise is metabolically important because it:
o: converts NAD+ to NADH to feed the electron transport chain
The reaction goes the other way, consuming NADH.
regenerates NAD+ for glycolysis
Correct: Lactate dehydrogenase oxidizes NADH to NAD+, supplying the NAD+ needed by glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase.
generates additional ATP through substrate-level phosphorylation
The LDH reaction produces no ATP; its benefit is NAD+ regeneration.
synthesizes glucose directly within muscle
Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase and does not make free glucose from lactate.
qs.x: Lactate dehydrogenase oxidizes NADH to NAD+, supplying the NAD+ needed by glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase. Trap: Thinking lactate formation produces ATP rather than regenerating the NAD+ cofactor.

qs.q: Higher citrate synthase activity in trained muscle most likely contributes to the higher lactate threshold because:
o: citrate synthase converts lactate directly to glucose
Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate; it does not act on lactate.
mitochondria in trained subjects produce lactate at a lower rate because they lack NADH
Mitochondria oxidize NADH; the differences arise from more oxidative capacity, not lack of NADH.
greater mitochondrial content allows more pyruvate to be oxidized aerobically, reducing reliance on lactate formation
Correct: More mitochondria increase oxidative capacity so that, at a given intensity, less pyruvate is diverted to lactate.
citrate synthase is a glycolytic enzyme that speeds lactate production
It is a citric acid cycle enzyme in the matrix.
qs.x: More mitochondria increase oxidative capacity so that, at a given intensity, less pyruvate is diverted to lactate. Trap: Assigning citrate synthase a glycolytic role instead of recognizing it as an index of mitochondrial content.

qs.q: In the liver, lactate taken up from the blood is mainly:
o: stored directly as lactate in glycogen granules
Glycogen is a polymer of glucose, not lactate.
made into glucose and released into blood
Correct: In the Cori cycle the liver oxidizes lactate to pyruvate and synthesizes glucose, which returns to muscle.
excreted unchanged in the bile through the biliary ducts
Bile does not serve as a route for lactate disposal.
converted to fatty acids that are exported as chylomicrons
Chylomicrons are made in intestinal cells from dietary fat, and lactate is not channeled this way.
qs.x: In the Cori cycle the liver oxidizes lactate to pyruvate and synthesizes glucose, which returns to muscle. Trap: Confusing the liver's gluconeogenic fate of lactate with lipid export pathways.

qs.q: Between 85% and 100% VO2max, how does the rise in lactate in trained subjects compare with that in untrained subjects?
o: It is larger in trained subjects, 6.0 mM compared with 4.5 mM
Correct: Trained: 9.0 - 3.0 = 6.0 mM; untrained: 11.0 - 6.5 = 4.5 mM.
It is larger in untrained subjects, because their final lactate is higher
The final value is higher in untrained subjects, but the rise is the difference from the 85% value.
It is smaller in trained subjects, 1.5 mM compared with 4.5 mM
1.5 mM is not a rise computed from the table for either group.
It is the same in both groups, 4.5 mM
Only the untrained subjects have a rise of 4.5 mM.
qs.x: Trained: 9.0 - 3.0 = 6.0 mM; untrained: 11.0 - 6.5 = 4.5 mM. Trap: Comparing endpoint values at 100% rather than the change between two stages.

graph.title: Figure 1. Blood lactate versus exercise intensity

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A biomechanics student models the human forearm as a uniform rigid rod of mass 1.6 kg hinged at the elbow and held horizontal. The biceps tendon attaches 4.0 cm from the elbow and pulls vertically upward. The center of mass of the forearm lies 15 cm from the elbow, and a hand grips a load 30 cm from the elbow. A force sensor in the tendon records the biceps force while the subject holds loads of several masses motionless, and the elbow joint force is then found from the force balance on the forearm. Results are in Table 1. Use g = 10 m/s², and treat the forearm as remaining horizontal and the biceps force as remaining vertical and approximately constant throughout any slow movement. In a second model, the student considers a surgical transfer that moves the tendon attachment to 6.0 cm from the elbow. The student reads all values from a calibrated sensor and repeats each measurement several times, and the scatter among repeats is small enough to be ignored. The subject keeps the upper arm vertical and the shoulder still during every trial, so that the only motion occurs at the elbow.

qs.q: What biceps force is needed to hold a 3.0 kg load motionless, based on the trend in Table 1?
o: This is 75 N per kilogram times 3.0 kg and leaves out the 60 N needed just to support the forearm itself.
Correct: Force rises linearly with load: 60 N plus 75 N per kilogram (torque balance F(0.04) = 16(0.15) + 10M(0.30)), so 60 + 225 = 285 N, which is also midway between the 2.0 kg and 4.0 kg entries.
This is the total weight of the forearm and load (16 N + 30 N), which ignores the lever arms entirely.
This is the value for a 4.0 kg load, not 3.0 kg.
qs.x: Force rises linearly with load: 60 N plus 75 N per kilogram (torque balance F(0.04) = 16(0.15) + 10M(0.30)), so 60 + 225 = 285 N, which is also midway between the 2.0 kg and 4.0 kg entries. Trap: Adding up weights as if the biceps pulled at the same distance from the elbow as the load.

qs.q: Treating the forearm as weightless, what is the ideal mechanical advantage of the forearm lever when the biceps lifts a load held in the hand?
o: This inverts the ratio (30/4.0); that would be the factor by which hand motion exceeds tendon motion, not the force advantage.
This uses the 15 cm center-of-mass distance (4.0/15) rather than the 30 cm distance of the load.
This applies only if effort and load act at equal distances from the pivot, which is not the case here.
Correct: Mechanical advantage is the effort arm divided by the load arm, 4.0 cm / 30 cm = 0.13; the biceps lies between the fulcrum and the load, a third-class lever.
qs.x: Mechanical advantage is the effort arm divided by the load arm, 4.0 cm / 30 cm = 0.13; the biceps lies between the fulcrum and the load, a third-class lever. Trap: Inverting the ratio of lever arms and expecting a force gain from a third-class lever.

qs.q: According to the force balance on the forearm, what is the force exerted by the elbow joint on the forearm when a 2.0 kg load is held?
o: 174 N upward
The magnitude is right, but the biceps force already exceeds the total weight, so the hinge must pull the forearm downward, not upward.
174 N downward
Correct: Net force is zero: 210 N (biceps, up) = 36 N (weights, down) + J, so the joint must push down with 210 - 36 = 174 N.
36 N upward
This would balance only the weights and forgets that the biceps itself supplies 210 N.
210 N down
This is the biceps force itself, not the difference between the biceps force and the weights.
qs.x: Net force is zero: 210 N (biceps, up) = 36 N (weights, down) + J, so the joint must push down with 210 - 36 = 174 N. Trap: Assuming the joint force simply supports the weight rather than balancing the large biceps force.

qs.q: If the tendon attachment were moved to 6.0 cm from the elbow, what biceps force would be required to hold the 2.0 kg load?
o: This multiplies 210 N by 6.0/4.0, moving the force the wrong way; a longer effort arm lowers the force needed.
This is the original value; the effort arm changed, so the force must change.
This scales 210 N by the ratio 4.0/12, which does not correspond to any lever arm in the problem.
Correct: Torque balance: F(0.060) = 16(0.15) + 20(0.30) = 8.4 N·m, so F = 140 N, which is 210 N × (4.0/6.0).
qs.x: Torque balance: F(0.060) = 16(0.15) + 20(0.30) = 8.4 N·m, so F = 140 N, which is 210 N × (4.0/6.0). Trap: Scaling the force directly with the effort arm instead of inversely.

qs.q: The subject slowly raises the 2.0 kg load by 0.20 m at the hand. Which value is closest to the work done by the biceps over this movement?
o: This is the work done only on the load (20 N × 0.20 m) and ignores the work needed to lift the forearm.
This multiplies the biceps force by the hand's displacement; the tendon moves only a fraction of that distance.
This is the work done on the forearm alone, leaving out the load.
Correct: The tendon moves 0.20 × (4.0/30) = 0.027 m, so W = 210 N × 0.027 m = 5.6 J, equal to the gain in potential energy of the load (4.0 J) plus the forearm (1.6 J).
qs.x: The tendon moves 0.20 × (4.0/30) = 0.027 m, so W = 210 N × 0.027 m = 5.6 J, equal to the gain in potential energy of the load (4.0 J) plus the forearm (1.6 J). Trap: Using the displacement of the hand rather than the displacement of the tendon.

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: A student releases steel spheres of different radii r (density 7800 kg/m³) from rest just below the surface of a tall cylinder of glycerol (density 1260 kg/m³, viscosity 1.2 Pa·s) held at 20 °C. A camera records each sphere after it reaches a constant speed, the terminal speed v_t. For slow flow, the drag force on a sphere is F = 6πηrv (Stokes' law), where η is the viscosity and v is the speed. The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid. The cylinder is wide enough that wall effects can be ignored, and each trial was repeated three times and averaged. Table 1 lists v_t for four steel spheres, and Figure 1 plots v_t against r². In a final trial, the student drops an aluminum sphere (density 2700 kg/m³) with the same radius as the 2.0 mm steel sphere. Use g = 10 m/s² and V = (4/3)πr³. The thermometers in the experiment can be read to 0.1 °C, and the cylinder is shielded from drafts. The student assumes that each sphere reaches its terminal speed well before it passes the first mark, so that all speeds in the table are steady values.

qs.q: What is the magnitude of the drag force on the 2.0 mm steel sphere when it moves at its terminal speed?
o: This is the sphere's weight alone, which forgets that buoyancy supports part of the weight.
Correct: At terminal speed drag equals weight minus buoyancy: (7800 - 1260)(10)(4/3)π(2.0 × 10⁻³)³ = 2.2 × 10⁻³ N; Stokes' law with 4.8 cm/s gives the same value.
This is the buoyant force, not the drag force.
This has the right digits but is off by a factor of ten, which comes from an error converting 2.0 mm to meters.
qs.x: At terminal speed drag equals weight minus buoyancy: (7800 - 1260)(10)(4/3)π(2.0 × 10⁻³)³ = 2.2 × 10⁻³ N; Stokes' law with 4.8 cm/s gives the same value. Trap: Equating drag to the full weight and ignoring buoyancy.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, which terminal speed is expected for a steel sphere of radius 2.5 mm?
o: 7.9 cm/s
This interpolates linearly in radius between 2.0 and 3.0 mm, but the graph shows speed depends on r².
6.0 cm/s
This assumes speed is proportional to r (4.8 × 2.5/2.0).
7.6 cm/s
Correct: The graph is a straight line of slope about 1.2 cm/s per mm², and r² = 6.25 mm², giving 1.21 × 6.25 = 7.6 cm/s.
9.4 cm/s
This assumes speed is proportional to r³ (4.8 × 1.25³).
qs.x: The graph is a straight line of slope about 1.2 cm/s per mm², and r² = 6.25 mm², giving 1.21 × 6.25 = 7.6 cm/s. Trap: Interpolating linearly in radius rather than using the r² dependence.

qs.q: The aluminum sphere is dropped in place of the 2.0 mm steel sphere. Its terminal speed is approximately what multiple of the steel sphere's terminal speed?
o: This is the ratio of the sphere densities (2700/7800) and ignores buoyancy.
This takes the square root of the density ratio, but speed depends linearly on the density difference.
This inverts the correct ratio, as if aluminum were the denser sphere.
Correct: Terminal speed is proportional to (ρ_sphere - ρ_fluid): (2700 - 1260)/(7800 - 1260) = 1440/6540 = 0.22.
qs.x: Terminal speed is proportional to (ρ_sphere - ρ_fluid): (2700 - 1260)/(7800 - 1260) = 1440/6540 = 0.22. Trap: Comparing raw densities instead of densities minus the fluid density.

qs.q: Immediately after the 2.0 mm steel sphere is released from rest, what is the magnitude of its acceleration?
o: 10 m/s²
This is free-fall acceleration and ignores buoyancy.
1.6 m/s²
This is the buoyancy term alone (g × ρ_fluid/ρ_steel) rather than the net.
8.4 m/s²
Correct: At v = 0 there is no drag, so a = g(1 - ρ_fluid/ρ_steel) = 10(1 - 1260/7800) = 8.4 m/s².
0 m/s²
This describes the sphere after it reaches terminal speed, not at release.
qs.x: At v = 0 there is no drag, so a = g(1 - ρ_fluid/ρ_steel) = 10(1 - 1260/7800) = 8.4 m/s². Trap: Assuming a released object starts with zero acceleration because forces are present.

graph.title: Figure 1. Terminal speed versus r²

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: Venous pressure in a standing person is influenced by the weight of the blood column between the heart and the vein. A physiologist measures gauge pressure in veins at several sites in a standing subject using fluid-filled catheters. The right atrium is taken as the reference height, with a gauge pressure of about 0 mmHg. Blood density is 1060 kg/m³, mercury density is 13,600 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², and 1 mmHg = 133 Pa. The hydrostatic prediction, ρgh, is compared with measured values in Table 1, and measured pressure is plotted against depth below the right atrium in Figure 1. Mean arterial pressure at heart level is 100 mmHg. When the subject later lies supine, the foot is only about 0.10 m below the right atrium. The venous valves are assumed to be open and the subject stands still, without muscle contraction, for several minutes before each reading so that flow in the veins is negligible. Catheter pressure transducers are zeroed at the level of the right atrium before every measurement.

qs.q: Which value is closest to the hydrostatic pressure increase produced by a 1.30 m column of blood?
o: 14 kPa
Correct: ΔP = ρgh = (1060)(9.8)(1.30) = 1.35 × 10⁴ Pa, which is about 14 kPa (101 mmHg).
1.4 kPa
This is off by a factor of ten; the product 1060 × 9.8 × 1.30 is about 13,500 Pa, not 1,350 Pa.
140 kPa
This is too large by a factor of ten and would exceed one atmosphere.
7.3 kPa
This uses the knee depth of 0.70 m instead of 1.30 m.
qs.x: ΔP = ρgh = (1060)(9.8)(1.30) = 1.35 × 10⁴ Pa, which is about 14 kPa (101 mmHg). Trap: Making a power-of-ten slip when multiplying density, g, and height.

qs.q: Why is the measured pressure in the raised hand near 0 mmHg, rather than the predicted -31 mmHg?
o: The thin-walled veins collapse when the pressure inside falls below the pressure outside, so the column cannot sustain a negative gauge pressure.
Correct: A collapsed vein carries pressure near atmospheric, so a catheter does not register the large negative value that ρgh predicts.
Blood density falls at the raised height, which cancels the hydrostatic term.
Density is essentially independent of the height of a limb.
Arterial pressure rises in the raised hand and offsets the venous value.
Arterial pressure falls at greater height, and it is a different vessel from the vein being measured.
The muscle pump pushes the blood forward and lowers the pressure to exactly 0 mmHg.
The muscle pump acts during movement and would not set a still limb to zero.
qs.x: A collapsed vein carries pressure near atmospheric, so a catheter does not register the large negative value that ρgh predicts. Trap: Assuming veins behave as rigid pipes at all pressures.

qs.q: If mean arterial pressure at heart level is 100 mmHg, what is the approximate mean arterial pressure in the dorsal foot artery of the standing subject?
o: 100 mmHg
This ignores the column of blood between the heart and the foot.
0 mmHg
This subtracts the hydrostatic term, which would apply to a site above the heart.
200 mmHg
Correct: Gravity adds the same hydrostatic term to the artery, so P ≈ 100 + 101 = about 200 mmHg.
131 mmHg
This adds the 1.30 m depth to 100 as if the depth were in mmHg.
qs.x: Gravity adds the same hydrostatic term to the artery, so P ≈ 100 + 101 = about 200 mmHg. Trap: Subtracting the hydrostatic term for a site below the heart.

qs.q: Which height of a column of blood exerts a pressure of 100 mmHg?
o: 7.8 mm
This inverts the density ratio (100 × 1060/13,600).
Correct: h(blood) = 100 mm × (13,600/1060) = 1283 mm, or about 1.3 m.
100 mm
This equates mmHg with mm of blood, though mercury is almost thirteen times denser.
This misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten.
qs.x: h(blood) = 100 mm × (13,600/1060) = 1283 mm, or about 1.3 m. Trap: Forgetting that mercury is much denser than blood when converting heights.

qs.q: When the subject lies supine, which measured pressure is expected in the dorsal foot vein?
o: 98 mmHg
This is the standing value, which depended on a 1.30 m column that is no longer present.
About 8 mmHg
Correct: With the foot only 0.10 m below the atrium, ρgh = 1060 × 9.8 × 0.10 = 1040 Pa, or about 8 mmHg.
0 mmHg exactly
A small depth below the atrium still adds a positive hydrostatic pressure.
78 mmHg
This is off by a factor of ten from the correct hydrostatic term for 0.10 m.
qs.x: With the foot only 0.10 m below the atrium, ρgh = 1060 × 9.8 × 0.10 = 1040 Pa, or about 8 mmHg. Trap: Assuming posture does not change the hydrostatic component of venous pressure.

graph.title: Figure 1. Measured venous pressure versus depth below right atrium

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: Gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane occurs by diffusion. According to Fick's law, the rate of transfer of a gas is proportional to the membrane area A, the partial-pressure difference ΔP, and a diffusion coefficient D, and inversely proportional to the membrane thickness d. D is proportional to the gas solubility S in the membrane fluid divided by the square root of the gas's molar mass M. Table 1 lists properties of three gases with typical partial pressures in alveolar gas and in blood entering the pulmonary capillaries of a resting subject. Solubility is in mmol/(L·atm) at 37 °C. Water vapor pressure at body temperature is 47 mmHg, and dry air is 21% O₂ by volume. A student also considers diseases that change A or d. Assume that each gas behaves ideally, that the alveolar gas and the capillary blood equilibrate across the same membrane, and that the temperature is 37 °C. Values in Table 1 are typical of a healthy adult breathing room air at sea level, where the barometric pressure is 760 mmHg.

qs.q: What is the ratio D(CO₂)/D(O₂) calculated from the data in Table 1?
o: This is the ratio of solubilities alone, with no molar mass correction.
This applies the molar mass ratio (32/44) without taking its square root.
Correct: D is proportional to S/√M, so the ratio is (34/1.3) × √(32/44) = 26.2 × 0.853 = about 22.
This is the inverse of the correct ratio.
qs.x: D is proportional to S/√M, so the ratio is (34/1.3) × √(32/44) = 26.2 × 0.853 = about 22. Trap: Leaving out the square root in the molar mass dependence.

qs.q: How does the net rate of CO₂ transfer compare with the net rate of O₂ transfer across the same membrane in a resting subject?
o: About 22 times as fast
This uses the ratio of diffusion coefficients and ignores the much smaller driving pressure for CO₂.
About 2.2 times as fast
Correct: Rate is proportional to D × ΔP: ratio = 22 × (6 mmHg/60 mmHg) = 2.2.
About 0.45 times as fast
This inverts the ratio and would mean O₂ moves faster, contradicting the large D difference.
About 10 times as slow
This uses only the pressure ratio (6/60) and ignores the diffusion coefficients.
qs.x: Rate is proportional to D × ΔP: ratio = 22 × (6 mmHg/60 mmHg) = 2.2. Trap: Using only the partial-pressure gradient to compare transfer rates.

qs.q: In a diseased lung, the effective membrane area is 40% of normal and the membrane is twice as thick. What fraction of the normal O₂ transfer rate is expected?
o: Correct: Rate is proportional to A/d: 0.40/2 = 0.20, or 20% of normal.
This multiplies the area fraction by the thickness factor instead of dividing.
This accounts for the loss of area alone and ignores the thickening.
This divides by the thickness twice, which is not required by Fick's law.
qs.x: Rate is proportional to A/d: 0.40/2 = 0.20, or 20% of normal. Trap: Multiplying by the thickness factor rather than dividing.

qs.q: A climber breathes humidified air at a total pressure of 253 mmHg. Which value is closest to the partial pressure of O₂ in the inspired air?
o: 43 mmHg
Correct: Inspired PO₂ = 0.21 × (253 - 47) = 0.21 × 206 = 43 mmHg.
53.1 mmHg
This applies 21% to the total pressure and forgets that water vapor occupies 47 mmHg of the humidified air.
206 mmHg
This subtracts water vapor but forgets to multiply by the 21% oxygen fraction.
21.0 mmHg
This treats the 21% oxygen fraction as a pressure in mmHg.
qs.x: Inspired PO₂ = 0.21 × (253 - 47) = 0.21 × 206 = 43 mmHg. Trap: Ignoring water vapor pressure in humidified air.

qs.q: By Graham's law, how does the effusion rate of N₂ compare with that of CO₂ at the same temperature?
o: N₂ effuses about 1.57 times faster
This uses the mass ratio without the square root.
N₂ effuses about 0.80 times as fast
This inverts the ratio, but lighter gases effuse faster.
N₂ and CO₂ effuse at the same rate
Gases with equal kinetic energy but different masses move at different speeds.
N₂ effuses about 1.25 times faster
Correct: Rate ratio = √(M_CO₂/M_N₂) = √(44/28) = 1.25.
qs.x: Rate ratio = √(M_CO₂/M_N₂) = √(44/28) = 1.25. Trap: Using the mass ratio directly rather than its square root.

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: Buried iron pipelines corrode in moist soil. To test cathodic protection, a technician connects iron coupons by wire to strips of other metals, buries each pair in moist soil for 30 days, and records the mass change of the iron coupon. Results appear in Table 1 with the standard reduction potentials of the strip metals. The reduction potential of Fe²⁺/Fe is -0.44 V. In soil, O₂ dissolved in water is reduced at the cathode: O₂ + 2 H₂O + 4 e⁻ → 4 OH⁻ (E° = +0.40 V). A control iron coupon with no attached strip lost 22 mg. The strips themselves are not weighed, and in every pair the soil water acts as the electrolyte that completes the circuit between the two metals. The technician also considers using a magnesium strip as a sacrificial anode on a long pipeline. Standard reduction potentials are for 25 °C and 1 M solutions, and the soil moisture and temperature were the same for every coupon. Each strip had a surface area about equal to that of the iron coupon, and the connecting wire did not corrode during the test.

qs.q: What is the standard cell potential when a zinc strip serves as anode and O₂ is reduced at the cathode?
o: Correct: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0.40 - (-0.76) = 1.16 V.
This uses Fe²⁺ as the cathode (-0.44 - (-0.76)), but oxygen is reduced under these conditions.
This adds the two potentials with their signs instead of subtracting the anode potential.
This is the potential of iron as anode (0.40 + 0.44), not zinc.
qs.x: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0.40 - (-0.76) = 1.16 V. Trap: Adding the half-cell potentials instead of subtracting the anode from the cathode.

qs.q: In the iron-copper pair, which statement describes the flow of electrons and the site of oxygen reduction?
o: Copper is the anode; electrons flow from copper to iron, which protects the iron.
Copper is much harder to oxidize than iron, so it cannot be the anode.
Iron is the cathode, so it is protected, and electrons flow from copper to iron.
The larger mass loss for the Fe-Cu pair shows iron corrodes faster, which means it is the anode.
Iron is the anode; electrons flow through the wire from iron to copper, where O₂ is reduced.
Correct: Fe is oxidized more readily than Cu (-0.44 V versus +0.34 V), so iron is the anode and the electrons travel to copper, which acts as the cathode surface.
No current flows because both metals are connected by the same wire.
The potential difference between the metals drives current through the wire.
qs.x: Fe is oxidized more readily than Cu (-0.44 V versus +0.34 V), so iron is the anode and the electrons travel to copper, which acts as the cathode surface. Trap: Assuming the metal with the higher reduction potential is the one that corrodes.

qs.q: A magnesium anode supplies a steady 0.20 A to a pipeline for 24 hours (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2 e⁻; molar mass 24.3 g/mol; F = 96,500 C/mol). What mass of magnesium is consumed?
o: This uses one electron per magnesium atom instead of two.
This uses four electrons per magnesium atom, a number that belongs to the O₂ half-reaction.
Correct: Charge = 0.20 × 86,400 = 17,280 C = 0.179 mol e⁻, so 0.0895 mol Mg × 24.3 g/mol = 2.2 g.
This uses the molar mass of zinc (65.4 g/mol) instead of magnesium.
qs.x: Charge = 0.20 × 86,400 = 17,280 C = 0.179 mol e⁻, so 0.0895 mol Mg × 24.3 g/mol = 2.2 g. Trap: Using the wrong number of electrons per mole of metal in the Faraday calculation.

qs.q: A steel can is coated with tin. Why does the iron corrode faster than uncoated iron once the coating is scratched?
o: Tin has a higher reduction potential than iron, so iron becomes the anode of a galvanic cell with the tin surface.
Correct: E°(Sn²⁺/Sn) = -0.14 V is greater than E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = -0.44 V, so exposed iron oxidizes in preference to tin, as the -31 mg entry in Table 1 shows.
Tin has a lower reduction potential than iron, so tin is oxidized and protects the iron.
Tin's reduction potential is higher than iron's, not lower; zinc and magnesium would behave this way.
Tin is a better electrical insulator, which traps water against the iron.
The corrosion rate increase arises from the galvanic couple, not insulation.
Tin reacts with O₂ to form a layer that dissolves iron.
Tin does not dissolve iron; iron loses mass through its own oxidation.
qs.x: E°(Sn²⁺/Sn) = -0.14 V is greater than E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = -0.44 V, so exposed iron oxidizes in preference to tin, as the -31 mg entry in Table 1 shows. Trap: Assuming any metal coating protects the iron even after the coating is damaged.

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: A heating element is made from a nichrome wire 2.0 m long with diameter 0.40 mm (cross-sectional area 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m²). The resistance of a wire is R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity, L the length, and A the cross-sectional area. Over a modest temperature range, ρ = ρ₂₀[1 + α(T - 20 °C)]. Table 1 lists ρ₂₀ and α for nichrome and for copper, the material of the leads supplying current to the element. A student heats the nichrome wire in a furnace, measures its resistance with a small test current at four temperatures, and plots the results in Figure 1. The student then connects the wire at 20 °C to a 24 V source through copper leads of the same length and diameter as the nichrome wire. The wire is straight, has uniform composition, and carries a current small enough that self-heating can be ignored during the resistance measurements in the furnace. The thermal expansion of the wire is small enough that its dimensions are treated as constant.

qs.q: Which value is closest to the power dissipated by the nichrome wire at 20 °C when connected directly to the 24 V source?
o: This is the current in amperes (24/17.5), not the power.
Correct: R = 17.5 Ω from Figure 1, so P = V²/R = 576/17.5 = 33 W.
This squares the voltage but omits division by the resistance.
This is 1/R, a conductance in siemens, not a power.
qs.x: R = 17.5 Ω from Figure 1, so P = V²/R = 576/17.5 = 33 W. Trap: Mixing up current and power or leaving out the resistance in P = V²/R.

qs.q: If the same length of nichrome wire had a diameter of 0.80 mm, what resistance would it have at 20 °C?
o: This halves the resistance as if it depended on diameter rather than area.
Correct: Doubling the diameter quadruples the area, so R = 17.5/4 = 4.4 Ω.
This doubles the resistance, the wrong direction for a thicker wire.
This quadruples the resistance, which would apply to a wire of half the diameter.
qs.x: Doubling the diameter quadruples the area, so R = 17.5/4 = 4.4 Ω. Trap: Treating resistance as inversely proportional to diameter instead of to diameter squared.

qs.q: According to Figure 1, by what percentage does the resistance of the nichrome wire increase between 20 °C and 620 °C?
o: This is a decimal error; 600 K times 4 × 10⁻⁴ is 0.24, which is 24%.
This is the ratio 21.7/17.5 expressed as a percentage of the original value, not the increase.
This treats the absolute rise in ohms as a percentage.
Correct: The graph rises from 17.5 Ω to 21.7 Ω, an increase of 4.2/17.5 = 24%, consistent with α ΔT = (4 × 10⁻⁴)(600) = 0.24.
qs.x: The graph rises from 17.5 Ω to 21.7 Ω, an increase of 4.2/17.5 = 24%, consistent with α ΔT = (4 × 10⁻⁴)(600) = 0.24. Trap: Reporting the final-to-initial ratio, or the rise in ohms, as the percent increase.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the increase in resistance of metals such as copper and nichrome as temperature rises?
o: The number of conduction electrons decreases as the metal is heated.
In metals the number of carriers barely changes; that explanation fits semiconductors in reverse.
Greater lattice vibration scatters conduction electrons more often, lowering their average drift speed for a given field.
Correct: In a metal, the number of charge carriers is nearly constant, but more frequent collisions with vibrating ions reduce drift velocity and raise resistivity.
The wire's length decreases on heating, which raises R.
Thermal expansion lengthens a wire, and the effect is far too small to explain a 24% change.
The wire's cross-sectional area rises, which increases R.
A larger area would lower the resistance, and again the expansion is very small.
qs.x: In a metal, the number of charge carriers is nearly constant, but more frequent collisions with vibrating ions reduce drift velocity and raise resistivity. Trap: Attributing the resistance change to geometry or carrier number rather than scattering.

qs.q: In the circuit with the copper leads, approximately what fraction of the 24 V source voltage is dropped across the leads at 20 °C?
o: This is the fraction across the nichrome wire, not the leads.
This is a power-of-ten error from 0.27/1.78.
Correct: R(leads) = (1.7 × 10⁻⁸)(2.0)/(1.26 × 10⁻⁷) = 0.27 Ω in series with 17.5 Ω, so the lead fraction is 0.27/17.8 = 1.5%.
This reports the lead resistance in ohms as a percentage.
qs.x: R(leads) = (1.7 × 10⁻⁸)(2.0)/(1.26 × 10⁻⁷) = 0.27 Ω in series with 17.5 Ω, so the lead fraction is 0.27/17.8 = 1.5%. Trap: Neglecting that series resistances divide the voltage in proportion to resistance.

graph.title: Figure 1. Resistance of the nichrome wire versus temperature

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: A glass pH electrode and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode form a cell whose potential depends linearly on pH: E = -s(pH - 7), where s = 2.303RT/F. The instrument is set so that E = 0 V in a pH 7.00 buffer. The reference electrode contains saturated KCl, so the AgCl + e⁻ → Ag + Cl⁻ half-reaction has a fixed potential. A student calibrates the meter with buffers at 25 °C and records the cell potential for two samples, as shown in Table 1. Figure 1 shows the calibration lines at 25 °C and at 37 °C. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), F = 96,500 C/mol, and 2.303RT/F = 0.0592 V at 25 °C. The calibration solutions are stirred and equilibrated for two minutes before each reading, and the electrodes are rinsed between solutions. The meter has a very high input impedance, so a negligible current passes through the cell during a measurement.

qs.q: What is the pH of Sample A?
o: This reverses the sign of the cell potential (7 + 1.50).
This is the quotient E/s alone, without subtracting it from 7.
This matches no step of the calculation; 0.0888 V is 1.50 pH units from neutral, not 1.00.
qs.x: pH = 7 - E/s = 7 - 0.0888/0.0592 = 7 - 1.50 = 5.50. Trap: Forgetting the pH 7 offset or reversing the sign of the slope.

qs.q: Why is the 37 °C line in Figure 1 steeper than the 25 °C line?
o: The reference electrode potential increases at higher temperature.
The reference potential would shift all points up or down, not change the slope.
Hydrogen ion concentration is higher at 37 °C for any buffer.
A buffer's pH is nearly constant; the change in slope is from the equation, not the solution.
The slope 2.303RT/F is proportional to absolute temperature, so it is about 4% larger at 310 K than at 298 K.
Correct: T enters the Nernst slope directly; 0.0592 × (310/298) = 0.0616 V per pH unit.
The Faraday constant rises with temperature.
F is a constant and does not depend on temperature.
qs.x: T enters the Nernst slope directly; 0.0592 × (310/298) = 0.0616 V per pH unit. Trap: Attributing the steeper slope to a change in the solution rather than to the T term in the Nernst equation.

qs.q: At 25 °C, what cell potential is expected for a solution of pH 8.50?
o: This has the right magnitude but the wrong sign; potential falls as pH rises.
This is the potential at pH 10.00, not 8.50.
This is the potential for a single pH unit above 7, not for 1.5 units.
qs.x: E = -0.0592 × (8.50 - 7.00) = -0.0888 V. Trap: Getting the sign wrong because acid solutions give positive potentials.

qs.q: Why does the potential of the Ag/AgCl reference electrode stay constant while the sample pH changes?
