o: The chloride concentration in the saturated KCl filling solution is fixed, so the AgCl/Ag half-cell potential is fixed.
Correct: By the Nernst equation, E for AgCl/Ag depends on [Cl⁻], which is held constant by the saturated KCl.
The reference electrode is not connected to the sample.
It must be connected through a junction to complete the circuit.
Silver ions are consumed in proportion to the hydrogen ion concentration.
Silver is not involved in the hydrogen ion response of the cell.
The reference electrode has no half-reaction.
AgCl + e⁻ → Ag + Cl⁻ is a real half-reaction at that electrode.
qs.x: By the Nernst equation, E for AgCl/Ag depends on [Cl⁻], which is held constant by the saturated KCl. Trap: Thinking a reference electrode does not take part in the cell reaction.

qs.q: What is the hydrogen ion concentration in Sample A?
o: This corresponds to pH 8.50.
This takes the pH value as the coefficient of the exponent.
Correct: [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵·⁵ = 3.2 × 10⁻⁶ M.
This corresponds to pH 1.50, the quotient E/s.
qs.x: [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵·⁵ = 3.2 × 10⁻⁶ M. Trap: Using the wrong sign or value when converting pH to concentration.

graph.title: Figure 1. Cell potential versus pH

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: Alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme in raw milk, is inactivated by heat, and the loss of activity follows first-order kinetics. A food scientist measured the first-order rate constant k for inactivation at four temperatures (Table 1) and plotted ln k against 1000/T in Figure 1. The Arrhenius equation, k = A e^(-Ea/RT), predicts that the plot of ln k versus 1/T is a straight line with slope -Ea/R. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and ln 2 = 0.693. The scientist assumes that the activation energy and the pre-exponential factor A do not depend on temperature over this range. A second question concerns the effect of a catalyst that lowers the activation energy of a reaction by 10 kJ/mol without changing A. Samples were held at each temperature long enough to reach thermal equilibrium, and the activity remaining was assayed with a colorimetric substrate. The scatter among replicate assays at each temperature was small, and each value in the table is an average of three runs.

qs.q: Which activation energy is obtained from the slope of the line in Figure 1?
o: 9.6 kJ/mol
This is the slope magnitude in thousands of kelvin with the factor of 1000 and R both ignored.
160 kJ/mol
This doubles the correct value, as if the slope were -Ea/(R/2).
80 kJ/mol
Correct: The slope is (-6.32 + 9.21)/(3.030 - 3.333) = -9.5 × 10³ K, so Ea = 9.5 × 10³ × 8.314 = 79 kJ/mol, about 80 kJ/mol.
40 kJ/mol
This halves the value, as if the slope were -2Ea/R.
qs.x: The slope is (-6.32 + 9.21)/(3.030 - 3.333) = -9.5 × 10³ K, so Ea = 9.5 × 10³ × 8.314 = 79 kJ/mol, about 80 kJ/mol. Trap: Forgetting to multiply the slope by R (or by the factor of 1000 in the axis).

qs.q: What is the half-life for inactivation at 300 K?
o: This is k divided by ln 2, which has the inverse of the units of time.
This is 1/k, the mean lifetime, not the half-life.
This is 0.5/k, which uses 0.5 in place of ln 2.
Correct: For first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k = 0.693/(1.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) = 6.9 × 10³ s.
qs.x: For first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2/k = 0.693/(1.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) = 6.9 × 10³ s. Trap: Using 1/k or k/ln 2 for the half-life of a first-order process.

qs.q: Why does the rate constant increase as temperature rises?
o: A larger fraction of molecular collisions has energy at or above the activation energy.
Correct: The Boltzmann distribution shifts toward higher energies, so exp(-Ea/RT) grows with T while Ea itself stays the same.
Raising the temperature lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
Ea is a property of the reaction pathway; heating does not change it (only a catalyst would).
Raising the temperature increases the concentration of enzyme.
The concentration in the sample does not change on heating, and k is independent of concentration.
Raising the temperature makes the reaction more exothermic.
The enthalpy change is not what k reflects, and it is nearly constant over this range.
qs.x: The Boltzmann distribution shifts toward higher energies, so exp(-Ea/RT) grows with T while Ea itself stays the same. Trap: Believing heat lowers the activation barrier rather than raising the fraction of molecules that can cross it.

qs.q: At 330 K, approximately how long does it take for 90% of the active enzyme to be lost?
o: This is the half-life, ln 2/k, which describes a loss of 50%.
This is 1/k, the time for the active fraction to fall to 37%.
This is off by a factor of ten.
qs.x: For 90% loss, ln(1/0.10) = 2.303, so t = 2.303/(1.8 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) = 1.3 × 10³ s. Trap: Using the half-life for a 90% loss.

qs.q: At 300 K, by what factor does the rate constant increase if a catalyst lowers Ea by 10 kJ/mol and leaves A unchanged?
o: This is the value of the exponent, not of the exponential.
This equates 10 kJ/mol with a tenfold increase.
This results from using Ea in kJ with R in J, which makes the exponent about 0.004.
qs.x: k₂/k₁ = exp(ΔEa/RT) = exp(10,000/(8.314 × 300)) = exp(4.01) = 55. Trap: Reporting the exponent rather than the exponential of the exponent.

graph.title: Figure 1. Arrhenius plot for enzyme inactivation

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A student uses a coffee-cup calorimeter to measure enthalpies of neutralization. In each trial 50.0 mL of an acid solution and 50.0 mL of a base solution, both at the same initial temperature, are mixed in an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid, and the highest temperature is recorded. Assume that all solutions have density 1.00 g/mL and specific heat capacity 4.18 J/(g·K), that no heat is lost to the surroundings, and that the heat absorbed by the cup is negligible. Results of two trials are shown in Table 1. In a third trial planned for later, the student will use 2.0 M HCl and 2.0 M NaOH, again 50.0 mL of each at 21.0 °C. All of the reactions are carried out at constant pressure. The acid and base solutions were allowed to reach thermal equilibrium with the room before mixing, and the mixture was stirred gently with the thermometer. The student recorded temperature every 15 seconds and used the highest value, which occurred about 45 seconds after mixing.

qs.q: Which value is closest to the enthalpy of neutralization per mole for Trial 1?
o: +56.8 kJ/mol
The temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.
-2.84 kJ/mol
This is the total heat, not divided by the moles of water formed.
-57 kJ/mol
Correct: q = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/g·K)(6.8 K) = 2.84 kJ released by 0.0500 mol of water formed; ΔH = -2.84/0.0500 = -57 kJ/mol.
-28.4 kJ/mol
This divides by 0.100 mol, the total moles of acid plus base, rather than the 0.0500 mol of limiting reagent.
qs.x: q = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/g·K)(6.8 K) = 2.84 kJ released by 0.0500 mol of water formed; ΔH = -2.84/0.0500 = -57 kJ/mol. Trap: Dividing by the wrong number of moles or dropping the negative sign of an exothermic reaction.

qs.q: Why is the temperature rise in Trial 2 smaller than in Trial 1?
o: Part of the energy released is consumed in ionizing the weak acid, which is endothermic, so the net heat released is smaller.
Correct: Acetic acid dissociates only partly; completing the dissociation as the base removes H⁺ absorbs energy, giving ΔH of about -53 kJ/mol rather than -57.
Acetic acid contains fewer moles of acid than HCl.
Both solutions contain 0.0500 mol of acid, so the amounts are equal.
Neutralization of a weak acid is endothermic overall.
The temperature rose, so the overall reaction is exothermic.
The specific heat capacity of acetic acid solution is lower than that of HCl.
Dilute solutions have nearly equal heat capacities, and a lower value would give a larger, not smaller, temperature rise.
qs.x: Acetic acid dissociates only partly; completing the dissociation as the base removes H⁺ absorbs energy, giving ΔH of about -53 kJ/mol rather than -57. Trap: Attributing the difference to amounts of reagent rather than the energy of ionization.

qs.q: If the cup itself absorbs a small amount of heat, but the student ignores this, how will the calculated enthalpy of neutralization compare with the true value?
o: The magnitude will be too large, because the cup adds extra heat to the solution.
The cup absorbs heat from the reaction; it does not supply heat.
It will be exactly correct, because the cup's heat capacity cancels in ΔT.
The heat taken up by the cup never reaches the thermometer, so it does not cancel.
The sign of ΔH will reverse.
The temperature still rises, so the reaction still appears exothermic.
The magnitude will be too small, because the temperature rise of the solution is smaller than if all the heat had gone to the solution.
Correct: Heat absorbed by the cup lowers the solution's temperature change, so q calculated from the solution alone underestimates the total heat released.
qs.x: Heat absorbed by the cup lowers the solution's temperature change, so q calculated from the solution alone underestimates the total heat released. Trap: Thinking heat absorbed by the apparatus would inflate the measured value.

qs.q: In the planned third trial, which final temperature is expected?
o: This is the Trial 1 result; doubling the moles of reaction in the same mass of solution doubles the temperature rise.
This doubles the final temperature rather than the temperature change.
This quadruples the temperature rise instead of doubling it.
Correct: The 2.0 M solutions give twice the moles (0.100 mol) in the same 100 g, so the heat and ΔT double: 6.8 × 2 = 13.6 K, and 21.0 + 13.6 = 34.6 °C.
qs.x: The 2.0 M solutions give twice the moles (0.100 mol) in the same 100 g, so the heat and ΔT double: 6.8 × 2 = 13.6 K, and 21.0 + 13.6 = 34.6 °C. Trap: Doubling the final temperature instead of the temperature change.

passages.title: Mini02 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: In cells, hydrolysis of ATP drives otherwise unfavorable reactions. For a reaction at constant temperature, ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q, where ΔG°′ is the standard free-energy change at pH 7 and Q is the reaction quotient. Table 1 lists ΔG°′ at 37 °C (310 K, RT = 2.58 kJ/mol) for four reactions. Figure 1 shows ΔG for ATP hydrolysis as ln Q varies, where Q = [ADP][Pᵢ]/[ATP] with concentrations in M. In a resting muscle cell, [ATP] = 5 mM, [ADP] = 0.5 mM, and [Pᵢ] = 5 mM, so Q = 5 × 10⁻⁴ and ln Q = -7.6. A coupled reaction is one whose overall ΔG°′ is the sum of the ΔG°′ values of its parts. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Assume that the activities of all species equal their molar concentrations. The values of ΔG°′ in Table 1 are for reactions in which each species is at 1 M except for H⁺, which is held at pH 7, and the temperature of all reactions is 37 °C.

qs.q: What is ΔG°′ for the coupled reaction glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP?
o: -44.3 kJ/mol
This adds the magnitudes of the two values instead of combining their signs.
-16.7 kJ/mol
Correct: Add the two reactions: -30.5 + 13.8 = -16.7 kJ/mol.
+16.7 kJ/mol
This has the right magnitude, but the sum is negative because the ATP term is larger in magnitude.
-30.5 kJ/mol
This is the ATP hydrolysis term by itself and leaves out the unfavorable glucose phosphorylation.
qs.x: Add the two reactions: -30.5 + 13.8 = -16.7 kJ/mol. Trap: Adding magnitudes instead of the signed values when coupling reactions.

qs.q: What is the equilibrium constant at 310 K for glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP?
o: This uses exp(-6.5), which applies to a reaction with a positive ΔG°′.
This takes the value of the exponent, 16.7/2.58, as K.
This results from using ΔG°′ in kJ with R in J, which makes the exponent nearly zero.
qs.x: K = exp(-ΔG°′/RT) = exp(16.7/2.58) = exp(6.5) = 6.5 × 10². Trap: Using the wrong sign in the exponent or leaving the exponent un-exponentiated.

qs.q: Using Figure 1, which ΔG is closest to the value for ATP hydrolysis in the resting muscle cell?
o: -50 kJ/mol
Correct: At ln Q = -7.6 the line lies between -51 (at -8) and -46 (at -6), so ΔG is about -50 kJ/mol: -30.5 + (2.58)(-7.6) = -50.1.
-30.5 kJ/mol
This is the standard value at ln Q = 0, which does not apply to the cell.
-10.9 kJ/mol
This adds the term RT ln Q to ΔG°′ with the wrong sign (-30.5 + 19.6).
+50.1 kJ/mol
ATP hydrolysis is spontaneous in the cell, so ΔG must be negative.
qs.x: At ln Q = -7.6 the line lies between -51 (at -8) and -46 (at -6), so ΔG is about -50 kJ/mol: -30.5 + (2.58)(-7.6) = -50.1. Trap: Using the standard-state value for conditions that are far from standard.

qs.q: Why is ΔG for ATP hydrolysis in the cell more negative than ΔG°′?
o: Cells hold Q well above 1 by keeping ADP and Pᵢ high.
If Q were above 1, ln Q would be positive and ΔG would be less negative than ΔG°′.
ΔG°′ is defined at a temperature far above 37 °C.
The standard state here is defined at pH 7 and the same temperature, not an elevated one.
Enzymes lower the ΔG of the hydrolysis reaction.
Enzymes change rates but not ΔG, which depends only on the states of reactants and products.
Cells keep Q well below 1 by holding ATP high and ADP and Pᵢ low, which makes ln Q negative.
Correct: Because ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q and ln Q is negative at Q < 1, the added term is negative.
qs.x: Because ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q and ln Q is negative at Q < 1, the added term is negative. Trap: Believing that a catalyst can change the free-energy change of a reaction.

qs.q: What is the slope of the line in Figure 1?
o: 8.31 kJ/mol
This is the value of R in J/(mol·K) with the temperature left out.
-30.5 kJ/mol
This is the intercept (ΔG°′) of the line, not its slope.
2.6 kJ/mol
Correct: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q, so the slope with respect to ln Q is RT = (8.314)(310)/1000 = 2.6 kJ/mol.
25.8 kJ/mol
This is RT expressed in J/mol with a factor of ten wrong in the conversion.
qs.x: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q, so the slope with respect to ln Q is RT = (8.314)(310)/1000 = 2.6 kJ/mol. Trap: Confusing the intercept with the slope or omitting T from RT.

graph.title: Figure 1. ΔG of ATP hydrolysis versus ln Q (310 K)

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Signal detection theory separates a listener's sensitivity from the criterion used to decide whether a stimulus was present. Forty adults listened for a faint 1,000-Hz tone embedded in white noise. In each of three payoff conditions, every listener completed 100 signal trials (tone present) and 100 noise trials (noise only) and responded "yes" or "no" after each trial. In the Liberal condition, a missed tone cost 5 points and a false alarm cost 1 point. In the Neutral condition, both errors cost 3 points. In the Conservative condition, a false alarm cost 5 points and a miss cost 1 point. Correct responses earned 1 point in all conditions. Tone intensity and noise level were identical across conditions, and condition order was counterbalanced across listeners. Pooled results are shown in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots hit rate against false-alarm rate for each condition. Listeners were screened to confirm normal hearing thresholds, wore the same headphones throughout, and received feedback on points earned after every block of 20 trials. The experimenter told them that the tone would be present on exactly half of the trials, so that the base rate was constant across conditions. A short practice block preceded each condition, and listeners were encouraged to maximize their total points.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: The Liberal condition made listeners more sensitive to the tone because they produced the largest number of hits.
A high hit rate alone can come from a lax criterion; the false-alarm rate rose from 8 to 40 as well, and d' did not increase.
The Conservative condition lowered the listeners' absolute threshold because they produced the fewest false alarms.
Fewer false alarms reflect a stricter criterion, not a change in the sensory threshold; d' was in fact slightly the highest here.
The payoff structure shifted the listeners' response criterion while sensitivity to the tone stayed roughly constant.
Correct: d' stays between 1.53 and 1.71 while hits and false alarms both rise as the criterion becomes more liberal.
Penalizing misses damaged the auditory system's ability to transduce the tone, which reduced d' in the Liberal condition.
Payoffs are decision-level manipulations that cannot change transduction, and d' differed only modestly across conditions.
qs.x: d' stays between 1.53 and 1.71 while hits and false alarms both rise as the criterion becomes more liberal. Trap: Treating a higher hit rate as better sensitivity without checking the false-alarm rate.

qs.q: In the Conservative condition, what proportion of the listener's "yes" responses were correct?
o: 0.62 of all yes responses
This is the hit rate, 62 of 100 signal trials, not the share of yes responses that were correct.
About 0.89
Correct: Yes responses = 62 hits + 8 false alarms = 70, and 62/70 is about 0.89.
0.77 of all yes responses
This is overall accuracy, (62 + 92)/200, which includes correct rejections that are not yes responses.
0.35 of all yes responses
This is the proportion of all 200 trials on which the listener said yes (70/200), not the proportion of those that were correct.
qs.x: Yes responses = 62 hits + 8 false alarms = 70, and 62/70 is about 0.89. Trap: Using the hit rate as the answer instead of dividing hits by all yes responses.

qs.q: If tone intensity were increased while the Neutral payoffs were kept, which change in Figure 1 is most likely?
o: The Neutral point would move along the same curve toward the lower left, matching the Conservative point.
Movement along one curve reflects a criterion change; a stronger tone changes sensitivity, which moves to a different curve.
The Neutral point would move toward the lower right, with more false alarms and fewer hits.
This would imply that a stronger tone is harder to detect, which contradicts the principle that sensitivity rises with signal strength.
The Neutral point would not move because payoffs, not stimulus intensity, determine the observed hit and false-alarm rates.
Payoffs influence only the criterion; stimulus intensity directly affects how well signal and noise trials can be separated.
The Neutral point would move toward the upper left, with a higher hit rate at a similar or lower false-alarm rate.
Correct: A stronger signal raises d', so hits rise with no increase in false alarms, shifting the point toward the upper-left corner.
qs.x: A stronger signal raises d', so hits rise with no increase in false alarms, shifting the point toward the upper-left corner. Trap: Assuming that only payoffs, not stimulus strength, can move a point on the plot.

qs.q: A researcher argues that signal detection theory is superior to a classical absolute-threshold procedure. Which feature supports that argument?
o: It shows that a stimulus below a fixed intensity is never perceived, whatever the observer's expectations.
SDT rejects a single fixed intensity cutoff; detection is probabilistic and depends on noise and criterion.
It eliminates internal noise in the nervous system so that responses depend only on the physical stimulus.
SDT assumes noise is always present in the system and builds it into the model rather than removing it.
It separates the observer's sensory sensitivity from motivation and decision bias.
Correct: Thresholds from yes/no data mix sensitivity with willingness to say yes; d' and the criterion are estimated separately.
It predicts that all observers have the same criterion once the stimulus intensity is held constant.
Criteria vary with payoffs, expectations, and motivation, as the three conditions show.
qs.x: Thresholds from yes/no data mix sensitivity with willingness to say yes; d' and the criterion are estimated separately. Trap: Believing that a threshold is a fixed property of the sensory system independent of motivation.

qs.q: On Figure 1, what coordinates would describe a listener who answered "yes" on every trial regardless of the stimulus?
o: False-alarm rate 1.0 and hit rate 1.0
Correct: Saying yes on all trials gives every signal trial a hit and every noise trial a false alarm, with zero sensitivity.
False-alarm rate 0 and hit rate 1.0, which would indicate perfect discrimination
This is perfect discrimination, which requires saying yes only when the tone is present.
False-alarm rate 0 and hit rate 0
This corresponds to answering "no" on every trial, the most conservative possible criterion.
False-alarm rate 1.0 and hit rate 0
This would mean answering yes only on noise trials, which is a systematic reversal of the task and not a bias.
qs.x: Saying yes on all trials gives every signal trial a hit and every noise trial a false alarm, with zero sensitivity. Trap: Confusing a maximally liberal criterion with perfect sensitivity.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Pooled trial counts (per 100 signal and 100 noise trials)

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: Taste sensitivity varies among people. Some individuals, called supertasters, report strong bitterness from 6-n-propylthiouracil (PROP), a compound that activates a bitter receptor encoded by the TAS2R38 gene. Researchers recruited 60 adults and stained the anterior tongue with blue food dye. They counted fungiform papillae (each of which holds taste buds) in a 6-mm circle. Participants then rated PROP bitterness, 0.5 M sucrose sweetness, and burn from a capsaicin solution on a 0 to 100 scale, with rinses between samples. Participants were sorted into three groups of 20 by papillae count. Across all 60 participants, papillae count correlated with PROP bitterness at r = +0.78. Group means are shown in Table 1. No participant had an olfactory or neurological disorder, and all wore nose clips during tasting. Papillae were counted by two raters who did not know the taste ratings, and their counts agreed closely. Participants were instructed to refrain from eating, drinking anything but water, and smoking for one hour before testing. Samples were presented in a randomized order, and participants used a labeled magnitude scale whose anchors were defined as the strongest sensation of any kind they had ever experienced.

qs.q: Capsaicin burn ratings were higher in the high-density group. Which factor best explains this result?
o: Capsaicin binds the same G protein-coupled bitter receptor as PROP, so more taste buds mean a larger signal.
Capsaicin acts on a pain-related ion channel (TRPV1) on nociceptors, not on a bitter receptor.
Free nerve endings of the trigeminal nerve surround fungiform papillae, so denser papillae carry more pain-sensitive fibers.
Correct: Capsaicin activates nociceptors, not taste receptors, and trigeminal fibers innervate the papillae.
Taste receptor cells for burn project directly to the olfactory bulb, which amplifies the sensation in people with more papillae.
Taste does not relay through the olfactory bulb, and burn is a somatosensory sensation rather than a taste.
Papillae density increases the number of rods in the tongue epithelium and therefore the sensitivity to heat.
Rods are photoreceptors in the retina and do not occur in the tongue.
qs.x: Capsaicin activates nociceptors, not taste receptors, and trigeminal fibers innervate the papillae. Trap: Assuming burn is a taste quality processed by taste receptor cells.

qs.q: Approximately what percentage of the variability in PROP bitterness ratings is statistically accounted for by papillae count?
o: About 78% of the variance
This treats r itself as the proportion of variance rather than squaring it.
About 22% of the variance
This is 1 - 0.78, which has no meaning as a variance share.
About 61%
Correct: r squared = 0.78 squared, which is about 0.61.
About 39% of the variance
This is the variance left unexplained, 1 - 0.61, not the variance accounted for.
qs.x: r squared = 0.78 squared, which is about 0.61. Trap: Reporting r as if it were the proportion of variance explained.

qs.q: Why can the researchers NOT conclude from these data that high papillae density causes stronger bitterness?
o: The sample of 60 is too small for any correlation coefficient to be calculated.
A correlation can be computed for any sample with variability; size affects precision, not feasibility.
A correlation of +0.78 is too high to be real and probably results from measurement error.
High correlations are not evidence of error; they only quantify the association.
Participants wore nose clips, which prevents inference about taste perception in everyday conditions in a way that would invalidate the correlation between taste ratings and counts.
Nose clips remove olfactory confounds and improve, not prevent, interpretation of taste ratings.
Papillae density was measured, not manipulated, so a third variable such as TAS2R38 genotype could influence both measures.
Correct: A correlational design leaves room for confounders; causal claims require manipulation or additional control.
qs.x: A correlational design leaves room for confounders; causal claims require manipulation or additional control. Trap: Reading a strong correlation as proof that one variable causes the other.

qs.q: Which pathway carries taste information from the tongue to the cortex region that gives rise to conscious taste perception?
o: Spinal dorsal columns to the medulla, then the thalamus, then the primary somatosensory cortex alone as it does for taste
Dorsal columns carry fine touch and proprioception from the body, and taste does not use this route.
Cranial nerves to the olfactory bulb, then directly to the amygdala, bypassing the thalamus
Bypassing the thalamus is characteristic of olfaction, not of taste, which uses the thalamic relay.
Optic nerve to the lateral geniculate nucleus, then to the occipital lobe for integration with taste
The optic pathway carries visual information; taste does not travel through the lateral geniculate nucleus.
Cranial nerves to the brainstem, then the thalamus, then the insular and frontal operculum gustatory cortex
Correct: Taste afferents synapse in the brainstem nucleus of the solitary tract, then relay through thalamus to gustatory cortex.
qs.x: Taste afferents synapse in the brainstem nucleus of the solitary tract, then relay through thalamus to gustatory cortex. Trap: Applying the olfactory exception of bypassing the thalamus to every sense.

qs.q: Which interpretation of Table 1 is best supported?
o: Papillae density affects only the perception of PROP, and sweetness is unrelated to density.
Sucrose ratings still rise from 55 to 68, so the association is smaller but not absent.
Ratings of all three stimuli rise with papillae density, but the increase is much steeper for PROP than for sucrose.
Correct: PROP rises from 12 to 71, whereas sucrose rises from 55 to 68, so density has the larger association with bitterness.
Low-density individuals cannot taste PROP at all, because their mean rating is close to zero.
A mean of 12 reflects weak but nonzero bitterness, and a mean cannot establish that every individual lacks sensitivity.
High-density individuals rated sucrose lower than low-density individuals, consistent with greater taste adaptation.
The table shows the opposite: high-density individuals gave higher sucrose ratings, 68 vs 55.
qs.x: PROP rises from 12 to 71, whereas sucrose rises from 55 to 68, so density has the larger association with bitterness. Trap: Overlooking that a smaller but real increase in sucrose ratings still exists.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Group means by fungiform papillae density

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: According to the levels-of-processing framework, memory depends on the depth at which information is encoded. Ninety undergraduates were randomly assigned to one of three orienting-task groups (n = 30 each) and saw 60 common nouns, one every 3 seconds. Each word was accompanied by a yes/no question requiring a different kind of processing. The structural group judged whether the word was printed in capital letters. The phonemic group judged whether the word rhymed with a target. The semantic group judged whether the word fit into a sentence frame. Participants were not told that memory would be tested. After a 10-minute filler task, each participant first completed free recall and then a recognition test containing the 60 studied words and 60 new words. Results are summarized in Figure 1 and Table 1. Words were presented on a computer screen in a different random order for each participant, and no word was repeated. The word list was matched for length and frequency of use in everyday English. The filler task consisted of simple arithmetic problems that prevented rehearsal of the list. All testing was done individually in a quiet room, and each session lasted about 40 minutes, including consent and debriefing.

qs.q: Which conclusion about encoding is best supported by Figure 1 and Table 1?
o: Phonemic encoding is as effective as semantic encoding, since both groups recognized more than half of the words.
Recognition of 0.74 vs 0.91 and recall of 27% vs 58% show a large advantage for semantic encoding.
Structural encoding produced the best performance because participants processed the visual appearance of each word and had the strongest traces.
The structural group had the lowest recall and hit rate, indicating the shallowest encoding.
Meaning-based encoding produces stronger memory traces than perceptual or sound-based encoding on both recall and recognition.
Correct: The semantic group had the highest recall and hit rate and the lowest false-alarm rate.
The effect of orienting task appeared only in free recall and disappeared when recognition cues were available.
Recognition hit rates also differed substantially across groups, so the effect did not disappear.
qs.x: The semantic group had the highest recall and hit rate and the lowest false-alarm rate. Trap: Assuming that any careful processing of a word helps memory equally.

qs.q: Semantic judgments are associated with greater activity in which brain region during encoding?
o: Primary visual cortex
This region processes basic visual features such as letter shapes, matching structural judgments instead.
Cerebellar vermis
This region is involved in coordination of movement and not in semantic encoding of words.
Left inferior prefrontal cortex
Correct: This region supports semantic elaboration and retrieval of word meaning during encoding.
Primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe
This region would be involved in analyzing sounds, relevant to phonemic judgments more than to meaning.
qs.x: This region supports semantic elaboration and retrieval of word meaning during encoding. Trap: Linking semantic tasks to sensory cortex rather than to prefrontal regions.

qs.q: Random assignment of participants to orienting tasks primarily helps the researchers do what?
o: Ensure that every participant is exposed to all three orienting tasks in the same order.
That describes a within-subjects design, whereas this study placed each participant in one group.
Increase the external validity by sampling participants from the whole population of adults.
Random assignment concerns allocation to groups; random sampling affects generalizability.
Prevent participants from guessing the purpose of the study, which eliminates demand characteristics from a single exposure.
Incidental learning handles awareness of the memory test; randomization does not prevent guessing.
Distribute preexisting differences in memory ability evenly across groups, so groups differ mainly in the task.
Correct: Randomization balances known and unknown participant characteristics across conditions on average.
qs.x: Randomization balances known and unknown participant characteristics across conditions on average. Trap: Confusing random assignment with random sampling.

qs.q: On average, how many more words did the semantic group recall than the structural group?
o: About 26 words
Correct: The difference is 58% - 14% = 44% of 60 words, which is 26.4 words.
44 words, the percentage-point gap
This reports the percentage-point difference as if it were a count of words.
About 35 words, the semantic mean
This is the semantic group's mean recall (58% of 60 is about 35), not the difference.
About 4 words, the ratio of the means
This is the ratio 58/14 (about 4.1) mistaken for a difference in words.
qs.x: The difference is 58% - 14% = 44% of 60 words, which is 26.4 words. Trap: Reporting a percentage-point gap as a number of words.

qs.q: Recognition performance exceeded free recall in every group. Which explanation is best?
o: Recognition presents the studied items as retrieval cues, whereas recall requires generating items without them.
Correct: Cues in the test make retrieval easier even when the memory trace is weak.
Recognition depends on implicit memory, which is stronger than explicit memory for studied words.
Both recall and recognition are explicit (declarative) tests that need conscious retrieval.
Recognition tests bypass the hippocampus, so storage in long-term memory is not required.
Recognition of studied words also depends on stored traces that require consolidation.
Recognition measures the capacity of sensory memory, which has a greater capacity than long-term memory within seconds of the test.
A 10-minute delay exceeds sensory memory, so recognition here reflects long-term storage.
qs.x: Cues in the test make retrieval easier even when the memory trace is weak. Trap: Calling recognition tests implicit simply because they are easier.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean free recall by orienting task

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: The linguistic relativity hypothesis proposes that the categories in a person's language influence perception and thought. Russian has separate basic words for light blue (goluboy) and dark blue (siniy), whereas English uses a single word, blue. Researchers tested 48 native Russian speakers and 48 native English speakers living in the same city. On each trial, a participant saw three blue squares, a target on top and two below, and pressed a key to indicate which lower square matched the target exactly. In half of the trials, the two lower squares fell on opposite sides of the Russian light/dark boundary (cross-category); in the other half, both fell on the same side (within-category). Color distances in perceptual space were equal across trial types. Half of each language group also performed the task while silently rehearsing an 8-digit string (verbal interference). Mean reaction times appear in Table 1. Accuracy was above 97% in every condition, so only correct trials were analyzed for reaction time. Participants were tested individually in a dimly lit room on a calibrated monitor, and all of them passed a standard color vision screening before the experiment began. Trials were presented in random order, and each participant completed 80 trials in each condition after a short practice block with feedback.

qs.q: Which result best supports a weak version of linguistic relativity?
o: English speakers responded at similar speeds across both pair types, showing that they cannot perceive the difference between shades.
Similar speeds do not mean the shades cannot be seen; English speakers could still perform the task correctly.
Both groups slowed under verbal interference, showing that all thought requires inner speech.
Interference mainly abolished the Russian advantage and did not slow everyone; the data do not show that thought requires speech.
Russian speakers performed faster than English speakers in every condition of the table.
Under interference Russian times (556, 559) were slower than English times on cross-category trials (545).
Russian speakers responded faster to cross-category pairs than to within-category pairs when no interference was present.
Correct: A 49-ms advantage appears only in the group whose language marks the boundary.
qs.x: A 49-ms advantage appears only in the group whose language marks the boundary. Trap: Mistaking equal speed across pair types for inability to discriminate colors.

qs.q: What does the loss of the Russian advantage under verbal interference suggest?
o: Digit rehearsal damaged color vision in Russian speakers while leaving English speakers unaffected.
Interference is cognitive, not sensory, and it cannot impair photoreceptors for only one language group.
The Russian color boundary is a purely perceptual feature that does not involve language.
If it were purely perceptual, verbal interference would not eliminate it.
The language effect depends on online use of verbal working memory resources during the task.
Correct: Rehearsing digits occupies the phonological loop, so labels cannot be used and the cross-category advantage vanishes.
The Russian advantage is a practice effect because Russian speakers had more experience with similar tasks.
A practice account would not predict that the advantage disappears only with concurrent verbal load.
qs.x: Rehearsing digits occupies the phonological loop, so labels cannot be used and the cross-category advantage vanishes. Trap: Attributing the interference effect to a sensory deficit rather than to competition for verbal working memory.

qs.q: Which finding contradicts strong linguistic determinism, the claim that language determines thought?
o: Russian speakers had two color words available for blue and English speakers had only one when they viewed the colors.
This is a premise of the study, which is consistent with, not contrary to, determinism.
Speakers of both languages discriminated cross- and within-category pairs, differing only in response speed.
Correct: If language limited thought, English speakers could not distinguish the shades; here the effect is only in speed.
Russian participants were faster on cross-category trials than on within-category trials.
This supports an influence of language on performance, consistent with a weaker claim.
The language groups were tested in the same city using identical equipment.
Holding conditions constant is a design feature and does not address the claim.
qs.x: If language limited thought, English speakers could not distinguish the shades; here the effect is only in speed. Trap: Treating any language influence as proof of strong determinism.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of comparing Russian and English speakers in this study?
o: Reaction time is an unreliable measure of perception because it varies from trial to trial.
Averaged over many trials, reaction time is a standard and sensitive measure.
The perceptual distance between color pairs was equal, which prevents detection of any language effect on their own and in all conditions.
Equating perceptual distance is a strength because it removes physical difference as an explanation.
Language group could not be randomly assigned, so cultural or educational differences may account for part of the difference.
Correct: This is a quasi-experimental comparison of preexisting groups, which weakens causal inference.
Using nonverbal stimuli means that results cannot be applied to language processing at all.
The aim was to test effects of language on perception, for which nonverbal stimuli are appropriate.
qs.x: This is a quasi-experimental comparison of preexisting groups, which weakens causal inference. Trap: Ignoring that participants could not be assigned to a native language.

qs.q: By what percentage did verbal interference reduce the Russian speakers' cross- versus within-category difference?
o: About 6% of the effect
This is the remaining effect, 3/49, not the reduction.
About 46% of the effect
This takes the 46-ms drop as if it were a percentage.
About 8% of the effect
This divides the 46-ms drop by the within-category mean of 561 ms instead of by the original 49-ms difference.
About 94%
Correct: The difference fell from 49 ms to 3 ms, a drop of 46 ms, and 46/49 is about 0.94.
qs.x: The difference fell from 49 ms to 3 ms, a drop of 46 ms, and 46/49 is about 0.94. Trap: Reporting the milliseconds of change as a percentage.

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: The two-factor theory of emotion proposes that an emotion arises from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label for the arousal. Excitation-transfer research suggests that leftover arousal from one event can intensify a reaction to an unrelated later event. Eighty undergraduates were randomly assigned to one of four groups (n = 20 each). Half ran in place for 90 seconds (high arousal) and half sat quietly (baseline arousal). Participants then viewed 12 mildly funny cartoons either 2 minutes later (short delay, while heart rate was still elevated) or 15 minutes later (long delay, after heart rate returned to baseline). They rated each cartoon's amusement from 1 (not at all) to 10 (extremely), and ratings were averaged per person. Participants were told the cartoons were part of a separate study of humor. Group means are shown in Table 1. Heart rate was recorded continuously with a chest strap and confirmed that it was elevated during the short delay and at baseline during the long delay. A research assistant, unaware of the exercise assignment, administered the cartoons. After the session, participants were asked what they thought the exercise was for, and none of them linked it to the cartoons. All participants gave informed consent and were debriefed fully.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the 7.4 rating in the Ran in place, short-delay group?
o: Exercise directly causes humor by raising the level of dopamine in the hippocampus.
The data show that exercise boosted ratings only when cartoons followed soon after, which a direct chemical effect on humor would not explain.
Participants who exercised had stronger intrinsic motivation to complete the rating task accurately.
Motivation would not explain why the long-delay exercise group, with the same motivation, rated near baseline.
Residual arousal from exercise was misattributed to the cartoons, strengthening the amusement label.
Correct: Arousal remained elevated, was not attributed to the exercise, and was therefore read as part of the emotional response to the cartoons.
Exercise lowered participants' arousal below baseline, so cartoons seemed more intense by contrast.
Exercise raised arousal, and short-delay measurements were taken while heart rate was still elevated.
qs.x: Arousal remained elevated, was not attributed to the exercise, and was therefore read as part of the emotional response to the cartoons. Trap: Assuming that exercise itself increases humor, regardless of timing.

qs.q: Why did exercise fail to raise ratings in the long-delay condition?
o: Participants forgot the cartoons during the longer wait and responded randomly.
Forgetting would lower reliability but not produce a mean equal to baseline in the long-delay group.
The long-delay group experienced a cognitive label of fear, which canceled the amusement.
No fear label was introduced, and ratings equaled those of the baseline group, not lower.
Delayed viewing activates the parasympathetic system more strongly, which increases humor during a delay of this length.
Parasympathetic activity lowers arousal, and ratings did not rise in this group.
Arousal had dissipated by the time of the cartoons, so there was no residual arousal to be misattributed.
Correct: After 15 minutes, heart rate had returned to baseline, and the mean (5.1) matched the seated group (5.2).
qs.x: After 15 minutes, heart rate had returned to baseline, and the mean (5.1) matched the seated group (5.2). Trap: Attributing an absent effect to forgetting instead of to dissipated arousal.

qs.q: The elevated heart rate after running reflects slowly declining activity of which system?
o: Parasympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system acting through the vagus nerve
Parasympathetic activity slows heart rate and promotes recovery, but it does not account for the elevation itself.
Somatic nervous system motor neurons controlling the heart's skeletal muscle
The heart is cardiac muscle controlled by the autonomic nervous system, not by somatic motor neurons.
Enteric nervous system through its control of gut motility
The enteric system regulates digestion and does not drive exercise-related changes in heart rate.
Sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system, with circulating epinephrine
Correct: Sympathetic activation and epinephrine raise heart rate and decline gradually after exertion.
qs.x: Sympathetic activation and epinephrine raise heart rate and decline gradually after exertion. Trap: Choosing the parasympathetic system because the arousal is declining.

qs.q: The pattern in Table 1 is best described as which kind of statistical effect?
o: A main effect of exercise only, because the exercise groups always rated cartoons higher.
The long-delay exercise group (5.1) did not exceed the seated group (5.2), so exercise had no consistent effect.
A main effect of delay only, because short-delay groups always rated cartoons higher.
Short-delay seated participants (5.0) rated cartoons lower than long-delay seated participants (5.2).
No effect of either factor, because the grand mean of the four cells is close to the scale midpoint.
The grand mean does not rule out strong differences among cells, as the 7.4 mean shows.
An interaction, because the effect of exercise depends on the delay.
Correct: Exercise raises ratings by 2.4 at the short delay but by -0.1 at the long delay, so the effect differs by delay.
qs.x: Exercise raises ratings by 2.4 at the short delay but by -0.1 at the long delay, so the effect differs by delay. Trap: Describing any difference between groups as a main effect instead of checking for an interaction.

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: The Yerkes-Dodson law proposes that performance is best at an intermediate level of arousal and that the optimum depends on task difficulty. One hundred twenty adults each performed a simple task (cancel all of the letter "e" characters in a text) and a complex task (solve logic puzzles requiring multi-step inference) at five arousal levels in separate sessions. Arousal was manipulated by combining background noise and time pressure, and each level was verified by recording mean heart rate. Every participant completed both tasks at all five levels. The order of the levels was randomized and counterbalanced across participants, and sessions were separated by at least two days. Performance was scored from 0 to 100. Mean scores are plotted in Figure 1, and heart rates for the five levels are in Table 1. Noise intensity ranged from 45 dB at level 1 to 85 dB at level 5, and the time limit for each task shortened as the level rose. Participants practiced both tasks until their scores stabilized before the formal sessions began. Task scores were calculated automatically by the computer program, and no feedback about scores was given until all sessions were complete. All participants were healthy adults who reported normal or corrected vision.

qs.q: Which statement best summarizes Figure 1?
o: Performance on both tasks rises steadily as arousal increases from level 1 to level 5.
Both curves decline at high arousal: the simple task after level 4 and the complex task after level 2.
The arousal level that maximizes performance is lower for the complex task than for the simple task.
Correct: The complex task peaks at level 2, whereas the simple task peaks at level 4.
Performance on the simple task is higher than on the complex task at every level of arousal because it was easier.
At levels 1 and 2 the complex task score is higher (52 vs 40, 80 vs 62).
The complex task is unaffected by arousal because its curve has no clear peak.
The complex curve has a clear peak at level 2 and drops sharply afterward.
qs.x: The complex task peaks at level 2, whereas the simple task peaks at level 4. Trap: Assuming that more arousal always helps performance or that the peak is identical for all tasks.

qs.q: By what percentage did the mean complex-task score fall between level 2 and level 5?
o: A fall of 37.5%
This is 30/80, the fraction of the level-2 score that remained, not the fall.
A fall of 50%
This gives the point drop of 50 as if it were a percentage.
Correct: The drop is 80 - 30 = 50 points, and 50/80 = 0.625.
A fall of 167%
This divides the 50-point drop by the final score (30) instead of by the original score (80).
qs.x: The drop is 80 - 30 = 50 points, and 50/80 = 0.625. Trap: Dividing the change by the final value rather than the starting value.

qs.q: Which structure plays a central role in regulating general cortical arousal and wakefulness that varied across the five levels?
o: Hippocampus
The hippocampus is primarily involved in forming declarative memories, not in setting the overall arousal level.
Reticular activating system in the brainstem
Correct: The reticular formation projects diffusely to the cortex and sets the general level of alertness.
Broca's area
This region is involved in speech production and does not regulate arousal.
Primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe
This region controls voluntary movement and does not set the level of alertness.
qs.x: The reticular formation projects diffusely to the cortex and sets the general level of alertness. Trap: Choosing a memory or language structure for a generalized arousal function.

qs.q: Why did the researchers counterbalance the order of the arousal levels?
o: To ensure that random assignment produced equivalent groups for the two tasks on the two tasks
Counterbalancing addresses order within participants, and each participant did both tasks.
To prevent practice and fatigue effects from being confounded with arousal level
Correct: Each participant completed all levels, so a fixed order would mix order effects with the arousal effect.
To increase the validity of heart rate as a measure of emotion
Order of presentation does not change what heart rate measures.
To eliminate the need for a control condition in the experiment
Counterbalancing does not replace controls; it handles order effects in within-subject designs.
qs.x: Each participant completed all levels, so a fixed order would mix order effects with the arousal effect. Trap: Confusing counterbalancing with random assignment to groups.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean heart rate at each arousal level

graph.title: Figure 1. Performance by arousal level and task

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Trait theories describe personality as relatively stable dispositions that predict behavior across situations. A company psychologist studied 300 customer-service employees hired over the past two years. Each employee completed a self-report Big Five inventory (each trait scored from 1 to 5). Supervisors independently rated job performance (0 to 100), and employees reported job satisfaction on a 1 to 7 scale. Only employees who passed a probationary period were included; those who left or were dismissed before it ended could not be studied. Pearson correlations for each trait appear in Table 1. Figure 1 shows conscientiousness and supervisor-rated performance for a random subset of 10 employees chosen to illustrate the relationship. Inventory items were scored so that higher values reflect more of each trait, and internal consistency of every scale exceeded 0.80. Supervisors did not see employees' personality scores, and employees did not see supervisors' ratings. Employees had been in their positions for at least one year when the measures were collected, and all data were collected within a single two-week window by an outside survey firm.

qs.q: Which interpretation of the neuroticism-satisfaction correlation of -0.42 is most appropriate?
o: Employees higher in emotional instability tended to report higher job satisfaction.
The sign is negative, which indicates an inverse relationship.
Neuroticism caused 42% of the variation in satisfaction among the employees.
A correlation does not show causation, and variance explained would be r squared, about 18%.
Employees higher in emotional instability tended to report lower job satisfaction.
Correct: A negative r means that as neuroticism rises, satisfaction tends to fall.
Neuroticism and satisfaction are unrelated because the correlation is below 0.50.
A correlation of -0.42 is a moderate, meaningful association, so unrelatedness is not implied.
qs.x: A negative r means that as neuroticism rises, satisfaction tends to fall. Trap: Reading the sign of a correlation backward, or treating r as percent of variance.

qs.q: Approximately what proportion of the variance in performance is shared with conscientiousness?
o: About 0.10
Correct: r squared = 0.31 squared, which is about 0.096.
About 0.31 of the variance
This reports r itself rather than squaring it.
About 0.56 of the variance
This is the square root of r, which is not a variance measure.
About 0.90 of the variance
This is 1 - 0.096, the variance not shared with conscientiousness.
qs.x: r squared = 0.31 squared, which is about 0.096. Trap: Using r in place of r squared to describe variance explained.

qs.q: What is the most reasonable conclusion about openness (r = +0.04 with performance)?
o: Openness has no influence of any kind on job performance, either directly or indirectly.
A near-zero correlation in one sample cannot prove the absence of all possible effects.
There is almost no linear relationship, although a nonlinear relationship cannot be ruled out by r alone.
Correct: Pearson r measures linear association, so a value near zero does not exclude a curved pattern.
Openness is the strongest predictor of job performance because the value is close to zero.
Values close to zero indicate the weakest, not strongest, linear association.
Openness has a perfect nonlinear relationship with job performance that Pearson r cannot capture.
Nothing in the table implies a perfect relationship of any form.
qs.x: Pearson r measures linear association, so a value near zero does not exclude a curved pattern. Trap: Concluding that a near-zero r proves the variables are completely unrelated.

qs.q: A limitation of self-reported personality scores is social desirability bias. Which procedure would best reduce it?
o: Increasing the sample size from 300 to 3,000 employees using the same inventory
A larger sample reduces random error but leaves a systematic bias in self-reports unchanged.
Asking employees to complete the inventory twice and averaging the two scores
Averaging repeated self-reports improves reliability but retains the same bias.
Using only employees with the highest conscientiousness scores to reduce variability
Selecting on the outcome range does not address bias and adds restriction of range.
Obtaining personality ratings from coworkers or supervisors who know the employee well in addition to self-reports
Correct: Informant reports provide an independent perspective that is not subject to the employee's own impression management.
qs.x: Informant reports provide an independent perspective that is not subject to the employee's own impression management. Trap: Assuming that bigger samples or repeated measures fix systematic bias.

qs.q: Because only employees who passed probation were included, how are the correlations in Table 1 most likely affected, compared with the full group of applicants?
o: They are probably weaker, because restriction of range reduces the observed correlation.
Correct: Excluding low performers narrows the range of scores, which tends to attenuate correlations.
They are probably stronger, because only successful employees can show clear associations.
Truncating the range typically weakens, not strengthens, associations.
They are unaffected, because correlations do not depend on which participants are sampled.
Correlation estimates depend strongly on the range of values in the sample.
They are exactly the same but have a different sign because of selection.
Selection does not reverse a correlation's direction on its own.
qs.x: Excluding low performers narrows the range of scores, which tends to attenuate correlations. Trap: Believing correlation is independent of the sampled range of the variables.

graph.title: Figure 1. Conscientiousness and job performance (10 employees)

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Self-determination theory distinguishes intrinsic motivation, doing an activity for its own sake, from extrinsic motivation, doing it for external rewards. Ninety children aged 5 to 7 who often chose to draw during free play were randomly assigned to three groups (n = 30 each). In session 1, children in the expected-reward group were told they would receive a "good player" certificate for drawing and then received it. Children in the unexpected-reward group drew without any mention of a reward and were surprised with a certificate afterward. Children in the no-reward group drew with no certificate. Two weeks later, in a separate session with no certificates available, each child had 10 minutes of free play with drawing materials and other toys. Observers, who did not know the group assignments, recorded minutes spent drawing. Baseline minutes (before session 1) and follow-up minutes are given in Table 1. Certificates were printed with the child's name and identical in all groups that received them. The drawing session lasted 10 minutes, and the materials were the same markers and paper that children could use in the follow-up session. Observers recorded minutes of drawing using a stopwatch, and agreement between two observers on a subset of sessions exceeded 90%. Parents consented to the study and children could stop at any time.

qs.q: Which concept best explains the drop in drawing time in the expected-reward group?
o: Learned helplessness, in which uncontrollable events produce passivity.
The children controlled their drawing and were not exposed to uncontrollable aversive events.
Overjustification, in which a reward given for an enjoyed activity shifts attributions away from intrinsic interest.
Correct: Children began to see the reward as the reason for drawing, and interest fell once it was absent.
Habituation, in which repeated exposure to the materials reduces the response to them.
Habituation would be seen in all groups, yet the control groups did not decline.
Drive reduction, in which behavior is motivated by reducing a physiological need.
Drawing does not reduce a biological deficit, and the theory would not predict a decline after a reward.
qs.x: Children began to see the reward as the reason for drawing, and interest fell once it was absent. Trap: Selecting a theory that would predict declines in all groups rather than only the rewarded one.

qs.q: Why did the unexpected-reward group show almost no change in drawing time?
o: The reward was not offered in advance, so children could not infer that they drew in order to earn it.
Correct: Without an expectation of reward, the activity was not seen as a means to an end.
Children in this group did not receive a certificate, which equated them with the no-reward group.
They received the certificate after drawing, as the passage states.
Unexpected rewards are always more reinforcing than expected rewards, which maintains behavior.
The result is explained by attribution, not by the strength of reinforcement, and the claim is not generally true.
The children forgot about the certificate during the two weeks, which restored their baseline.
The finding is explained more simply by the missing expectation, and forgetting is not supported.
qs.x: Without an expectation of reward, the activity was not seen as a means to an end. Trap: Assuming the unexpected reward is simply stronger reinforcement.

qs.q: What was the percentage decrease in drawing time in the expected-reward group from baseline to follow-up?
o: About 53% of baseline
This is 3.1/5.8, the share of baseline drawing that remained, not the size of the fall.
About 87% of baseline
This divides the 2.7-minute drop by the follow-up value of 3.1 minutes instead of by baseline.
A decrease of 2.7%
This reports the drop in minutes as a percentage.
About 47%
Correct: The change is 5.8 - 3.1 = 2.7 minutes, and 2.7/5.8 is about 0.47.
qs.x: The change is 5.8 - 3.1 = 2.7 minutes, and 2.7/5.8 is about 0.47. Trap: Dividing by the follow-up value rather than the baseline.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the no-reward group?
o: It ensures that the observers cannot determine which children received a certificate.
Observer blinding was achieved by hiding group assignments, not by the existence of this group.
It estimates how drawing time changes over two weeks without any reward, controlling for time and familiarity.
Correct: Comparing against this baseline shows that the expected-reward drop is not just a time effect.
It provides a treatment group whose motivation is fully extrinsic.
This group had no extrinsic reward at all.
It allows measurement of the placebo effect from the experimenter's friendly attention.
The group does not control for experimenter attention unless all groups were treated identically, and it is a no-treatment control.
qs.x: Comparing against this baseline shows that the expected-reward drop is not just a time effect. Trap: Mistaking a no-treatment control for a placebo control.

qs.q: A strict operant-conditioning account predicts that, once certificates are removed, drawing in the expected-reward group should do which of the following?
o: Increase above the level during the reward period because the reinforcer is no longer present.
Removing a reinforcer cannot increase the reinforced behavior in an operant account.
Decline toward baseline through extinction, but not fall well below it.
Correct: Removing the reinforcer should return responding to its pre-reinforcement level, not below it.
Remain at the level during reward because behavior is permanent after conditioning.
Reinforced behavior diminishes after reinforcement ends.
Fall to zero immediately because operant behaviors vanish when rewards stop.
Extinction is gradual and typically returns to baseline, and baseline here was above zero.
qs.x: Removing the reinforcer should return responding to its pre-reinforcement level, not below it. Trap: Thinking removal of reinforcement should push behavior below its natural baseline.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Mean minutes spent drawing during 10-minute free play

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: A case-control study examined whether frequent use of headphones at high volume is associated with persistent tinnitus. Investigators identified 200 adults with persistent tinnitus (cases) from audiology clinics and 400 adults without tinnitus (controls) from the same clinics' patients seeking routine hearing screening, frequency-matched to cases by age group and sex. Interviewers asked each participant about listening habits during the preceding five years. "High exposure" was defined as listening at high volume for more than 2 hours per day. Interviewers knew case status. Results are shown in Table 1, with age stratified at 40 years. The odds ratio (OR) for each row is the odds of high exposure among cases divided by the odds of high exposure among controls. Cases were adults aged 20 to 65 who had reported tinnitus lasting at least six months, confirmed by a clinician using a standard questionnaire. Controls reported no tinnitus on the same questionnaire. The interviewers followed a written script but could ask clarifying questions. Participants with noisy occupations or a history of ear surgery were excluded from both groups to limit other explanations for hearing symptoms.

qs.q: What is the crude odds ratio for all participants?
o: An OR of 1.5
This is the ratio of cases high to cases low, 120/80, which ignores the controls.
An OR of 1.2
This is 120/100, exposed cases divided by exposed controls, which ignores the unexposed groups entirely.
An OR of 0.22
This is the reciprocal of the correct value, from placing the cross-products in the wrong order.
qs.x: OR = (120 x 300)/(80 x 100) = 36,000/8,000 = 4.5. Trap: Calculating a ratio from only the cases or only one cell pair instead of the cross-product.

qs.q: Why can this study design not provide an estimate of the incidence of tinnitus among high-exposure listeners?
o: Participants were selected by outcome status, so the proportion of cases in the sample is fixed by the investigators.
Correct: In case-control sampling the case-to-control ratio is chosen, so risk or incidence cannot be calculated directly.
Tinnitus is a subjective symptom that cannot be counted in epidemiologic studies.
Case-control studies of subjective conditions are common and valid when a case definition exists.
Odds ratios can only be computed in randomized trials with a placebo group.
Odds ratios are the standard measure in case-control studies and are used widely in observational research.
The matching of controls to cases by age and sex makes all exposures equally common.
Matching ensures balance for age and sex only; it does not equalize exposure prevalence.
qs.x: In case-control sampling the case-to-control ratio is chosen, so risk or incidence cannot be calculated directly. Trap: Applying cohort-study measures such as risk to a study that samples by outcome.

qs.q: Interviewers who knew case status asked participants about listening habits. Which bias is the most direct concern?
o: Recall bias, because cases may search their memories and report past exposure differently than controls.
Correct: People with the condition often recall or report past exposures more thoroughly, inflating the odds ratio.
Survivorship bias, because only participants who survived a long follow-up were interviewed.
This study has no follow-up of survivors; it compares existing cases and controls.
Attrition bias, because many participants dropped out between treatment and outcome measurement.
There was no treatment period or follow-up that could produce attrition.
Lead-time bias, because screening detects the disease earlier than it would otherwise appear.
Lead-time bias applies to screening and survival timing, not to exposure reporting in a case-control study.
qs.x: People with the condition often recall or report past exposures more thoroughly, inflating the odds ratio. Trap: Naming a bias that belongs to cohort studies or screening rather than retrospective exposure reporting.

qs.q: What can be concluded from comparing the age-specific ORs (5.6 and 3.4) with the crude OR?
o: Age is a strong confounder, because the crude OR is smaller than both of the stratum-specific ORs.
The crude OR (4.5) lies between the two stratum ORs, so this description is incorrect.
Headphone use protects older adults, because the age 40 or older OR is lower.
An OR of 3.4 is still above 1 and indicates greater odds of exposure among cases.
Age does not completely explain the association, because the odds ratio remains well above 1 in both age groups.
Correct: Confounding by age would be expected to disappear within strata, which did not happen.
High exposure caused tinnitus in both age groups, since both ORs exceed 3.
Stratified associations remain observational and cannot establish causation by themselves.
qs.x: Confounding by age would be expected to disappear within strata, which did not happen. Trap: Interpreting a lower but still elevated OR as protective or as proof of causation.

qs.q: Which design would best establish that high-volume listening precedes tinnitus onset?
o: A prospective cohort that measures listening habits in tinnitus-free adults and follows them for new-onset tinnitus
Correct: Measuring exposure before the outcome occurs establishes temporal order without recall problems.
A larger case-control study with additional controls from the general population
More controls improve precision but do not establish that exposure came first.
A cross-sectional survey of current listening habits and tinnitus status in one sitting
Both variables are measured at once, so temporal order cannot be determined.
A case report describing one patient with tinnitus and a history of high-volume listening
A single case provides no comparison group and cannot establish temporal or causal relationships.
qs.x: Measuring exposure before the outcome occurs establishes temporal order without recall problems. Trap: Assuming that bigger or more varied retrospective samples can establish temporal order.

tbl.cap: Table 1. High and low exposure by group

passages.title: Mini03 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: A randomized trial tested an 8-week mindfulness program for work-related anxiety. One hundred twenty employees were randomly assigned to the program (n = 60) or to a waitlist (n = 60) and completed measures at weeks 0, 4, and 8. The prespecified primary outcome was the change in an anxiety questionnaire score (lower is better). Four secondary outcomes were also analyzed. All tests were two-sided with a significance threshold of 0.05 unless adjusted. Participants knew their group assignments. Table 1 reports the mean change from week 0 to week 8 in each group, with the difference between groups, its 95% confidence interval (CI), and the p value. Figure 1 shows the mean anxiety score at each time point. Randomization was performed by computer using a list that was concealed from the staff enrolling participants. The program involved weekly group sessions of 90 minutes and a daily 10-minute home practice. Outcomes were self-reported on tablets in a private room. Participants who dropped out before week 8 were analyzed in their assigned groups using the last available measurement, and 5 participants in each group were lost to follow-up.

qs.q: Which statement about the 95% CI for the anxiety score difference is accurate?
o: Because the interval is wide, the difference is not statistically significant.
Width reflects precision, and this interval still excludes 0.
The interval shows that 95% of employees improved by between 2.6 and 8.0 points.
A CI describes uncertainty about the group-level mean difference, not the range of individual responses.
Because the interval excludes 0, the difference is statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
Correct: A 95% CI that does not contain the null value corresponds to p below 0.05.
The interval shows a 95% probability that the study results were due to chance.
A confidence interval does not give the probability that chance produced the results.
qs.x: A 95% CI that does not contain the null value corresponds to p below 0.05. Trap: Interpreting a confidence interval as the range of individual outcomes.

qs.q: If the five outcomes were all truly unaffected by the program and independent, about what is the probability that at least one would reach p < 0.05?
o: About 5%
This is the error rate for a single test, not for five.
About 25%
This is 5 x 5%, which overstates the probability because tests overlap.
About 77%
This is the probability of no false positives, 0.95^5, not of at least one.
About 23%
qs.x: 1 - (0.95)^5 = 1 - 0.774 = 0.226. Trap: Adding error rates together or reporting the chance of none rather than at least one.

qs.q: If a Bonferroni correction is applied across the four secondary outcomes, what would be concluded?
o: None of the secondary outcomes would be significant, because the adjusted threshold is 0.0125.
Correct: 0.05/4 = 0.0125, and the smallest secondary p value is 0.04.
Sleep quality alone would remain significant, because it has the smallest confidence interval.
Its p value of 0.049 exceeds 0.0125, and the CI width does not determine significance.
Both sleep quality and depressive symptoms would remain significant, since both p values are below 0.05.
The corrected threshold is lower than 0.05, so both would be nonsignificant.
All four would become significant, because correction lowers the p value for each test.
Bonferroni lowers the threshold for significance rather than the p values.
qs.x: 0.05/4 = 0.0125, and the smallest secondary p value is 0.04. Trap: Thinking that correction for multiple tests makes it easier to reach significance.

qs.q: The waitlist group's anxiety score also fell by 3.1 points. Which explanation is most reasonable?
o: Nonspecific factors such as regression to the mean, natural remission, and participation in a study
Correct: The waitlist did not receive the intervention, so any improvement reflects factors other than the program.
A direct effect of the mindfulness program on participants who had not yet received it
Waitlist participants did not receive the program during the 8 weeks.
Measurement error that always lowers scores on repeated administration of the questionnaire
Random error does not systematically lower scores.
A carryover effect from an earlier phase in which the waitlist group had received treatment
The design did not include a prior treatment phase for these participants.
qs.x: The waitlist did not receive the intervention, so any improvement reflects factors other than the program. Trap: Attributing any change in a control group to the intervention itself.

tbl.cap: Table 1. Change from week 0 to week 8

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean anxiety score

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Cadherins are calcium-dependent adhesion proteins. To test how E-cadherin supports cell aggregation, researchers used mouse L cells, which express no cadherins and do not aggregate. L cells were stably transfected with a vector encoding full-length E-cadherin (L-Ecad) or with an empty vector (L-vec). Cells were released from plates with a mild treatment that preserves surface proteins, suspended at equal density, and rotated gently for 60 minutes. Aggregation was reported as the percentage decrease in the number of single, unattached cells relative to time zero. Buffers contained 2 mM Ca2+ unless stated. In one condition, 2 mM EGTA, a Ca2+ chelator, replaced Ca2+. In another, Fab fragments of an antibody against the extracellular region of E-cadherin were added. In a mixing experiment, L-Ecad and L-vec cells were combined 1:1. In a final experiment, L-Ecad cells were combined 1:1 with L-Ncad cells, which express N-cadherin, and the aggregates were examined by microscopy. Table 1 summarizes results at 2 mM Ca2+ or as noted. Figure 1 shows aggregation of L-Ecad cells as the Ca2+ concentration was varied.

qs.q: Why did L-Ecad cells fail to aggregate when Ca2+ was replaced with EGTA?
o: Ca2+ is consumed as an energy source when cadherins link adjacent cells, so removing it halts ATP-dependent adhesion
Ca2+ is a structural cofactor, not a fuel; cadherin binding does not consume ATP.
EGTA causes the cells to swell and burst, which removes the single cells from the suspension that are counted
Cell lysis would lower the count of all cells, but the L-Ecad cells in EGTA stayed as single cells (5% aggregation), consistent with intact cells that simply do not adhere.
Ca2+ binding to the extracellular repeats rigidifies the ectodomain so it can bind a cadherin on a neighboring cell

Correct: Ca2+ ions bind between the extracellular repeats and stiffen the ectodomain; without Ca2+ the protein is floppy and cannot form trans interactions, so chelation abolishes aggregation (84% to 5%).
EGTA activates proteases that digest the cytoplasmic tail of E-cadherin, which uncouples the protein from the cell membrane
Nothing in the data suggests proteolysis of the cytoplasmic tail; cadherin loss of function in EGTA is due to loss of Ca2+ binding in the extracellular region and is reversible.
qs.x: Ca2+ ions bind between the extracellular repeats and stiffen the ectodomain; without Ca2+ the protein is floppy and cannot form trans interactions, so chelation abolishes aggregation (84% to 5%). Trap: Assuming Ca2+ acts as a metabolic cofactor or energy source rather than as a structural ion that stabilizes the cadherin ectodomain.

qs.q: In the 1:1 mixture of L-Ecad and L-vec cells, aggregation was 41%, about half that of L-Ecad cells alone. Which interpretation is most consistent with this result?
o: L-vec cells release a soluble factor that blocks E-cadherin on the L-Ecad cells and halves their binding ability
A blocking factor would also have reduced aggregation of L-Ecad cells alone and in other conditions; there is no evidence for it, and the observed value is predicted by simple cell counting.
E-cadherin on L-Ecad cells binds the empty vector protein on L-vec cells with about half the strength of its homophilic binding
The empty vector encodes no cell-surface protein, so there is nothing for E-cadherin to bind on L-vec cells.
E-cadherin binds a different, unidentified receptor present on all L cells, and half of the mixed cells lacked that receptor
L-vec cells aggregated only 6% alone, so they carry no functional receptor; L-Ecad aggregation requires E-cadherin on both partners.
E-cadherin binds E-cadherin on another cell, so only the L-Ecad cells in the mixture could join aggregates
Correct: Cadherin binding is homophilic. L-vec cells lack cadherin, so only the L-Ecad half of the population (about 84% of half the cells, roughly 42%) can aggregate, matching the observed 41%.
qs.x: Cadherin binding is homophilic. L-vec cells lack cadherin, so only the L-Ecad half of the population (about 84% of half the cells, roughly 42%) can aggregate, matching the observed 41%. Trap: Concluding that L-vec cells actively interfere, when the data simply reflect half of the cells lacking the homophilic binding partner.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, the Ca2+ concentration at which aggregation of L-Ecad cells is about half of its plateau value is closest to
o: 0.3 mM
Correct: The plateau is about 84%, so half-maximal is about 42%. Aggregation is 35% at 0.25 mM and 62% at 0.5 mM, so 42% falls at about 0.3 mM.
1.0 mM
At 1.0 mM aggregation is already 80%, close to the plateau.
2.0 mM
At 2.0 mM aggregation is at the plateau of 84%.
At 0.05 mM aggregation would be only about 8%, far below half-maximal.
qs.x: The plateau is about 84%, so half-maximal is about 42%. Aggregation is 35% at 0.25 mM and 62% at 0.5 mM, so 42% falls at about 0.3 mM. Trap: Taking the midpoint of the x-axis range rather than reading the concentration that gives half of the maximum y-value.

qs.q: Which comparison in Table 1 provides the most direct evidence that the extracellular region of E-cadherin is needed for aggregation?
o: L-Ecad cells with and without the anti-E-cadherin Fab in 2 mM Ca2+
Correct: The Fab binds only the extracellular region, and it lowers aggregation from 84% to 14%, so that region is directly implicated.
L-Ecad cells alone compared with the 1:1 mixture of L-Ecad and L-vec cells in 2 mM Ca2+
The mixing result shows that binding is homophilic; it does not test the role of the extracellular region.
L-vec cells compared with L-Ecad cells, each suspended in 2 mM Ca2+ buffer for 60 minutes
This comparison shows that expressing the E-cadherin gene is required, but not which part of the protein does the work.
L-Ecad cells in 2 mM Ca2+ compared with L-Ecad cells in 2 mM EGTA without any added Ca2+
The EGTA comparison shows that aggregation needs Ca2+, but Ca2+ could be required for many processes and does not identify the domain involved.
qs.x: The Fab binds only the extracellular region, and it lowers aggregation from 84% to 14%, so that region is directly implicated. Trap: Choosing a comparison that shows E-cadherin or Ca2+ matters without isolating the specific domain that mediates adhesion.

qs.q: Inside the cell, the cytoplasmic tail of E-cadherin is linked through catenins primarily to which cytoskeletal element at adherens junctions?
o: Actin filaments
Correct: Adherens junctions anchor cadherins to the actin cytoskeleton through beta-catenin and alpha-catenin.
Intermediate filaments
Intermediate filaments attach to desmosomes (desmosomal cadherins) and hemidesmosomes, not classical adherens junctions.
Microtubules
