Microtubules are not the principal cytoskeletal partners of adherens junction cadherins.
Septins
Septins are filament-forming GTPases involved in cytokinesis and cell shape, not the standard link to adherens junction catenins.
qs.x: Adherens junctions anchor cadherins to the actin cytoskeleton through beta-catenin and alpha-catenin. Trap: Confusing adherens junctions (actin) with desmosomes (intermediate filaments), since both use cadherin-family proteins.

r: 80, in separate aggregates of each cell type

graph.title: Figure 1. Aggregation of L-Ecad cells versus extracellular Ca2+

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Aquaporin-1 (AQP1) is a tetrameric membrane protein in which each monomer forms a water-selective pore. To measure its effect on water permeability, researchers injected Xenopus laevis oocytes with water (control) or with AQP1 cRNA and incubated them for three days. Oocytes have a low basal permeability to water. Each oocyte, in a buffer of 200 mOsm, was transferred to a buffer of 70 mOsm, and its volume was recorded by video microscopy. The osmotic water permeability coefficient (Pf) was calculated from the initial rate of swelling. Mercury (HgCl2) reacts covalently with cysteine side chains, and AQP1 contains a cysteine near the narrowest part of its pore. Some AQP1-expressing oocytes were exposed to 0.3 mM HgCl2 for 5 minutes before the transfer. Others were exposed to HgCl2 and then to 5 mM beta-mercaptoethanol (BME), a thiol-containing reducing agent, for 15 minutes. Results are shown in Table 1. In a separate group, AQP1 oocytes were kept in 200 mOsm buffer, with no change in osmolarity.

qs.q: The swelling of AQP1 oocytes after transfer to 70 mOsm buffer is best described as
o: active transport of water into the cell, powered by ATP hydrolysis at the AQP1 pore
Aquaporins are channels, not pumps; water flows passively and does not require ATP.
movement of solutes out of the oocyte through AQP1, which draws water in behind them
AQP1 is water-selective, and the volume increase reflects net water entry, not solute exit; solute loss would shrink the cell.
passive osmosis of water into the more concentrated cytoplasm
Correct: Water moves by osmosis toward the compartment with the higher solute concentration; AQP1 only raises the permeability of the membrane to water.
secondary active transport in which water enters coupled to the inward movement of sodium
No sodium-coupled step is involved; aquaporin-mediated flow is driven only by the osmotic gradient.
qs.x: Water moves by osmosis toward the compartment with the higher solute concentration; AQP1 only raises the permeability of the membrane to water. Trap: Treating the channel as a pump that spends energy, rather than a pore through which water follows the osmotic gradient.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why BME restored swelling of the HgCl2-treated AQP1 oocytes?
o: BME hydrolyzes peptide bonds in AQP1 so that the mercury-modified region is removed from the pore
Cleaving AQP1 would destroy rather than restore its function.
BME induces synthesis of new AQP1 protein from the injected cRNA during the 15-minute treatment, which replaces the inhibited channels
Protein synthesis and insertion within 15 minutes cannot account for a nearly complete recovery, and the original protein had been present all along.
The thiol groups of BME displace mercury from the cysteine sulfhydryl groups of AQP1 and reopen the pore
Correct: Mercury inhibits through reaction with cysteine thiols; a reagent rich in thiols competes for the mercury and returns the pore to normal, which fits Pf returning from 35 to 195.
BME raises the osmolarity of the buffer, which increases the driving force for water entry
BME at 5 mM adds negligible osmolarity relative to the 70 mOsm buffer, and the oocytes were tested in the same buffers as the other groups.
qs.x: Mercury inhibits through reaction with cysteine thiols; a reagent rich in thiols competes for the mercury and returns the pore to normal, which fits Pf returning from 35 to 195. Trap: Overlooking that the inhibition was chemical and reversible, and attributing recovery to new protein or osmotic changes.

qs.q: The AQP1-dependent portion of permeability is the Pf of AQP1 oocytes minus the Pf of water-injected oocytes. About what percentage of that portion was eliminated by HgCl2?
o: 83% is 175/210, which fails to subtract the basal permeability of the oocyte before computing the fraction.
Correct: AQP1-dependent Pf = 210 - 20 = 190. After mercury it is 35 - 20 = 15. The fraction eliminated is (190 - 15)/190 = 175/190, about 92%.
8% is about the AQP1-dependent portion that remained (15/190), not the portion that was eliminated.
17% is 35/210, the fraction of the total Pf that remained, not the fraction removed.
qs.x: AQP1-dependent Pf = 210 - 20 = 190. After mercury it is 35 - 20 = 15. The fraction eliminated is (190 - 15)/190 = 175/190, about 92%. Trap: Failing to subtract the basal permeability of water-injected oocytes, or reporting the remaining fraction instead of the eliminated fraction.

qs.q: Water-injected oocytes still swelled slightly (relative volume 1.06). The most likely reason is that
o: sodium channels in the oocyte membrane open in dilute buffer and carry water along with sodium
Ion channels do not carry bulk water in the way described; water flow follows osmotic gradients.
the lipid bilayer itself is slightly permeable to water, even without aquaporins
Correct: Water can diffuse across phospholipid bilayers slowly, which explains a small basal Pf of 20 micrometers per second.
water-injection itself delivers hypotonic solution that expands the oocyte before the transfer
The control oocytes were incubated for three days and are at osmotic equilibrium with 200 mOsm buffer before the transfer.
oocytes contain endogenous AQP1 at levels equal to the injected cells, but the pores are partly closed
If endogenous AQP1 were equal in both groups, the Pf values would be identical, but AQP1 oocytes swelled about 10 times faster in Pf.
qs.x: Water can diffuse across phospholipid bilayers slowly, which explains a small basal Pf of 20 micrometers per second. Trap: Assuming that no water crosses a membrane lacking aquaporins, so that any swelling must reflect a specific protein.

qs.q: For AQP1 oocytes kept in 200 mOsm buffer (relative volume 1.00), which explanation is most appropriate?
o: Water still crosses AQP1 in both directions, but with no osmotic gradient the two fluxes are equal and there is no net volume change
Correct: Channels allow bidirectional movement; net flux requires a difference in water potential across the membrane.
The oocyte actively pumps out water at the same rate as it enters to maintain constant volume
No water pump exists in oocytes; volume is constant because the net flux is zero.
Water cannot cross the membrane unless the osmolarity inside is higher than outside by at least 100 mOsm, because smaller gradients cannot overcome the barrier of the bilayer
Water flux has no threshold gradient; any gradient produces some net flow.
Aquaporins close in isotonic buffer because they are gated by changes in membrane tension
Nothing in the passage suggests aquaporin gating by tension, and the pores function whenever water gradients exist.
qs.x: Channels allow bidirectional movement; net flux requires a difference in water potential across the membrane. Trap: Equating a lack of net volume change with a lack of water movement.

h: Relative volume 3 min after transfer to 70 mOsm

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: Escherichia coli swims by rotating flagella. When the flagella rotate counterclockwise they form a bundle and the cell runs in a nearly straight line; when they rotate clockwise the bundle flies apart and the cell tumbles and then runs in a new direction. In a capillary assay, a glass capillary containing buffer with or without the amino acid attractant aspartate was placed for 60 minutes in a chamber of motile bacteria, and the number of cells that entered the capillary was counted. The aspartate receptor Tar signals through the kinase CheA, which phosphorylates CheY; phosphorylated CheY binds the flagellar motor and promotes clockwise rotation. The strains were wild type (WT), a tar deletion (Dtar), and a cheA deletion (DcheA). The tumbling rate of each strain was measured in uniform buffer. Table 1 gives the results, and Figure 1 shows the accumulation of WT cells in capillaries containing a range of aspartate concentrations.

qs.q: Compared with the buffer-only capillary, the accumulation of WT cells in the 100 micromolar aspartate capillary was about
o: 18-fold greater
Correct: 21,500 divided by 1,200 is about 17.9, or about 18-fold.
21-fold greater
21-fold results from comparing 21,500 with about 1,000 rather than 1,200, or from reading the thousands of cells as a ratio to 1.
5-fold greater
5-fold would result if the value were compared with the 1 micromolar condition (5.8/1.2 = 4.8), not with 100 micromolar.
9-fold greater
9-fold is not obtained from the table or from Figure 1; it would correspond to a count of about 10,800 cells.
qs.x: 21,500 divided by 1,200 is about 17.9, or about 18-fold. Trap: Dividing by the wrong control value or misreading the units of the graph versus the table.

qs.q: Which mechanism best explains how WT cells move up an aspartate gradient?
o: When attractant concentration rises over time, the tumbling frequency drops, so runs that happen to point up the gradient are prolonged
Correct: Bacteria are too small to sense spatial gradients; they sense changes over time and bias a random walk by suppressing tumbling when conditions improve.
Cells compare receptor occupancy between the front and the back of the cell and steer by rotating the flagella on the side facing the attractant
E. Coli is only about 2 micrometers long, so it cannot detect a meaningful difference in concentration between its two ends.
Tumbles are directed toward the attractant, so each reorientation points the cell up the gradient
Tumbles produce random new directions, not directed ones; the bias comes from longer runs when moving in a favorable direction.
Aspartate binding increases the number of flagella on the cell, which increases swimming speed up the gradient
Flagellar number does not change in seconds; attractant changes tumbling frequency.
qs.x: Bacteria are too small to sense spatial gradients; they sense changes over time and bias a random walk by suppressing tumbling when conditions improve. Trap: Thinking bacteria steer like larger cells by sensing a spatial gradient, rather than biasing a random walk through time-dependent signaling.

qs.q: The Dtar strain tumbled normally in uniform buffer but did not accumulate in the aspartate capillary. This result indicates that Tar
o: is required to detect aspartate, while the motility machinery of the cell is intact
Correct: The normal tumbling rate (1.0 per second) and normal buffer-only counts show that the cells swim; they fail only when the attractant must be sensed.
is required for flagellar rotation, because cells lacking Tar cannot swim at all
Dtar cells tumble and move normally in buffer, so Tar is not needed for flagellar rotation.
is required to import aspartate for use as an energy source, so Dtar cells starve in the capillary
Nothing in the data concerns nutrient uptake; Tar is a chemoreceptor, and starvation would not occur within 60 minutes.
inhibits CheA, so its deletion locks cells in constant tumbling
Constant tumbling would give a tumble rate well above 1.0 per second, not the normal value reported.
qs.x: The normal tumbling rate (1.0 per second) and normal buffer-only counts show that the cells swim; they fail only when the attractant must be sensed. Trap: Reading a failure to respond to a signal as a global defect in motility or metabolism.

qs.q: DcheA cells did not tumble and did not accumulate in the aspartate capillary. The best explanation is that
o: without CheA the Tar receptor cannot bind aspartate, so the cells never detect the gradient
Receptor binding happens upstream of CheA and is not prevented by its deletion; the defect is in the signal output.
without CheA the flagellar motor cannot rotate, so DcheA cells cannot swim into the capillary
The reported counts in buffer (900) show that DcheA cells still swim; tumbling is absent, not motility.
without CheA the cells tumble constantly, which prevents them from swimming in a straight line and so from moving steadily toward the attractant
A tumble rate of 0.0 per second means these cells do not tumble at all.
without CheA, CheY is not phosphorylated, so the cells never tumble and cannot bias their random walk toward the attractant
Correct: Tumbling requires CheY-P. Cells that only run still move randomly, but they lack the ability to change direction in response to the gradient, so they do not accumulate.
qs.x: Tumbling requires CheY-P. Cells that only run still move randomly, but they lack the ability to change direction in response to the gradient, so they do not accumulate. Trap: Equating loss of tumbling with loss of motility, when the strain can still swim but cannot change direction.

qs.q: In Figure 1, accumulation of WT cells declines between 100 and 1000 micromolar aspartate. Which explanation is most plausible?
o: The cells run out of CheY, so tumbling can no longer be suppressed at any aspartate concentration
CheY is a catalytic signaling protein that is regenerated; a limit on its amount would not explain a decrease only at high attractant.
High aspartate concentrations are toxic to the cells that enter the capillary, so their count falls as they die there
Aspartate at 1 mM is an ordinary amino acid concentration and is not toxic; the data show a decline in the count, not cell death.
Receptors near the capillary mouth become saturated and adapt, so cells can no longer detect a useful gradient there
Correct: Chemotaxis depends on sensing changes in receptor occupancy; saturation and adaptation reduce the response at high concentrations.
Aspartate at 1 mM is converted by the cells into a repellent that causes them to swim away
No evidence indicates conversion into a repellent, and the cells respond to attractant at lower concentrations.
qs.x: Chemotaxis depends on sensing changes in receptor occupancy; saturation and adaptation reduce the response at high concentrations. Trap: Attributing a drop in response at high stimulus to toxicity rather than to receptor saturation and adaptation.

h: Tumbles per second in uniform buffer

graph.title: Figure 1. Accumulation of WT cells in capillaries versus aspartate concentration

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Influenza A virus has a segmented, negative-sense RNA genome. The viral surface protein hemagglutinin binds terminal sialic acid on host cells, and the enzyme neuraminidase (NA) cleaves sialic acid, which allows newly formed virions to leave the infected cell. The drug oseltamivir carboxylate inhibits NA. A plaque assay was used to test two viral isolates: wild type (WT) and a variant carrying the substitution H275Y in NA. Confluent monolayers of MDCK cells were infected with 0.1 mL of a 10^-5 dilution of each virus stock, and after a 1-hour adsorption the inoculum was removed and replaced with an agarose overlay containing the drug at the concentrations shown. After 48 hours, cells were fixed and stained, and plaques (clear zones of dead cells) were counted. The mean plaque diameter was also measured. Table 1 shows the results of the experiment, each value the mean of three wells. Plaque number reports how many infectious particles started a spreading infection, whereas plaque diameter reflects how efficiently virus spread from cell to cell during the 48-hour incubation.

qs.q: What is the titer of the WT virus stock, in plaque-forming units (PFU) per milliliter?
o: 9.8 x 10^6 results from dividing by the dilution but forgetting to account for the 0.1 mL volume.
9.8 x 10^8 results from using 0.01 mL, which is not the volume plated.
Correct: Titer = plaques / (dilution x volume plated) = 98 / (10^-5 x 0.1 mL) = 98 / 10^-6 = 9.8 x 10^7 PFU/mL.
9.8 x 10^5 results from dividing by the dilution twice or multiplying by the volume instead of dividing.
qs.x: Titer = plaques / (dilution x volume plated) = 98 / (10^-5 x 0.1 mL) = 98 / 10^-6 = 9.8 x 10^7 PFU/mL. Trap: Forgetting to divide by the volume plated, which gives a titer ten-fold too low.

qs.q: In the WT virus, the drug reduced plaque diameter even at 1 nM, a concentration that did not reduce plaque number. The best explanation is that inhibiting NA
o: prevents the host cell from undergoing lysis, so infected cells survive longer
The size of the plaques reflects cell death and spread; the data do not show that infected cells survive longer, and the mechanism of the drug concerns release.
prevents the virus from binding sialic acid on the first host cell, so fewer initial infections occur
Hemagglutinin, not NA, mediates attachment; blocking NA would not reduce initial infection at 1 nM, where plaque number was unchanged.
blocks viral RNA synthesis inside infected cells, so that these cells produce no progeny virions at all
NA acts at release, after replication; if RNA synthesis were blocked there would be no plaques at all.
traps newly made virions on the surface of the infected cell, which limits spread to neighboring cells
Correct: Plaque number reflects initial infection events and plaque size reflects cell-to-cell spread, which depends on release of progeny virions by NA.
qs.x: Plaque number reflects initial infection events and plaque size reflects cell-to-cell spread, which depends on release of progeny virions by NA. Trap: Mixing up the roles of hemagglutinin (attachment) and neuraminidase (release) in the infection cycle.

qs.q: Which feature of influenza A most directly accounts for the rapid emergence of drug-resistant variants such as H275Y?
o: The virus carries a large DNA genome that undergoes frequent recombination with host DNA
Influenza has a segmented RNA genome, not a DNA genome.
The virus integrates into the host genome, where mutations accumulate over many cell divisions
Influenza does not integrate; it replicates in the nucleus as RNA without entering the host chromosomes.
The viral reverse transcriptase is error prone and introduces many mutations as it copies the RNA genome into DNA
Influenza is not a retrovirus and has no reverse transcriptase; it never makes a DNA intermediate.
The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase lacks proofreading activity, which creates many mutations in progeny genomes
Correct: Influenza replicates its RNA genome with an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that does not proofread, so the mutation rate is high.
qs.x: Influenza replicates its RNA genome with an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that does not proofread, so the mutation rate is high. Trap: Applying features of retroviruses such as HIV to a negative-sense RNA virus.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: Oseltamivir carboxylate kills infected MDCK cells directly, since plaque counts fall at high doses
Plaques are formed by dead cells; fewer plaques in the presence of drug means fewer successful rounds of infection, not direct killing of cells.
H275Y spreads between cells more efficiently than WT in the absence of drug, as shown by plaque diameter at 0 nM
At 0 nM the diameters are 2.0 mm and 2.1 mm, which is no evidence for more efficient spread.
H275Y cannot infect cells because plaque numbers decline at 1000 nM
The H275Y virus infected cells at all concentrations and had 60 plaques per well even at 1000 nM.
H275Y requires more than 100 times as much drug as WT to reduce plaque number by about half
Correct: WT plaque number fell to about half (52 of 98) at 10 nM, whereas H275Y still had 60 of 96 at 1000 nM, so at least 100-fold more drug is needed.
qs.x: WT plaque number fell to about half (52 of 98) at 10 nM, whereas H275Y still had 60 of 96 at 1000 nM, so at least 100-fold more drug is needed. Trap: Reading a partial reduction at the highest dose as a total loss of infectivity.

qs.q: The influenza A genome is negative-sense RNA. Which of the following must be present in the virion to start infection of a new cell?
o: A viral ribosome to translate the genome directly into protein
Viruses lack ribosomes; they use host ribosomes, but only on mRNA, which the negative strand is not.
A viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase to transcribe the genome into mRNA
The viral genome is RNA, not DNA, so a DNA-dependent polymerase would have no template.
A viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Correct: A negative strand cannot be translated, and host cells do not copy RNA into RNA, so the virion carries its own polymerase for transcription.
A viral integrase to insert the genome into the host chromosome
Integrase is characteristic of retroviruses; influenza does not integrate.
qs.x: A negative strand cannot be translated, and host cells do not copy RNA into RNA, so the virion carries its own polymerase for transcription. Trap: Assuming a negative-strand RNA can be read directly by host ribosomes.

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Bacillus subtilis forms endospores when nutrients are scarce. A mother cell packages a copy of its chromosome in a spore with a dehydrated core, a thick protective coat, and a high content of dipicolinic acid (DPA) chelated with Ca2+. Small acid-soluble proteins (SASPs) bind the spore DNA. To compare heat resistance, researchers prepared vegetative cells, wild-type (WT) spores, and spores of a mutant lacking the two major SASP genes (DSASP). Each preparation, containing about 10^8 colony-forming units (CFU) per mL, was heated at 90 degrees C. Samples were removed at intervals, cooled, and plated, and the log10 of CFU per mL was calculated. The core water content and DPA content of spores and cells were also measured. Table 1 shows the composition of each type, and Figure 1 shows survival over time. The D-value is the time required for a 10-fold (one log) reduction in viable count. Assume that survival declines linearly on a log scale during the heating period and that all preparations began with the same number of cells.

qs.q: From Figure 1, what is the D-value at 90 degrees C for vegetative cells?
o: 2.5 min
Correct: The count drops by 2 logs (8.0 to 6.0) in 5 minutes, that is 1 log per 2.5 minutes.
10 min
10 min is the D-value of the DSASP spores, not of the vegetative cells.
5.0 min
5.0 min is the time for a 2-log drop, not a 1-log drop.
1.0 min
1.0 min would imply a 5-log drop in 5 minutes, which the graph does not show.
qs.x: The count drops by 2 logs (8.0 to 6.0) in 5 minutes, that is 1 log per 2.5 minutes. Trap: Reporting the time of the whole interval rather than the time for a single 10-fold decrease.

qs.q: Assuming the WT spore curve continues linearly, about how long at 90 degrees C would be needed to reduce a WT spore population by 3 logs?
o: 60 min
60 min is close to a single D-value and would give only a 1-log reduction.
150 min
Correct: WT spores lose 0.4 log in 20 minutes, which is 0.1 log per 5 minutes, a D-value of 50 minutes; 3 logs requires 3 x 50 = 150 minutes.
30 min
30 min is the time for a 3-log drop of DSASP spores (D = 10 min), not WT spores.
300 min
300 min would result from doubling the D-value or using a 6-log reduction.
qs.x: WT spores lose 0.4 log in 20 minutes, which is 0.1 log per 5 minutes, a D-value of 50 minutes; 3 logs requires 3 x 50 = 150 minutes. Trap: Using a D-value of a different preparation, or using an inconsistent time scale when extrapolating.

qs.q: Table 1 and Figure 1 together support which conclusion about heat resistance of spores?
o: Core dehydration alone accounts for all of the heat resistance, since WT and DSASP spores have identical core water
WT and DSASP have identical core water but different survival, so dehydration cannot account for all of the resistance.
DPA content has no relation to heat resistance, since vegetative cells with no DPA die at about the same rate as WT spores
WT spores survive far better than the vegetative cells, which lack DPA, so DPA is plausibly relevant.
SASPs alone account for the heat resistance of spores, because DSASP spores die as fast as vegetative cells
DSASP spores have a D-value four times that of vegetative cells, so SASPs are not the only factor.
Low core water and high DPA help, but SASPs add protection, since DSASP and WT spores differ with equal water and DPA

Correct: The DSASP spores survive far better than vegetative cells (D = 10 vs 2.5 min), which suggests that dehydration and DPA matter, and WT spores survive better still (D = 50 min), which implicates SASPs.
qs.x: The DSASP spores survive far better than vegetative cells (D = 10 vs 2.5 min), which suggests that dehydration and DPA matter, and WT spores survive better still (D = 50 min), which implicates SASPs. Trap: Attributing an effect to a single factor when the comparison among three groups reveals more than one.

qs.q: Spores are not killed by boiling water at 100 degrees C for several minutes. Which sterilization method is therefore preferred for surgical instruments?
o: Refrigerating the instruments at 4 degrees C, which prevents germination of endospores
Cold storage does not kill spores and may even preserve them.
Autoclaving at 121 degrees C under pressure
Correct: Endospores withstand 100 degrees C; the higher temperature of a pressurized autoclave achieves sterility.
Soaking in 70% ethanol, which is sporicidal at room temperature
Ethanol kills vegetative cells but does not reliably kill spores.
Boiling the instruments for 30 minutes at 100 degrees C, which kills all bacterial forms
Boiling is not reliable against spores, as Figure 1 shows for WT spores even at 90 degrees C.
qs.x: Endospores withstand 100 degrees C; the higher temperature of a pressurized autoclave achieves sterility. Trap: Believing that boiling sterilizes everything, which ignores the existence of heat-resistant endospores.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes endospore formation from bacterial reproduction?
o: Each spore divides by binary fission after formation, which increases the number of cells
Spores are dormant and do not divide until they germinate.
Spores form from a fusion of two bacteria and thereby produce a new genetic combination
Spore formation is not sexual; no fusion with another cell occurs.
Each cell makes one spore, so cell number does not increase
Correct: A starving cell converts itself into one spore; viable cell number rises only after germination and growth.
Spores are formed by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number of the mother cell
Bacteria do not undergo meiosis; the spore receives a full copy of the chromosome.
qs.x: A starving cell converts itself into one spore; viable cell number rises only after germination and growth. Trap: Treating spores as a reproductive stage, as in fungi, rather than as a dormant survival form.

graph.title: Figure 1. Survival at 90 degrees C

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: A human epithelial cell line has a doubling time of 20 hours. Researchers used flow cytometry to measure DNA content per cell after propidium iodide staining and sorted cells into G1 (2N DNA), S (between 2N and 4N), and G2/M (4N) groups. Asynchronous cultures were left untreated or treated for 24 hours with one of three agents. Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and so depletes deoxyribonucleotides. Nocodazole prevents polymerization of microtubules. Drug R inhibits CDK4/6, kinases that phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein (Rb). The percentage of cells in each group is shown in Table 1. In a separate time course, cells were treated with nocodazole and sampled every 6 hours; Figure 1 shows the percentage of cells with 4N DNA content, with a series for untreated cells. Assume that the untreated culture is in exponential growth, that the percentage of cells in a phase is proportional to the duration of that phase, and that cell death was negligible.

qs.q: Cells in G2/M have 4N DNA content because, at this stage,
o: the cell has completed meiosis I, so each daughter has twice the haploid DNA content
This is a mitotic culture; meiosis does not occur in this cell line.
the cell has not yet replicated DNA but has doubled the number of chromosomes by fusing with another cell
DNA doubling occurs by replication, not by cell fusion.
the cell has undergone cytokinesis, producing two cells that each contain 4N DNA
Cytokinesis returns each daughter cell to 2N.
DNA was replicated in S phase but sister chromatids remain joined
Correct: After S phase each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, giving 4N DNA until anaphase and cytokinesis divide them.
qs.x: After S phase each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, giving 4N DNA until anaphase and cytokinesis divide them. Trap: Confusing the chromosome number with the DNA content, which doubles in S phase while the chromosome count stays the same.

qs.q: Drug R caused 88% of cells to accumulate in G1. The most likely mechanism is that CDK4/6 inhibition
o: blocks DNA polymerase directly, so cells that enter S phase cannot continue and remain in G1
A DNA polymerase block would cause accumulation in S, as seen with hydroxyurea, not in G1.
keeps Rb hypophosphorylated and bound to E2F, so genes required for S phase are not expressed
Correct: CDK4/6 phosphorylation of Rb releases E2F; the drug blocks that release, so the G1/S transition is not made.
activates the anaphase-promoting complex, which degrades the cyclins required for S phase
Activation of APC/C drives mitotic exit and is not how a CDK4/6 inhibitor works; the drug acts on Rb phosphorylation.
prevents microtubule assembly, so cells stall before the metaphase spindle can form
Microtubule disruption causes arrest in G2/M (as in the nocodazole row), not in G1.
qs.x: CDK4/6 phosphorylation of Rb releases E2F; the drug blocks that release, so the G1/S transition is not made. Trap: Choosing an arrest point that matches a different drug in the table rather than the pathway the drug inhibits.

qs.q: Using the assumptions in the passage, the duration of S phase in the untreated culture is closest to
o: 14 h is not obtained from any phase fraction; it would be 70% of the cycle, the time outside S.
3.6 h is 18% of 20 h, the duration of G2/M.
10.4 h is 52% of 20 h, the duration of G1.
6 h
Correct: S phase is 30% of the cell cycle, and 0.30 x 20 h = 6 h.
qs.x: S phase is 30% of the cell cycle, and 0.30 x 20 h = 6 h. Trap: Using the percentage of a different phase to calculate the duration.

qs.q: In Figure 1, the percentage of nocodazole-treated cells with 4N DNA content rises gradually rather than all at once. The best explanation is that
o: other cells keep cycling until they reach mitosis, where the spindle checkpoint arrests them
Correct: Each cell is arrested only when it reaches M phase, so the 4N fraction rises as cells arrive from earlier phases, in about 20 hours.
nocodazole enters cells slowly and takes about 24 hours to reach an effective concentration
Drugs of this kind act within minutes to hours; the gradual rise reflects cell cycle progression, not drug uptake.
cells in G1 and S duplicate their DNA twice in the presence of nocodazole and become 4N
A cell that is arrested in M phase has 4N DNA only after a single replication in S phase; rereplication does not explain the data.
nocodazole kills cells in G1 and S, so the fraction of 4N cells rises as other cells are lost
The passage states that cell death was negligible, and the 4N count was already 58% at 12 h.
qs.x: Each cell is arrested only when it reaches M phase, so the 4N fraction rises as cells arrive from earlier phases, in about 20 hours. Trap: Attributing a time-dependent change to drug kinetics instead of to cell-cycle progression of an asynchronous population.

qs.q: Which observation in Table 1 is most consistent with hydroxyurea's effect on ribonucleotide reductase?
o: The fraction of cells in S rises from 30% to 47%, which shows that DNA replication is faster after treatment
A larger S fraction means that cells spend longer in S, not that replication is faster.
The S fraction rises from 30% to 47% while G2/M falls from 18% to 5%, as cells cannot finish replication without dNTPs
Correct: Without dNTPs, DNA replication stalls, so cells accumulate in S and fewer reach G2/M.
The fraction of cells in G2/M falls from 18% to 5%, which shows that nucleotides are also needed for the mechanics of mitosis itself
The lower G2/M fraction arises because fewer cells complete S phase, not because mitosis needs nucleotides.
The fraction of cells in G1 falls from 52% to 48%, which shows that cells cannot enter S phase
G1 fraction changed only slightly and cells still entered S, as the S fraction increased.
qs.x: Without dNTPs, DNA replication stalls, so cells accumulate in S and fewer reach G2/M. Trap: Reading an increase in the S-phase fraction as faster replication rather than a slowed or stalled replication.

graph.title: Figure 1. Cells with 4N DNA content over time

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Skeletal muscle regenerates from satellite cells, quiescent stem cells that lie beside muscle fibers. When activated, satellite cells proliferate as myoblasts, then stop dividing, express myogenin, and fuse to form multinucleated myotubes. To study this process, researchers cultured C2C12 myoblasts in growth medium with 10% fetal bovine serum. At day 0, the medium was changed to differentiation medium with 2% horse serum. Cells were fixed on the indicated days and stained for Ki67, a marker present in cycling cells and absent in cells that have exited the cell cycle, and for myogenin. The fusion index is the percentage of all nuclei located within cells containing three or more nuclei. In one group, cells were transfected with an siRNA against myogenin (siMyog) at day 0, and the same measurements were made on day 4. Table 1 shows the results. About 800 nuclei were counted for each time point. Myogenin is a muscle-specific transcription factor of the basic helix-loop-helix family, and myoblasts that have exited the cell cycle remain viable and capable of fusion.

qs.q: Which observation in Table 1 best supports the idea that cell cycle exit precedes myoblast fusion?
o: Between day 0 and day 1, Ki67-positive nuclei fall from 85% to 40% while the fusion index rises only from 0% to 3%
Correct: The loss of cycling cells occurs before the appearance of multinucleated cells, which fits an ordered series of events.
At day 4, siMyog cells have 5% Ki67-positive nuclei, which shows that myogenin is required for cell cycle exit
The siMyog cells exited the cell cycle (5% Ki67-positive) despite lacking myogenin, so myogenin is not required for cell cycle exit.
At day 4 the fusion index is 65%, which shows that most nuclei are in myotubes
A high final fusion index shows that fusion occurred but not the order of events.
At day 2, 28% of nuclei are fused, which is lower than the 62% that are myogenin-positive
Comparing myogenin and fusion shows that myogenin expression precedes fusion, but does not address exit from the cycle.
qs.x: The loss of cycling cells occurs before the appearance of multinucleated cells, which fits an ordered series of events. Trap: Reading the final state of the cells as evidence for the sequence of events.

qs.q: The siMyog cells at day 4 were mostly Ki67-negative but had a fusion index of 4%. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Myogenin is a cell-cycle inhibitor, since siMyog cells divide faster than control cells at day 4
The data do not show faster division; Ki67 is 5% in siMyog versus 4% in the day 4 control, which are essentially equal.
Myogenin is needed for exit from the cell cycle, since siMyog cells lack the fusion that accompanies exit
Exit from the cell cycle occurred in the siMyog group (5% Ki67-positive).
Myogenin is needed for the terminal differentiation program, including fusion, but not for exit from the cell cycle
Correct: siMyog cells left the cycle (5% Ki67-positive), but they did not differentiate and fuse, which shows that exit alone is insufficient.
Myoblasts can fuse without leaving the cell cycle, since siMyog cells remain 95% Ki67-positive
The table shows that siMyog cells are only 5% Ki67-positive, not 95%.
qs.x: siMyog cells left the cycle (5% Ki67-positive), but they did not differentiate and fuse, which shows that exit alone is insufficient. Trap: Assuming that cells lacking the differentiation program must also have failed to exit the cell cycle.

qs.q: Switching from 10% to 2% serum most likely promotes differentiation because
o: reduced mitogen signaling lowers growth-factor-driven cycling, which permits cells to exit the cycle and differentiate
Correct: Serum supplies growth factors that sustain proliferative signaling; their withdrawal favors exit and differentiation.
serum contains myogenin, and a lower dose of serum avoids repression of the endogenous myogenin gene in the cells
Serum is not a source of myogenin, an intracellular transcription factor made by the cells.
low serum is toxic to myoblasts, which stimulates the apoptotic program that leads to fusion
Differentiating cells in low serum remain viable and become myotubes; fusion is not an apoptotic process.
low serum increases the concentration of cholesterol in the medium, which forces the cells to fuse
Serum contains lipids and cholesterol; lowering serum does not raise them or compel fusion.
qs.x: Serum supplies growth factors that sustain proliferative signaling; their withdrawal favors exit and differentiation. Trap: Explaining a change in cell fate as the result of toxicity or stress instead of altered signaling.

qs.q: Which property must satellite cells have in order to be classified as stem cells of muscle?
o: The ability to self-renew and to give rise to differentiated muscle cells
Correct: Stem cells both self-renew and produce differentiated progeny; satellite cells are unipotent (muscle) stem cells.
The ability to remain proliferative indefinitely and never express myogenin
Satellite cells do express myogenin as they differentiate; a stem cell does not remain undifferentiated in all progeny.
The ability to form every cell type of the body, including nerve cells and blood cells
That describes pluripotent stem cells, whereas satellite cells are restricted to the muscle lineage.
The ability to form myotubes without ever dividing, so the pool is not depleted
Satellite cells must divide to produce the myoblasts that regenerate muscle.
qs.x: Stem cells both self-renew and produce differentiated progeny; satellite cells are unipotent (muscle) stem cells. Trap: Assuming that all stem cells are pluripotent.

qs.q: About how many of the 800 nuclei counted at day 2 were myogenin-positive?
o: About 96
96 is 12% of 800, the number of Ki67-positive nuclei.
About 496
Correct: 62% of 800 = 496.
About 560
560 is 70% of 800, the myogenin-positive count at day 4.
About 224
224 is 28% of 800, the number of nuclei in myotubes.
qs.x: 62% of 800 = 496. Trap: Reading the percentage from a different column or a different day.

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: TRPV1 is a cation channel found in the sensory endings of nociceptive neurons. It opens in response to capsaicin, the pungent compound in chili peppers, and to noxious heat. To characterize it, HEK293 cells, which do not normally express TRPV1, were transfected with the TRPV1 gene or left untransfected. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were made with the membrane potential held at -60 mV. The standard external solution contained Na+ and 2 mM Ca2+. Capsaicin was applied by perfusion at 1 micromolar unless otherwise stated, and the peak inward current was recorded. Capsazepine, a competitive antagonist at the capsaicin site, was applied at 10 micromolar with capsaicin. In one group, external Na+ was replaced with N-methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG+), a large cation that does not pass through the channel. Table 1 shows peak currents, and Figure 1 shows the current in TRPV1 cells at different capsaicin concentrations. Inward current is reported as a magnitude in picoamperes (pA).

qs.q: The inward current evoked by capsaicin in TRPV1 cells is best explained by
o: pumping of Na+ into the cell by the Na+/K+ ATPase, which is stimulated by capsaicin
The pump is not stimulated by capsaicin and is too slow to give a current of this size within seconds.
entry of Na+ and Ca2+ down their electrochemical gradients through the open channel, which depolarizes the cell
Correct: TRPV1 is a nonselective cation channel; at -60 mV Na+ (and Ca2+) enter, and the current falls when Na+ is replaced by impermeant NMDG+.
exit of K+ through the open channel, which hyperpolarizes the cell
K+ exit would be an outward current and would not be the inward current recorded.
entry of Cl- through the open channel, which depolarizes the cell
Cl- entry would be an outward current by convention and would hyperpolarize the cell; the NMDG+ result also implicates cations.
qs.x: TRPV1 is a nonselective cation channel; at -60 mV Na+ (and Ca2+) enter, and the current falls when Na+ is replaced by impermeant NMDG+. Trap: Confusing the direction of current with the direction of ion movement, so that anion entry or cation exit is mistaken for inward current.

qs.q: By what percentage did capsazepine reduce the peak current evoked by 1 micromolar capsaicin in TRPV1 cells?
o: About 99%
99% would require a final current of about 15 pA, the vehicle-only level, which was not reached.
About 93%
Correct: The current fell from 1450 to 95 pA, a decrease of 1355 pA, and 1355/1450 = 0.93.
About 7%
7% is about the remaining fraction (95/1450 = 6.6%), not the fraction removed.
About 66%
66% is not obtained from the data; it would correspond to a current of about 490 pA.
qs.x: The current fell from 1450 to 95 pA, a decrease of 1355 pA, and 1355/1450 = 0.93. Trap: Reporting the fraction remaining rather than the fraction inhibited.

qs.q: Based on Figure 1, the capsaicin concentration that produces half of the maximal current is closest to
o: 0.6 micromolar
Correct: The maximum is about 2200 pA, so half is about 1100 pA; the curve passes through 850 pA at 0.3 micromolar and 1450 pA at 1 micromolar, so 1100 pA occurs at about 0.6 micromolar.
10 micromolar
At 10 micromolar the current is 2150 pA, near saturation.
0.06 micromolar
At 0.06 micromolar the current is only about 200 pA, far below half the maximum.
3 micromolar
At 3 micromolar the current is 1900 pA, about 86% of the maximum.
qs.x: The maximum is about 2200 pA, so half is about 1100 pA; the curve passes through 850 pA at 0.3 micromolar and 1450 pA at 1 micromolar, so 1100 pA occurs at about 0.6 micromolar. Trap: Choosing the concentration at which the current is nearly maximal, rather than the one giving half of the maximal response.

qs.q: Capsaicin applied to the skin causes a burning sensation. Which sequence best accounts for this sensation?
o: Channel opening depolarizes the nociceptor ending until voltage-gated Na+ channels fire action potentials that are relayed to the brain

Correct: Cation influx depolarizes the sensory ending; when threshold is reached, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and action potentials propagate along the afferent fiber toward the central nervous system.
Channel opening causes the release of acetylcholine at the skin, which activates muscarinic receptors on keratinocytes to heat the tissue
The effect arises from activation of the sensory neuron, not from acetylcholine release in the skin or a literal rise in temperature.
Channel opening activates motor neurons that contract skin muscle, which stretches pain receptors
Capsaicin acts on sensory (afferent) neurons, not motor neurons.
Channel opening hyperpolarizes the nociceptor ending, which releases inhibitory neurotransmitter onto pain-carrying neurons
The current is inward, so the ending depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizes.
qs.x: Cation influx depolarizes the sensory ending; when threshold is reached, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and action potentials propagate along the afferent fiber toward the central nervous system. Trap: Assuming that capsaicin literally heats tissue, rather than activating the same channel that detects heat.

r: TRPV1, capsaicin, external Na+ replaced by NMDG+

graph.title: Figure 1. Peak inward current versus capsaicin concentration in TRPV1 cells

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: Leptin is a hormone secreted by adipose tissue in proportion to fat mass. Two strains of obese mice were studied. Mice homozygous for the ob mutation (ob/ob) are severely obese; those homozygous for the db mutation (db/db) are equally obese. To determine whether each strain lacks a circulating factor or the ability to respond to it, researchers used parabiosis, a surgery that joins the circulatory systems of two animals so that blood-borne factors are shared. Pairs were joined at 6 weeks of age, and the daily food intake and change in body mass of each partner were measured over the next 4 weeks. Unjoined mice served as controls. In each case, the partners were of the same sex and similar size. Table 1 shows the results. Hormone injection experiments in the same strains gave consistent findings. Assume that circulating blood factors exchange freely between partners within a few days of surgery, and that any change in intake reflects hormonal signaling rather than stress from the surgery.

qs.q: The wild-type mouse joined to a db/db partner ate much less and lost weight. The best explanation is that
o: the db/db partner secretes a satiety factor that acts only on its own hypothalamus and spreads by gap junctions to the wild-type partner
Gap junctions link cells, not separate animals; the factor travels in the blood.
the wild-type partner makes antibodies against the db/db partner's tissues, which reduces its food intake
The data do not suggest an immune response, and the effect is explained by the hormone's known action.
the db/db partner lacks leptin, so the wild-type partner's leptin is diverted to the db/db partner and is no longer available to the wild type
db/db mice are not leptin deficient; if leptin were lacking, the wild-type partner's intake would not fall below 4.0 g.
the db/db partner secretes large amounts of leptin, which reaches the wild-type partner through the shared circulation and suppresses its appetite
Correct: db/db mice cannot respond to leptin, so fat accumulates and leptin rises; the high circulating leptin acts on the functional receptors of the wild-type partner.
qs.x: db/db mice cannot respond to leptin, so fat accumulates and leptin rises; the high circulating leptin acts on the functional receptors of the wild-type partner. Trap: Assuming the db mutation, like ob, is a lack of the hormone rather than a failure to respond to it.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the db/db mouse is best supported by the table?
o: It is lacking the satiety center in the hypothalamus, since its partner lost weight
The conclusion concerns a receptor defect, not an absence of an entire brain region; the table cannot establish anatomy.
It produces leptin but cannot respond to it, since its own intake stayed high when joined to a wild-type partner that stopped eating

Correct: db/db intake stayed at 7.9 g and mass rose by 17 g even when joined to a wild-type partner, while that partner ate only 1.5 g and lost weight, so db/db makes active leptin but does not respond to it.
It produces no leptin, since its intake was unchanged when joined to a wild-type partner
The unchanged intake would be seen in either case; the starvation of the partner shows that the db/db mouse makes active hormone.
It produces leptin that is inactive, since its leptin has no effect on the intake of a partner with normal receptors
The wild-type partner joined to db/db ate 1.5 g instead of 4.0 g, which shows that db/db leptin is active.
qs.x: db/db intake stayed at 7.9 g and mass rose by 17 g even when joined to a wild-type partner, while that partner ate only 1.5 g and lost weight, so db/db makes active leptin but does not respond to it. Trap: Concluding that a failure to respond to a signal means the signal is absent.

qs.q: Compared with wild-type mice, which of the following pairs of plasma leptin concentrations would be expected in ob/ob and db/db mice?
o: ob/ob: high; db/db: high
ob/ob mice cannot produce functional leptin, so levels cannot be high.
ob/ob: high; db/db: very low or undetectable
This reverses the genotypes.
ob/ob: very low or undetectable; db/db: very low or undetectable
db/db mice are obese and secrete leptin in proportion to their fat mass.
ob/ob: very low or undetectable; db/db: high
Correct: ob/ob mice have no functional hormone, and db/db mice have large fat stores and no feedback, so they secrete high levels.
qs.x: ob/ob mice have no functional hormone, and db/db mice have large fat stores and no feedback, so they secrete high levels. Trap: Reversing the two mutant strains or expecting both strains to have the same hormone level.

qs.q: Leptin lowers food intake mainly by acting on neurons of which brain region?
o: The cerebellar cortex of the hindbrain
The cerebellar cortex coordinates movement and is not a site of leptin action on appetite.
The posterior pituitary gland and its stalk
The posterior pituitary stores and releases oxytocin and ADH and is not the main leptin target.
The arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus
Correct: Leptin receptors in the arcuate nucleus regulate NPY/AgRP (appetite-stimulating) and POMC (appetite-suppressing) neurons.
The primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe
The primary visual cortex processes visual information.
qs.x: Leptin receptors in the arcuate nucleus regulate NPY/AgRP (appetite-stimulating) and POMC (appetite-suppressing) neurons. Trap: Selecting a structure that is part of the endocrine system but not the site where leptin acts.

passages.title: Mini04 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Mammalian behavior shows circadian rhythms that persist in constant darkness (DD) with a period near, but not exactly, 24 hours. The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is thought to be the master pacemaker. Hamsters kept in DD were studied by wheel-running activity. Circadian time (CT) is defined so that CT0 is the start of the subjective day and CT12 is the onset of activity in a nocturnal animal. Animals were given a brief light pulse at different CTs, and the shift in the next day's activity onset was measured. Table 1 shows the rhythm of animals under different conditions, including an SCN lesion and SCN lesion followed by transplantation of fetal SCN tissue from a donor with a short free-running period (tau mutant). Figure 1 shows the shift in activity onset as a function of CT of the light pulse (positive values are advances, negative values are delays). Light pulses lasted 15 minutes and were given at an intensity of 100 lux to animals that had been in constant darkness for at least two weeks, so that their free-running rhythms were established.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the results of the SCN lesion and graft groups?
o: The SCN is not required for rhythms, since grafted animals recover a rhythm
Lesioned animals lost the rhythm, which shows that the SCN is required; the graft restored it.
The SCN generates the period of the rhythm, since grafted tissue imposes the donor's period on a lesioned host
Correct: An animal with no rhythm after lesion regains one whose period matches that of the donor tissue, so the period is a property of the SCN cells.
The rhythm is set by the host's remaining tissues, since the host retains its wild-type period after grafting
Grafted animals had donor periods (20.1 h and 23.9 h), not the host's.
The SCN produces rhythms only if connected to the retina, since grafted animals have no retinal input
The experiment does not address retinal input, and the rhythm persisted in constant darkness, in which light cues are absent.
qs.x: An animal with no rhythm after lesion regains one whose period matches that of the donor tissue, so the period is a property of the SCN cells. Trap: Reading the recovery of rhythmicity as evidence that the SCN is dispensable.

qs.q: A hamster with a free-running rhythm receives a light pulse at CT16. Compared with an unpulsed animal, its activity onset on the following day is predicted to occur
o: about 0.5 h later
A delay of 0.5 hour is the shift near CT12, not CT16.
about 2 h earlier
An advance of 2 hours would require a shift of +2.0 h, as seen near CT22 (+1.8 h) but with the opposite sign.
about 2 h later
Correct: Figure 1 shows a phase shift of -2.0 h at CT16, and negative values are delays, so activity begins later.
at the same time
No shift occurs during the subjective day (CT2 to CT10), not at CT16.
qs.x: Figure 1 shows a phase shift of -2.0 h at CT16, and negative values are delays, so activity begins later. Trap: Mixing up the sign convention for advances and delays.

qs.q: Light information reaches the SCN mainly through
o: the vestibulocochlear nerve, from the hair cells of the inner ear
The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance information.
the optic radiations, from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the visual cortex
The optic radiations carry image-forming information to visual cortex and are not the main route to the SCN.
photoreceptors in the pineal gland, which sense light through the skull
In mammals the pineal gland does not sense light directly; it receives information from the SCN.
the retinohypothalamic tract, from retinal ganglion cells that contain the photopigment melanopsin
Correct: A subset of retinal ganglion cells is intrinsically photosensitive and projects directly to the SCN.
qs.x: A subset of retinal ganglion cells is intrinsically photosensitive and projects directly to the SCN. Trap: Assuming that all light information is processed through the visual cortex pathway.

qs.q: Which statement best describes how the SCN influences melatonin secretion?
o: The SCN has no effect on melatonin, which is regulated solely by blood glucose concentration
Melatonin secretion is controlled by the circadian system and light, not by glucose.
The SCN inhibits the adrenal medulla, which causes melatonin to be released at night
Melatonin is not secreted by the adrenal medulla, which makes catecholamines.
The SCN drives the pineal gland through a multisynaptic pathway, so melatonin is high at night and light at night suppresses it
Correct: SCN output travels via the hypothalamus and sympathetic ganglia to the pineal gland, and melatonin is secreted mainly at night; light suppresses it.
The SCN secretes melatonin directly into the blood during the day, which signals the pineal gland to rest
Melatonin is made by the pineal gland, not by the SCN, and it is secreted at night.
qs.x: SCN output travels via the hypothalamus and sympathetic ganglia to the pineal gland, and melatonin is secreted mainly at night; light suppresses it. Trap: Assuming the SCN itself secretes the hormone.

r: SCN lesion, graft of tau mutant SCN
SCN lesion, graft of wild-type SCN

graph.title: Figure 1. Phase shift in activity onset after a light pulse
graph.x_label: Circadian time of light pulse (CT, h)

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A student studies Rayleigh scattering by suspending polystyrene spheres, each about 50 nm in diameter, in water. A monochromator selects one visible wavelength at a time, and the beam passes through the suspension with the incident intensity held constant at every wavelength. A detector placed at 90° to the beam records the scattered intensity. Because the spheres are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light, the scattered intensity is expected to vary as 1/λ⁴. The student normalizes each reading to the value at 700 nm; the results are shown in Table 1 and plotted in Figure 1. The student then repeats the experiment with spheres about 2 µm in diameter and finds that the scattered intensity is nearly independent of wavelength, so the suspension appears white. The student also notes that the transmitted beam, viewed end-on through a long tube of the 50 nm suspension, looks orange-red. Table 1 lists the intensities relative to the 700 nm reading.

qs.q: According to the 1/λ⁴ dependence, how many times more strongly are 400 nm photons scattered than 700 nm photons by the 50 nm spheres?
o: 1.8 times
1.75 is the wavelength ratio itself, with no exponent applied.
3.1 times
1.75² ≈ 3.1 applies a square instead of the fourth power.
9.4 times
Correct: Intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴, so I(400)/I(700) = (700/400)⁴ = 1.75⁴ ≈ 9.4, matching the first row of Table 1 (9.38).
5.4 times
1.75³ ≈ 5.4 applies a cube instead of the fourth power.
qs.x: Intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴, so I(400)/I(700) = (700/400)⁴ = 1.75⁴ ≈ 9.4, matching the first row of Table 1 (9.38). Trap: Applying the wavelength ratio to the wrong power instead of the fourth power.

qs.q: Based on the 1/λ⁴ relationship, what is the relative scattered intensity at 500 nm (700 nm = 1.00)?
o: Correct: (700/500)⁴ = 1.4⁴ ≈ 3.84, which agrees with the 500 nm row of Table 1.
1.40 is the wavelength ratio, not raised to the fourth power.
1.96 is 1.4², a square rather than a fourth power.
0.26 is (500/700)⁴, the inverse ratio, which would apply if intensity increased with wavelength.
qs.x: (700/500)⁴ = 1.4⁴ ≈ 3.84, which agrees with the 500 nm row of Table 1. Trap: Inverting the ratio so that longer wavelengths scatter more.

qs.q: If the student plotted the natural log of the relative scattered intensity against the natural log of the wavelength using the data in Table 1, the plot would be:
o: a straight line with a slope of +4, because the intensity increases with wavelength.
The sign is wrong; intensity decreases as wavelength increases.
a curve with a slope that steepens toward longer wavelengths, because the data in Figure 1 are curved.
Figure 1 is curved on linear axes, but a power law is linear on log-log axes.
a straight line with a slope of −1/4, because the wavelength varies as the fourth root of intensity.
The exponent, not its reciprocal, is the slope of ln I versus ln λ.
a straight line with a slope of −4, because I ∝ λ⁻⁴.
Correct: Taking logs of I = kλ⁻⁴ gives ln I = ln k − 4 ln λ, a straight line with slope −4.
qs.x: Taking logs of I = kλ⁻⁴ gives ln I = ln k − 4 ln λ, a straight line with slope −4. Trap: Reading the curvature on linear axes as evidence against a power law.

qs.q: The larger 2 µm spheres scatter all visible wavelengths about equally. The most likely reason is that:
o: the scattering is no longer governed by the 1/λ⁴ dependence when the particle size is comparable to or larger than the wavelength.

Correct: The 1/λ⁴ law holds only for particles much smaller than the wavelength; for particles near or above it (Mie regime) scattering is only weakly wavelength dependent, so the suspension looks white.
larger spheres absorb all visible wavelengths equally, so none are scattered.
Absorption is not the explanation; the suspension remains white and scatters strongly.
light of longer wavelength has more energy per photon, which offsets the 1/λ⁴ dependence.
Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so longer wavelengths have less energy.
the larger spheres are transparent, so no light is scattered.
Transparency of the material does not prevent scattering by refractive index differences at the interface.
qs.x: The 1/λ⁴ law holds only for particles much smaller than the wavelength; for particles near or above it (Mie regime) scattering is only weakly wavelength dependent, so the suspension looks white. Trap: Assuming bigger particles must absorb rather than scatter the light.

qs.q: Why does the transmitted beam through a long tube of the 50 nm suspension look orange-red?
o: Red light has the highest frequency and is therefore the most strongly absorbed by the spheres.
Red has the lowest frequency of visible light, and the effect arises from scattering, not absorption.
Blue light is scattered out of the beam more than red light is.
Correct: Blue and violet light are scattered sideways much more strongly than red, so the transmitted beam is depleted of short wavelengths and appears orange-red, as in a sunset.
The spheres emit orange-red light after absorbing blue light in the beam.
Re-emission after absorption is not Rayleigh scattering and would not depend on the wavelength this way.
Longer wavelengths are scattered out at 90°, leaving blue light in the transmitted beam.
This reverses the wavelength dependence; shorter wavelengths scatter more.
qs.x: Blue and violet light are scattered sideways much more strongly than red, so the transmitted beam is depleted of short wavelengths and appears orange-red, as in a sunset. Trap: Reversing which end of the visible spectrum is scattered more strongly.

graph.title: Figure 1. Relative scattered intensity versus wavelength

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: Diagnostic ultrasound transducers emit short pulses of sound that travel through soft tissue at about 1540 m/s, reflect from boundaries, and return to the transducer. As the pulse travels, the tissue absorbs and scatters sound, and the intensity level falls in proportion to distance and to frequency. A change in intensity level in decibels (dB) is ΔL = 10 log(I2/I1), so a loss of 10 dB corresponds to a factor of 10 in intensity. A sonographer examining the liver compares five transducer frequencies. Table 1 lists the wavelength of each pulse in tissue and the attenuation of the sound in liver, in dB per cm of one-way travel. Figure 1 plots attenuation against frequency. The instrument can display an echo only if the total loss on the round trip, to the reflector and back, does not exceed a preset limit. Shorter wavelengths allow the instrument to distinguish reflectors that lie closer together along the beam.

qs.q: At 5.0 MHz, what is the total loss, in dB, for an echo that returns from a reflector 4.0 cm deep?
o: 28 dB
Correct: The pulse travels 4.0 cm down and 4.0 cm back, 8.0 cm in all. The loss is 8.0 cm × 3.5 dB/cm = 28 dB.
14 dB
This counts only the one-way trip to the reflector (4.0 cm × 3.5 dB/cm) and omits the return trip.
3.5 dB
This is the attenuation per centimeter, not the total loss over the distance traveled.
7.0 dB
This multiplies the attenuation by 2 cm, using the depth divided by two rather than the doubled path.
qs.x: The pulse travels 4.0 cm down and 4.0 cm back, 8.0 cm in all. The loss is 8.0 cm × 3.5 dB/cm = 28 dB. Trap: Forgetting that the echo must travel to the reflector and back.

qs.q: If the instrument can display echoes with a total round-trip loss of up to 63 dB, what is the greatest depth that can be imaged at 7.5 MHz?
o: 12 cm
This uses one-way travel, 63 dB ÷ 5.25 dB/cm, ignoring the round trip.
6.0 cm
Correct: Round-trip loss per centimeter of depth is 2 × 5.25 = 10.5 dB. Depth = 63 dB ÷ 10.5 dB/cm = 6.0 cm.
3.0 cm
This divides the loss by twice the round-trip loss per centimeter, counting the return trip twice.
8.4 cm
This divides the 63 dB limit by the frequency, 7.5 MHz, which is not a loss per centimeter.
qs.x: Round-trip loss per centimeter of depth is 2 × 5.25 = 10.5 dB. Depth = 63 dB ÷ 10.5 dB/cm = 6.0 cm. Trap: Dividing by one-way attenuation without doubling for the round trip.

qs.q: A sonographer must image a structure 2 cm deep, and then a structure 12 cm deep. Which statement best describes the trade-off between frequency choices?
o: A higher frequency has a longer wavelength and so penetrates deeper, though it resolves fine detail poorly.
Higher frequency in a given medium means shorter, not longer, wavelength, and it attenuates more.
A lower frequency gives finer detail because it has more cycles per unit time, but it cannot reach deep structures.
Lower frequency gives longer wavelengths and poorer detail, yet it penetrates better.
A higher frequency gives shorter wavelengths and finer detail, but its greater attenuation limits the depth reached.
Correct: Table 1 shows that wavelength shrinks and attenuation rises as frequency increases. High frequency suits superficial structures; low frequency is needed for deep ones.
Frequency affects only the speed of sound, so the two choices differ only in the time delay of the echo.
The speed of sound in tissue is set by the medium, not by frequency.
qs.x: Table 1 shows that wavelength shrinks and attenuation rises as frequency increases. High frequency suits superficial structures; low frequency is needed for deep ones. Trap: Assuming a higher frequency always gives a better image regardless of depth.

qs.q: How long after the pulse is emitted does an echo from a reflector 4.0 cm deep arrive back at the transducer?
o: 26 µs
This counts only the one-way travel time and ignores the return trip.
52 µs
Correct: The round trip is 8.0 cm = 0.080 m. t = d/v = 0.080 m ÷ 1540 m/s ≈ 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ s = 52 µs.
104 µs
This doubles the round trip, effectively using a distance of 16 cm.
5.2 ms
This results from using centimeters rather than meters when dividing distance by speed.
qs.x: The round trip is 8.0 cm = 0.080 m. t = d/v = 0.080 m ÷ 1540 m/s ≈ 5.2 × 10⁻⁵ s = 52 µs. Trap: Using the one-way distance for the time of an echo.

qs.q: A total loss of 28 dB corresponds to which ratio of returning intensity to original intensity?
o: This is the ratio for 14 dB, the one-way loss, not the round-trip loss.
This treats the decibel value as the exponent of 10 without dividing by 10.
This takes 28 dB as 2.8 and treats it as a coefficient rather than an exponent.
qs.x: I2/I1 = 10^(−28/10) = 10^(−2.8) ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻³. Trap: Forgetting that decibels are one tenth of a base-10 logarithm of the ratio.

graph.title: Figure 1. Attenuation in liver versus ultrasound frequency

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: Cesium-137 decays with a half-life of about 30 years. The decay is a beta emission that produces barium-137 in an excited state (¹³⁷ᵐBa), which relaxes to the ground state by emitting a 662 keV gamma ray. A student places a sealed ¹³⁷Cs source at a fixed distance from a Geiger-Müller detector and inserts lead sheets of increasing total thickness between them. At each thickness the detector counts for several minutes, and the background rate is subtracted. For a narrow beam of gamma rays, the transmitted rate follows I = I0e^(−μx), where x is the thickness of absorber and μ is the linear attenuation coefficient. The half-value layer (HVL) is the thickness that reduces the rate by half. Table 1 gives the net count rate and the natural logarithm of that rate. Figure 1 shows the net rate as a function of lead thickness. The lead sheets were of uniform composition and the geometry was not altered between runs.

qs.q: What thickness of lead is needed to reduce the net count rate to 125 counts/min?
o: 30 mm
This assumes the rate falls by half for each 6 mm but miscounts the halvings by one, stopping at 250 counts/min.
48 mm
This corresponds to eight half-value layers, which would reduce the rate to about 31 counts/min.
384 mm
This multiplies the HVL by the factor of reduction needed (64 × 6.0 mm = 384 mm), instead of counting halvings.
36 mm
Correct: 8000 → 125 is a factor of 64 = 2⁶, requiring six half-value layers: 6 × 6.0 mm = 36 mm.
qs.x: 8000 → 125 is a factor of 64 = 2⁶, requiring six half-value layers: 6 × 6.0 mm = 36 mm. Trap: Multiplying the HVL by the ratio of rates rather than counting the number of halvings.

qs.q: What is the linear attenuation coefficient μ for lead, as indicated by Table 1?
o: 8.7 mm⁻¹
This takes the reciprocal, HVL/ln 2, which is a length (the mean free path), not an attenuation coefficient.
This is 1/HVL and leaves out the ln 2 factor from the exponential decay.
Correct: Because I/I0 = ½ at x = 6.0 mm, μ = ln 2 / HVL = 0.693 / 6.0 mm ≈ 0.12 mm⁻¹. The slope of ln(rate) versus x is −0.115 mm⁻¹ for the same reason.
4.2 mm⁻¹
This multiplies the HVL by ln 2, which gives neither μ nor the mean free path.
qs.x: Because I/I0 = ½ at x = 6.0 mm, μ = ln 2 / HVL = 0.693 / 6.0 mm ≈ 0.12 mm⁻¹. The slope of ln(rate) versus x is −0.115 mm⁻¹ for the same reason. Trap: Using 1/HVL for the attenuation coefficient and forgetting ln 2.

qs.q: Which equation correctly represents the nuclear decay of cesium-137 described in the passage?
o: ¹³⁷₅₅Cs → ¹³⁷₅₆Ba + ⁰₋₁e + antineutrino
Correct: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, raising Z from 55 to 56 and leaving the mass number at 137. Barium has Z = 56, and an electron and an antineutrino are emitted.
¹³⁷₅₅Cs → ¹³³₅₃I + ⁴₂He
This is an alpha decay, which would lower the mass number by 4; the passage describes beta emission.
¹³⁷₅₅Cs → ¹³⁷₅₄Xe + ⁰₊₁e + neutrino
This is positron emission, which lowers Z by 1; the passage's product, barium, has Z = 56.
¹³⁷₅₅Cs → ¹³⁶₅₅Cs + ¹₀n
This is neutron emission, which does not produce barium.
qs.x: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, raising Z from 55 to 56 and leaving the mass number at 137. Barium has Z = 56, and an electron and an antineutrino are emitted. Trap: Choosing a decay mode that changes Z in the wrong direction for the stated product.

qs.q: The source emits an unshielded net rate of 8000 counts/min today. What would the unshielded net rate be 60 years from now, ignoring background?
o: 2000 counts/min
Correct: 60 years is two half-lives of 30 years, so the rate is 8000 × (½)² = 2000 counts/min.
4000 counts/min
This applies only one half-life (30 years) instead of two.
1000 counts/min
This applies three half-lives, which corresponds to 90 years.
6000 counts/min
This subtracts a fixed amount of 2000 per 30 years, treating decay as linear rather than exponential.
qs.x: 60 years is two half-lives of 30 years, so the rate is 8000 × (½)² = 2000 counts/min. Trap: Treating radioactive decay as a linear decrease with time.

qs.q: The values of ln(rate) in Table 1 fall by about 0.69 for every 6.0 mm of lead. What does this show?
o: Each equal thickness of lead removes the same number of gamma rays per minute.
A constant number removed per layer would make the rate itself decrease linearly, which Figure 1 does not show.
Each equal thickness of lead removes the same fraction of the gamma rays that reach it, whatever the rate.
Correct: A constant decrease of ln(rate) per unit thickness means exponential attenuation: the same fraction (here one half per 6.0 mm) is removed from whatever reaches each layer.
Lead absorbs more of the beam as the beam becomes weaker.
The fraction removed per layer is constant, not larger, for a weaker beam.
Photons lose energy gradually, so their frequency drops with increasing thickness.
In the narrow-beam model the photons are either removed or transmitted unchanged; their energy is not gradually lowered.
qs.x: A constant decrease of ln(rate) per unit thickness means exponential attenuation: the same fraction (here one half per 6.0 mm) is removed from whatever reaches each layer. Trap: Confusing a constant fractional decrease with a constant absolute decrease.

graph.title: Figure 1. Net count rate versus lead thickness

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: When a high-energy electron removes a 1s electron from an atom, an electron from the n = 2 level can fall into the vacancy and emit an X-ray photon, called Kα radiation. In 1913 Moseley found that the frequency of this emission depends on the atomic number Z of the target element, which led to the modern periodic table ordered by Z. A simple model treats the outer electron as moving in the field of a nucleus whose charge is partly screened by the single remaining 1s electron, so that E(Kα) ≈ k(Z − 1)², where k is a constant. A laboratory measured the Kα energy of four known targets and of an unknown target X. Table 1 lists the results, along with the square root of each energy. Figure 1 plots the square root of E against Z. An energy in keV corresponds to a wavelength in nanometers of λ = 1.240 / E.

qs.q: Using Table 1 and the model in the passage, what is the atomic number of target X?
o: This subtracts 1 from the value of Z − 1 (33) instead of adding 1 to reach Z.
Correct: √E ≈ 0.1015(Z − 1) for the known targets (for Cu, 2.84/28 = 0.1015). For X, Z − 1 = 3.35/0.1015 ≈ 33, so Z = 34.
This is the value of Z − 1 itself, not Z.
This results from rounding √E/0.1015 up and adding 2 for screening.
qs.x: √E ≈ 0.1015(Z − 1) for the known targets (for Cu, 2.84/28 = 0.1015). For X, Z − 1 = 3.35/0.1015 ≈ 33, so Z = 34. Trap: Reporting Z − 1 as the atomic number.

qs.q: Which process produces Kα radiation?
o: An n = 1 electron is promoted to n = 2, absorbing a photon.
This is absorption, not emission, and it requires an empty n = 2 level.
An outer electron is removed from the atom, producing a free electron.
Ionization of an outer electron does not give a characteristic X-ray line.
An n = 2 electron falls into a vacancy in the n = 1 shell, emitting a photon.
Correct: Kα arises after a 1s electron is ejected: an electron from the L shell (n = 2) falls into the K-shell vacancy, and the energy difference is carried off by an X-ray photon.
The nucleus emits a photon as it drops from an excited nuclear state.
That would be gamma emission, not an atomic electron transition.
qs.x: Kα arises after a 1s electron is ejected: an electron from the L shell (n = 2) falls into the K-shell vacancy, and the energy difference is carried off by an X-ray photon. Trap: Confusing characteristic X-ray emission with nuclear gamma emission.

qs.q: The model uses (Z − 1) instead of Z. Which phrase best explains the −1?
o: One proton in the nucleus is neutralized by the electron that was removed from the atom.
The nuclear charge is unchanged by removing an electron.
Only Z − 1 of the electrons in the atom are able to fall into the vacancy.
The number of electrons that could transition does not enter the energy formula.
The remaining 1s electron screens one unit of nuclear charge.
Correct: The n = 2 electron sees the full nuclear charge Z reduced by about one unit because the other 1s electron lies between it and the nucleus.
The photon carries away one unit of charge from the atom when it is emitted.
Photons are uncharged and do not change the atom's charge.
qs.x: The n = 2 electron sees the full nuclear charge Z reduced by about one unit because the other 1s electron lies between it and the nucleus. Trap: Assuming screening comes from nuclear changes rather than other electrons.

qs.q: Using the relationship shown in Table 1 and Figure 1, what would be the approximate Kα energy of phosphorus (Z = 15)?
o: 2.3 keV
This uses Z rather than Z − 1 in the formula: (0.1015 × 15)² = 2.3.
1.4 keV
This reports √E = 1.42 as if it were the energy, without squaring.
0.14 keV
This results from using 0.1015 × 14 = 1.42 and then dividing by ten rather than squaring.
2.0 keV
qs.x: √E = 0.1015 × (15 − 1) = 1.42, so E = 1.42² ≈ 2.0 keV. Trap: Using Z in place of Z − 1 in the formula.

qs.q: What is the wavelength of the Kα radiation from the copper target?
o: 6.5 nm
This inverts the formula (E/1.240) and so gives the wrong order of magnitude.
This shifts the decimal place by one.
This results from using the energy in eV instead of keV in the formula.
qs.x: λ = 1.240 / E = 1.240 / 8.05 ≈ 0.154 nm. Trap: Inverting the wavelength-energy relationship.

graph.title: Figure 1. Square root of Kα energy versus atomic number

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: The autoionization of water, 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, is described by the ion-product constant Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻]. Kw is not truly constant; it depends on temperature. A physiology student measured the pH of pure, carbon-dioxide-free water at several temperatures with a calibrated electrode and then calculated Kw from the readings. In pure water the concentrations of H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ are equal, so a neutral solution has pH = ½ pKw. Table 1 gives Kw and the pH of neutral water at five temperatures, and Figure 1 plots the pH of neutral water against temperature. In the laboratory, solutions made for biological work are generally prepared and used near 37 °C rather than 25 °C, and the student wondered how this affects the meaning of a pH reading and what pH should be called neutral at body temperature. Assume all solutions are dilute enough that concentrations may be used in place of activities.

qs.q: What can be concluded about the autoionization of water from the trend in Table 1?
o: It is exothermic, because Kw increases as the temperature increases.
An exothermic reaction would have an equilibrium constant that decreases with increasing temperature.
It is endothermic, because Kw increases with temperature.
Correct: Raising the temperature shifts an endothermic equilibrium toward products. Kw increases from 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ at 0 °C to 5.1 × 10⁻¹³ at 100 °C, so autoionization absorbs heat.
It is endothermic, because the pH of neutral water increases as the temperature increases.
The pH of neutral water decreases with temperature in Table 1.
Its enthalpy change is zero, because water remains neutral at every temperature.
Water stays neutral because [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], but that does not imply a zero enthalpy change.
qs.x: Raising the temperature shifts an endothermic equilibrium toward products. Kw increases from 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ at 0 °C to 5.1 × 10⁻¹³ at 100 °C, so autoionization absorbs heat. Trap: Equating 'neutral' with pH 7 at every temperature.

qs.q: What is the pH of a 1.0 × 10⁻³ M NaOH solution at 37 °C?
o: This applies the 25 °C relationship pH = 14 − pOH instead of the value of pKw at 37 °C.
This subtracts the pOH from 13.38, using an arithmetic error in pKw.
This is the pOH of the solution, not its pH.
qs.x: At 37 °C, pKw = −log(2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 13.62. [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M, so pOH = 3.00, and pH = 13.62 − 3.00 = 10.62. Trap: Using pH + pOH = 14 at temperatures other than 25 °C.

qs.q: At 50 °C, a solution is found to have a pH of 6.8. This solution is best described as:
o: slightly basic, since its pH exceeds neutral at 50 °C.
Correct: Neutral water at 50 °C has pH 6.63. A solution with pH 6.8 has a lower [H₃O⁺] than neutral water, so [OH⁻] > [H₃O⁺] and the solution is slightly basic.
acidic, because its pH of 6.8 is below the familiar neutral value of 7.00.
The definition of neutrality at 50 °C is pH 6.63, not 7.
neutral, because its pH is within 0.2 of 7 and so close to the neutral point.
Neutrality is defined by [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], which occurs at pH 6.63 at this temperature.
strongly acidic, because pH values below 7 indicate a high H₃O⁺ concentration.
A pH of 6.8 is far from strongly acidic by any definition.
qs.x: Neutral water at 50 °C has pH 6.63. A solution with pH 6.8 has a lower [H₃O⁺] than neutral water, so [OH⁻] > [H₃O⁺] and the solution is slightly basic. Trap: Using pH 7 as the neutral point at all temperatures.

qs.q: By what factor is [H₃O⁺] in neutral water at 100 °C greater than in neutral water at 25 °C?
o: This is the ratio of the Kw values, which is the ratio of products of two concentrations, not of one.
This is the inverse of the correct factor, which would indicate a decrease.
Correct: In neutral water [H₃O⁺] = √Kw. The ratio is √(5.1 × 10⁻¹³ / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = √51 ≈ 7.1 (pH 6.14 vs 7.00 differ by 0.86, and 10^0.86 ≈ 7.2).
This is the difference between the pH values of the two solutions, not the ratio of concentrations.
qs.x: In neutral water [H₃O⁺] = √Kw. The ratio is √(5.1 × 10⁻¹³ / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) = √51 ≈ 7.1 (pH 6.14 vs 7.00 differ by 0.86, and 10^0.86 ≈ 7.2). Trap: Using the ratio of Kw values for the ratio of H₃O⁺ concentrations.

qs.q: What is [H₃O⁺] in neutral water at 0 °C?
o: Correct: [H₃O⁺] = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ M, in agreement with to the table value of pH 7.47 (10⁻⁷·⁴⁷ ≈ 3.4 × 10⁻⁸ M).
