This is Kw itself, not the square root of Kw.
This is the value at 25 °C and ignores the temperature dependence.
This is off by a factor of 10 from the square root of 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵.
qs.x: [H₃O⁺] = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ M, in agreement with to the table value of pH 7.47 (10⁻⁷·⁴⁷ ≈ 3.4 × 10⁻⁸ M). Trap: Reporting Kw or its 25 °C value instead of its square root at the stated temperature.

graph.title: Figure 1. pH of neutral water versus temperature

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: Fatty acids are carboxylic acids with long unbranched hydrocarbon tails. Their melting points influence the fluidity of the membranes and fats they form. Researchers compared the melting points of several fatty acids with chains of 12 to 18 carbons. Saturated fatty acids have only single carbon-carbon bonds in the tail. Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more double bonds. Naturally occurring double bonds are nearly always cis, which puts a rigid bend in the chain. Elaidic acid is the trans isomer of oleic acid, and it is produced during the partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils. Table 1 lists the number of carbons, the number and geometry of double bonds, and the melting point of each acid. In the solid state fatty acids pack in layers, with pairs of carboxyl groups held together by hydrogen bonds. Melting requires enough thermal energy to overcome the attractions between neighboring molecules, so stronger or more extensive contacts between chains should produce a higher melting point.

qs.q: Which intermolecular force best explains the increase in melting point from lauric acid to stearic acid?
o: Stronger hydrogen bonding between the carboxyl groups of longer chains.
Each molecule has one carboxyl group regardless of chain length, so hydrogen bonding per molecule does not change.
Stronger ion-dipole attractions between the tails and the surrounding solvent.
The acids melt as pure solids; no solvent or ions are involved.
Greater London dispersion forces between the longer tails.
Correct: Each additional CH₂ group adds surface area and polarizability, so dispersion forces between adjacent tails grow stronger and more energy is needed to melt the solid.
Stronger covalent bonding between neighboring molecules in the solid.
Melting disrupts intermolecular attractions only; covalent bonds within molecules remain intact.
qs.x: Each additional CH₂ group adds surface area and polarizability, so dispersion forces between adjacent tails grow stronger and more energy is needed to melt the solid. Trap: Attributing a trend in chain length to hydrogen bonding at the unchanging carboxyl group.

qs.q: Why is the melting point of oleic acid (18:1, cis) much lower than that of stearic acid (18:0)?
o: The cis double bond kinks the chain, so the molecules pack less tightly and have weaker contact between tails.
Correct: Both have 18 carbons and one carboxyl group. The cis double bond puts a bend in the tail, which prevents close packing and lowers the dispersion contacts between neighbors.
The double bond makes the molecule more polar, so it is more soluble in water and melts sooner.
A single C=C bond adds little polarity and solubility is not what determines melting of the pure solid.
Oleic acid has fewer carbons than stearic acid, so it has weaker dispersion forces.
Both acids have 18 carbons.
The double bond blocks the carboxyl group from forming hydrogen bonds.
Both acids retain a carboxyl group and the ability to hydrogen bond.
qs.x: Both have 18 carbons and one carboxyl group. The cis double bond puts a bend in the tail, which prevents close packing and lowers the dispersion contacts between neighbors. Trap: Assuming that any double bond lowers the melting point through polarity.

qs.q: Elaidic acid (trans) melts at 45 °C, much higher than oleic acid (cis). What is the best explanation?
o: The trans isomer has more carbons than oleic acid and therefore stronger dispersion forces.
The two isomers have the same formula and the same number of carbons.
The trans isomer has stronger hydrogen bonds because its carboxyl group sits in a different position.
The carboxyl group is at the same position in both isomers.
The trans bond leaves the chain nearly straight, so molecules pack closely.
Correct: A trans double bond keeps the tail extended, resembling a saturated chain. Tight packing in the solid raises the melting point toward that of stearic acid (70 °C).
The trans isomer forms covalent cross-links between neighboring chains in the solid state.
No covalent cross-links form in a pure fatty acid solid.
qs.x: A trans double bond keeps the tail extended, resembling a saturated chain. Tight packing in the solid raises the melting point toward that of stearic acid (70 °C). Trap: Thinking that isomers differing only in geometry differ in carbon count or functional group.

qs.q: Based on the trend for saturated acids in Table 1, which melting point is the most reasonable estimate for arachidic acid (20:0)?
o: This equals the melting point of stearic acid and assumes no increase with two more carbons.
This extrapolates the early increments of about 10 °C per two carbons, though the increments shrink to 7 °C by stearic acid.
This assumes the melting point falls as the chain gets longer, opposite to the trend.
Correct: The increments for each added pair of carbons are 10, 9, and 7 °C, and are decreasing. An increase of about 5 °C gives roughly 75 °C for a chain of 20 carbons.
qs.x: The increments for each added pair of carbons are 10, 9, and 7 °C, and are decreasing. An increase of about 5 °C gives roughly 75 °C for a chain of 20 carbons. Trap: Extrapolating a linear trend when the increments are clearly shrinking.

qs.q: Compared with a hydrocarbon of similar size, a fatty acid melts at a higher temperature primarily because the carboxyl groups of two molecules can:
o: form a hydrogen-bonded pair in addition to the dispersion forces between tails.
Correct: The O–H of one carboxyl group donates a hydrogen bond to the C=O of its partner, forming cyclic dimers. This adds to the dispersion forces and raises the melting point.
form ionic bonds with each other, producing a salt.
The carboxylic acid is neutral in the pure solid and does not form ionic bonds.
form covalent bonds that join the pairs into a polymer.
No covalent bond forms between fatty acid molecules on melting or freezing.
repel each other, which pushes the molecules into an ordered lattice.
Repulsion would not stabilize the solid; hydrogen bonding is the attraction involved.
qs.x: The O–H of one carboxyl group donates a hydrogen bond to the C=O of its partner, forming cyclic dimers. This adds to the dispersion forces and raises the melting point. Trap: Treating hydrogen bonding as an ionic or covalent interaction.

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: Caffeine can be removed from an aqueous solution by liquid-liquid extraction with dichloromethane, an organic solvent that is denser than water and not miscible with it. A student shakes 100 mL of an aqueous solution containing 0.500 g of caffeine with dichloromethane in a separatory funnel, lets the layers separate, and drains the lower layer. Caffeine distributes between the two phases according to the partition coefficient K = [caffeine in dichloromethane] / [caffeine in water], which is 4.6 at the temperature used. For an aqueous volume Va extracted with an organic volume Vo, the fraction of the solute that remains in the aqueous phase after one extraction is 1 / (1 + K·Vo/Va). The student compares three procedures that use a total of 100 mL of dichloromethane. Table 1 gives the fraction of caffeine remaining in the water and the total mass of caffeine collected in the organic phase. In each case equilibrium is reached before the layers are separated, and the organic portions are combined.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why four 25 mL extractions recover more caffeine than one 100 mL extraction?
o: A smaller volume of solvent has a larger partition coefficient for caffeine, so more solute enters each portion.
K is a property of the solute and the two solvents; it does not change with the volume used.
Each fresh solvent portion re-establishes equilibrium and removes the same fraction of what remains.
Correct: Each extraction removes a fixed fraction of what is left. Fractions multiply, and (0.465)⁴ is smaller than 0.179 for the same total solvent volume.
Smaller portions dissolve a greater mass of caffeine per milliliter of solvent because they reach saturation sooner.
The extraction operates far below saturation, and the gain does not result from solubility limits.
The caffeine is chemically changed by repeated shaking, which converts it to a form that moves into the organic layer.
Shaking only helps the solute reach equilibrium; no chemical change occurs.
qs.x: Each extraction removes a fixed fraction of what is left. Fractions multiply, and (0.465)⁴ is smaller than 0.179 for the same total solvent volume. Trap: Believing that the partition coefficient depends on how the solvent is divided.

qs.q: According to Table 1, how much caffeine remains in the aqueous layer after the single 100 mL extraction?
o: This is the mass collected in the organic layer, not the mass left in the water.
Correct: 0.500 g − 0.411 g = 0.089 g, consistent with 0.500 g × 0.179 = 0.0895 g.
This results from dividing the starting mass by K (0.500 / 4.6), which is not how the partition is calculated.
This is the fraction remaining, 0.179, read as a mass in grams.
qs.x: 0.500 g − 0.411 g = 0.089 g, consistent with 0.500 g × 0.179 = 0.0895 g. Trap: Reading a fraction as a mass or dividing by K.

qs.q: Using the fractions in Table 1, how much caffeine is left in the aqueous phase after the two 50 mL extractions?
o: This is the mass collected in the organic phase for the 2 × 50 mL procedure, not the mass left in water.
Correct: The fraction remaining is 0.092, so the mass left is 0.500 g × 0.092 ≈ 0.046 g, which equals 0.500 g − 0.454 g.
This is the fraction remaining, 0.092, read as a mass in grams.
This assumes caffeine is split evenly between the phases, which ignores K = 4.6.
qs.x: The fraction remaining is 0.092, so the mass left is 0.500 g × 0.092 ≈ 0.046 g, which equals 0.500 g − 0.454 g. Trap: Reporting the collected mass or the fraction instead of the mass left behind.

qs.q: After the layers separate in the separatory funnel, where is most of the caffeine found?
o: In the upper layer, which is the dichloromethane.
Dichloromethane is denser than water, so it forms the lower layer.
In the lower layer, which is the dichloromethane.
Correct: Because K > 1, caffeine favors dichloromethane, and since dichloromethane is denser than water, it is drained from the bottom of the funnel.
In the lower layer, which is the water.
The lower layer is the denser solvent, dichloromethane, not the water.
Evenly in both layers, because K is greater than 1.
K = 4.6 means caffeine is about 4.6 times more concentrated in the organic phase, so the distribution is not equal.
qs.x: Because K > 1, caffeine favors dichloromethane, and since dichloromethane is denser than water, it is drained from the bottom of the funnel. Trap: Assuming the organic layer is always on top.

qs.q: Adding sodium chloride to the aqueous layer before extracting (salting out) is expected to increase the amount of caffeine collected. The most likely reason is that the added salt:
o: makes caffeine less soluble in the aqueous phase, increasing the effective partition coefficient.
Correct: Dissolved ions tie up water molecules, so less water is available to dissolve a neutral organic solute. More caffeine moves into dichloromethane, effectively raising K.
reacts with caffeine to form a salt that dissolves in dichloromethane.
Sodium chloride does not react with neutral caffeine, and an ionic product would favor water, not dichloromethane.
increases the solubility of dichloromethane in water, enlarging the organic phase.
Salt lowers the mutual solubility of the two solvents.
lowers the density of water so that the layers separate faster.
Dissolved salt raises the density of water; the effect on extraction is not due to density.
qs.x: Dissolved ions tie up water molecules, so less water is available to dissolve a neutral organic solute. More caffeine moves into dichloromethane, effectively raising K. Trap: Assuming that added salt must react chemically with the solute.

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: Esters can be made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol under acid catalysis, a process called Fischer esterification. In one study, acetic acid reacted with ethanol in the presence of a catalytic amount of concentrated sulfuric acid: CH₃CO₂H + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃CO₂CH₂CH₃ + H₂O. The mixtures were heated until no further change occurred, and the equilibrium constant at the reaction temperature was Keq ≈ 4.0. The mechanism begins when the catalyst protonates the carbonyl oxygen of the acid. The alcohol then adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate, and proton transfers followed by loss of water give the ester. Each mixture began with 1.00 mol of acetic acid and varying amounts of ethanol. Table 1 gives the moles of ester present at equilibrium, calculated from Keq, for each ratio. In one additional experiment, ethanol enriched in oxygen-18 was used, and the labeled oxygen was tracked by mass spectrometry in the products.

qs.q: What is the role of the sulfuric acid in this reaction?
o: It protonates the carbonyl oxygen, activating the carbon toward attack, and is regenerated.
Correct: Protonation of the C=O increases the partial positive charge on carbon, so the weakly nucleophilic alcohol can add. The proton is returned at the end, so the acid is a catalyst.
It deprotonates the alcohol to make it a stronger nucleophile, and it is consumed in the reaction.
Under strongly acidic conditions the alcohol is not deprotonated, and a catalyst is not consumed.
It shifts the equilibrium constant toward the ester by absorbing the water that is produced during the reaction.
A catalyst changes the rate, not the value of Keq, and the equilibrium is the same without it.
It oxidizes the alcohol to an aldehyde, which then adds to the carboxylic acid to form the ester.
The reaction does not involve oxidation of the alcohol.
qs.x: Protonation of the C=O increases the partial positive charge on carbon, so the weakly nucleophilic alcohol can add. The proton is returned at the end, so the acid is a catalyst. Trap: Assuming a catalyst alters the equilibrium constant or is consumed.

qs.q: Why does using 10.0 mol of ethanol give a higher yield of ester than using 1.00 mol?
o: Increasing a reactant concentration shifts the equilibrium toward products.
Correct: Le Chatelier's principle applies: more of one reactant drives the reaction forward until Q = Keq again, so more acid is converted (0.97 mol versus 0.67 mol).
The excess ethanol increases the value of Keq at the reaction temperature.
Keq depends only on temperature, and it is given as constant (4.0).
The excess ethanol acts as a catalyst and lowers the activation energy.
The excess affects the position of equilibrium, not the rate or activation energy.
The excess ethanol absorbs the water, converting it to ethyl acetate.
Water is not converted to the ester; the reaction is not changed by this route.
qs.x: Le Chatelier's principle applies: more of one reactant drives the reaction forward until Q = Keq again, so more acid is converted (0.97 mol versus 0.67 mol). Trap: Believing that adding reactant changes the equilibrium constant.

qs.q: In the oxygen-18 experiment, the labeled oxygen of ethanol would be found in:
o: the water only, because the alcohol hydroxyl group is lost.
The water formed comes from the carboxylic acid's OH group and the carbonyl oxygen after protonation, not from the alcohol.
both the ester and the water, in equal amounts.
The alcohol oxygen is incorporated into the ester and is not lost.
the ester only, on the ethyl group.
Correct: The alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon and stays bonded to the ethyl group. The water that leaves is derived from the acid, so the label ends up in the ester.
neither product, because it exchanges with the sulfuric acid.
The oxygen of the alcohol stays bonded to its carbon throughout.
qs.x: The alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon and stays bonded to the ethyl group. The water that leaves is derived from the acid, so the label ends up in the ester. Trap: Assuming water is formed from the alcohol hydroxyl group.

qs.q: Which change, with the reagent ratio kept at 1:1, would most increase the ester yield above 0.67 mol?
o: Increasing the amount of sulfuric acid catalyst tenfold.
A larger amount of catalyst speeds approach to equilibrium but does not change the equilibrium yield.
Lowering the reaction temperature to slow the reverse reaction only.
Lowering the temperature slows both the forward and reverse reactions and does not by itself raise the yield.
Removing water as it forms, for example with molecular sieves.
Correct: Water is a product. Removing it keeps Q below Keq, so the reaction continues forward and the yield can approach 1.00 mol.
Heating for less time once equilibrium is reached.
The mixture is already at equilibrium; shortening the heating time cannot give more ester.
qs.x: Water is a product. Removing it keeps Q below Keq, so the reaction continues forward and the yield can approach 1.00 mol. Trap: Confusing speeding up the approach to equilibrium with moving the equilibrium.

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: The acidity of benzoic acid derivatives depends on substituents on the ring. A substituent that stabilizes the benzoate anion makes the acid stronger. Hammett substituent constants (σ) describe the electron-donating or electron-withdrawing effect of a group at the para position, with σ = 0 for hydrogen, positive values for electron-withdrawing groups, and negative values for electron-donating groups. For the ionization of benzoic acids in water at 25 °C, a plot of pKa against σ is a straight line with a slope of about −1.0. A chemist compared six para-substituted benzoic acids, as listed in Table 1. The pKa values were measured by titration and σ values were taken from the reference column. Figure 1 shows pKa as a function of σ. A group that withdraws electrons through both inductive and resonance effects can delocalize the negative charge of the carboxylate. A group that donates electrons by resonance has the opposite effect.

qs.q: Which acid in Table 1 has the greatest tendency to ionize in water?
o: p-Nitrobenzoic acid, since its group best stabilizes the anion.
Correct: The strongest acid has the lowest pKa, 3.44 for the nitro compound, which has the largest positive σ (0.78). Delocalizing the carboxylate charge stabilizes the anion.
p-Methoxybenzoic acid, because the methoxy group donates electron density to the carboxylate.
Donation of electron density destabilizes the carboxylate and gives the highest pKa, the weakest acid.
Benzoic acid, because it has no substituent to interfere with ionization.
Benzoic acid has a pKa of 4.20, higher than five of the others, so it is weaker than several.
p-Chlorobenzoic acid, because chlorine has the largest σ of the six groups.
Chlorine's σ is 0.23, smaller than that of CN or NO₂.
qs.x: The strongest acid has the lowest pKa, 3.44 for the nitro compound, which has the largest positive σ (0.78). Delocalizing the carboxylate charge stabilizes the anion. Trap: Selecting the acid with the highest pKa as the strongest.

qs.q: How many times larger is Ka for p-nitrobenzoic acid than for benzoic acid?
o: This is the difference in pKa values, not the ratio of Ka values.
This is the inverse of the correct ratio, showing the p-nitro acid as weaker.
This is 10^1.76, adding 1 to the exponent by an arithmetic slip.
qs.x: Ka ratio = 10^(4.20 − 3.44) = 10^0.76 ≈ 5.8. Trap: Reporting the pKa difference as a ratio.

qs.q: A substituent has σ = +0.35. Using the line in Figure 1, what pKa would be predicted for the corresponding para-substituted benzoic acid?
o: This adds σ to 4.20 rather than subtracting, reversing the slope of the line.
This is the pKa for σ = 0.66 (CN), not for 0.35.
Correct: The slope is about −1.0 and the intercept is 4.20, so pKa ≈ 4.20 − 0.35 = 3.85.
This reports σ itself as a pKa.
qs.x: The slope is about −1.0 and the intercept is 4.20, so pKa ≈ 4.20 − 0.35 = 3.85. Trap: Using a positive slope when the plot clearly decreases.

qs.q: Why does a para-methoxy group raise the pKa of benzoic acid above 4.20?
o: It withdraws electron density through the sigma bond, which stabilizes the carboxylate.
Methoxy is a net donor at the para position, as shown by its negative σ.
It protonates the carboxylate group, which prevents ionization.
An ether oxygen is not acidic enough to protonate the carboxylate in water.
It increases the size of the molecule, so it is less soluble in water.
Solubility does not determine pKa, which describes equilibrium of the dissolved species.
It donates electron density by resonance, which destabilizes the negatively charged carboxylate.
Correct: A negative σ means electron donation. The extra electron density on the ring opposes the delocalization of negative charge, so the anion is less stable and the acid is weaker.
qs.x: A negative σ means electron donation. The extra electron density on the ring opposes the delocalization of negative charge, so the anion is less stable and the acid is weaker. Trap: Treating oxygen-containing groups as electron-withdrawing in all cases.

graph.title: Figure 1. pKa of para-substituted benzoic acids versus Hammett σ

passages.title: Mini05 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: Surfactants such as sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) have a charged sulfate head group and a long hydrocarbon tail. In water the molecules gather at the air-water interface, with the tails directed toward the air. This lowers the surface tension, which is a measure of the energy cost of exposing the interface. At a concentration called the critical micelle concentration (CMC), the molecules also begin to assemble into spherical micelles, in which the tails form a hydrocarbon core and the head groups face the water. A student measured the surface tension of SDS solutions at 25 °C with a tensiometer. Pure water has a surface tension of 72 mN/m. The data are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. A second series of experiments was carried out in 0.10 M sodium chloride, and the break in the curve appeared at a lower SDS concentration than in pure water, while the plateau value of the surface tension was nearly unchanged.

qs.q: Why does adding SDS lower the surface tension of water below 8 mM?
o: SDS dissolves in the bulk and strengthens the hydrogen-bond network among the water molecules at the surface.
Strengthening the surface network would raise the surface tension, not lower it.
SDS molecules react with dissolved gases at the surface, which removes the inward pull on surface water.
No such chemical reaction is involved in surface activity.
SDS forms micelles at every concentration, and these shield the surface from the water beneath it.
Micelles form only at and above the CMC, and the tension drops below that point.
SDS adsorbs at the surface and replaces water there, reducing cohesive hydrogen bonding.
Correct: Surface water molecules are pulled inward by hydrogen bonds. SDS tails at the surface interact only weakly with the air and with each other, which lowers the energy cost of the interface.
qs.x: Surface water molecules are pulled inward by hydrogen bonds. SDS tails at the surface interact only weakly with the air and with each other, which lowers the energy cost of the interface. Trap: Assuming a solute always raises surface tension by increasing the solution's cohesion.

qs.q: Why does the surface tension remain at 38 mN/m for concentrations above about 8 mM?
o: The surface becomes saturated with water molecules that block further SDS adsorption.
The surface is saturated with SDS monomers, not with water.
The SDS molecules stop dissolving because the solution is supersaturated with them.
The added SDS remains in solution as micelles; it does not precipitate.
Added SDS forms micelles in the bulk, so the concentration of free monomer at the surface stays roughly constant.
Correct: Above the CMC, extra surfactant goes into micelles. The free monomer concentration, which sets the surface coverage and the tension, stays near its value at the CMC.
The SDS molecules decompose when the concentration exceeds the CMC.
SDS is chemically stable under these conditions and does not decompose at higher concentration.
qs.x: Above the CMC, extra surfactant goes into micelles. The free monomer concentration, which sets the surface coverage and the tension, stays near its value at the CMC. Trap: Thinking the plateau means the surfactant has stopped dissolving.

qs.q: What is the approximate CMC of SDS in pure water, according to Figure 1?
o: 4 mM
This is the concentration at which the surface tension is 52 mN/m, in the middle of the falling portion.
20 mM
This is the highest concentration measured, well into the plateau.
38 mM
This is the value of the surface tension on the plateau, not a concentration.
8 mM
Correct: The CMC is where the curve breaks from a steep decrease to a plateau. The tension reaches 38 mN/m at 8 mM and does not change thereafter.
qs.x: The CMC is where the curve breaks from a steep decrease to a plateau. The tension reaches 38 mN/m at 8 mM and does not change thereafter. Trap: Reading the plateau's y-value as the concentration.

qs.q: In 0.10 M NaCl, the CMC of SDS is lower than in pure water. Which explanation is most consistent with this?
o: The chloride ions bond covalently to the hydrocarbon tails, which makes the tails more hydrophobic and favors micelles.
Chloride does not form covalent bonds with hydrocarbon tails.
The added salt raises the surface tension of the water, which pushes SDS molecules out of the surface into micelles.
The reasoning is incorrect; salt has a small effect on surface tension and does not drive micelle formation this way.
The sodium ions convert SDS into a nonionic surfactant that can no longer adsorb at the air-water surface.
SDS remains an anionic surfactant in the presence of sodium ions.
Ions screen repulsion between the sulfate head groups, so micelles form at lower SDS concentration.
Correct: Micelles bring many negatively charged heads into close contact. Counterions shield the electrostatic repulsion among heads, which lowers the energetic cost and lowers the CMC.
qs.x: Micelles bring many negatively charged heads into close contact. Counterions shield the electrostatic repulsion among heads, which lowers the energetic cost and lowers the CMC. Trap: Believing that ions alter the tails rather than screening the charged head groups.

graph.title: Figure 1. Surface tension versus SDS concentration

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Group polarization is the tendency for group discussion to strengthen the position members held beforehand. Researchers recruited 120 undergraduates and formed 24 five-person groups, each made up of members whose private ratings of a risky financial option were similar. Each participant first rated, on a scale from 1 (never) to 9 (definitely), willingness to take the option. Twelve groups (discussion condition) then talked for 15 minutes about whether the option was wise. The other 12 groups (control condition) sat in the same room for 15 minutes working on unrelated puzzles without talking. Everyone then rated the option again, privately. A group was classed as risk-leaning if its mean first rating exceeded 5 and cautious-leaning if it was below 5. Coders also tallied arguments voiced in the discussion groups: 78% of arguments in risk-leaning groups favored the option, and 74% of arguments in cautious-leaning groups opposed it. Table 1 and Figure 1 show group-level means.

qs.q: Which result in Table 1 best demonstrates group polarization?
o: Both kinds of discussion group moved toward the scale midpoint after talking, reflecting a compromise among members.
Movement toward 5 would indicate convergence; the discussion means moved away from 5 in both subgroups.
Discussion groups ended farther from the scale midpoint in the direction of their initial lean, whereas control groups barely changed.
Correct: Risk-leaning discussion groups rose from 6.2 to 7.4 and cautious-leaning discussion groups fell from 3.8 to 2.7, both moving away from 5, while controls stayed essentially flat.
Every group, including those that never talked, became more extreme after 15 minutes, so the change reflects time alone.
Control groups changed by 0.1 point or less, so time and repeated rating did not produce the shifts.
After discussion, risk-leaning and cautious-leaning groups became more similar to each other than they had been before.
The gap between lean types widened (about 2.4 points before, 4.7 after), so the groups became less similar.
qs.x: Risk-leaning discussion groups rose from 6.2 to 7.4 and cautious-leaning discussion groups fell from 3.8 to 2.7, both moving away from 5, while controls stayed essentially flat. Trap: Assuming that any change after discussion is a compromise toward the middle, instead of checking the direction of each group's shift.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the control condition in this study?
o: To guarantee that participants in the discussion condition had been assigned to groups of the same size as the other condition.
Group sizes were fixed at five in both conditions by design; the control does not serve this function.
To supply the coded arguments that allowed researchers to estimate how persuasive each position was in the discussion groups.
Only the discussion groups produced arguments to code; control groups did not talk.
To show that the shifts seen in the discussion groups were not produced merely by the passage of time and rating the option twice.
Correct: Control groups had the same delay, setting, and repeated rating but no discussion, so any difference from the discussion groups can be attributed to talking.
To remove demand characteristics entirely, since control participants cannot guess the hypothesis being tested by the researchers.
Control participants can still form guesses about the study, so demand characteristics are not eliminated.
qs.x: Control groups had the same delay, setting, and repeated rating but no discussion, so any difference from the discussion groups can be attributed to talking. Trap: Treating a control group as a way to remove every bias rather than as a baseline for the manipulated variable.

qs.q: Which additional finding would favor the persuasive-arguments explanation of polarization over a social-comparison explanation?
o: Polarization occurred only when members learned how their own ratings compared with the ratings of the other group members.
This outcome depends on seeing others' ratings, which is what a social-comparison account predicts.
Groups polarized even when members heard one another's arguments but never learned each other's ratings.
Correct: If arguments alone, without information about others' positions, produce a shift, then exposure to novel arguments rather than comparison with others is the driver.
Polarization was larger in groups whose members said they liked and wanted to impress one another.
Stronger effects with greater liking and impression management fit a social-comparison account.
Polarization vanished when members were told the group's average rating before they spoke.
Disappearance when only the average is known would suggest that comparison information, not arguments, matters.
qs.x: If arguments alone, without information about others' positions, produce a shift, then exposure to novel arguments rather than comparison with others is the driver. Trap: Choosing a result that fits both explanations rather than one that separates them.

qs.q: Why did the researchers treat the 12 groups per condition, rather than the 60 individuals, as the units of analysis?
o: Ratings on a 9-point scale are too coarse to be compared across individual participants in a meaningful way.
Scale coarseness is not the issue; individual ratings could still be analyzed if they were independent.
Averaging within groups removes the influence of initial lean, which would otherwise hide the effect of discussion.
Initial lean was used to classify groups and is still visible in the means, so it is not removed.
After discussion, members influenced one another, so their ratings are not independent observations.
Correct: Independence of observations is a core assumption of standard tests; using individuals would inflate the effective sample size and exaggerate significance.
Group means vary more than individual ratings, which lowers the risk of a Type I error in the comparison.
Group means actually vary less than individual scores, and the choice is about independence, not Type I error control per se.
qs.x: Independence of observations is a core assumption of standard tests; using individuals would inflate the effective sample size and exaggerate significance. Trap: Counting the 120 participants as 120 independent data points even though discussion makes group members' responses dependent.

qs.q: What was the average shift in the direction of initial lean across the two discussion subgroups?
o: 0.05 points
Subtracting the signed changes (+1.2 and -1.1) cancels the shifts and ignores their direction relative to lean.
2.30 points
Adding the two shifts gives the total, not the average.
0.58 points
Dividing the total by four rather than by two halves the correct average again.
1.15 points
Correct: Risk-leaning groups moved +1.2 in their lean direction and cautious-leaning groups moved 1.1 in theirs, so the average is (1.2 + 1.1) / 2 = 1.15.
qs.x: Risk-leaning groups moved +1.2 in their lean direction and cautious-leaning groups moved 1.1 in theirs, so the average is (1.2 + 1.1) / 2 = 1.15. Trap: Averaging signed changes (+1.2 and -1.1), which cancels two shifts that are both movements toward greater extremity.

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean willingness to take the risky option

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 2
text: The overjustification effect holds that rewarding an activity people already enjoy can reduce later interest in it. Researchers observed 90 children, ages 4 and 5, during one week of free play with markers and paper, and enrolled children who chose to draw for a substantial share of the time. A week later, children were randomly assigned to three conditions (n = 30 each). In the expected-reward condition, children were told before drawing that they would earn a certificate. In the unexpected-reward condition, children drew with no mention of a prize and were given a certificate afterward. In the no-reward condition, children drew and received nothing. Two weeks after that session, observers who did not know the conditions recorded the percentage of free-play time each child spent drawing. Table 1 lists condition means, with standard deviations in parentheses. Children whose parents had not consented to observation were not enrolled, and all children were treated kindly and given a small gift at the end of the study regardless of condition. Sessions took place in the same classroom with the same materials, and an adult stayed nearby in every session.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the drop in drawing time in the expected-reward group?
o: Children inferred that they had drawn for the certificate, which weakened their view of drawing as something they did because they enjoyed it.
Correct: This is the self-perception and overjustification account: a salient external reward becomes the perceived cause of the behavior, undermining intrinsic motivation.
Children felt dissonance about being paid too little for drawing and so changed their attitude toward the activity.
A small reward producing dissonance would predict more, not less, liking; the reward here was framed as a prize, and drawing time fell.
Children observed peers who stopped drawing after earning certificates and imitated that behavior during later free play.
There was no peer modeling in the design; children drew individually.
Repeated exposure to the markers caused habituation, so the children stopped responding to the drawing materials.
Habituation would also have affected the unexpected-reward and no-reward groups, whose drawing time stayed near baseline.
qs.x: This is the self-perception and overjustification account: a salient external reward becomes the perceived cause of the behavior, undermining intrinsic motivation. Trap: Reaching for a familiar concept (imitation or habituation) without checking whether the design could produce it in only one group.

qs.q: What is the main reason the study included an unexpected-reward group?
o: To see whether receiving a reward without expecting it lowers later interest.
Correct: The only difference between the expected-reward and unexpected-reward groups is whether the reward was anticipated while drawing, isolating expectation as the key factor.
To check that children in all three groups drew for equal amounts of time at baseline.
Baseline equivalence is checked with the baseline column, not with this extra group.
To serve as a placebo condition in which children cannot tell that they are being observed.
A placebo group is not defined by hidden observation, and observation was equal across groups anyway.
To determine whether the observers could correctly guess which condition each child had been in.
Observers were meant to be unaware of conditions; guessing accuracy was not the purpose.
qs.x: The only difference between the expected-reward and unexpected-reward groups is whether the reward was anticipated while drawing, isolating expectation as the key factor. Trap: Confusing a comparison group that isolates one variable with a baseline or blinding check.

qs.q: By what percentage did mean drawing time decrease from baseline to follow-up in the expected-reward group?
o: 27 is the absolute decrease in percentage points, not the percent decrease relative to baseline.
About 44%
Correct: The drop was 61 - 34 = 27 percentage points, and 27 / 61 is about 0.44, or 44% of the baseline value.
34 / 61 is about 56%, which is the share of baseline time remaining rather than the share lost.
27 / 34 is about 79%, which wrongly uses the follow-up value as the denominator.
qs.x: The drop was 61 - 34 = 27 percentage points, and 27 / 61 is about 0.44, or 44% of the baseline value. Trap: Reporting the point difference (27) as a percent decrease, or dividing by the follow-up value instead of the baseline.

qs.q: Which situation is most consistent with the overjustification effect?
o: A teenager who loved reading for fun joins a program that pays her for each book, then reads less on her own once the program ends.
Correct: An already enjoyed activity, a contingent expected reward, and a later decline in voluntary engagement is the pattern the effect describes.
A worker pays closer attention to details while a quarterly bonus is available, and relaxes when it is not offered.
Effort that tracks an available bonus shows ordinary extrinsic motivation, not erosion of an existing intrinsic interest.
A student given a surprise gift after a strong exam continues to study at the same rate as before.
An unexpected gift is not predicted to change interest, matching the unexpected-reward group.
A dog trained with treats sits reliably when a treat is visible but ignores the command when none is shown.
This is learned dependence on a reinforcer, not a loss of intrinsic interest in the activity.
qs.x: An already enjoyed activity, a contingent expected reward, and a later decline in voluntary engagement is the pattern the effect describes. Trap: Picking any example involving rewards without requiring prior intrinsic interest and a later drop after the reward.

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 3
text: Social comparison theory proposes that people evaluate themselves by comparing their abilities and outcomes with those of others. Eighty college students were told that a study concerned problem-solving styles. Each completed a short creativity test and then waited for results in a room with another 'participant' who was actually a trained confederate. The confederate revealed a score that was either better (upward) or worse (downward) than the participant's own, and was presented as either a student in the same major (similar) or in an unrelated major (dissimilar). A fifth group waited alone (control). Sixteen participants were randomly assigned to each of the five conditions. Afterward, all completed a 0 to 100 state self-esteem scale. Table 1 lists the results, and Figure 1 plots the four comparison conditions. The confederates followed a written script, wore similar clothing, and were rotated across conditions so that no single confederate was linked to one condition. Participants were fully informed about the study only after the final questionnaire.

qs.q: Which outcome in Table 1 is consistent with social comparison theory?
o: Downward comparison with a dissimilar student produced lower self-esteem than the control condition.
The downward dissimilar mean (71) was slightly above control (70), not below it.
Upward comparison with a dissimilar student produced higher self-esteem than the control condition.
The upward dissimilar mean (68) was below control (70), not above it.
Upward comparison with a similar student produced lower self-esteem than the control condition.
Correct: Falling behind a comparable other (58 versus 70 in control) lowers self-evaluation, as the theory predicts.
The control group showed higher self-esteem than every group that made a comparison.
Both downward conditions (76 and 71) exceeded the control mean of 70.
qs.x: Falling behind a comparable other (58 versus 70 in control) lowers self-evaluation, as the theory predicts. Trap: Assuming control must be the highest group, or ignoring which direction each comparison moved self-esteem relative to control.

qs.q: Why might upward comparison with a dissimilar student lower self-esteem less than upward comparison with a similar student?
o: Dissimilar students are likely to be perceived as less intelligent, which makes the participant feel more capable by contrast.
The mechanism is relevance of the standard, not a belief that the other student is less intelligent.
Participants in the dissimilar conditions had higher self-esteem before the study, so they had more to lose from the comparison.
Random assignment makes pre-existing self-esteem equal across conditions on average.
Dissimilar targets reduce the effect of the confederate's score because participants cannot hear what the confederate says.
Both conditions heard the same kind of score disclosure; hearing was not manipulated.
A dissimilar person is a less relevant standard, so that person's better performance says less about the participant's own ability.
Correct: Comparison matters most when the target is similar on relevant attributes; a different-major peer offers less diagnostic information about one's own standing.
qs.x: Comparison matters most when the target is similar on relevant attributes; a different-major peer offers less diagnostic information about one's own standing. Trap: Inventing a baseline difference between groups despite random assignment.

qs.q: Which statement about Figure 1 describes an interaction between comparison direction and similarity?
o: Both upward and downward comparisons lower self-esteem when the target is similar to the participant.
Downward comparison with a similar target gave the highest self-esteem (76), not a lowered score.
Self-esteem is higher in the dissimilar conditions regardless of whether the comparison is upward or downward.
Downward dissimilar (71) was below downward similar (76), so the statement fails for downward comparisons.
The effect of target similarity runs in opposite directions for upward and downward comparisons.
Correct: Upward comparison scored higher with dissimilar targets (68 versus 58), but downward comparison scored lower with dissimilar targets (71 versus 76), so the lines cross.
Upward and downward lines are parallel, showing that direction has an effect independent of similarity.
The lines are not parallel: they slope in opposite directions and cross.
qs.x: Upward comparison scored higher with dissimilar targets (68 versus 58), but downward comparison scored lower with dissimilar targets (71 versus 76), so the lines cross. Trap: Calling any two effects an interaction instead of checking whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.

qs.q: Because participants were deceived about the purpose of the study, what is the most important ethical step after data collection?
o: Destroying all data from participants in the upward-comparison conditions so that the lowered scores cannot be used.
Data are not discarded because they are unflattering; the issue is participant welfare.
Excluding participants who suspected the confederate from being told the true purpose of the study.
All participants, including those who suspected the confederate, are owed an explanation.
Debriefing participants about the deception and addressing any lowered self-esteem.
Correct: Deception is acceptable only when needed and when participants are fully informed afterward and any distress is mitigated.
Offering the control participants the opportunity to repeat the study in a comparison condition.
Offering a repeat does not address the deception or any harm already experienced.
qs.x: Deception is acceptable only when needed and when participants are fully informed afterward and any distress is mitigated. Trap: Confusing data quality procedures with obligations to the participants after deception.

qs.q: Using the standard error of the mean, which interval best approximates the 95% confidence interval for the upward-similar group?
o: 46 to 70 is the mean plus or minus 1 SD (12), the spread of individual scores rather than the uncertainty of the mean; it wrongly reaches the control mean.
55 to 61 uses only 1 SE on each side, a roughly 68% interval.
Correct: SE = SD / square root of n = 12 / 4 = 3, and 58 plus or minus about 2 SE (6 points) gives 52 to 64, which excludes the control mean of 70.
56 to 60 corresponds to about 0.7 SE and is too narrow for a 95% interval.
qs.x: SE = SD / square root of n = 12 / 4 = 3, and 58 plus or minus about 2 SE (6 points) gives 52 to 64, which excludes the control mean of 70. Trap: Using the standard deviation in place of the standard error, which widens the interval and makes the group look indistinguishable from control.

graph.title: Figure 1. State self-esteem by comparison direction and target similarity

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 4
text: Researchers tested whether teacher expectations influence student performance. At the start of the school year, teachers in 24 elementary classrooms (eight each in grades 1, 3, and 5) were told that a new test had identified about one in five students as 'bloomers' who were likely to show unusual intellectual growth. In fact, the bloomers had been chosen by lottery, and the test had not been scored. Eight months later, testers who did not know which students had been labeled gave an alternate form of the same ability test. Observers also recorded that teachers gave labeled first graders more feedback and more challenging assignments than their classmates. Table 1 shows the mean gain in test score (points) for labeled and unlabeled students. The classrooms came from three schools serving similar neighborhoods. Within each classroom, labeled students were chosen by lottery regardless of their earlier performance, and teachers were asked not to discuss the labels with students or parents.

qs.q: Why does the random selection of 'bloomers' allow the researchers to attribute gain differences to the label?
o: Random selection ensures that testers cannot tell which students were labeled when they score the tests.
Hiding labels from testers was a separate step; random selection does not blind anyone.
Random selection guarantees that teachers treat labeled and unlabeled students in the same way during the year.
Teachers evidently did not treat students alike; observers saw more feedback for labeled first graders.
Random selection increases the number of labeled students, which gives the study greater statistical power.
The labeled fraction was fixed at about one in five; randomization does not enlarge it.
Random selection makes labeled and unlabeled students similar in ability at the start, so the label is the only systematic difference.
Correct: Because the lottery is unrelated to ability, preexisting differences should balance out on average, supporting a causal claim about the label.
qs.x: Because the lottery is unrelated to ability, preexisting differences should balance out on average, supporting a causal claim about the label. Trap: Mixing up random assignment, which equates groups, with blinding, which prevents biased measurement.

qs.q: Why was it important that the testers did not know which students had been labeled?
o: So that labeled students would not realize they had been selected and change their own behavior.
Student awareness is a different concern; the students were never told about the labels.
So that the testers could be matched to classrooms with the same number of labeled students.
Matching testers to classrooms has nothing to do with blinding.
So that their own expectations could not influence how they administered or scored the tests.
Correct: Observer or experimenter bias is itself an expectancy effect; blinding testers prevents it from contaminating the outcome measure.
So that the alternate test form would be certain to measure the same ability as the original form.
Test-form equivalence is a property of the test, not of tester knowledge.
qs.x: Observer or experimenter bias is itself an expectancy effect; blinding testers prevents it from contaminating the outcome measure. Trap: Treating blinding as a way to hide information from participants rather than from the people who measure outcomes.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?
o: The advantage of labeled students was largest in grade 1 and was nearly absent by grade 5.
Correct: The labeled-minus-unlabeled gap was 5.8 points in grade 1, 0.7 in grade 3, and 0.3 in grade 5.
The new test accurately identified students who were about to show unusual intellectual growth.
The labels came from a lottery and the test was never scored, so it could not have predicted anything.
Teachers in grades 3 and 5 ignored the labels entirely and treated all students identically.
A small gap does not show that teachers ignored labels; the table has no behavioral data for those grades.
Unlabeled first graders showed no improvement in test scores over the eight months.
Unlabeled first graders gained 7.0 points, so they did improve.
qs.x: The labeled-minus-unlabeled gap was 5.8 points in grade 1, 0.7 in grade 3, and 0.3 in grade 5. Trap: Overstating a pattern in the data into a claim about teacher behavior or test accuracy that the table cannot support.

qs.q: Labeled first graders received more feedback and harder assignments and then gained more. Which concept does this sequence best illustrate?
o: The fundamental attribution error, in which observers explain students' performance by their dispositions rather than the situation.
The fundamental attribution error concerns explaining behavior, not expectations that change outcomes.
The halo effect, in which one positive trait colors judgments about unrelated traits of the same student.
The halo effect is about generalizing one trait; the key element here is behavior that confirms the label.
Confirmation bias in scoring, in which testers interpret ambiguous answers to fit what they expect.
Testers were blind to labels, so biased scoring cannot account for the result.
A self-fulfilling prophecy, in which an initially false expectation leads to behavior that makes it come true.
Correct: Teachers' expectations altered their treatment of students, which in turn produced the improvement the label had predicted.
qs.x: Teachers' expectations altered their treatment of students, which in turn produced the improvement the label had predicted. Trap: Choosing a social-cognition bias that describes a judgment rather than the loop from expectation to behavior to outcome.

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 5
text: To study how proximity affects friendship formation, researchers followed 500 first-year students who were randomly assigned to rooms along dormitory hallways. At the end of the first term, each student named close friends among hallmates. Researchers then coded pairs of hallmates as adjacent (rooms next to each other) or far (four or more doors apart), and as high or low in attitude similarity based on a questionnaire completed at orientation, before rooms were assigned. Table 1 gives the percentage of pairs in which at least one student named the other as a close friend, for the 1,000 pairs that were either adjacent or far apart. Figure 1 adds pairs two and three doors apart and shows friendship rates for all pairs by distance in doors. Students could request a room change after the first week, but fewer than 5% did so, and requests were not included in the analysis. Friendship reports were collected privately, and students did not see one another's answers.

qs.q: Which principle best explains why friendship rates decline with distance in Figure 1?
o: Cognitive dissonance, in which people change their attitudes after acting against them.
Dissonance is about conflict between attitudes and behavior and does not predict declining friendship with distance.
The mere exposure effect, in which repeated contact increases familiarity and liking.
Correct: Closer neighbors encounter each other more often, and repeated exposure tends to raise liking, which makes friendships more likely.
The bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each person's willingness to act.
The bystander effect concerns helping in emergencies.
Reciprocity of liking, in which people dislike anyone who does not first express interest in them.
Reciprocal liking can help friendships form but does not explain why distance matters.
qs.x: Closer neighbors encounter each other more often, and repeated exposure tends to raise liking, which makes friendships more likely. Trap: Selecting a well-known social psychology effect that does not address how frequency of contact changes attraction.

qs.q: What is the main advantage of randomly assigning students to rooms?
o: It guarantees that every pair of hallmates would have the same attitude similarity.
Random assignment of rooms does not equalize similarity between pairs; similarity varied across pairs.
It ensures that friendships formed in the dormitory are stronger than those formed elsewhere.
Nothing about room assignment tells us about friendships formed elsewhere.
It rules out the possibility that students chose to live near people they already liked.
Correct: Without random assignment, self-selection of neighbors could create the proximity-friendship link, so random assignment supports a causal reading of proximity.
It makes the sample of 500 students representative of all first-year students nationwide.
Representativeness depends on how students were sampled, not on room assignment.
qs.x: Without random assignment, self-selection of neighbors could create the proximity-friendship link, so random assignment supports a causal reading of proximity. Trap: Confusing random assignment, which supports internal validity, with random sampling, which supports generalization.

qs.q: Which conclusion is NOT justified by the study?
o: Pairs of adjacent hallmates were more likely to be friends than pairs far apart.
Adjacent pairs showed 38% and 17% friendship against 12% and 4% for far pairs, so this is justified.
Attitude similarity causes friendship, because similarity was measured, not manipulated, and friends may become alike over time.
Correct: Similarity was an observed characteristic; only room placement was randomized, so a causal claim about similarity is unsupported.
Far pairs with high similarity were more likely to be friends than far pairs with low similarity.
Far pairs with high similarity (12%) exceeded far pairs with low similarity (4%), so this is justified.
Friendship rates declined as the distance between rooms increased.
Figure 1 shows a steady decline across the four distance categories, so this is justified.
qs.x: Similarity was an observed characteristic; only room placement was randomized, so a causal claim about similarity is unsupported. Trap: Treating a correlational association between measured similarity and friendship as causal because the rest of the design was experimental.

qs.q: What percentage of all 500 adjacent pairs were friends?
o: 27.5% is the simple average of 38% and 17%, which ignores that there are more low-similarity pairs.
Correct: Friends among adjacent pairs = 0.38(200) + 0.17(300) = 76 + 51 = 127, and 127 / 500 = 25.4%, which is the value plotted at 1 door in Figure 1.
21.2% does not follow from weighting the two adjacent percentages by their numbers of pairs.
30.5% overweights the high-similarity pairs and does not match the table.
qs.x: Friends among adjacent pairs = 0.38(200) + 0.17(300) = 76 + 51 = 127, and 127 / 500 = 25.4%, which is the value plotted at 1 door in Figure 1. Trap: Averaging the two percentages without weighting by the number of pairs in each group.

qs.q: Which statement about the effect of proximity is supported by Table 1?
o: Proximity was associated with friendship only among pairs that were high in attitude similarity.
Among low-similarity pairs, adjacent pairs (17%) also exceeded far pairs (4%).
Far pairs with high similarity were more likely to be friends than adjacent pairs with low similarity.
Far high-similarity pairs were 12%, below adjacent low-similarity pairs at 17%.
Similarity was associated with friendship only among pairs that were adjacent.
Among far pairs, high similarity (12%) still exceeded low similarity (4%).
Proximity went with higher friendship rates at both similarity levels.
Correct: Adjacent pairs exceeded far pairs in both similarity levels (38 versus 12 and 17 versus 4).
qs.x: Adjacent pairs exceeded far pairs in both similarity levels (38 versus 12 and 17 versus 4). Trap: Inferring that an effect is limited to one subgroup after comparing only one pair of cells in the table.

graph.title: Figure 1. Friendship rate by distance between rooms
graph.x_label: Distance between rooms (doors apart; 4 = four or more)

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 6
text: Sociologists distinguish strong ties, close relationships maintained through frequent contact, from weak ties, acquaintances seen rarely. A researcher surveyed 400 workers who had started a new job within the previous year. Of these, 250 learned about the job through a personal contact; the others used advertisements or agencies. Contacts seen at least twice a week were coded as strong ties, and contacts seen once a year or less as weak ties. For each contact-based lead, respondents also reported whether the information was new, meaning that no one in their close circle knew of the opening. Respondents reported an average of 12 strong ties and 120 weak ties. Table 1 summarizes the 250 contact-based hires. Respondents were drawn from a random sample of employers in one region, and interviews were conducted by phone with trained interviewers. Industries and job levels were similar for strong-tie and weak-tie hires, according to the researcher.

qs.q: Why would weak ties tend to supply new information about job openings?
o: Acquaintances belong to social circles that do not overlap with the respondent's close friends, so they hear different things.
Correct: Weak ties act as bridges between otherwise separate networks (bridging social capital), carrying non-redundant information.
Acquaintances have more formal authority over hiring decisions than friends or relatives do.
Nothing in the study suggests weak ties hold more hiring power.
Strong ties are less trustworthy and therefore withhold information about openings from respondents.
Strong ties are typically more trusted; their information is simply more redundant.
People tell acquaintances more about their own lives, so weak ties know more about the respondent.
Weak ties by definition know less about the respondent, and the point concerns what they know about other networks.
qs.x: Weak ties act as bridges between otherwise separate networks (bridging social capital), carrying non-redundant information. Trap: Assuming weak ties are valuable because of power or trust, not because of their position in different networks.

qs.q: Of all the new leads reported in Table 1, approximately what percentage came through weak ties?
o: Correct: New leads: strong = 0.20 x 100 = 20; weak = 0.60 x 150 = 90. Weak share = 90 / 110, about 82%.
60% is the weak-tie rate of new leads within weak ties, not the share of all new leads.
36% is 90 / 250, the proportion of all hires who got a new lead through a weak tie.
18% is 20 / 110, the strong-tie share of new leads.
qs.x: New leads: strong = 0.20 x 100 = 20; weak = 0.60 x 150 = 90. Weak share = 90 / 110, about 82%. Trap: Using the within-group percentage (60%) as if it were the share of all new leads.

qs.q: About how many times more likely was a given strong tie than a given weak tie to produce a hire?
o: About 0.7 times
0.67 is 100 / 150, the ratio of total hires without adjusting for number of ties.
About 6.7 times

Correct: Per respondent, 12 strong ties yielded 100/400 hires on average and 120 weak ties yielded 150/400; per tie, 100/(400 x 12) is about 2.1% versus 150/(400 x 120), about 0.31%, a ratio of about 6.7.
About 10 times
10 is the ratio of the numbers of weak to strong ties, not of hire rates per tie.
About 1.5 times
1.5 is 150 / 100, which compares total hires and ignores the number of ties.
qs.x: Per respondent, 12 strong ties yielded 100/400 hires on average and 120 weak ties yielded 150/400; per tie, 100/(400 x 12) is about 2.1% versus 150/(400 x 120), about 0.31%, a ratio of about 6.7. Trap: Comparing raw hire counts and ignoring that respondents had ten times as many weak ties to draw from.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of surveying only workers who had recently found jobs?
o: The workers cannot report how frequently they see each contact, so tie strength cannot be determined.
Respondents can report frequency of contact, and the study coded tie type from it.
It cannot show how often each tie type failed to produce a job for unsuccessful searchers.
Correct: Sampling on a successful outcome omits unsuccessful searches, so the effectiveness of each tie type is not fully estimable.
The survey includes workers who used advertisements, which makes the contact-based sample too large.
The 250 contact-based hires were analyzed separately, so advertisement users do not inflate the sample.
Workers who changed jobs recently cannot report how many ties they have, so tie counts are unreliable.
Counting ties is a self-report issue but not the main design limitation described.
qs.x: Sampling on a successful outcome omits unsuccessful searches, so the effectiveness of each tie type is not fully estimable. Trap: Focusing on measurement details rather than the sampling-on-outcome problem that limits the conclusions.

qs.q: Who would most likely benefit from activating weak ties?
o: A widow who needs emotional comfort and practical help in the weeks after a loss.
Emotional support and practical care are typically provided by strong ties.
A graduate seeking openings in an industry where no close friend works.
Correct: Information from outside one's own circle is the main strength of weak ties.
A manager who needs to coordinate daily work with colleagues on her own team.
Daily coordination relies on frequent, dense contact within the team.
A student who wants a trusted friend to lend him money during a financial emergency.
Trust and willingness to lend money are characteristic of strong ties.
qs.x: Information from outside one's own circle is the main strength of weak ties. Trap: Choosing a scenario involving support or trust rather than access to new information.

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 7
text: Demographers compare age structures to anticipate social needs. Table 1 gives population (in millions) by broad age group for Country J in 1990 and 2020 and for Country K in 2020. Estimates come from national censuses adjusted for undercount. The total dependency ratio is the number of people aged 0 to 14 plus those aged 65 and older, per 100 people aged 15 to 64. Both countries have low death rates, and Country J had little net migration over the period. Figure 1 plots the total fertility rate (TFR, the average number of births per woman) for both countries; replacement-level fertility in low-mortality countries is about 2.1. Country K is a lower-middle-income country with a growing urban population and expanding school enrollment, whereas Country J is a high-income country with universal pension coverage financed by taxes on current workers. Ages were grouped by completed years at the census date, and all figures are rounded to the nearest million.

qs.q: What was the total dependency ratio of Country J in 2020?
o: About 36 per 100
45 / 125 is about 36, which divides by the total population instead of the working-age group.
About 38 per 100
30 / 80 is about 38, which counts only the older dependents.
About 19 per 100
15 / 80 is about 19, which counts only the child dependents.
About 56 per 100
Correct: Dependents = 15 + 30 = 45 and working-age = 80, so 45 / 80 = 0.5625, or about 56 per 100.
qs.x: Dependents = 15 + 30 = 45 and working-age = 80, so 45 / 80 = 0.5625, or about 56 per 100. Trap: Dividing dependents by the total population or counting only one dependent group instead of using the working-age group as the denominator.

qs.q: Between 1990 and 2020, the total population of Country J grew from 110 million to 125 million. Which statement is supported by Table 1?
o: Growth in the 65+ group (18 million) exceeded net population growth (15 million).
Correct: The 65+ group rose from 12 to 30 (+18), the 0-14 group fell by 3, and the 15-64 group was unchanged, so older adults more than account for net growth.
The working-age group accounted for most of the net growth in the population over the 30 years.
The 15-64 group stayed at 80 million, so it contributed none of the growth.
Increases in the number of children were the main source of growth during the 30 years.
The 0-14 group shrank from 18 to 15 million.
The population aged 65 and older grew more slowly than the population aged 0 to 14.
The 65+ group grew by 150%, while the 0-14 group declined.
qs.x: The 65+ group rose from 12 to 30 (+18), the 0-14 group fell by 3, and the 15-64 group was unchanged, so older adults more than account for net growth. Trap: Assuming that population growth must come from births rather than from longevity.

qs.q: Country J's TFR in Figure 1 has been below replacement level for decades. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Without immigration or further gains in longevity, Country J's population would eventually shrink because births fall short of what is needed to replace parents.
Correct: Below-replacement fertility leads to eventual decline, but momentum and longer life spans can keep the total from falling for years.
Country J's population must already be declining, because a TFR below 2.1 immediately lowers the total population.
Population momentum and longevity delay decline; J actually grew from 110 to 125 million.
Below-replacement fertility cannot affect the age structure unless death rates also rise sharply.
Persistently low fertility changes age structure on its own, producing an older population.
Country J's falling TFR shows that it has not completed the demographic transition.
Low births and low deaths describe a completed transition; low TFR is consistent with it.
qs.x: Below-replacement fertility leads to eventual decline, but momentum and longer life spans can keep the total from falling for years. Trap: Equating a below-replacement TFR with immediate population decline and forgetting about momentum and longevity.

qs.q: Which stage of demographic transition best describes Country K in 2020?
o: Stage 1, with high birth rates and high death rates that keep growth near zero
High death rates are inconsistent with the stated low mortality in K.
Stage 3, with falling fertility that is still well above replacement
Correct: K has few older adults, a large child population, a TFR of 3.9 and declining, and low mortality, which matches the late stage 2 to stage 3 pattern in which growth is still substantial.
Stage 4, with low birth rates and low death rates and a roughly stable population
A TFR of 3.9 is far above the near-replacement level that characterizes stage 4.
A post-transition stage with fertility far below replacement and an aging population
J, not K, fits the description with TFR 1.3 and an older population.
qs.x: K has few older adults, a large child population, a TFR of 3.9 and declining, and low mortality, which matches the late stage 2 to stage 3 pattern in which growth is still substantial. Trap: Matching a country to a stage by its falling fertility alone, without checking how far it is above replacement.

qs.q: How did the number of working-age people per person aged 65 and older in Country J change from 1990 to 2020?
o: It rose from 15 to 38.
15 and 38 are the old-age dependency ratios (65+ per 100 working-age), which rose, not workers per older person.
It fell from 12 to 30.
12 and 30 are the raw counts of older people, which rose.
It fell from about 4.5 to about 2.7.
4.5 does not match 80 / 12, and the 1990 value was about 6.7.
It fell from about 6.7 to about 2.7.
Correct: In 1990, 80 / 12 is about 6.7; in 2020, 80 / 30 is about 2.7, so fewer workers support each older person.
qs.x: In 1990, 80 / 12 is about 6.7; in 2020, 80 / 30 is about 2.7, so fewer workers support each older person. Trap: Reporting the old-age dependency ratio, which rose, when the question asks for its reciprocal, which fell.

graph.title: Figure 1. Total fertility rate

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 8
text: Researchers surveyed 2,000 households in one metropolitan area to compare income, wealth (assets minus debts), and homeownership between two social groups, labeled Group P and Group Q, which have differed historically in access to credit and housing. Table 1 reports medians for all households and for households headed by a college graduate. Data were collected at a single time point. Researchers reported medians rather than means, and noted that Group Q households were more likely to be renters in neighborhoods where property values have risen slowly, whereas Group P households were more likely to own homes in neighborhoods where values have risen quickly. Households were sampled at random from tax and housing records, interviews were conducted in person, and wealth was reported for the previous calendar year. Respondents who declined to report an asset value were excluded from the wealth calculations. Income was reported before taxes, and households were classified by the group of the person who owned or rented the home.

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares the gaps for all households in Table 1?
o: The ratio of Group P to Group Q was about 1.3 for median income but about 7.9 for median wealth.
Correct: 68,000 / 52,000 is about 1.3, and 190,000 / 24,000 is about 7.9, so the wealth gap is much wider than the income gap.
The ratio of Group P to Group Q was about 7.9 for median income but about 1.3 for median wealth.
The ratios are reversed in this option.
The ratios of Group P to Group Q were nearly identical for median income and median wealth.
A 1.3 ratio and a 7.9 ratio are far from identical.
Group Q had a higher homeownership rate than Group P but a lower median wealth.
Group P's homeownership (74%) was higher than Group Q's (46%).
qs.x: 68,000 / 52,000 is about 1.3, and 190,000 / 24,000 is about 7.9, so the wealth gap is much wider than the income gap. Trap: Reading a modest income gap as evidence of a similarly modest wealth gap.

qs.q: Which factor best explains why the wealth gap is wider than the income gap?
o: Wealth is calculated only from annual earnings, so any gap in income is automatically magnified in wealth.
Wealth is assets minus debts, not a function of earnings alone.
Households in the lower-wealth group save a smaller fraction of every dollar of income than households in the other group.
Nothing in the table shows saving rates differ; the passage points to housing and credit access.
Wealth is measured at the individual level, while income is measured at the household level.
Both measures here are reported at the household level.
Wealth accumulates over time and across generations through assets such as home equity and inheritance, whereas income is a yearly flow.
Correct: Historical differences in credit and housing access produce cumulative advantage or disadvantage that shows up more strongly in assets than in income.
qs.x: Historical differences in credit and housing access produce cumulative advantage or disadvantage that shows up more strongly in assets than in income. Trap: Attributing the gap to individual choices when structural, cumulative factors are described in the passage.

qs.q: Which conclusion about education is supported by Table 1?
o: College education eliminated the wealth gap between the two groups.
A gap of $249,000 in median wealth between college graduates is not eliminated.
College-educated Group Q households held about one-fifth the median wealth of college-educated Group P households.
Correct: 61,000 / 310,000 is about 0.20, so a large wealth gap remained at the same education level.
College-educated Group Q households owned homes at a higher rate than all Group P households.
Group Q college graduates owned homes at 63%, below the 74% rate for all Group P households.
College-educated households in both groups had lower median incomes than non-college households.
Median incomes were higher for college graduates in both groups (98,000 and 79,000 versus 68,000 and 52,000).
qs.x: 61,000 / 310,000 is about 0.20, so a large wealth gap remained at the same education level. Trap: Assuming equal educational attainment should equalize wealth.

qs.q: Why did the researchers report medians rather than means for wealth?
o: A few extremely wealthy households would pull the mean far above what a typical household holds.
Correct: Wealth distributions are strongly right-skewed, so the median better represents a typical household.
Medians can be calculated even when some households did not report their wealth, whereas means cannot.
Missing data affect both statistics; this is not why medians are preferred.
Medians are less affected by the number of households and therefore needed no measure of sample size.
Sample size still matters for any statistic.
Wealth is a categorical variable, and only medians can be computed for categorical data.
Wealth is a continuous variable, not a categorical one.
qs.x: Wealth distributions are strongly right-skewed, so the median better represents a typical household. Trap: Believing the choice of median is about missing data or variable type rather than skewness.

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 9
text: Researchers developed an 8-item Brief Loneliness Scale (BLS; scores range from 8 to 40, higher scores indicating greater loneliness) and administered it to 150 adults. Internal consistency was assessed with Cronbach's alpha. A subgroup of 60 adults completed the BLS again two weeks later, during which no major life events were reported. All 150 adults also completed an established 20-item loneliness measure, an extraversion measure, and a social desirability measure (tendency to answer so as to look good). Table 1 summarizes the statistics. Figure 1 plots first and second BLS scores for 12 participants selected at random from the retest subgroup. The adults were recruited from community centers and online notices and were paid a small fee for each session. Items such as 'I feel left out' were rated for frequency over the past month, from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Higher scores on the established measure also indicate greater loneliness.

qs.q: What does a Cronbach's alpha of 0.88 indicate about the BLS?
o: The scale measures loneliness and not some other construct.
That describes validity, which alpha does not establish.
Participants' scores remain stable over a two-week interval.
Stability over time is test-retest reliability, reported separately as 0.81.
The items tend to vary together, indicating good internal consistency.
Correct: Alpha summarizes how strongly items correlate with each other, an index of internal-consistency reliability.
The scale predicts later social isolation better than other measures do.
Predictive power is a validity question that is not addressed here.
qs.x: Alpha summarizes how strongly items correlate with each other, an index of internal-consistency reliability. Trap: Treating a reliability coefficient as evidence that the scale measures the intended construct.

qs.q: Approximately what proportion of the variance in BLS scores is shared with the established loneliness measure?
o: Correct: The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.74 x 0.74 is about 0.55.
0.74 is the correlation coefficient itself, not the shared variance.
0.86 is the square root of 0.74, which is an incorrect transformation.
0.45 is the unshared variance (1 - 0.55).
qs.x: The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.74 x 0.74 is about 0.55. Trap: Reporting r as if it were the proportion of variance explained.

qs.q: What does the correlation of 0.05 with social desirability suggest?
o: The BLS is highly reliable because it does not depend on social desirability.
Low correlation with an unrelated measure is evidence of validity, not reliability.
Participants who are more socially desirable are unlikely to be lonely.
A near-zero correlation says there is essentially no relationship, not a negative one.
Responses on the BLS are not strongly influenced by a tendency to look good, supporting discriminant validity.
Correct: A scale should correlate weakly with constructs it is not meant to measure; 0.05 indicates little overlap with social desirability.
The BLS measures extraversion rather than loneliness.
The correlation with extraversion is moderate (-0.35), but it does not show the BLS measures extraversion.
qs.x: A scale should correlate weakly with constructs it is not meant to measure; 0.05 indicates little overlap with social desirability. Trap: Confusing discriminant validity with reliability.

qs.q: Suppose every participant's BLS score at the second testing was exactly 3 points lower than at the first. What would happen to the test-retest correlation?
o: It would fall, because the scores would no longer be the same on both occasions.
Correlation does not require equal scores, only a consistent linear relationship.
It would be unchanged, since correlation reflects relative standing.
Correct: Adding or subtracting a constant shifts all scores equally and leaves their relative ordering and the correlation unchanged.
It would become negative, because scores moved in the opposite direction.
