A uniform decrease still ranks participants the same way, so the correlation does not turn negative.
It would rise to 1.0 only if the scores also became more spread out.
Changing spread alone would not change the correlation either.
qs.x: Adding or subtracting a constant shifts all scores equally and leaves their relative ordering and the correlation unchanged. Trap: Assuming that a correlation measures agreement of exact scores rather than similarity in rank order.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the BLS is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
o: The BLS has been shown to measure loneliness without error because its correlations are all strong.
Not all correlations are strong, and no scale is error-free.
Scores were stable, but that does not prove the BLS measures loneliness.
Correct: A retest r of 0.81 means good stability, whereas validity needs evidence like the correlation with an established measure.
Participants' scores did not change at all between the two administrations.
The scatter plot shows individual score changes between times, so scores did vary.
A correlation of -0.35 with extraversion shows that low extraversion causes loneliness.
A correlation cannot establish causal direction.
qs.x: A retest r of 0.81 means good stability, whereas validity needs evidence like the correlation with an established measure. Trap: Equating reliability with validity or reading a correlation as causal.

graph.title: Figure 1. BLS scores at first and second administration (12 participants)

passages.title: Mini06 · Psych/Soc · Passage 10
text: A new blood test screens for a disease. Researchers applied the test and a definitive diagnostic procedure to 1,000 adults from a clinic where 10% of patients have the disease. A test result was positive if the biomarker concentration exceeded 40 units/mL. Table 1 gives the results. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive, specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative, and positive predictive value (PPV) is the proportion of positive results that are true positives. Researchers are also considering using the test for population screening in a community where disease prevalence is 1%, and 10,000 adults would be tested. Assume that sensitivity and specificity are the same as in the clinic. The clinic sample was drawn at random from consecutive patients who came for evaluation of symptoms, and the people who performed the diagnostic procedure did not know the blood test results.

qs.q: What is the sensitivity of the test in the clinic sample?
o: 50% is the PPV (90 / 180), not sensitivity.
99% is not obtainable from the table; 810 / 820 is the negative predictive value, about 98.8%.
10% is the proportion of those with the disease who test negative (false negatives).
Correct: Sensitivity = true positives / all with disease = 90 / 100 = 90%.
qs.x: Sensitivity = true positives / all with disease = 90 / 100 = 90%. Trap: Using the positive result column as the denominator, which gives PPV rather than sensitivity.

qs.q: What is the PPV of the test in the clinic sample?
o: 90% is sensitivity and specificity, not PPV.
Correct: PPV = 90 true positives / 180 positive results = 50%.
10% is the prevalence in the clinic sample.
90.9% does not follow from the table.
qs.x: PPV = 90 true positives / 180 positive results = 50%. Trap: Confusing PPV with sensitivity because the number 90 appears in both calculations.

qs.q: In the 10,000-person community screening scenario, what would the PPV be?
o: About 50%
50% is the clinic value, which depends on 10% prevalence.
About 90%
90% is the sensitivity and does not equal PPV.
About 1%
1% is the prevalence, not the PPV.
About 8%
Correct: Disease present = 100, of whom 90 test positive; disease absent = 9,900, of whom 10% (990) test positive. PPV = 90 / (90 + 990), about 8%.
qs.x: Disease present = 100, of whom 90 test positive; disease absent = 9,900, of whom 10% (990) test positive. PPV = 90 / (90 + 990), about 8%. Trap: Carrying the clinic PPV over to a population with a different prevalence.

qs.q: Why is the PPV lower when the same test is used in a lower-prevalence population?
o: False positives from the large disease-free group outnumber true positives from the small affected group.
Correct: PPV depends on prevalence; with a rare disease, even a small false-positive rate yields many false positives relative to true cases.
The test's sensitivity falls when fewer people in the sample have the disease.
Sensitivity is a property of the test given the disease and does not change with prevalence.
The specificity of the test increases, which reduces the number of correct positive results.
Specificity stays the same by assumption, and a higher specificity would raise PPV.
Fewer people agree to testing in low-prevalence communities, which lowers the number of true positives.
Participation rates are not part of the PPV calculation.
qs.x: PPV depends on prevalence; with a rare disease, even a small false-positive rate yields many false positives relative to true cases. Trap: Thinking that prevalence changes the test's sensitivity or specificity instead of the predictive values.

qs.q: If researchers lowered the positivity cutoff from 40 to 25 units/mL, what would most likely happen?
o: Both sensitivity and specificity would increase.
Both cannot improve by shifting a single cutoff when the distributions overlap.
Sensitivity would decrease and specificity would increase.
This describes raising the cutoff rather than lowering it.
Sensitivity would increase and specificity would decrease.
Correct: A lower threshold labels more people positive, catching more true cases but also more healthy people.
Both sensitivity and specificity would decrease.
Moving a single cutoff trades one for the other, not a decline in both.
qs.x: A lower threshold labels more people positive, catching more true cases but also more healthy people. Trap: Forgetting that the two accuracy measures trade off with the cutoff.

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Short stature in childhood has several endocrine causes. Growth hormone (GH) is released in pulses from anterior pituitary somatotrophs under the control of two hypothalamic peptides: GHRH, which stimulates release, and somatostatin, which inhibits it. GH acts on the liver and other tissues to raise insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which promotes bone growth and feeds back negatively on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary. Because GH secretion is pulsatile, a single random GH level is uninformative, so clinicians give a provocative stimulus (arginine) and measure peak GH. In some cases GHRH is also injected to test pituitary responsiveness. Three children with short stature were evaluated, and each was then treated with recombinant human GH (rhGH) for one year. Results are shown in Table 1. A normal peak GH after stimulation is above 10 ng/mL, and normal IGF-1 is defined as 100% of the age-matched mean. Children were measured at the same clinic with standard stadiometers.

qs.q: The results for Patient 1 are most consistent with a defect located in which structure?
o: The anterior pituitary somatotrophs, because they fail to release GH even when stimulated directly by GHRH
Correct: Patient 1 has low GH after both arginine and GHRH, so the pituitary cannot respond even to direct GHRH stimulation; the pituitary is the site of the lesion.
The hypothalamic neurons that secrete GHRH, because the pituitary would then respond normally to injected GHRH
Patient 2, not Patient 1, shows that pattern: a normal response to GHRH after a failed arginine response.
The liver, because it cannot synthesize IGF-1 even though pituitary GH release is normal
Patient 1 has low GH, and a liver defect would give normal or high GH with low IGF-1.
The GH receptor on target tissues, because GH levels would then be high after stimulation
A receptor defect gives high GH, as in Patient 3; Patient 1 has low GH.
qs.x: Patient 1 has low GH after both arginine and GHRH, so the pituitary cannot respond even to direct GHRH stimulation; the pituitary is the site of the lesion. Trap: Choosing the hypothalamus because low GH after arginine looks like a hypothalamic problem, ignoring the failed GHRH response that localizes the defect to the pituitary.

qs.q: Patient 3 has a high peak GH but a low IGF-1 level and does not grow in response to rhGH. The best explanation is
o: a defective GH receptor or post-receptor pathway, which prevents IGF-1 production and removes negative feedback on GH release
Correct: High GH with low IGF-1 and no response to exogenous GH indicates the tissues cannot respond to GH; low IGF-1 then fails to feed back, so GH stays high.
a deficiency of somatostatin, which would raise GH release but leave IGF-1 production and the growth response to rhGH completely normal
Without somatostatin, GH is high, but receptors would still respond to it, so IGF-1 and rhGH response would be normal.
a pituitary tumor secreting GH autonomously, which would raise IGF-1 above the age norm
An autonomous GH-secreting tumor gives high IGF-1 because the receptors are working.
a deficiency of GHRH, which would give a low GH peak and a good growth response to rhGH
Low GHRH gives low GH, as in Patient 2, with a strong rhGH response.
qs.x: High GH with low IGF-1 and no response to exogenous GH indicates the tissues cannot respond to GH; low IGF-1 then fails to feed back, so GH stays high. Trap: Assuming that high GH must mean high IGF-1; the liver makes IGF-1 only if the GH receptor signals.

qs.q: Why is serum IGF-1, rather than a random GH measurement, used to screen for GH deficiency?
o: GH is destroyed by the liver within seconds, so it can never be detected in plasma
GH has a short half-life (minutes) but is detectable; it is not destroyed within seconds.
IGF-1 is secreted in pulses that are larger than those of GH, which makes it easier to detect
IGF-1 is not pulsatile; its stability is the reason it is useful.
IGF-1 is long-lived and stable, so it reflects GH secretion integrated over time
Correct: GH is released in short pulses and cleared quickly, whereas IGF-1 is bound to carrier proteins and stays at a stable level that reflects average GH exposure.
IGF-1 is produced by the pituitary itself, so it directly measures somatotroph mass
IGF-1 is made mainly by the liver in response to GH, not by the pituitary.
qs.x: GH is released in short pulses and cleared quickly, whereas IGF-1 is bound to carrier proteins and stays at a stable level that reflects average GH exposure. Trap: Believing IGF-1 is a pituitary hormone; it is a liver-derived (and locally produced) mediator of GH action.

qs.q: If Patient 1 continues rhGH treatment, approximately how many additional centimeters will Patient 1 grow over two years compared with no treatment?
o: 6.3 cm
6.3 cm is the one-year gain, not the two-year gain.
9.5 cm
9.5 cm is the on-treatment velocity for a single year, not the gain over the untreated rate.
19.0 cm is two years of total treated growth, not the difference from untreated growth.
Correct: Growth gain per year is 9.5 - 3.2 = 6.3 cm; over two years this is 2 x 6.3 = 12.6 cm.
qs.x: Growth gain per year is 9.5 - 3.2 = 6.3 cm; over two years this is 2 x 6.3 = 12.6 cm. Trap: Using the treated velocity directly instead of subtracting the untreated growth rate.

qs.q: Which treatment would be most likely to improve growth in Patient 3?
o: Higher-dose rhGH, because overcoming a receptor defect only requires more ligand
The receptor pathway is defective, so more GH gives no extra benefit; Patient 3 already shows 2.1 cm/yr on rhGH.
Recombinant IGF-1, because it bypasses the nonfunctional GH receptor signaling that normally generates IGF-1
Correct: Patient 3 cannot make IGF-1 in response to GH, so supplying IGF-1 directly replaces the missing mediator.
A GHRH analog, because GH release is the limiting step in this patient
GH is already high after stimulation, so more GHRH adds nothing.
Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, because it lowers the elevated GH and thereby corrects the growth failure of this child
Lowering GH further would not help; IGF-1 is the missing mediator, and octreotide would reduce a hormone that is not the problem.
qs.x: Patient 3 cannot make IGF-1 in response to GH, so supplying IGF-1 directly replaces the missing mediator. Trap: Treating the elevated GH level rather than the missing IGF-1 effect.

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: Diuretics increase urinary salt and water excretion by inhibiting transporters along the nephron. In a crossover study, healthy volunteers on a fixed diet received a single oral dose of placebo, furosemide (a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter), hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ, which inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter), or spironolactone (an aldosterone receptor antagonist) on separate days. Urine was collected for 6 hours after each dose. Results are shown in Table 1. Assume that each volunteer had a glomerular filtration rate of 120 mL/min and a plasma sodium concentration of 140 mmol/L throughout the study, so that about 6,000 mmol of sodium was filtered during the 6 hours. Volunteers refrained from caffeine and alcohol for 24 hours, drank 500 mL of water 30 minutes before dosing, and remained seated during the collection period. Urine osmolality was measured by freezing-point depression, and electrolytes by ion-selective electrodes. Each treatment was separated by a one-week washout, and the order of treatments was randomized.

qs.q: The fall in urine osmolality after furosemide is best explained by which effect?
o: Increased ADH secretion, which opens aquaporins in the collecting duct and dilutes the urine
More ADH would make urine more concentrated, not less.
Reduced solute reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, which collapses the medullary gradient that concentrates urine

Correct: The thick ascending limb normally pumps NaCl out of the lumen to build the medullary interstitial gradient; blocking NKCC2 dissipates the gradient, so the collecting duct cannot concentrate urine.
Increased reabsorption of water in the proximal tubule, which concentrates the filtrate
Proximal water reabsorption is not the target of furosemide, and it would reduce volume.
Blockade of aldosterone receptors in principal cells, which raises water excretion without changing the gradient
Aldosterone antagonism is the mechanism of spironolactone and does not account for the furosemide result.
qs.x: The thick ascending limb normally pumps NaCl out of the lumen to build the medullary interstitial gradient; blocking NKCC2 dissipates the gradient, so the collecting duct cannot concentrate urine. Trap: Attributing the dilute urine to the collecting duct rather than to loss of the medullary gradient from the loop of Henle.

qs.q: Spironolactone lowers urinary K+ excretion below the placebo value because it
o: inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, which reduces K+ delivery to the distal nephron
Inhibiting NKCC2 is the action of furosemide, which increased K+ loss.
blocks aldosterone-driven Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in the principal cells of the collecting duct
Correct: Aldosterone increases ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase activity in principal cells; blocking its receptor reduces Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion, so K+ is retained.
inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter, which raises distal flow and K+ secretion
NCC inhibition is the action of HCTZ, and it increased K+ excretion.
inhibits proximal K+ reabsorption, which leaves more K+ in the tubular fluid
Spironolactone does not act in the proximal tubule, and blocking K+ reabsorption would increase, not lower, K+ excretion.
qs.x: Aldosterone increases ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase activity in principal cells; blocking its receptor reduces Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion, so K+ is retained. Trap: Confusing the K+-sparing aldosterone antagonist with loop and thiazide diuretics, which raise K+ loss.

qs.q: What is the most likely reason that furosemide increased K+ excretion?
o: More Na+ and fluid reaching the collecting duct raises Na+ reabsorption through ENaC, which makes the lumen negative and drives K+ secretion
Correct: Greater distal delivery of Na+ and high tubular flow increase Na+ entry via ENaC and sweep secreted K+ away, so K+ excretion rises.
Furosemide directly opens K+ channels in the thick ascending limb, which lets K+ escape from the lumen into the urine, independent of any change in distal sodium delivery or tubular flow
Furosemide acts on NKCC2; it does not open K+ channels, and K+ secretion occurs mainly in the collecting duct.
Furosemide lowers plasma aldosterone, which reduces K+ reabsorption in the distal nephron
Furosemide tends to raise renin and aldosterone through volume depletion, which also contributes to K+ loss.
Furosemide inhibits H+/K+-ATPase in intercalated cells, which removes K+ reabsorption
Inhibition of H+/K+-ATPase is not the mechanism of furosemide, and that pump mediates K+ reabsorption of minor extent.
qs.x: Greater distal delivery of Na+ and high tubular flow increase Na+ entry via ENaC and sweep secreted K+ away, so K+ excretion rises. Trap: Looking for a direct effect of the drug on K+ transport instead of the downstream effect of increased distal flow and sodium delivery.

qs.q: Under furosemide, the fractional excretion of sodium (Na+ excreted divided by Na+ filtered) was approximately
o: Correct: Filtered Na+ is about 6,000 mmol, and 250 / 6,000 is approximately 0.042, or about 4%.
1% is the placebo value (60 / 6,000), not the furosemide value.
10% would require about 600 mmol of Na+ in the urine.
42% results from dividing by 600 mmol instead of 6,000 mmol.
qs.x: Filtered Na+ is about 6,000 mmol, and 250 / 6,000 is approximately 0.042, or about 4%. Trap: Dividing by the wrong filtered load or using the placebo excretion.

qs.q: A patient with recurrent calcium kidney stones and high urinary calcium would be best treated with which drug, based on Table 1?
o: Furosemide, because it increases urine volume the most and dilutes urinary calcium
Furosemide more than doubled Ca2+ excretion (7.5 mmol), which would worsen stone formation despite higher volume.
Spironolactone, because it has the largest effect on Na+ excretion of the drugs tested
Spironolactone did not change Ca2+ excretion (3.1 mmol) and had the smallest Na+ effect among the drugs.
Placebo, because none of the drugs changes Ca2+ excretion in a clinically useful direction
HCTZ clearly lowered Ca2+ excretion, so the claim that none of the drugs changes it is incorrect.
HCTZ, because it lowers urinary Ca2+ excretion below the placebo value
Correct: HCTZ reduced Ca2+ excretion from 3.0 to 1.5 mmol, consistent with enhanced distal Ca2+ reabsorption, lowering supersaturation and stone risk.
qs.x: HCTZ reduced Ca2+ excretion from 3.0 to 1.5 mmol, consistent with enhanced distal Ca2+ reabsorption, lowering supersaturation and stone risk. Trap: Choosing the diuretic with the greatest volume effect without checking the calcium column.

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: Lactase, a brush-border enzyme of the small intestine, hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose. In most mammals and in many human populations, lactase activity declines after weaning (lactase non-persistence). Unabsorbed lactose passes to the colon, where bacteria ferment it. A hydrogen breath test detects this process. After an overnight fast, adults drank 50 g of lactose in water, and breath hydrogen was measured over 3 hours (Figure 1). Participants were lactase-persistent, lactase-nonpersistent, or lactase-nonpersistent after taking an oral lactase supplement with the lactose. Jejunal biopsy lactase activity, the rise in blood glucose after 50 g of lactose, and stool pH measured the next morning were also recorded (Table 1). Participants avoided high-fiber foods and antibiotics for the preceding four weeks, since both can change the colonic flora, and did not smoke or exercise during testing because these affect breath hydrogen. Symptoms were scored by questionnaire, and each test was performed on a separate day in randomized order.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the small blood glucose rise in the lactase-nonpersistent group?
o: Lactose cannot be absorbed intact, so with little brush-border lactase there is little glucose and galactose available for uptake
Correct: Disaccharides must be hydrolyzed at the brush border before monosaccharide transporters can absorb them; low lactase activity limits glucose release from lactose.
Lactase-nonpersistent intestinal cells lack the SGLT1 transporter, so no glucose from any source can be absorbed and the lactose-derived sugars stay in the lumen
The supplement group absorbed glucose normally, so transporters are intact; only the enzyme is deficient.
The liver converts all absorbed glucose to glycogen before it reaches the blood
Hepatic glycogen synthesis would not eliminate the rise in the first hour and does not distinguish the groups.
Colonic bacteria consume the glucose released by lactase before it can be absorbed
The bacteria act in the colon, after the main site of absorption, and ferment unabsorbed lactose rather than glucose already hydrolyzed.
qs.x: Disaccharides must be hydrolyzed at the brush border before monosaccharide transporters can absorb them; low lactase activity limits glucose release from lactose. Trap: Assuming a transporter defect rather than a missing hydrolase step.

qs.q: In the lactase-nonpersistent group, breath hydrogen rose substantially only after about 60 minutes. The best explanation is that
o: the small intestine produces hydrogen gas only after prolonged exposure to lactose
Human cells do not generate hydrogen from lactose; bacteria do.
lactose must first be converted to galactose in the liver and then metabolized by hepatocytes, which releases hydrogen into the blood
Hydrogen arises from colonic fermentation, not hepatic metabolism of galactose.
pancreatic enzymes produce hydrogen slowly as they digest lactose in the duodenum
Pancreatic enzymes do not digest lactose, and they do not produce hydrogen.
unabsorbed lactose first has to travel to the colon, where bacteria ferment it and release hydrogen that is absorbed and exhaled
Correct: H2 is a product of bacterial fermentation, and the colonic bacteria need the lactose to arrive from the small intestine, which takes time.
qs.x: H2 is a product of bacterial fermentation, and the colonic bacteria need the lactose to arrive from the small intestine, which takes time. Trap: Attributing hydrogen production to human digestion instead of bacterial fermentation.

qs.q: The lower stool pH in the lactase-nonpersistent group most likely reflects
o: short-chain fatty acids and lactic acid produced when colonic bacteria ferment unabsorbed lactose
Correct: Bacterial fermentation of lactose produces organic acids, which lower fecal pH to 5.4 and also generate gas.
increased bicarbonate secretion by the pancreas in response to lactose
Bicarbonate secretion would raise, not lower, the pH.
bile acids that are not reabsorbed in the ileum and that acidify the stool
Unreabsorbed bile acids can cause diarrhea but are not the cause here and do not account for the supplement effect.
gastric acid that is not neutralized because lactose delays gastric emptying
Gastric acid is neutralized in the duodenum by bicarbonate and does not set stool pH.
qs.x: Bacterial fermentation of lactose produces organic acids, which lower fecal pH to 5.4 and also generate gas. Trap: Choosing an upper GI explanation for a colonic finding.

qs.q: Lactase-nonpersistent individuals often develop watery diarrhea after consuming lactose. The most direct cause is that unabsorbed lactose
o: raises the osmolarity of luminal contents and holds water in the intestine
Correct: An unabsorbed, osmotically active solute draws water into the lumen, an osmotic diarrhea that stops with fasting or lactose avoidance.
activates adenylyl cyclase in the crypt cells and drives active Cl- secretion
Cl- secretion driven by cAMP is the mechanism of cholera toxin, not of lactose malabsorption.
damages the intestinal villi and thereby reduces the surface area for absorption
Lactase non-persistence is not associated with villous damage; the mucosa is normal.
stimulates gastrin release, which increases motility throughout the small intestine
Lactose does not stimulate gastrin to an appreciable degree, and increased motility is not the main mechanism.
qs.x: An unabsorbed, osmotically active solute draws water into the lumen, an osmotic diarrhea that stops with fasting or lactose avoidance. Trap: Linking lactose to secretory diarrhea rather than to the osmotic effect of unabsorbed solute.

qs.q: Peak breath hydrogen in lactase-nonpersistent participants was how many times that of participants who took the supplement?
o: About 0.2
0.2 is the reciprocal (15 / 70).
About 11.7
11.7 is the ratio of the nonpersistent peak to the lactase-persistent peak (70 / 6).
About 4.7
Correct: Peak H2 was 70 ppm without the supplement and 15 ppm with it, so 70 / 15 is approximately 4.7.
About 55
55 is the difference in ppm (70 - 15), not a ratio.
qs.x: Peak H2 was 70 ppm without the supplement and 15 ppm with it, so 70 / 15 is approximately 4.7. Trap: Computing a difference instead of a ratio, or using the wrong comparison group.

graph.title: Figure 1. Breath hydrogen after 50 g lactose

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Ovulation requires a surge of luteinizing hormone (LH). During most of the menstrual cycle, estradiol from the ovarian follicles suppresses GnRH and gonadotropin release (negative feedback), but late in the follicular phase high estradiol switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge. To test the conditions for this switch, researchers infused estradiol at a constant concentration into women in the early follicular phase whose own ovarian steroid output had been suppressed, and measured serum LH over 72 hours (Figure 1). One infusion maintained serum estradiol at 50 pg/mL and the other at 250 pg/mL. Table 1 summarizes typical hormone and endometrial values across the natural cycle in other volunteers. Estradiol was measured by immunoassay, and LH by a two-site immunometric assay. Ultrasound confirmed that no dominant follicle was developing at the start of each infusion, and each woman received both concentrations in separate cycles, in randomized order. Values in Table 1 are means from regularly cycling women.

qs.q: The results for the 50 pg/mL infusion are best explained by
o: positive feedback by estradiol, which raises LH release as soon as the concentration exceeds a fixed threshold in the pituitary
Positive feedback was seen only at 250 pg/mL after about 36 hours.
direct inhibition of the ovary by LH, which lowers estradiol production
LH acts on the ovary rather than being inhibited by it, and estradiol was fixed by the infusion.
negative feedback by estradiol on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, which lowers GnRH and LH release
Correct: A modest, sustained estradiol level suppressed LH from 6 to about 4.5 mIU/mL, the signature of negative feedback.
stimulation of the corpus luteum, which secretes inhibin and lowers LH
The women were in the follicular phase with no corpus luteum.
qs.x: A modest, sustained estradiol level suppressed LH from 6 to about 4.5 mIU/mL, the signature of negative feedback. Trap: Predicting a surge at any estradiol level instead of recognizing that both concentration and duration determine the feedback direction.

qs.q: In the natural cycle, the rapid rise in estradiol late in the follicular phase is produced mainly by
o: theca cells of the corpus luteum, which convert progesterone to estradiol under the control of LH during the follicular phase
No corpus luteum exists in the follicular phase, and the luteal source is secondary.
granulosa cells of the dominant follicle, which use aromatase to convert androgens made by theca cells
Correct: Under FSH stimulation, granulosa cells express aromatase and convert thecal androgens to estradiol; the dominant follicle becomes the main source.
the anterior pituitary, which secretes estradiol in response to GnRH
The pituitary secretes FSH and LH, not estradiol.
the adrenal medulla, which converts cortisol to estradiol
The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines, not sex steroids.
qs.x: Under FSH stimulation, granulosa cells express aromatase and convert thecal androgens to estradiol; the dominant follicle becomes the main source. Trap: Assigning estradiol synthesis to theca cells alone, which make androgens but lack significant aromatase.

qs.q: In the mid-luteal phase, FSH and LH are low (3 and 4 mIU/mL). Which explanation fits the data in Table 1?
o: Low progesterone removes inhibition of the hypothalamus, which lowers GnRH release
Progesterone is highest, not low, in this phase.
High FSH from the developing follicle inhibits its own secretion through a short-loop pathway that involves the endometrium and uterine tubes
FSH is low, not high, in this phase, and the endometrium is not an endocrine source of gonadotropin suppression.
High progesterone, together with estradiol and inhibin from the corpus luteum, suppresses gonadotropin secretion by negative feedback
Correct: Progesterone is 14 ng/mL in the mid-luteal phase, and with estradiol and inhibin from the corpus luteum it strongly inhibits GnRH, FSH, and LH.
The endometrium secretes LH-suppressing factors when it reaches 12 mm
The endometrium is a target tissue; it does not secrete factors that control pituitary LH.
qs.x: Progesterone is 14 ng/mL in the mid-luteal phase, and with estradiol and inhibin from the corpus luteum it strongly inhibits GnRH, FSH, and LH. Trap: Remembering that progesterone suppresses gonadotropins only for the LH surge phase and overlooking its role in the luteal phase.

qs.q: A combined oral contraceptive supplies a steady daily dose of estrogen and progestin. Based on Figure 1, it prevents ovulation mainly because
o: it raises FSH and LH continuously, which exhausts the follicles
Contraceptives lower, not raise, gonadotropins.
it blocks LH receptors on the oocyte, which prevents fertilization
LH acts on granulosa and theca cells, and blocking oocyte receptors is not the mechanism.
constant steroid levels maintain negative feedback and prevent the high, sustained estradiol pattern needed for the LH surge
Correct: Steady modest steroid levels keep LH and FSH low (like the 50 pg/mL infusion), so follicular development and the surge do not occur.
it increases GnRH pulse frequency, which causes premature luteolysis and prevents the endometrium from supporting implantation of an embryo
Contraceptives suppress GnRH pulses; they do not raise them.
qs.x: Steady modest steroid levels keep LH and FSH low (like the 50 pg/mL infusion), so follicular development and the surge do not occur. Trap: Believing that hormonal contraceptives work by raising gonadotropins rather than by suppressing them.

qs.q: According to Table 1, the endometrium reaches its greatest thickness in the mid-luteal phase because
o: falling estradiol and progesterone cause the endometrium to proliferate
Falling steroid levels trigger menstruation, not growth.
FSH acts directly on the endometrium, which causes it to thicken
FSH acts on ovarian follicles, not on endometrial cells.
the LH surge triggers the endometrium to double in thickness within 24 hours by direct stimulation of uterine stromal cells
The mid-cycle endometrium is 10 mm, with only a small change from the late follicular phase, so no doubling occurs.
progesterone from the corpus luteum promotes secretory development of an endometrium previously primed by estradiol
Correct: Estradiol drives proliferation in the follicular phase; progesterone then converts the endometrium to a secretory, nutrient-rich state suitable for implantation.
qs.x: Estradiol drives proliferation in the follicular phase; progesterone then converts the endometrium to a secretory, nutrient-rich state suitable for implantation. Trap: Assigning endometrial growth to pituitary hormones rather than to ovarian steroids.

graph.title: Figure 1. Serum LH during sustained estradiol infusion

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Premature infants are at risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) because their lungs are deficient in pulmonary surfactant, a mixture of phospholipids and proteins made by alveolar type II cells. Surfactant lowers the surface tension at the air-liquid interface of the alveoli. Researchers studied lungs excised from preterm lambs. One group had received no treatment, and the other received intratracheal surfactant before delivery. Each lung was inflated to a pressure of 30 cm H2O and then deflated stepwise, and the retained volume was recorded at each pressure. Figure 1 shows the deflation pressure-volume curves, with volume expressed per kilogram of body weight. Compliance was defined as the change in volume divided by the change in pressure over the steep linear portion of each curve, between 5 and 15 cm H2O. Lambs were delivered at 128 days of gestation, which is comparable to about 28 weeks in humans, and lungs were degassed before the pressure-volume measurements began.

qs.q: What was the compliance of the surfactant-treated lungs between 5 and 15 cm H2O?
o: 0.8 mL/kg per cm H2O
0.8 is the compliance of the untreated lungs ((9 - 1) / 10).
3.6 mL/kg per cm H2O
3.6 divides the final volume at 15 cm H2O by 10 and ignores the starting volume.
2.6 mL/kg per cm H2O
Correct: Volume rose from 10 to 36 mL/kg (26 mL/kg) over a 10 cm H2O interval, so compliance = 26 / 10 = 2.6 mL/kg per cm H2O.
26 mL/kg per cm H2O
26 is the volume change and has not been divided by the pressure change.
qs.x: Volume rose from 10 to 36 mL/kg (26 mL/kg) over a 10 cm H2O interval, so compliance = 26 / 10 = 2.6 mL/kg per cm H2O. Trap: Dividing the final volume by the pressure rather than the change in volume by the change in pressure.

qs.q: According to the Law of Laplace, why does absence of surfactant promote alveolar collapse?
o: Pressure in a sphere is proportional to radius, so large alveoli have the highest pressure and collapse first and empty their air into the smaller alveoli that remain open
Pressure is inversely, not directly, related to radius.
Surface tension is unaffected by surfactant, so collapse results only from reduced blood flow
Surfactant specifically lowers surface tension, which is the point of the passage.
Collapsing pressure is proportional to surface tension and inversely proportional to radius, so small alveoli empty into larger ones
Correct: Laplace's law (P = 2T/r) shows that, for equal tension, smaller alveoli have a higher collapsing pressure; surfactant reduces T more in small alveoli, stabilizing them.
Surfactant increases the elastic recoil of the lung, so its absence lowers the collapsing pressure
Surfactant reduces the recoil from surface tension and thus increases compliance, which is opposite to the stated claim.
qs.x: Laplace's law (P = 2T/r) shows that, for equal tension, smaller alveoli have a higher collapsing pressure; surfactant reduces T more in small alveoli, stabilizing them. Trap: Reversing the radius relationship in Laplace's law, so that large alveoli appear to be at greatest risk.

qs.q: Which hormone, given to a mother before preterm delivery, most effectively accelerates surfactant production in the fetal lung?
o: A glucocorticoid such as betamethasone
Correct: Antenatal glucocorticoids induce maturation of type II cells and increase surfactant synthesis, lowering the incidence and severity of RDS.
Oxytocin, to induce contractions and shorten pregnancy
Oxytocin does not affect lung maturation and would promote preterm labor.
Progesterone, to maintain the uterine lining
Progesterone may delay labor but does not induce surfactant production.
Epinephrine, to dilate the fetal bronchioles
Epinephrine is a bronchodilator but does not stimulate surfactant synthesis.
qs.x: Antenatal glucocorticoids induce maturation of type II cells and increase surfactant synthesis, lowering the incidence and severity of RDS. Trap: Selecting a hormone associated with labor or pregnancy rather than lung maturation.

qs.q: Compared with a healthy neonate, an infant with RDS is most likely to show
o: hyperoxemia caused by reduced alveolar surface tension
Surfactant deficiency raises, not lowers, surface tension.
an increased lung compliance, which reduces the work of breathing and improves the ventilation of the alveoli at low pressure
Figure 1 shows the untreated lung has a lower, not higher, compliance.
decreased alveolar-capillary membrane permeability to oxygen
The problem is collapse of alveoli, not diffusion across the membrane.
hypoxemia caused by atelectasis, which leaves perfused alveoli unventilated and produces a right-to-left shunt
Correct: Collapsed alveoli receive blood but no ventilation, so shunted blood remains deoxygenated; stiff lungs also make breathing harder.
qs.x: Collapsed alveoli receive blood but no ventilation, so shunted blood remains deoxygenated; stiff lungs also make breathing harder. Trap: Linking RDS to a diffusion barrier rather than to alveolar collapse and shunt.

qs.q: What is the most likely reason the surfactant-treated curve flattens between 20 and 30 cm H2O?
o: Surfactant is washed away from the alveoli as pressure rises
Surfactant is not removed by pressure; its effect is largest at low volumes.
The lung approaches its elastic limit, as collagen and elastin fibers resist further stretching
Correct: At high volumes the connective tissue limits distensibility, so large pressure changes yield small volume changes, regardless of surface tension.
The alveoli collapse completely at high pressure, which reduces volume
Alveoli collapse at low, not high, pressure.
The airway resistance becomes very high at large volumes, which stops airflow even in a static measurement
The measurements are static and not determined by airway resistance.
qs.x: At high volumes the connective tissue limits distensibility, so large pressure changes yield small volume changes, regardless of surface tension. Trap: Attributing the plateau to surfactant behavior rather than to the elastic properties of the tissue.

graph.title: Figure 1. Deflation pressure-volume curves of preterm lamb lungs

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization. NK cells carry inhibitory receptors that bind class I MHC molecules; when class I MHC is abundant, inhibitory signals dominate, and when it is low, activating signals can trigger killing through the release of perforin and granzymes. CD8+ T cells, by contrast, recognize viral peptides presented by class I MHC. Researchers incubated target cells with NK cells or with virus-specific CD8+ T cells at an effector-to-target ratio of 10:1 for 4 hours and measured specific lysis. Surface class I MHC was measured by flow cytometry and expressed relative to uninfected Line A (set to 1.0). K562 is a leukemia line that expresses almost no class I MHC. Virus V is known to reduce class I MHC expression. Results are shown in Table 1. Data are the means of triplicate wells from three independent experiments, and spontaneous release was below 10% in all conditions.

qs.q: The high NK cell lysis of K562 cells is best explained by
o: strong recognition of K562 antigens by NK cell T-cell receptors
NK cells do not use clonal T-cell receptors.
the absence of class I MHC on the target, which removes inhibitory signals to the NK cell
Correct: NK cells detect missing self: when class I MHC is nearly absent, inhibitory receptors are not engaged, and activating signals lead to lysis.
high class I MHC levels, which activate NK cell killing
High class I MHC inhibits NK cells, as the uninfected Line A result (5%) shows.
the production of antibodies against K562 by NK cells
NK cells do not secrete antibodies; B cells do.
qs.x: NK cells detect missing self: when class I MHC is nearly absent, inhibitory receptors are not engaged, and activating signals lead to lysis. Trap: Thinking that NK cell activation requires recognition of antigen presented on MHC like a T cell.

qs.q: What do the results with the Fab fragment of the class I MHC blocking antibody show?
o: Masking class I MHC on a normal cell is sufficient to make it susceptible to NK cell lysis
Correct: Lysis by NK cells rose from 5% to 41% when the inhibitory ligand was masked, while CD8+ T cell lysis stayed low (1%).
Class I MHC is required for NK cell perforin production
The NK cells killed effectively, so perforin was produced when the inhibitory signal was removed.
Class I MHC is activating for NK cells and increases killing
Killing went up when class I MHC was blocked, so it is an inhibitory, not an activating, ligand.
CD8+ T cells require NK cells to kill Line A cells
The data show no interaction between NK cells and CD8+ T cells.
qs.x: Lysis by NK cells rose from 5% to 41% when the inhibitory ligand was masked, while CD8+ T cell lysis stayed low (1%). Trap: Reading the antibody as damaging the cell rather than masking the ligand; a Fab fragment cannot recruit complement or other effectors.

qs.q: Virus V reduces class I MHC. Based on Table 1, what is the likely advantage and the likely cost for the virus?
o: Fewer viral peptides reach NK cells, but the infected cell becomes a stronger CD8+ T cell target
NK cells do not need peptides; their killing rises when class I MHC falls.
Fewer viral peptides reach CD8+ T cells, but the infected cell is a stronger NK cell target
Correct: T cell lysis was reduced to 18% and NK cell lysis increased to 38%, a trade-off.
Greater viral antigen display to CD8+ T cells, with no change in NK cell sensitivity
Lower class I MHC means less peptide display, not more, and NK killing was higher.
Reduced NK cell lysis and increased CD8+ T cell lysis because the cell has less class I MHC
Both predicted effects are reversed relative to the data.
qs.x: T cell lysis was reduced to 18% and NK cell lysis increased to 38%, a trade-off. Trap: Thinking that lowering class I MHC should help the virus evade every kind of lymphocyte.

qs.q: A cell line lacks TAP, the transporter that moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum, and displays low surface class I MHC. Compared with a normal line, this line would most likely be
o: less susceptible to NK cell lysis and more susceptible to CD8+ T cell lysis
This reverses both effects.
equally susceptible to both cell types because TAP acts after antigen presentation
TAP acts before presentation and determines how much class I MHC reaches the surface.
more susceptible to NK cell lysis and less to CD8+ T cell lysis
Correct: Without peptide loading, class I MHC is unstable and poorly expressed, which releases NK inhibition and removes the T cell target.
more susceptible to lysis by both cell types because it cannot degrade antigens
Antigen degradation by the proteasome is unaffected, and low class I MHC reduces T cell recognition.
qs.x: Without peptide loading, class I MHC is unstable and poorly expressed, which releases NK inhibition and removes the T cell target. Trap: Overlooking that class I MHC surface expression depends on peptide loading.

qs.q: Which feature distinguishes NK cells from CD8+ T cells in this study?
o: NK cells use the T-cell receptor and V(D)J recombination to recognize antigens presented on class I MHC
NK cells do not rearrange receptor genes.
NK cells need previous infection and develop immunologic memory
Immunologic memory is a characteristic of adaptive cells.
NK cells use Fas ligand only, and not perforin and granzymes
NK cells use perforin and granzymes as stated in the passage.
NK cells kill without clonal selection or previous exposure, so they can act within hours
Correct: NK cells are part of innate immunity and use germline-encoded receptors, whereas CD8+ T cells require clonal expansion for specificity.
qs.x: NK cells are part of innate immunity and use germline-encoded receptors, whereas CD8+ T cells require clonal expansion for specificity. Trap: Treating NK cells as a type of T cell with antigen-specific receptors.

r: Line A infected with virus V
Line A + class I MHC blocking antibody Fab

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Long-term potentiation (LTP), a persistent strengthening of synapses after brief high-frequency activity, is a leading cellular model of memory. In hippocampal slices, a pathway of Schaffer collaterals onto CA1 neurons was stimulated at low frequency while the field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fEPSP) slope was recorded and expressed as a percentage of baseline. At time 0, a brief high-frequency tetanus was delivered. In control slices, the fEPSP stayed elevated. Other slices were bathed in APV, an antagonist of the NMDA receptor, or in anisomycin, an inhibitor of protein synthesis, beginning 20 minutes before the tetanus. Figure 1 shows fEPSP slope over four hours. NMDA receptors are blocked at resting potential by Mg2+ and become permeable to Ca2+ when glutamate is bound and the membrane is depolarized. Slices were maintained at 32 degrees C in oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid, and responses were recorded from the stratum radiatum of CA1. The tetanus consisted of 100 pulses at 100 Hz.

qs.q: Why does APV prevent LTP in these experiments?
o: APV blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, which prevents the action potential in the presynaptic terminal and therefore stops the release of glutamate from the Schaffer collaterals
Na+ channel blockade would eliminate baseline transmission, but the baseline was unchanged.
NMDA receptors act as coincidence detectors that allow Ca2+ entry only when glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization occur together
Correct: NMDA receptor-mediated Ca2+ entry triggers LTP; blocking it leaves baseline transmission intact but prevents the potentiation (fEPSP stays near 100%).
APV blocks the presynaptic release of glutamate, which means the tetanus is not transmitted
APV acts on postsynaptic NMDA receptors and does not alter glutamate release.
APV blocks AMPA receptors, which prevents any baseline fEPSP before the tetanus
Baseline fEPSP was normal before the tetanus, which AMPA receptors would not allow if they were blocked.
qs.x: NMDA receptor-mediated Ca2+ entry triggers LTP; blocking it leaves baseline transmission intact but prevents the potentiation (fEPSP stays near 100%). Trap: Assuming that the antagonist blocks all glutamatergic transmission instead of only the NMDA receptor component.

qs.q: Which postsynaptic change most directly increases the fEPSP during the first hour after the tetanus?
o: Ca2+ activates CaMKII, which promotes insertion and phosphorylation of AMPA receptors in the postsynaptic membrane
Correct: Early LTP is expressed as more and more active AMPA receptors, increasing the response to a given quantity of glutamate.
Ca2+ activates acetylcholinesterase, which increases the clearance of glutamate
Faster glutamate clearance would reduce, not increase, the response.
Ca2+ closes the NMDA receptor channels permanently, which prevents desensitization and limits further Ca2+ entry during the tetanus
The channel isn't closed permanently, and the response increased.
Ca2+ activates voltage-gated Cl- channels, which depolarize the postsynaptic cell
Cl- channels would hyperpolarize or clamp the membrane near the Cl- equilibrium potential.
qs.x: Early LTP is expressed as more and more active AMPA receptors, increasing the response to a given quantity of glutamate. Trap: Proposing a presynaptic or glial change for an effect that the data localize to the postsynaptic neuron.

qs.q: Anisomycin produced a significant divergence from control beginning at about 60 minutes. These data best support the conclusion that
o: early LTP does not require new protein synthesis, whereas maintenance of potentiation for hours does
Correct: At 10 and 30 minutes anisomycin slices matched control (188 and 172 versus 190 and 180), but the potentiation decayed to baseline by 240 minutes.
LTP induction needs protein synthesis, because potentiation was reduced at 10 minutes
Potentiation at 10 minutes was almost identical to control (188 versus 190), so induction was intact.
protein synthesis is needed only for the baseline response before the tetanus
Baseline was not altered by anisomycin before the tetanus.
anisomycin blocks NMDA receptors, as APV does
Anisomycin allowed an initial LTP, whereas APV prevented it, so their mechanisms differ.
qs.x: At 10 and 30 minutes anisomycin slices matched control (188 and 172 versus 190 and 180), but the potentiation decayed to baseline by 240 minutes. Trap: Reading any drug effect as a block of induction without comparing the early time points.

qs.q: In the control slices, what fraction of the initial potentiation (the increase above baseline at 10 minutes) remained at 240 minutes?
o: About 55%
55% would correspond to a drop to about 150%.
About 87%
87% results from dividing 165 by 190, which does not subtract the baseline.
About 72%
Correct: Initial potentiation was 190 - 100 = 90 points; at 240 minutes it was 165 - 100 = 65 points; 65 / 90 is approximately 0.72.
About 165%
165% is the fEPSP value itself rather than a fraction of potentiation.
qs.x: Initial potentiation was 190 - 100 = 90 points; at 240 minutes it was 165 - 100 = 65 points; 65 / 90 is approximately 0.72. Trap: Dividing raw fEPSP values without subtracting the 100% baseline.

qs.q: A patient with bilateral damage to the hippocampus is most likely to show which deficit?
o: Loss of all memories from before the injury, with preserved ability to form new ones
This describes retrograde amnesia, which is not the typical pattern for hippocampal damage.
Loss of the ability to learn new motor skills but preservation of declarative memory
This reverses the roles: procedural memory is spared by hippocampal damage.
Loss of language comprehension, with no effect on memory formation
Language comprehension is mainly a function of Wernicke's area in the temporal cortex.
Inability to form new explicit (declarative) memories, while previously learned motor skills remain intact
Correct: The hippocampus is needed for consolidating new declarative memories, as in patient H.M.; procedural learning depends on other structures.
qs.x: The hippocampus is needed for consolidating new declarative memories, as in patient H.M.; procedural learning depends on other structures. Trap: Confusing anterograde amnesia from hippocampal damage with retrograde amnesia.

graph.title: Figure 1. fEPSP slope after a tetanus delivered at time 0

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix and requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) as a cofactor of its E1 subunit. Lactic acidosis can arise from impaired PDC activity or from defects of the respiratory chain. Cultured fibroblasts were grown under four conditions, and PDC activity was assayed in lysates with and without added 1 mM TPP. Lactate and pyruvate in the culture medium were also measured. The lactate-to-pyruvate (L/P) ratio reflects the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio because lactate dehydrogenase equilibrates the two couples. Results are in Table 1. The E1 variant cells carry a missense mutation in the E1 subunit. Cells were cultured in glucose-containing medium for 48 hours before analysis, and lysates were prepared with detergent to release mitochondrial enzymes. Thiamine-depleted cells were grown in thiamine-free medium for two weeks, and the complex I defect arose from a mutation in a subunit of that complex. All assays were done in triplicate.

qs.q: Which set of cofactors is required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex as a whole?
o: Biotin, lipoic acid, FAD, NADP+, and coenzyme A, with ATP as the energy source
Biotin carries CO2 in carboxylases and is not used by PDC, and NADP+ is not the acceptor.
Thiamine pyrophosphate, pyridoxal phosphate, FMN, NAD+, and ATP
Pyridoxal phosphate is used in transamination, and ATP is not a cofactor.
Biotin, thiamine pyrophosphate, FAD, NADPH, and tetrahydrofolate
Biotin and tetrahydrofolate are not PDC cofactors, and NADH, not NADPH, is generated.
Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD+, and coenzyme A
Correct: The E1, E2, and E3 subunits use TPP, lipoamide, and FAD, respectively, with NAD+ as the final electron acceptor and CoA as the acyl acceptor.
qs.x: The E1, E2, and E3 subunits use TPP, lipoamide, and FAD, respectively, with NAD+ as the final electron acceptor and CoA as the acyl acceptor. Trap: Mixing up the cofactors of PDC with those of the carboxylases or transaminases.

qs.q: Why does lactate accumulate in the thiamine-depleted cells?
o: Lactate is formed from acetyl-CoA, which accumulates when PDC is overactive
PDC activity was lower, not higher, and acetyl-CoA is not a lactate precursor.
Without PDC activity, gluconeogenesis converts glucose to lactate in the matrix
Gluconeogenesis builds glucose, not lactate, and does not occur in the matrix of fibroblasts.
Reduced PDC activity lets pyruvate build up and be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, which regenerates NAD+
Correct: Pyruvate not oxidized by PDC is diverted to lactate; in these cells the L/P ratio is nearly unchanged (12), so the excess is of both metabolites.
Lactate dehydrogenase is inhibited when PDC activity is low, so lactate stays in the cell and is not released into the medium
If LDH were inhibited, lactate would fall rather than rise.
qs.x: Pyruvate not oxidized by PDC is diverted to lactate; in these cells the L/P ratio is nearly unchanged (12), so the excess is of both metabolites. Trap: Assuming that lactic acidosis always signals an elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio rather than a pyruvate surplus.

qs.q: The L/P ratio is 42 in the complex I-defective cells but 10 to 13 in the other cells. This difference is best explained by
o: increased pyruvate carboxylase activity in the matrix, which converts lactate to pyruvate and lowers the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the cytosol
Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, not lactate to pyruvate.
enhanced thiamine uptake, which drives pyruvate into acetyl-CoA
Thiamine would raise PDC flux and lower lactate, but PDC activity is normal here.
an inability to take up glucose, which decreases pyruvate levels
Glucose uptake is not limited; pyruvate is 0.12 mM and lactate is high.
impaired reoxidation of NADH in mitochondria, which raises the NADH/NAD+ ratio and drives lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate
Correct: A complex I defect leaves NADH unoxidized, which raises NADH/NAD+ and favors lactate over pyruvate; PDC itself is normal (11.5).
qs.x: A complex I defect leaves NADH unoxidized, which raises NADH/NAD+ and favors lactate over pyruvate; PDC itself is normal (11.5). Trap: Treating all lactic acidosis as the same disorder, ignoring what the L/P ratio says about redox state.

qs.q: The E1 variant cells recovered most of their PDC activity with 1 mM TPP. The most likely explanation is that the mutation
o: destroys the catalytic site of E1, so that no amount of cofactor restores activity
A destroyed catalytic site would not show an almost fourfold recovery with TPP.
increases the production of E1 mRNA, so excess TPP is required for degradation
Higher E1 mRNA would not be corrected by TPP and does not fit the lysate assay.
blocks entry of pyruvate into the mitochondria, so TPP bypasses the transporter
The lysate assay does not depend on the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier.
lowers the affinity of E1 for TPP, so excess cofactor restores saturation
Correct: Activity rose from 2.5 to 10.8 nmol/min/mg, consistent with a higher Km for TPP overcome by raising the cofactor concentration; such patients may respond to high-dose thiamine.
qs.x: Activity rose from 2.5 to 10.8 nmol/min/mg, consistent with a higher Km for TPP overcome by raising the cofactor concentration; such patients may respond to high-dose thiamine. Trap: Assuming any loss of enzyme activity must be irreversible instead of considering cofactor binding.

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: In Xenopus egg extracts, the cell cycle can be driven in a test tube. Entry into mitosis requires activation of the cyclin B-CDK1 complex, and exit requires the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) to ubiquitinate cyclin B for proteasomal degradation. In a time course, extracts containing sperm nuclei were sampled every 20 minutes for cyclin B level and for histone H1 kinase activity, a readout of CDK1 activity (Figure 1; both normalized to the peak value). In additional extracts, sampled at 100 minutes, researchers added either a mutant cyclin B that lacks the destruction box recognized by the APC/C (cyclin B-delta90) or the CDK inhibitor roscovitine. The fraction of nuclei with condensed chromosomes was scored (Table 1). Extracts were prepared from eggs arrested in metaphase of meiosis II and then released by calcium addition, so that they cycled in vitro through repeated rounds of interphase and mitosis at 23 degrees C. Chromosomes were visualized with a DNA dye.

qs.q: What is the best interpretation of the drop in both cyclin B and kinase activity between 60 and 80 minutes in the control extract?
o: Activation of CDK1 by degradation of its catalytic subunit at the end of S phase
CDK1 is not degraded in this process; the cyclin is.
Translation of cyclin B is inhibited by roscovitine, so that CDK1 remains inactive
Roscovitine was not added to the control extract.
Phosphorylation of cyclin B by CDK1 stabilizes the protein and shuts down the cycle
Stabilizing cyclin B would keep kinase activity high, not turn it off.
APC/C destroys cyclin B, which inactivates CDK1 and permits exit from mitosis
Correct: CDK1 requires cyclin B for activity; degradation by the APC/C removes the regulatory subunit, and kinase activity falls with it.
qs.x: CDK1 requires cyclin B for activity; degradation by the APC/C removes the regulatory subunit, and kinase activity falls with it. Trap: Thinking that the catalytic CDK subunit, not the cyclin, is the one destroyed at each cycle.

qs.q: Cells in the roscovitine extract accumulate cyclin B (0.9) but do not condense chromosomes. This shows that
o: cyclin B is the catalytic kinase that phosphorylates histone H1 and nuclear lamins, so its presence alone drives condensation
Cyclins are regulatory and have no catalytic activity of their own.
cyclin B alone is insufficient; the kinase activity of CDK1 is needed to drive chromosome condensation
Correct: Roscovitine inhibits CDK1, so kinase activity (0.04) is low despite high cyclin B, and condensation (3%) fails; the CDK is the catalytic subunit.
roscovitine increases the rate of cyclin B degradation
Degradation was not increased; cyclin B in this extract remained high.
chromosome condensation is independent of the cell cycle
Condensation was driven by CDK1 activity, so it is dependent on the cycle.
qs.x: Roscovitine inhibits CDK1, so kinase activity (0.04) is low despite high cyclin B, and condensation (3%) fails; the CDK is the catalytic subunit. Trap: Assuming that the level of cyclin by itself reports the kinase activity.

qs.q: The extract containing cyclin B-delta90 arrests with condensed chromosomes (92%). This outcome indicates that
o: destruction of cyclin B is needed to enter mitosis
The control shows cyclin B accumulating before mitosis, not being destroyed.
CDK1 activity is required for completion of DNA replication but not for mitosis
Condensation shows mitosis was entered, which is a function of CDK1.
CDK1 activity is sufficient to enter mitosis, but cyclin B destruction is needed to exit it
Correct: The non-degradable cyclin keeps CDK1 active (1.00), driving and holding the mitotic state.
the delta90 mutant cyclin B inhibits the proteasome and stops the cell in G1
A non-degradable cyclin lacks the recognition site, but it does not inhibit the proteasome, and cells were in mitosis, not G1.
qs.x: The non-degradable cyclin keeps CDK1 active (1.00), driving and holding the mitotic state. Trap: Reading mitotic arrest as a failure to enter mitosis.

qs.q: In the control extract, by what factor was kinase activity at 60 minutes greater than at 100 minutes?
o: About 0.1
0.1 would be the ratio of the 100-minute value to the 60-minute value, which is the inverse.
About 3.3
3.3 comes from dividing the cyclin B levels (1.0 / 0.3).
About 90
90 results from a decimal error, since 0.95 / 0.10 is not 90.
About 9.5
Correct: At 60 minutes the activity was 0.95 and at 100 minutes it was 0.10; 0.95 / 0.10 = 9.5.
qs.x: At 60 minutes the activity was 0.95 and at 100 minutes it was 0.10; 0.95 / 0.10 = 9.5. Trap: Inverting the ratio, or comparing cyclin B levels instead of kinase activity.

graph.title: Figure 1. Cyclin B level and H1 kinase activity in control extract

passages.title: Mini07 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Ethanol is metabolized mainly in the liver. Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde, and mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetate; each step reduces NAD+ to NADH. About 40% of people of East Asian ancestry carry the ALDH2*2 allele, which encodes a nearly inactive enzyme. Healthy adult volunteers received either placebo or ethanol (0.5 g/kg). Blood was sampled 4 hours later. Participants were studied either after an overnight fast or after a meal, and a group heterozygous for ALDH2*2 was included. Plasma glucose, lactate, lactate/pyruvate (L/P) ratio, and acetaldehyde are shown in Table 1. Ethanol was given as a drink over 20 minutes, and peak blood ethanol concentrations were similar in all groups. Participants abstained from alcohol for one week before testing. The fed groups consumed a standard mixed meal containing about 600 kcal 30 minutes before the drink. Acetaldehyde was measured by gas chromatography. Each participant was studied once.

qs.q: Why did fasted volunteers develop hypoglycemia after ethanol?
o: Ethanol stimulates insulin secretion strongly, which causes the liver to store glucose as glycogen and the muscle to take up the remaining glucose from blood
Insulin secretion is not the main mechanism; the fed group, which had glycogen available, did not become hypoglycemic.
The high NADH/NAD+ ratio diverts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, which lowers the substrates available for gluconeogenesis

Correct: In the fasted state glucose is supplied by gluconeogenesis; NADH from ethanol oxidation shifts the LDH and malate dehydrogenase equilibria away from pyruvate and oxaloacetate, and glucose falls to 58 mg/dL.
Ethanol inhibits glycogen phosphorylase directly, which raises glucose uptake by muscle
Glycogen phosphorylase is not the target; the fasted state has depleted glycogen and relies on gluconeogenesis.
Acetaldehyde is converted to glucose in the liver, which uses up the available glucose
Acetaldehyde is oxidized to acetate and does not form glucose.
qs.x: In the fasted state glucose is supplied by gluconeogenesis; NADH from ethanol oxidation shifts the LDH and malate dehydrogenase equilibria away from pyruvate and oxaloacetate, and glucose falls to 58 mg/dL. Trap: Attributing alcohol-induced hypoglycemia to insulin rather than to redox-impaired gluconeogenesis.

qs.q: In the ALDH2*1/*2 group, plasma acetaldehyde was 45 uM, 15 times that of ALDH2*1/*1 participants. The most likely explanation is that
o: the variant allele increases ADH activity, which lowers the production of acetaldehyde
A higher ADH activity would raise, not lower, acetaldehyde production.
the variant allele blocks the formation of acetaldehyde from ethanol, which leaves ethanol unmetabolized and lowers the plasma acetaldehyde concentration
If acetaldehyde formation were blocked, acetaldehyde would be low.
the variant ALDH2 subunits reduce the oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate, so acetaldehyde accumulates after ADH makes it

Correct: ALDH2 is the main acetaldehyde-clearing enzyme; reduced activity leaves it elevated, which produces facial flushing and nausea. Lactate and L/P values were similar to wild type, so NADH generation by ADH was unaffected.
acetaldehyde cannot be filtered by the kidney in heterozygous carriers
Renal filtration is not the main route of acetaldehyde clearance.
qs.x: ALDH2 is the main acetaldehyde-clearing enzyme; reduced activity leaves it elevated, which produces facial flushing and nausea. Lactate and L/P values were similar to wild type, so NADH generation by ADH was unaffected. Trap: Choosing a step upstream of acetaldehyde rather than the enzyme that removes it.

qs.q: In the fasted ethanol group with a lactate of 2.8 mM and an L/P ratio of 28, the pyruvate concentration was approximately
o: 0.01 mM results from a tenfold arithmetic error.
Correct: L/P = 28, so pyruvate = lactate / 28 = 2.8 / 28 = 0.10 mM.
0.36 mM is the reciprocal of the lactate value (1 / 2.8) and ignores the ratio.
78 mM
78 mM is the product of 2.8 and 28, which multiplies instead of divides.
qs.x: L/P = 28, so pyruvate = lactate / 28 = 2.8 / 28 = 0.10 mM. Trap: Multiplying lactate by the ratio instead of dividing.

qs.q: High hepatic NADH/NAD+ after heavy ethanol use contributes to fatty liver mainly because it
o: inhibits beta-oxidation of fatty acids and favors triglyceride synthesis
Correct: Oxidation steps in beta-oxidation and the TCA cycle need NAD+, so excess NADH slows them; fatty acids are re-esterified into triglycerides that accumulate in hepatocytes.
stimulates beta-oxidation, which raises acetyl-CoA, and thereby depletes triglycerides
Beta-oxidation is slowed, not stimulated, when NAD+ is scarce.
activates the pentose phosphate pathway, which generates NADPH and degrades fatty acids
The pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH for biosynthesis and does not degrade fatty acids.
increases carnitine uptake into mitochondria, which accelerates fatty acid oxidation
Faster mitochondrial oxidation would reduce fat accumulation, the opposite of what occurs.
qs.x: Oxidation steps in beta-oxidation and the TCA cycle need NAD+, so excess NADH slows them; fatty acids are re-esterified into triglycerides that accumulate in hepatocytes. Trap: Thinking more NADH means more fuel oxidation, when it actually inhibits NAD+-dependent steps.

passages.title: Mini08 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Philosophers lean on thought experiments the way laboratory scientists lean on apparatus. A runaway trolley, a violinist plugged into a stranger's circulatory system, a factory of beings physically identical to us but lacking inner experience: each is a small invented world built to isolate one variable and elicit a verdict. The verdict is then treated as data. If nearly everyone judges that it would be wrong to push a man from a footbridge to stop the trolley, any adequate moral theory must either explain that judgment or explain it away. Defenders of the method say that it is indispensable, since many philosophical questions cannot be settled by observation, and that the alternative to consulting intuitions is not to consult nothing but to consult them carelessly.

Critics reply that the analogy with apparatus fails at the first step. A telescope has a known relationship to the thing it measures, established by comparing its readings against independent checks. No such calibration is available for intuition. We cannot step outside our judgments to learn whether they track moral or metaphysical facts or merely record the accidents of upbringing, evolutionary history, and the particular wording of the scenario. Experimental philosophers have sharpened the worry by showing that verdicts shift with factors that seem irrelevant: the order in which cases are presented, whether the agent is described in the first or third person, even the cultural background of the respondent. If a judgment flips when the same case is merely reordered, the critics say, it is not a reading of reality but a reading of our psychology.

The defender has two replies, neither fully satisfying. The first is that instability afflicts only some intuitions. Judgments about extreme cases, the ones that survive reordering and rewording and that recur across cultures, may deserve more trust than judgments about delicate ones, and the practice of philosophy already involves sorting the robust from the fragile. The second reply is subtler. Thought experiments, it holds, are not meant to deliver verdicts that are simply accepted; they are meant to put pressure on a principle. When a proposed theory implies that a certain invented case is permissible, and the implication strikes us as monstrous, the thought experiment has not proved the theory false, but it has raised its price. The theorist may pay the price by bullet-biting, accepting the odd consequence, but then the cost is visible and can be weighed against the theory's other virtues.

This defense has a limit. The fictional cases that serve best as pressure points are often those stripped of every realistic feature: the trolley has no history, the people on the track have no names. Our intuitions evolved and were trained in a messy world, and there is no guarantee that they behave reliably when asked about a world that has been tidied for the purpose. A judgment about a scenario that could never occur may reflect the mind's best guess about a nearby real scenario, filling in missing details with defaults, rather than a verdict on the case as stipulated. If so, two philosophers who give different answers may not disagree about the case at all; they may simply have imagined different details.

The most defensible position may therefore be a modest one. Thought experiments are neither instruments of proof nor mere rhetorical ornaments. They are tools for making our commitments explicit, for discovering which of our principles we are unwilling to give up, and for revealing where we disagree. What they cannot do is certify themselves.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Thought experiments should be abandoned because intuitive verdicts shift with wording, order, and culture.
This is the critics' position, which the author qualifies rather than adopts.
Thought experiments work just like laboratory apparatus and so yield data of the same kind that experiments do.
The author reports this analogy only to show where critics say it fails.
Only verdicts about extreme cases can legitimately be used to evaluate moral theories.
This is one of the defender's two replies, not the passage's overall conclusion.
Thought experiments are valuable for clarifying and putting pressure on our principles, though their verdicts cannot be treated as self-certifying evidence.
Correct: This matches the closing paragraph, which settles on a modest role for the method: it exposes commitments without proving anything.
qs.x: This matches the closing paragraph, which settles on a modest role for the method: it exposes commitments without proving anything. Trap: Picking the critics' view because it receives the most detailed discussion, when the final paragraph settles on a middle position.

qs.q: According to the passage, critics claim that the analogy between thought experiments and a telescope breaks down because:
o: thought experiments describe worlds that could never physically exist.
Impossibility of the scenario appears only in paragraph four and is not the calibration complaint.
telescopes give different readings depending on the order of observations.
Order effects are attributed to intuition, not to telescopes.
philosophers disagree about which scenarios are worth examining at all.
The passage does not raise disagreement over case selection as the critics' point.
intuition cannot be checked against independent tests.
Correct: Paragraph two says a telescope can be calibrated against independent checks and intuition cannot.
qs.x: Paragraph two says a telescope can be calibrated against independent checks and intuition cannot. Trap: Confusing the order-effect evidence with the calibration objection; they are separate steps in the critics' case.

qs.q: The author mentions that verdicts shift with the order in which cases are presented primarily in order to:
o: show that moral intuitions are entirely relative to culture and therefore of no value to philosophers.
The passage never says intuitions are entirely relative or worthless; the defender keeps a role for robust ones.
provide evidence that verdicts can reflect the presentation of a case rather than its facts.
Correct: Order effects show that a verdict can track our psychology rather than the case, supporting the critics.
illustrate how laboratory methods have made philosophical judgment more reliable.
The finding is used to cast doubt on reliability, not to praise laboratory methods.
introduce the defender's claim that unstable intuitions must be discarded outright.
The defender argues only some intuitions are unstable and others are trustworthy.
qs.x: Order effects show that a verdict can track our psychology rather than the case, supporting the critics. Trap: Overgeneralizing from a finding about some verdicts to the claim that all intuitions are worthless.

qs.q: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the statement that a monstrous implication 'has raised its price'?
o: Any theory that conflicts with a widely shared intuition should be given up at once.
This contradicts the claim that the thought experiment has not proved the theory false.
Thought experiments matter only for theories that have no other virtues to weigh.
The passage says the cost is weighed against a theory's other virtues, so such virtues matter.
A theory implying a monstrous verdict about an invented case is not thereby refuted, but its defenders must accept and justify that cost.
Correct: The passage says the case does not prove the theory false but makes its cost visible and weighable.
Bullet-biting is evidence that a theorist has misunderstood the case as described.
Bullet-biting is described as a legitimate way to pay the price, not as a misunderstanding.
qs.x: The passage says the case does not prove the theory false but makes its cost visible and weighable. Trap: Treating a raised cost as equivalent to a refutation, when the author separates the two.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most weaken the defender's first reply?
o: Verdicts about delicate cases differ across cultures more than verdicts about extreme cases do, even when the cases are reworded and reordered.
This supports the claim that extreme cases are more robust.
Philosophers can reliably tell in advance which of their intuitions will prove robust.
This supports the reply's claim that sorting robust from fragile is already practiced.
Verdicts about extreme cases change as readily with wording and order as verdicts about delicate cases do.
Correct: The first reply depends on extreme-case verdicts being more stable; this removes that difference.
Respondents give the same answers to extreme cases whether told in the first or third person.
This shows stability for extreme cases, which strengthens the reply.
qs.x: The first reply depends on extreme-case verdicts being more stable; this removes that difference. Trap: Selecting a finding that sounds critical of intuition but in fact reinforces the defender's distinction.

qs.q: Which of the following situations is most similar to the worry raised in the fourth paragraph?
o: Two jurors disagree about a hypothetical because they hold incompatible theories of justice and rights.
Here the disagreement is about principle, whereas the passage's worry is about unnoticed differences in imagined details.
Two jurors reach opposite verdicts on a sparse case because each supplies different unstated facts.
Correct: Like the philosophers, the jurors answer different cases because each fills gaps with their own defaults.
A juror reverses her verdict after the order of the testimony is rearranged.
This resembles the order-effect worry of paragraph two, not the gap-filling worry of paragraph four.
Two jurors reach the same verdict on a hypothetical for entirely different reasons.
Agreement for different reasons is not the problem of imagined details producing apparent disagreement.
qs.x: Like the philosophers, the jurors answer different cases because each fills gaps with their own defaults. Trap: Matching on the surface similarity of disagreement rather than on its source in unstated details.

passages.title: Mini08 · CARS · Passage 2
text: Popular usage has made "stoic" a synonym for unfeeling, and the Stoics of the ancient world are often pictured as men whose calm nothing could stir. This picture is a caricature, but it is a revealing one, because it rests on a confusion about what the Stoics took emotions to be. For the Stoics, an emotion was not a raw sensation that happens to a person, like a shiver or a blush. It was a judgment: a rational assent to the proposition that something good or bad is present or approaching. Fear is the judgment that a coming event is a genuine evil, and grief is the judgment that a genuine evil has already occurred. On this view there is nothing to be done about a passion by suppressing it; the only remedy is to examine the judgment that constitutes it and to ask whether it is true.

The truth of such judgments depends, for the Stoics, on a sharp doctrine about value. Only virtue is good and only vice is bad. Health, wealth, reputation, and even the life of a loved one are "indifferents": they may be preferred to their opposites, and a sensible person will pursue them, but they do not affect whether one's life goes well, because they lie at least partly outside one's control. Someone who grieves the death of a friend as though a genuine evil had befallen him has therefore misjudged, and the misjudgment is the source of the suffering. The sage, having corrected every such error, experiences no passions, only good feelings such as joy in virtue and wariness in place of fear.

Critics from antiquity onward have objected that this program is either impossible or inhuman. Grief, they say, seems to express love, and a person incapable of it would be diminished rather than perfected. Yet the Stoics were not blind to this. Seneca concedes that tears may come unbidden, and the school developed the notion of "first movements" or preliminary affects: the flinch at a sudden noise, the pallor at bad news, the welling of tears. These reactions are involuntary and do not yet involve assent; the sage feels them as anyone does. What distinguishes the sage is what follows: she does not endorse the impression that something terrible has happened, and so the first movement subsides instead of hardening into a passion.

This distinction deserves more credit than it usually receives, because it anticipates a modern clinical idea. Contemporary cognitive therapies teach patients to distinguish an automatic thought from the belief they form about it, and to test the belief against evidence. The resemblance is not accidental; the founders of those therapies acknowledged the debt. But the resemblance also exposes a difficulty. Therapy aims to replace distorted beliefs with accurate ones, and it does not claim that the world contains nothing worth fearing. The Stoic claim is far stronger: that nothing outside one's own character is worth fearing at all. If this strong doctrine is false, then the Stoic method loses its guarantee, since the judgments the sage refuses to make may sometimes be true.
