Style is not at issue; the letters are said to be written in haste or distress.
qs.x: The paragraph contrasts the letter writer's ignorance of the outcome with a retrospective narrator. Trap: Reading the phrase as a literal reference to timing instead of to the writer's ignorance of the ending.

qs.q: The discussion of Les Liaisons dangereuses mainly serves to show how the epistolary form:
o: keeps the reader ignorant of the characters' true motives until the final letters of the novel.
The reader can assemble the truth from the correspondence.
makes any narrator unnecessary because letters are always truthful.
No one in the book tells the whole truth.
depends on a single scheming character to narrate the whole story.
The passage describes multiple correspondents.
allows the reader to weigh competing accounts and detect irony in their discrepancies.
Correct: The paragraph says discrepancies among the letters are the novel's instrument of irony and the reader acts as judge.
qs.x: The paragraph says discrepancies among the letters are the novel's instrument of irony and the reader acts as judge. Trap: Assuming that without a narrator the reader must be left uninformed.

qs.q: The author's view of the plausibility objection to the epistolary novel is best described as:
o: regarding it as completely baseless.
The author says the complaints have a point.
valid but outweighed.
Correct: The author says the complaints have a point and that implausibility was the price paid for effects.
treating it as the reason the form disappeared.
The author attributes disappearance to new forms meeting the same needs.
agreeing that it makes the form unworthy of study.
The author says the letters remain valuable as evidence of what writers attempted.
qs.x: The author says the complaints have a point and that implausibility was the price paid for effects. Trap: Reading a concession as agreement with the critics' overall verdict.

qs.q: Which of the following would most strengthen the author's claim that later techniques met the same needs as the epistolary form?
o: Many readers today find letters in novels implausible and prefer more direct narration.
This repeats the plausibility objection and does not connect later forms to the same needs.
Pioneers of free indirect style described their aim as rendering thoughts as they occur.
Correct: This links the later technique to the effect of immediacy the letters provided.
Letter writing declined in the nineteenth century.
This concerns social practice, not narrative technique meeting the same needs.
Richardson's novels sold more copies than later novels.
Sales say nothing about whether later techniques produced similar effects.
qs.x: This links the later technique to the effect of immediacy the letters provided. Trap: Choosing evidence about readers' views rather than about the aims of later techniques.

qs.q: Which of the following would be the best modern parallel to the 'self-presentation' effect described in the fourth paragraph?
o: A novel narrated by an omniscient voice that summarizes events after they occur.
This is retrospective narration, the contrast the passage draws.
A novel consisting of one long letter that is never answered.
This lacks the multiple addressees whose contrast reveals motive.
A novel told through emails and messages in which a character's tone shifts with each recipient, revealing her motives.
Correct: The shifting presentation for different addressees is the effect the paragraph describes.
A novel with a table of dates and places in the front.
This is reference material, not self-presentation.
qs.x: The shifting presentation for different addressees is the effect the paragraph describes. Trap: Choosing a work that merely uses letters, rather than one where addressees shape what is said.

passages.title: Mini08 · CARS · Passage 9
text: It is hard now to imagine a time when Shakespeare was regarded as a flawed genius whose plays required repair, yet for much of the century after his death that was the prevailing view. When the theaters reopened in 1660, after the Puritan ban, audiences found the old plays rough, irregular, and sometimes shocking. Restoration adapters set about improving them. Nahum Tate rewrote King Lear in 1681 with a happy ending in which Cordelia survives and marries Edgar, and this version held the stage for about a century and a half. Samuel Johnson, who admired Shakespeare deeply and edited his works in 1765, nonetheless defended the substitution on the ground that Cordelia's death offended his sense of poetic justice. The playwright, in other words, was a great writer who needed to be corrected by his heirs.

The transformation of this reputation into something close to worship, which a critic mockingly named "bardolatry" in the nineteenth century, has been told as a story of rising taste. Readers, it is said, eventually developed the sensitivity to appreciate what had been there all along. A less flattering and more informative account emphasizes the circumstances in which the reputation was made. David Garrick's Shakespeare Jubilee of 1769 at Stratford, an extravagant festival in which, notoriously, not one of the plays was performed, helped establish the poet as a national symbol; Stratford became a place of pilgrimage, and relics such as a supposed mulberry tree he had planted were sold to the devout. The rise of an English national identity, the demand for a native writer who could stand against the French classical dramatists, and the growth of a commercial publishing market for annotated editions all contributed. The poet's greatness was, in part, manufactured by those who needed a national poet.

This account has sometimes been taken as a debunking, as though to explain a reputation were to show it unearned. That inference is mistaken. The fact that a writer's prestige served cultural and commercial purposes does not show that his work lacked qualities that merited it. The more reasonable interpretation is that reputations require both: the work must offer something capable of sustaining prolonged attention, and a society must have reasons to give it that attention. Many works of high quality have lacked the second condition and have been forgotten; Shakespeare enjoyed both. The sociological explanation answers the question of why this writer and not another was lifted to the status of national poet. It does not answer, and does not claim to answer, the question of whether the lifting was deserved.

The point has a practical consequence for teaching. A common approach presents the canon as a body of timeless masterpieces whose value is self-evident to any sensitive reader, so that a student who finds Shakespeare difficult must be at fault. An approach that treats the canon purely as the residue of power, on the other hand, invites students to dismiss the plays without ever reading them closely enough to judge. Both approaches evade the harder task, which is to ask what the plays make possible: the compression of thought in a line, the way a character changes his mind in front of us, the fashioning of speech that can carry both an argument and its undermining. Knowing the history of a reputation can make a reader more skeptical about the claims made for a work; it cannot spare the reader the labor of finding out whether those claims are true.

qs.q: Which of the following is the main point of the passage?
o: Shakespeare's reputation is undeserved because it was manufactured for national purposes.
The author calls this inference mistaken.
Explaining the social history of Shakespeare's reputation does not settle whether the plays deserve it, which readers must judge by studying the plays.
Correct: The third and fourth paragraphs separate how a reputation arose from whether it is deserved.
Shakespeare's plays were always recognized as masterpieces by every generation.
The first paragraph says they were long regarded as flawed and needed repair.
Teachers should avoid discussing the history of literary reputations.
The author says such knowledge can make readers usefully skeptical.
qs.x: The third and fourth paragraphs separate how a reputation arose from whether it is deserved. Trap: Treating a sociological explanation as a debunking, the inference the author rejects.

qs.q: According to the passage, Johnson defended Tate's version of King Lear because:
o: poetic justice required it.
Correct: The first paragraph gives this as his ground.
he believed Tate was a better playwright than Shakespeare.
The passage says Johnson admired Shakespeare deeply.
audiences at the time demanded tragic endings.
The passage says the adaptation had a happy ending.
he edited Tate's version in 1765.
He edited Shakespeare's works in 1765, not Tate's.
qs.x: The first paragraph gives this as his ground. Trap: Assuming that admiration for Shakespeare would prevent any defense of Tate's changes.

qs.q: The fact that no play was performed at Garrick's Jubilee is mentioned primarily to suggest that:
o: the celebration honored Shakespeare as a symbol more than it engaged his work.
Correct: The author uses it as an example of symbolic and commercial uses of the poet.
Garrick disliked Shakespeare's plays.
Nothing in the passage suggests this.
the plays were too difficult and too rough to stage in the eighteenth century.
The adaptations of Tate and others were staged for a century and a half.
Stratford had no theater at the time.
The passage does not discuss Stratford's theaters.
qs.x: The author uses it as an example of symbolic and commercial uses of the poet. Trap: Reading the omission as a statement about the plays' difficulty rather than as a mark of symbolic use.

qs.q: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?
o: A work's prestige can be explained socially without implying it is unworthy.
Correct: This is the claim of the third paragraph.
A work that lacks social support is probably of low quality and deserves its neglect.
The author says many high-quality works were forgotten for lack of such support.
Prestige is determined only by the quality of the work.
The author says reputations require both quality and a social reason.
Any canon is the product of power alone.
The author says this approach invites dismissal without reading.
qs.x: This is the claim of the third paragraph. Trap: Collapsing the author's two necessary conditions into one.

qs.q: Which of the following would most strengthen the claim that many works of high quality have been forgotten?
o: A poet whose work was praised by critics immediately and has remained in print.
This is a case of recognition, not of forgotten quality.
A playwright whose reputation rose after a national festival honored him.
This resembles Shakespeare's case, not a forgotten work.
A novelist whose work sold poorly because critics found it poor.
This is low quality, not forgotten high quality.
A poet whom later critics rank with the best of her era was ignored in her lifetime for lack of patrons and rediscovered by a later movement.
Correct: It gives a case of quality without social support, which was forgotten.
qs.x: It gives a case of quality without social support, which was forgotten. Trap: Picking a case where recognition followed quality, which does not show forgotten quality.

qs.q: Which of the following teaching approaches is most consistent with the author's recommendation in the last paragraph?
o: Telling students the novel is a timeless masterpiece and that any difficulty reflects their own failings.
This is the first approach the author criticizes.
Telling students the novel is canonical only because of power and so need not be read.
This is the second approach the author criticizes.
Telling students how a novel became canonical and then having them read it closely to test its claims.
Correct: The approach combines historical skepticism with the labor of close reading.
Asking students to memorize the dates and publishers of the novel's editions.
This concerns the history alone and omits evaluating the work itself.
qs.x: The approach combines historical skepticism with the labor of close reading. Trap: Choosing an approach that adopts only one of the two halves of the author's advice.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 1
text: In the early 1960s, a group of American filmmakers set out to make documentaries that would, in their own phrase, simply happen in front of the camera. Lightweight cameras and portable sound had just made it possible to follow people through a day without lights or scripts. The resulting style, which its practitioners called direct cinema, rested on a principle of withdrawal: the filmmaker would observe, never interview, never stage, and never explain.

The ambition was admirable, but it concealed a confusion between two different things the word objectivity can mean. In one sense, objectivity names a method: a set of procedures, such as keeping notes, disclosing sources, and checking claims against rivals, that allow others to evaluate how a conclusion was reached. In another sense, it names a posture: the absence of a point of view. Direct cinema aspired to the second, and the second is not available to any film. A camera must be pointed somewhere, and pointing is choosing. A cinematographer who follows a politician into a hotel room has already decided that the room, not the crowd outside, is where the story lives. An editor who reduces two hundred hours of footage to ninety minutes has decided, with every cut, which gesture will count as typical and which as an accident. The absence of narration does not remove these judgments; it merely removes the place where they could be stated and contested.

Critics have sometimes accused direct cinema of bad faith, as though its makers knew they were shaping the material and pretended otherwise. This charge is too harsh. Most of the filmmakers understood that selection was unavoidable. What they believed was that restraint could discipline selection: if the filmmaker refused to intervene in events, then at least the raw material would be unmanipulated, and the viewer could trust that what appeared on screen had happened. Trust of this limited kind is real: a viewer can be fairly confident that the confrontation shown was not rehearsed.

Yet the restraint carried a cost that its defenders were slower to notice. Because the filmmakers declined to ask questions, they could not learn what their subjects thought was happening. Subjects who were aware of the camera behaved accordingly, and the filmmaker, unwilling to talk about the camera's presence, had no way to separate performance from habit. A later tradition, sometimes called cinema verite in its French usage, took the opposite course. Its filmmakers openly provoked their subjects, asked them to account for themselves, and left the questions in the finished film. They claimed that the camera was a catalyst, and that people under its gaze revealed truths they would not reveal otherwise. This claim has its own difficulties, since a provoked confession is no more innocent than a staged one, but it places the filmmaker inside the frame, where the viewer can weigh the interference.

The lesson is not that documentary should abandon the aim of fidelity. It is that fidelity cannot be purchased by silence. A film earns credibility when its makers make visible, in the film or around it, the choices that produced it: where the camera stood, what was left out, and what the subjects knew. Viewers are quite capable of discounting a perspective they can see. What they cannot discount is a perspective that insists it is not there. The most trustworthy documentaries, on this view, are not the ones that appear to have no author but the ones that behave as honest authors do, by letting the audience know who is speaking and from where.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?
o: Direct cinema failed because its practitioners deliberately staged scenes while claiming to observe events as they unfolded naturally.
The author explicitly rejects the charge of deliberate staging as 'too harsh'; the problem was confusion about objectivity, not fraud.
Provocation of subjects is the only reliable way for a documentary to capture the truths that people would otherwise conceal.
The passage calls verite's provocation a mixed strategy with 'its own difficulties' and does not name it the only reliable method.
A documentary earns trust not by hiding the filmmaker's point of view but by making the choices that shaped the film visible to viewers.
Correct: The passage moves from the impossibility of a perspective-free film to the conclusion that credibility comes from disclosing where the camera stood, what was cut, and what subjects knew.
Portable cameras and synchronous sound finally allowed documentary filmmakers to eliminate selection from the filmmaking process.
The author argues that selection is unavoidable for any film, so equipment could not eliminate it.
qs.x: The passage moves from the impossibility of a perspective-free film to the conclusion that credibility comes from disclosing where the camera stood, what was cut, and what subjects knew. Trap: Choosing the first detail the passage discusses at length (staging or provocation) instead of the conclusion the whole argument builds toward.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as objective in the sense of a method rather than a posture?
o: A film with no narration, in which the camera never leaves the room where its main subject is speaking.
Absence of narration is the 'posture' of having no point of view, which the author says no film can have.
A film shot with a hidden camera so that none of the subjects ever changes behavior because of being filmed.
A hidden camera still involves choices about placement and editing, and it reveals nothing about the procedures that produced the film.
A film whose makers release their shooting log and state which hours of footage were left out of the final cut.
Correct: Method-style objectivity consists of procedures such as disclosing sources that let others evaluate how a conclusion was reached; releasing a log and the omissions does exactly that.
A film in which the director interviews every participant at length but does not mention the editing process or the reasons for choosing those participants.
Interviews would alter what subjects say, and without disclosure of the editing, viewers still cannot evaluate how the film was shaped.
qs.x: Method-style objectivity consists of procedures such as disclosing sources that let others evaluate how a conclusion was reached; releasing a log and the omissions does exactly that. Trap: Equating objectivity with the absence of narration, which is the posture the author says is unavailable.

qs.q: Suppose a study found that viewers who were told a documentary's funding source and editing choices judged its claims more cautiously than viewers who were not told. This finding would most directly support which claim in the passage?
o: Direct cinema films are generally more trusted than films that include interviews.
The study compares disclosure with nondisclosure and says nothing about direct cinema versus interview-based films.
Subjects who know they are filmed always behave differently from how they otherwise would.
The study measures viewer judgment, not subject behavior in front of a camera.
Editors who cut hundreds of hours of footage cannot avoid favoring dramatic events.
The study concerns what viewers do with disclosed information, not what editors favor.
Viewers are capable of discounting a perspective that is made visible to them.
Correct: The author states that viewers can discount a perspective they can see; caution after disclosure is exactly that behavior.
qs.x: The author states that viewers can discount a perspective they can see; caution after disclosure is exactly that behavior. Trap: Picking a claim that is also in the passage but is not the one the study tests.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward cinema verite is best described as:
o: unqualified admiration, since it solves the problem of selection that direct cinema left unresolved.
Verite is said to have 'its own difficulties', so admiration is not unqualified, and it does not solve selection.
open disdain, since provoking subjects is as manipulative as staging a scene for the camera.
The author credits verite with a merit, so the tone is not disdainful.
detached neutrality, since the passage reports its methods without evaluating them in any way.
The author offers explicit evaluation ('merit', 'difficulties'), so the stance is not neutral.
qualified approval, since it exposes the filmmaker's role but provokes its subjects.
Correct: The author says verite has 'the merit' of placing the filmmaker inside the frame but adds that a provoked confession is no more innocent than a staged one.
qs.x: The author says verite has 'the merit' of placing the filmmaker inside the frame but adds that a provoked confession is no more innocent than a staged one. Trap: Reading a single negative clause as the author's overall verdict.

qs.q: A television series advertises that 'no producers interfered with what you see' but does not reveal how many hours were shot or how scenes were ordered. Based on the passage, the series' claim to credibility is weakest because it:
o: relies on lightweight cameras, which cannot record synchronous sound with enough clarity.
Equipment quality is not part of the author's concern about credibility.
fails to ask its subjects any questions on camera, which limits what the audience learns.
Declining to ask questions is a cost of direct cinema, but the author's final argument is about concealed choices.
presents an edited result as though it had no author while keeping the choices that produced it hidden.
Correct: The author concludes that what viewers cannot discount is a perspective that insists it is not there; the series makes just such an insistence.
allows its subjects to know they are being filmed, which causes them to perform for the camera and obscures their ordinary habits.
Subject awareness is raised as a difficulty for direct cinema, but it is not what the passage says makes a claim of credibility weakest.
qs.x: The author concludes that what viewers cannot discount is a perspective that insists it is not there; the series makes just such an insistence. Trap: Selecting a real limitation mentioned in the passage rather than the one tied to the author's conclusion.

qs.q: The author states that a viewer of a direct cinema film 'can be fairly confident that the confrontation shown was not rehearsed.' This statement serves primarily to:
o: prove that direct cinema achieved the posture of objectivity that the author earlier defined.
The author maintains that the posture of objectivity is unavailable to any film.
concede a genuine strength of direct cinema before explaining the limits of its restraint.
Correct: The concession acknowledges a limited but real value of restraint, after which the author turns to its costs.
suggest that cinema verite films are generally less trustworthy than films made by direct cinema.
The sentence does not compare trustworthiness across the two traditions in this way.
illustrate how editors decide which gesture will count as typical in a long stretch of footage.
The editing example appears elsewhere and concerns selection, not rehearsal.
qs.x: The concession acknowledges a limited but real value of restraint, after which the author turns to its costs. Trap: Treating a concession as the author's thesis.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 2
text: Every city contains buildings that have outlived their purpose: grain elevators without grain, power stations without turbines, schools without pupils. For much of the twentieth century, the choices for such structures were thought to be two. A building could be demolished, its site cleared for something useful, or it could be preserved, frozen as a monument to the period that produced it. Preservation, in this older conception, meant arresting change. The ideal was the museum-piece building in which every surface was restored to its original condition and every later alteration was stripped away as a kind of contamination.

Adaptive reuse, the practice of converting an old building to a new function, has increasingly complicated this picture. A cotton mill becomes apartments; a rail depot becomes a market hall; a cathedral-like pumping station becomes a concert venue. Enthusiasts praise such projects on partly practical grounds: old structures are often sturdier than their replacements, their large windows and high ceilings are costly to build today, and the energy embodied in their bricks and beams would be wasted by demolition. But the deeper appeal is cultural. A converted building keeps a visible conversation going between past and present, and passers-by experience the layering of time directly rather than reading about it on a plaque.

Purists object that the practice is a form of quiet vandalism. To insert floors into a factory hall is to destroy the very volume that made it a factory hall; to cut a doorway through a load-bearing wall is to erase evidence of how the structure carried its loads. The objection has force, but it relies on a premise that deserves scrutiny, namely that a building has a single authentic state to which it ought to be returned. Almost none does. A medieval church was extended, burned, rebuilt, and refitted across centuries, and to restore it to any single moment is to decide that the other moments do not matter. The mill itself was altered many times; the loom hall of 1880 was not the loom hall of 1840. What the purist calls the original is usually an editorial choice.

A more useful distinction, then, may be between alterations that respect a building's legibility and those that destroy it. A conversion is legible when a visitor can still understand what the structure was and how it worked: when the great hall remains a great hall, when the iron columns remain exposed, when new insertions are clearly distinguishable from old fabric and could in principle be removed. It is illegible when the old structure survives only as a facade, a decorative shell behind which an unrelated building has been constructed. Facade retention, in which a historic front is propped up while everything behind it is demolished, is the clearest example of the second kind. It preserves the picture of the past while discarding its substance, and it treats history as a matter of appearance.

This standard has its own difficulties. Legibility is partly a matter of the observer's knowledge, and a building that seems perfectly clear to an architectural historian may be opaque to a tenant who has never seen a mill. Moreover, a building that is not used tends not to survive, so a standard that makes conversion too demanding may in practice condemn buildings to decay or demolition. Still, the criterion at least directs attention to the right question. The issue is not whether a building has been changed, since all living buildings change, but whether the change leaves the building able to tell the truth about its own history.

qs.q: The main point of the passage is that:
o: buildings that no longer serve their original purpose should be restored to the single condition in which they were first built.
The author argues that almost no building has a single authentic state to which it could be returned.
facade retention is the best way to combine economic redevelopment with the historical record of a structure.
Facade retention is the author's clearest example of an illegible conversion.
adaptive reuse is chiefly justified by the energy and construction costs saved when demolition is avoided.
Practical savings are mentioned as one of two kinds of appeal, but the author calls the deeper appeal cultural and builds the argument on legibility.
changes to old buildings are acceptable when the buildings can still reveal what they were and how they worked.
Correct: The author replaces the question of whether a building has changed with whether the change leaves it legible about its own history.
qs.x: The author replaces the question of whether a building has changed with whether the change leaves it legible about its own history. Trap: Treating a supporting reason, such as cost savings, as the thesis.

qs.q: According to the passage, why do critics describe facade retention as an example of illegible alteration?
o: It keeps the appearance of a historic front while discarding the structure behind it, treating history as a matter of appearance.
Correct: The passage says facade retention preserves the picture of the past while discarding its substance.
It requires the front of a building to be propped up with new materials that cannot be told apart from old fabric.
Propping is mentioned as how the front is held up, not as the cause of illegibility.
It cuts new doorways through load-bearing walls and so erases evidence of how the building carried its loads.
The doorway example is used to illustrate the purists' complaint about conversion in general.
It divides a large hall into floors, destroying the volume that identified the building as a factory.
Inserted floors are also part of the purists' objection and not the passage's discussion of facade retention.
qs.x: The passage says facade retention preserves the picture of the past while discarding its substance. Trap: Confusing the purists' general objections with the author's specific criticism of facades.

qs.q: Which conversion would the author be most likely to consider successful?
o: A brick power station keeps its smokestack and front wall while a glass office block rises behind them.
Keeping only the stack and front wall is facade retention, the author's example of illegibility.
A warehouse becomes offices while its open hall and iron columns remain exposed and the new mezzanines are demountable steel.
Correct: Visible original features and removable, distinguishable new insertions match the author's description of a legible conversion.
A cathedral is restored to the way it looked in a single century, with later additions removed.
The author criticizes restoration to a single moment as an editorial choice.
A school is converted into apartments by adding floors that hide the original classroom spaces and corridors.
Hiding the original spaces would make the building unable to show what it had been.
qs.x: Visible original features and removable, distinguishable new insertions match the author's description of a legible conversion. Trap: Choosing an option that keeps a visible feature but hides the building's structure.

qs.q: Which of the following discoveries would most weaken the author's response to the purists?
o: Many converted mills have lower heating costs than comparable new apartment blocks.
Heating costs concern practical benefits, not the question of authenticity.
Most historic buildings were built in one campaign and never altered.
Correct: The author argues that almost no old building has a single authentic state because buildings were altered repeatedly; if most were never altered, that premise fails.
Visitors often misjudge a building's original function when they see only the outside.
Visitor misjudgment bears on legibility, not on whether buildings have an authentic state.
Several well-known cathedrals were extended and rebuilt across several centuries.
Repeated rebuilding would support the author's argument rather than weaken it.
qs.x: The author argues that almost no old building has a single authentic state because buildings were altered repeatedly; if most were never altered, that premise fails. Trap: Picking evidence that supports the author because it is on the same topic.

qs.q: The author's discussion of the tenant who has never seen a mill suggests that:
o: Legibility depends on what visitors already know, so it is not purely objective.
Correct: The author notes that legibility is partly a matter of the observer's knowledge, so a clear conversion to an expert may be opaque to a layperson.
historians should be barred from judging whether a conversion respects the original structure.
The author does not suggest excluding experts.
residents of converted buildings care less about history than architects and historians do.
The passage makes no claim about how much tenants care about history.
a legible conversion must include explanatory plaques that tell visitors what the building once was.
The author mentions plaques only as how people otherwise read about the past, not as required.
qs.x: The author notes that legibility is partly a matter of the observer's knowledge, so a clear conversion to an expert may be opaque to a layperson. Trap: Overreading an example into a recommendation the author never makes.

qs.q: The final paragraph acknowledges difficulties with the legibility standard in order to:
o: demonstrate that the purists' objection to conversion is ultimately correct.
The author continues to reject the purists' premise about a single authentic state.
show that the criterion is imperfect but still directs attention to the proper question.
Correct: The author says the criterion 'at least directs attention to the right question', so the difficulties are conceded without abandoning it.
argue that buildings that are not used should be demolished rather than altered.
The author fears that demanding standards may condemn buildings to decay, and so does not recommend demolition.
withdraw the earlier claim that adaptive reuse conserves a building's embodied energy in favor of the purists' preference.
The embodied energy argument is not retracted or revisited.
qs.x: The author says the criterion 'at least directs attention to the right question', so the difficulties are conceded without abandoning it. Trap: Reading a concession as a reversal.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 3
text: In 1945, the Dutch painter Han van Meegeren was arrested for selling a national treasure to the occupying Nazis. The treasure was a painting attributed to Vermeer, and its buyer was a high-ranking German official. Faced with a charge of treason, Van Meegeren made an extraordinary defense: the picture was not a Vermeer at all, he said, but a forgery that he had painted himself. Skeptics demanded proof, and he produced it by painting another in his cell under the eyes of witnesses. Art experts, who had hailed the pictures as masterpieces, were embarrassed; the public briefly made the forger a hero.

The episode raises a puzzle that philosophers of art have long enjoyed. If a painting hailed as sublime is discovered to be fake, what has changed? The canvas is the same, the pigment is the same, and the light still falls on it exactly as before. If the experience of looking at it was valuable on Tuesday, why should it be worthless on Wednesday? One answer, favored by those who believe that aesthetic value resides entirely in what can be seen, is that nothing of value is lost, and that the sense of disappointment is a mere prejudice, a snobbery about signatures. On this view, a perfect forgery would be as good as the original, and the market for authenticated masterworks is a superstition kept alive by collectors.

The answer is tempting, but it overlooks what we are actually valuing when we admire a work. A painting is not only an arrangement of colors; it is also an achievement, the result of a particular person solving particular problems at a particular time. Part of what moves us in a Vermeer is the recognition that someone in a Delft room, with the tools available in the 1660s, found a way to make light seem to rest on a woman's sleeve. To learn that the picture was made in the 1930s by a man imitating that achievement is to learn that the achievement we were admiring never occurred. The surface is unchanged, but the thing it was evidence of is gone. Our response was, so to speak, addressed to a person, and the person turns out not to exist.

This explains why forgeries are so often detected by the passage of time rather than by chemistry. Van Meegeren's Vermeers look, to modern eyes, conspicuously like the 1930s: the faces have the large-eyed sentimentality of film stars of that decade, a resemblance invisible to the experts of the day who wanted to see a lost Vermeer. A forger can reproduce a style, but he cannot step outside his own period, and the features he does not know he is contributing give him away. In this respect, forgery differs from legitimate imitation, such as the copies made by art students, or a pastiche acknowledged as such, in which the borrowed style is displayed rather than disguised.

None of this proves that authenticity is the only value a painting can have. A forgery may still be skillful, and one can admire the skill, as long as it is understood to be the forger's and not Vermeer's. What the case shows is that aesthetic appreciation is not a closed transaction between eye and surface. It reaches back to the history of making, and the knowledge we bring to a work belongs to the experience rather than being an unwelcome intrusion upon it.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
o: Han van Meegeren should be regarded as a hero because he exposed the gullibility of experts and the powerful.
The public's reaction to Van Meegeren is mentioned in passing and is not the author's concern.
A perfect forgery is as valuable as an original because the pigment and the light on the canvas are identical.
The author attributes this view to others and rejects it.
Forgeries are best detected by chemical analysis, since style can be reproduced by any skilled painter.
The author says forgeries are typically given away by period features, not chemistry.
The discovery that a celebrated painting is a forgery matters because appreciating art involves knowing who made the work and what was achieved.
Correct: The author argues that admiration is directed at an achievement in history, so exposure of a forgery changes the experience even though the surface is unchanged.
qs.x: The author argues that admiration is directed at an achievement in history, so exposure of a forgery changes the experience even though the surface is unchanged. Trap: Adopting the view that the author presents as the tempting but mistaken answer.

qs.q: When the author says the response to a forged Vermeer 'was addressed to a person, and the person turns out not to exist,' the author most nearly means that:
o: viewers of a forged painting are mistaken about what colors the canvas contains.
The author states that the pigment and surface are unchanged.
Vermeer himself may not have painted any of the works attributed to him.
The author never questions Vermeer's authorship of genuine works.
viewers who admire a painting generally want to meet the person who painted it.
The sentence is figurative; it concerns the object of admiration, not a wish to meet anyone.
part of the admiration is for a maker's achievement, absent in a forgery.
Correct: The 'person' is the seventeenth-century painter whose achievement viewers believed they were admiring.
qs.x: The 'person' is the seventeenth-century painter whose achievement viewers believed they were admiring. Trap: Taking the figurative phrase literally and choosing an option about the canvas itself.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's explanation of why forgeries tend to be exposed over time?
o: Chemical analysis of pigments has become more precise since the 1940s.
Better chemistry would offer another route to detection and would not undermine the author's account.
Experts who authenticate paintings are often wrongly confident because they want to find a lost masterwork.
Expert wishfulness is the author's own explanation for why the forgeries were accepted initially.
Forgers who deliberately study the sensibilities of their own era can eliminate every trace of it from their imitations.
Correct: The explanation rests on forgers unknowingly contributing features of their own period; if they could eliminate every trace, later viewers would have nothing to detect.
Facial styles in portraits change with each generation of painters.
Changing styles would help later viewers notice period differences, supporting the author.
qs.x: The explanation rests on forgers unknowingly contributing features of their own period; if they could eliminate every trace, later viewers would have nothing to detect. Trap: Choosing a statement that is related to forgery detection but supports the passage.

qs.q: A listener treasures a recording of a famous pianist's performance, then learns it was generated by software imitating the pianist's style. Which description best parallels the author's analysis of this situation?
o: The sound is unchanged, but the listener learns that the human achievement the recording seemed to document never took place.
Correct: This mirrors the author's claim that the surface is unchanged but the thing it was evidence of is gone.
The listener should feel no disappointment, since the sound is identical to what she enjoyed before.
That is the view the author calls tempting but incomplete.
The listener should admire the software because skill in imitation is the only thing that makes any performance valuable.
The author allows that skill can be admired but says it is the imitator's, and does not call it the only value.
The listener's disappointment shows that music is valued mainly for its price and rarity rather than for any feature of the sound or its makers.
The author does not link disappointment to market value; she describes the market for masterworks only as the argument of others.
qs.x: This mirrors the author's claim that the surface is unchanged but the thing it was evidence of is gone. Trap: Reasoning from the market comment instead of the achievement argument.

qs.q: The author would most likely regard an openly acknowledged pastiche in the style of Vermeer as:
o: legitimate imitation, because the borrowed style is displayed rather than disguised.
Correct: The passage contrasts forgery with acknowledged imitation, where the style is displayed and not disguised.
morally equivalent to a forgery, since both reproduce another painter's style without permission.
The author separates disguised imitation from acknowledged imitation and does not discuss permission.
worthless, because a painting made in the twentieth century cannot achieve anything.
The author allows that skill can be admired when attributed to the right person.
more valuable than a forgery of equal skill, since pastiche requires no knowledge of the earlier period.
The passage says nothing about the knowledge pastiche requires.
qs.x: The passage contrasts forgery with acknowledged imitation, where the style is displayed and not disguised. Trap: Assuming all imitation is condemned.

qs.q: Which of the following positions does the author explicitly reject?
o: Forgeries can display real technical skill that is worth admiring.
The author concedes that skill in a forgery can be admired as the forger's.
Only the visible surface matters, never authenticity.
Correct: The author calls this view tempting but says it overlooks that a painting is also an achievement.
Aesthetic appreciation reaches back to the history of how a work was made.
This is the author's own position.
The knowledge a viewer brings to a work is part of the experience of it.
This is the author's own conclusion.
qs.x: The author calls this view tempting but says it overlooks that a painting is also an achievement. Trap: Choosing a view the passage endorses because it sounds like a qualification.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 4
text: For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, hunting and gathering was imagined as the bottom rung of a ladder. People who lived by foraging were assumed to spend every waking hour searching for food, to live on the edge of starvation, and to have no time for anything else. Yet when anthropologists in the mid-twentieth century began to measure how foraging peoples actually spent their days, the evidence did not fit the story. Studies in southern Africa and northern Australia suggested that adults obtained their food in a few hours a day, several days a week, and spent much of the remainder resting, visiting, and talking.

These findings prompted the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins to propose that hunter-gatherers were, in an unexpected sense, the original affluent society. His argument turned on the observation that wealth can be defined in two ways. One can make many goods, or one can want few. The conventional picture assumes that human wants are infinite and means are scarce, so that the task of economy is to close an ever-open gap. Foragers, Sahlins suggested, closed the gap from the other end. Their material wants were modest and could be satisfied with the resources at hand, and because they traveled frequently, possessions were a burden. A people who carry everything they own do not accumulate.

The thesis was widely discussed, and has since been criticized. The working-hours data came from short observation periods, often in seasons of plenty, and often did not count tasks such as making tools and processing plant foods. Several of the best-known groups were by the time of study living in marginal environments, pressed there by neighbors, and may have differed from foragers of richer lands in earlier eras. Archaeological evidence from other regions shows that some foraging societies were sedentary, stored food, and maintained inequalities of rank, so that the portrait of a uniformly egalitarian and unhurried existence is too simple. And infant mortality and injury were serious hazards, so leisure alone is a poor measure of well-being.

These objections correct the details of Sahlins' account without disturbing its central contribution. The contribution was not a claim that the Paleolithic was a paradise but a challenge to an inference. The inference ran from the technology of a society to the quality of its life: simpler tools, it was assumed, must mean harder lives. Sahlins showed that this reasoning depends on a hidden premise about what people want. If the premise is dropped, scarcity ceases to be a fixed condition of existence and becomes the product of a particular set of institutions, in particular, those that cultivate unlimited desire. A market society manufactures wants as well as goods, and it is therefore always poor in its own eyes, however much it produces.

The point has a modern application that does not depend on any romantic view of the past. When economists compare nations by income per person, they implicitly assume that a rise in consumption is a rise in welfare. Foraging societies serve as a reminder that this assumption is a cultural commitment rather than a finding. Whether a life is rich depends on the standard of counting, itself a product of social arrangements. An anthropologist who describes a society as poor because it has few possessions has therefore said something about the describer's own world at least as much as about the people described. The proper lesson is humility about the yardstick, and that lesson holds even if every one of the particular figures in the original studies is eventually revised.

qs.q: The central purpose of the passage is to:
o: demonstrate that hunting and gathering was a more comfortable way of life than agriculture in every region.
The author says the Paleolithic was not claimed to be a paradise and notes the hazards foragers faced.
refute Sahlins' thesis by showing that foragers worked longer hours than early observers recorded.
The author treats the criticisms as correcting details, not disturbing the central contribution.
argue that the lasting value of Sahlins' work lies in exposing a hidden assumption about wants, even if its data are revised.
Correct: The passage defends Sahlins' challenge to an inference about technology and well-being while conceding errors in detail, and ends by urging humility about the yardstick.
explain how modern economists measure national welfare using income per person.
Income comparison is only used in the last paragraph as an application.
qs.x: The passage defends Sahlins' challenge to an inference about technology and well-being while conceding errors in detail, and ends by urging humility about the yardstick. Trap: Taking the criticisms as the passage's verdict.

qs.q: As used in the passage, the phrase 'closed the gap from the other end' most nearly means that foragers:
o: produced goods more efficiently than agricultural societies did.
Efficient production is the opposite of the 'other end' described.
accumulated stores of food that exceeded the needs of their neighbors.
The passage says foragers did not accumulate possessions.
narrowed the gap by wanting less, not producing more.
Correct: The preceding sentence contrasts making many goods with wanting few; foragers did the latter.
closed the gap by moving to regions where food was most abundant.
Movement is mentioned only as making possessions a burden.
qs.x: The preceding sentence contrasts making many goods with wanting few; foragers did the latter. Trap: Reading a metaphor through the nearest concrete word (travel) instead of the contrast just stated.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine Sahlins' claim that foragers had modest material wants that they could satisfy with what they had?
o: Foraging groups in marginal environments spent less time on food acquisition than groups in richer environments.
This concerns work time and environment, not whether wants were modest.
Foraging groups routinely traded and raided to obtain more manufactured goods than they could carry or use.
Correct: Persistent effort to acquire surplus goods suggests that wants were not modest and bounded.
Foraging groups suffered from high rates of infant mortality and injury.
Hazards bear on well-being, not on the extent of desire for goods.
Foraging groups moved camp several times each year in response to seasonal changes.
Mobility is what the passage gives as the reason possessions were a burden.

is invalid, because only the number of hours worked can measure a society's welfare.

rests on a cultural commitment about what counts as well-being rather than on a demonstrated finding.

must be false, since consumption is unrelated to welfare in modern nations.
The author calls the assumption unproven, not demonstrably false.
qs.x: The author says that treating a rise in consumption as a rise in welfare is an assumption, not a finding. Trap: Swinging from 'unproven' to 'false'.

qs.q: Suppose later research showed that the foraging groups in the original studies actually worked twice as many hours as first reported. According to the passage, this would:
o: barely touch the core argument, which concerns wants, not hours.
Correct: The author states the lesson would hold even if every particular figure were revised.

The author separates the numbers from the argument about wants.

qs.x: The author states the lesson would hold even if every particular figure were revised. Trap: Treating a factual revision as fatal to a conceptual argument.

qs.q: The third paragraph, which lists criticisms of Sahlins' thesis, serves mainly to:
o: prove that foraging societies were uniformly egalitarian and unhurried.
The paragraph says the portrait of uniform egalitarianism is too simple.
show that modern economists have abandoned the assumption that wants are infinite.

Correct: The following paragraph begins by saying these objections correct details without disturbing the central contribution.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 5
text: A common way of thinking about crime begins with the act. Some acts, it is assumed, are inherently deviant: they violate norms that nearly everyone shares, and the people who commit them are different from those who do not. The sociologist's task, on this view, is to find what causes the difference, whether poverty, broken homes, or personality. In the middle of the twentieth century, a group of sociologists proposed that this approach had the problem backward. Howard Becker, whose formulation became the best known, argued that deviance is not a quality of the act itself but of the response to it. Social groups create deviance by making rules whose infraction constitutes deviance and by applying those rules to particular people, labeling them outsiders.

The claim is easily misunderstood. It does not say that harmful acts do not occur, or that it is arbitrary what societies forbid. Its point is that the label attached to an act depends on who does it, who sees it, and who has the power to make an accusation stick. The same drinking by two teenagers may be treated as high spirits at a well-off address and as delinquency in a poor neighborhood. Almost everyone breaks some rule; only some are caught, charged, and publicly named. If the offenders who come before courts are a sample drawn by the decisions of police, neighbors, and school officials, then characteristics that seem to distinguish offenders from others may reflect the selection process rather than the acts.

Labeling theorists drew a further, more controversial conclusion. Being named a deviant, they argued, can itself alter a person's course. A young man caught with a small quantity of drugs and expelled from school finds that conventional paths have narrowed: employers are wary, former friends keep their distance, and the remaining open group consists of others who have also been labeled. Over time, he may come to see himself as the sort of person the label describes. The initial act, which might have been a passing episode, is followed by a career of deviance that the reaction helped produce. The theory distinguishes between primary deviance, the original and often casual act, and secondary deviance, the behavior that develops as a response to the consequences of being labeled.

Critics replied that the theory exaggerated the power of labels and neglected the plain fact that some acts do harm whether or not anyone labels them. Empirical tests of the secondary deviance thesis have also been mixed. Some studies find that youths who are formally sanctioned go on to offend more than similar youths who escape notice, as the theory predicts, while others find no difference or a deterrent effect. The ambiguity may arise because the effect depends on circumstances: a sanction that preserves a person's standing in the community seems less damaging than one that publicly excludes him.

What the theory ultimately offers is not a complete account of crime but a corrective to a habit of mind. It reminds investigators that the categories they use to sort people were made by institutions with interests of their own, and that a statistic recording who was arrested is, in part, a record of who was watched. The theory's lasting value is therefore methodological: it directs attention to the questions of who defines the rule, who enforces it, and what happens to those who are named.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Labeling theory has been conclusively confirmed by studies showing that formal sanctions increase later offending.
The passage says tests of the secondary deviance thesis have been mixed.
Labeling theory is most valuable as a reminder that deviance categories and offender statistics are shaped by institutional decisions.
Correct: The final paragraph calls the theory's value methodological, directing attention to who defines the rule and who enforces it.
Harmful acts are not really harmful unless society names them as deviant.
The author says the theory does not claim that harmful acts fail to occur.
Poverty and personality are the true causes of deviance, which labeling theory fails to explain.
The author does not treat poverty or personality as established causes.
qs.x: The final paragraph calls the theory's value methodological, directing attention to who defines the rule and who enforces it. Trap: Overstating empirical support for the theory.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best example of secondary deviance as the passage defines it?
o: A student takes a small item from a store on a dare and then regrets it and returns it.
A single casual act that is not followed by labeling resembles primary deviance.
A police officer ignores a minor theft by a well-off student but arrests another student for the same act.
The unequal treatment illustrates selective labeling, not behavior developed in response to it.
A student expelled for a minor theft joins a group of other expelled youths and begins to steal regularly.
Correct: Secondary deviance is behavior that develops as a response to the consequences of being labeled, as in the narrowed paths and new peer group.
A criminologist finds that arrested youths have more unstable families than youths who are not arrested.

qs.q: The example of two teenagers drinking is used in the passage to illustrate that:
o: how an act is classified depends on who commits it and who has the power to name it.
Correct: The same behavior is treated as high spirits in one setting and delinquency in another.
well-off teenagers commit fewer rule violations than teenagers in poor neighborhoods.
The passage says that almost everyone breaks rules; it does not compare rates.
drinking by teenagers is not harmful if it is done in a wealthy household.
The author does not make a claim about harm.
police are the main source of deviant behavior in neighborhoods.
The point concerns classification, not police causing behavior.
qs.x: The same behavior is treated as high spirits in one setting and delinquency in another. Trap: Reading unequal treatment as unequal behavior.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the suggestion that differences between arrested and non-arrested youths may reflect the selection process rather than the acts?
o: Anonymous surveys show that the traits distinguishing arrested youths also predict higher self-reported rule breaking among all youths.
Correct: If the same traits predict actual rule breaking among unarrested youths, the difference is not just an artifact of who gets caught.

qs.x: If the same traits predict actual rule breaking among unarrested youths, the difference is not just an artifact of who gets caught. Trap: Choosing evidence that supports the author's position.

qs.q: Which of the following would critics of labeling theory most likely cite against Becker's claim that deviance is not a quality of the act itself?
o: Teenagers in wealthy neighborhoods are treated more leniently than teenagers elsewhere.
Differences in treatment are evidence for the theory.
Some studies show that sanctioned youths go on to offend more than similar youths who escape notice.
Increased offending after sanction is the effect the theory predicts.
Employers are more reluctant to hire people who have been publicly labeled.
Employer reluctance is part of the labeling theorists' account.
An assault injures its victim whether or not anyone ever calls the assailant a deviant.
Correct: The critics' point, as stated, is that some acts do harm regardless of how others react.
qs.x: The critics' point, as stated, is that some acts do harm regardless of how others react. Trap: Choosing evidence that supports the theory.

qs.q: A report finds that Neighborhood A has twice as many drug arrests as Neighborhood B. Based on the passage, the most cautious interpretation is that the figures may partly record:
o: that residents of Neighborhood A have personalities that make drug use likely.
The passage warns against assuming causes exist in the offenders when they may lie in selection.
where police concentrate their attention, as well as how much drug use occurs.
Correct: The author says an arrest statistic is in part a record of who was watched.
that drug use is harmless in Neighborhood B because it is not punished.
The author does not claim that unpunished acts are harmless.
that labeling theory has been disproved by the difference in arrest rates.
The report does not test the theory at all.
qs.x: The author says an arrest statistic is in part a record of who was watched. Trap: Reading a statistic as a direct measure of behavior.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Consider a minor ritual of modern life: the line. People who wait for a bus, a bank teller, or a concert ticket arrange themselves in single file, in order of arrival, and no one in authority needs to tell them to. Someone who steps to the front is met with glares and murmurs, sometimes with open protest, and the feeling of outrage seems out of all proportion to the few minutes that the offender gains. Yet the queue is a revealing case, because it is an institution with no founder, no written code, and no official enforcement that is nonetheless remarkably stable.

The rule governing the queue is that of first come, first served, and it is worth noticing how particular a rule it is. Resources could be allotted in other ways: to the strongest, the wealthiest, the most deserving, or the person whose need is greatest. Emergency rooms use the last criterion, and some airlines sell priority to the second. First come, first served has a distinctive moral character. It treats every person as equivalent in everything except the time of arrival, and it makes that single difference the basis of precedence. It is blind to status, to merit, and to need. In this sense, waiting in line expresses an egalitarian conception of persons, which helps explain why violations feel like insults: the line-jumper has not merely saved time but has claimed to be worth more than others who were present before him.

The queue also reveals what sociologists mean by a social fact. No individual in a line chooses the rule, and any one person can decline to follow it. Yet the pressure to conform is real, and it is applied by the participants themselves. Those who wait enforce the order against those who might break it, at some cost to themselves in time and discomfort, with no reward other than the preservation of the arrangement. This is the kind of enforcement that a theorist of norms would expect: a rule is genuinely a norm only when its violation is sanctioned by the group even though the sanctioner gains little personally.

The rule is not universal, and its limits are instructive. Observers of markets, ticket windows, and bus stops in different cultures report that the single-file line is by no means the only solution to the problem of crowding. In some places people gather in a loose cluster, and precedence is negotiated through eye contact, small gestures, and a shared sense of who arrived when. Such arrangements can work smoothly, and members of those cultures may find the rigid line unnatural. Travelers who are accustomed to one convention and who enter a place that follows the other often feel at once that they are being treated rudely, though no one has intended an offense. The discomfort is a sign of how deeply the rule has been absorbed: it feels not like a convention but like a plain requirement of fairness.

The ordinary experience of waiting thus offers a lesson that sociologists have drawn from larger structures. Social order is not only a matter of laws and police. It depends on millions of small agreements that are maintained because people internalize them, enforce them upon each other, and mistake them for the nature of things. To see the queue as a convention rather than a law of nature is to begin to see what many other apparently natural arrangements might be.

qs.q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: argue that first come, first served is the fairest method of allocating scarce resources in settings from hospitals to ticket windows.
The author calls the rule 'particular' and notes alternatives rather than defending it as the fairest.
prove that cultures that do not use single-file lines are less orderly than those that do.
The author says other arrangements work smoothly.
describe the history of the queue from its origin in the nineteenth century.
The queue is described as having no founder and no history is given.
use the queue as an everyday example of how conventions sustain social order while seeming natural.
Correct: The passage concludes that seeing the queue as a convention is the start of seeing other apparently natural arrangements as conventions.
qs.x: The passage concludes that seeing the queue as a convention is the start of seeing other apparently natural arrangements as conventions. Trap: Treating a description of the rule as the author's endorsement.

qs.q: According to the passage, why does line-jumping provoke outrage out of proportion to the time gained?
o: The jumper breaks a written code that is enforced by a recognized authority.
The queue has no written code or official enforcement.

The rule is blind to status, and the passage does not say that jumpers are of higher status.
qs.x: The author says the rule treats everyone as equivalent except for time of arrival, so cutting claims special worth. Trap: Supplying a plausible practical reason that the passage dismisses.

qs.q: According to the passage, a rule counts as a genuine norm when:
o: it is written into law and enforced by police.
The queue is cited precisely because it has no official enforcement.
violators are sanctioned by unrewarded peers.
Correct: The author defines genuine norms by group sanctions that cost the sanctioners something and reward them little.
every member of the group has agreed to it in advance.
The author notes that no individual chooses the rule.
violations are punished by those who stand to gain from the sanction.
The passage says the sanctioners receive no reward beyond preserving the arrangement.
qs.x: The author defines genuine norms by group sanctions that cost the sanctioners something and reward them little. Trap: Importing a legal definition of rules.

qs.q: The author mentions emergency rooms and airlines in order to:
o: argue that emergency rooms and airlines should adopt the queue as their method.
The author makes no recommendation for those institutions.

The author does not rank the criteria.

The passage does not discuss the queue's origins.

Correct: The examples demonstrate need-based and wealth-based alternatives before the author describes the moral character of the queue's rule.
qs.x: The examples demonstrate need-based and wealth-based alternatives before the author describes the moral character of the queue's rule. Trap: Missing the contrast function of an example.

qs.q: A traveler from a country with single-file lines visits a place where people gather loosely and feels she is being treated rudely. The passage suggests that her reaction shows:
o: how deeply she has absorbed a rule that feels like fairness.
Correct: The author says the discomfort is a sign of how deeply the rule has been absorbed and mistaken for a requirement of fairness.
that the local people are in fact behaving rudely according to a universal standard.
The author states that no one has intended an offense.

The author says other arrangements can work smoothly.

qs.x: The author says the discomfort is a sign of how deeply the rule has been absorbed and mistaken for a requirement of fairness. Trap: Accepting the traveler's perception as objective.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely cite as another instance of a convention mistaken for the nature of things?
o: The law of gravity, which causes dropped objects to fall at the same rate everywhere.
A law of nature is not a convention.
A court ruling that applies a written statute to a particular dispute.

The distance people stand from one another in conversation, which varies across cultures yet feels like simple courtesy to those who follow it.
Correct: This is an unwritten, culturally variable arrangement that members regard as natural and enforce through discomfort.
A hospital rule that treats the most critically ill patient first.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 7
text: Among the ideas in economics that are widely accepted by specialists and widely doubted by everyone else, comparative advantage holds a prominent place. David Ricardo stated the principle in the early nineteenth century using cloth and wine. Suppose that one country can produce both goods with less labor than another. It might seem that this country has nothing to gain from trade. Ricardo's insight was that what matters is not absolute efficiency but relative cost. If the first country is much better at making wine than at making cloth, while the second is only slightly worse at cloth than at wine, then each does best by specializing where its disadvantage is smallest and buying the rest. Both end up with more of both goods than either could have made alone.

The argument is mathematically secure. Yet the theorem is a statement about totals. It says that the gains of those who benefit are large enough that they could, in principle, compensate those who lose and still come out ahead. It does not say that they will do so, or that the losers are the same people as the winners. A country that opens its markets to cheap imported textiles lowers prices for every consumer, but it also eliminates jobs in its textile towns. The consumers' savings are spread thinly over millions of households; the workers' losses are concentrated on a few thousand, and they do not come back when the economy adjusts, because a person who has spent thirty years operating a loom cannot readily become a software engineer.

Critics of free trade have long pointed to this asymmetry, and the evidence of recent decades has given their argument fresh force. Studies of regions that were exposed to a surge of imports found that displaced workers did not smoothly move to new industries. Many left the labor force, and wages in the affected areas remained depressed for years. Economists who had expected quick adjustment had to concede that their models assumed a mobility real people lack.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that the theory of comparative advantage has been refuted. The critics' evidence concerns the distribution of gains, not their existence, and the theory never claimed otherwise. The accurate conclusion is that the principle is incomplete as a guide to policy, rather than false as an account of the economy. A defender of trade can grant every fact about displaced workers and still hold that the right response is to keep borders open while compensating the losers through retraining and wage insurance. Protecting an industry forgoes the gains from cheaper goods, and the protected workers are often not helped in the long run because the industry's decline continues anyway.

Why then has the compensation so rarely been paid? The answer lies partly in politics. The beneficiaries of trade are numerous and diffuse, and no one of them has an incentive to lobby for a program that would transfer their gains to strangers. The losers are few and concentrated, and they have every incentive to organize in opposition to trade itself, which is the visible cause of their hardship. The result is a debate in which defenders speak of aggregate benefits and critics of particular suffering. A sounder debate would hold two things together at once: that the theory of comparative advantage describes a real source of wealth, and that its promise of compensation is a promissory note that societies have too often failed to honor. The principle is a reason to trade; it is not a reason to ignore those who pay for it.

qs.q: Which of the following best captures the author's position on comparative advantage?
o: It correctly explains a source of national wealth but is incomplete as a policy guide unless losers are compensated.
Correct: The author says the principle is incomplete as a guide to policy rather than false as an account of the economy, and that compensation is the missing piece.
It has been refuted by evidence that import competition permanently harms displaced workers in the regions most exposed to imports.
The author says the critics' evidence concerns distribution, not existence of gains.
It proves that protective barriers are always harmful to the workers they are intended to help.
The author says protection often fails to help workers, but does not claim that barriers are always harmful.
It applies only to countries that are more productive than their trading partners in every good.
Ricardo's example shows that the principle holds even when one country is more productive in everything.
qs.x: The author says the principle is incomplete as a guide to policy rather than false as an account of the economy, and that compensation is the missing piece. Trap: Treating criticism of a theory's policy use as refutation of the theory.

qs.q: According to Ricardo's example, a country that can make both goods with less labor than its partner should:
o: produce everything itself, since trade could not improve on its efficiency.
The passage says absolute efficiency is not what matters.
specialize in the good at which it is least productive in order to protect its workers.
Producing the good with the largest disadvantage would reverse the logic of the example.

Correct: What matters is relative cost, so each country specializes where its relative disadvantage is smallest.

The passage gives no requirement that productivity be equal.
qs.x: What matters is relative cost, so each country specializes where its relative disadvantage is smallest. Trap: Equating the most productive country with the one that needs no trade.

qs.q: The author mentions that 'a person who has spent thirty years operating a loom cannot readily become a software engineer' in order to:
o: show that technological change is more harmful to workers than trade is.
The passage does not compare technology and trade.

The author does not recommend any limits on who may hold jobs.
suggest that consumers are unaffected by the loss of jobs in textile towns.
The passage says consumers gain through lower prices, which is a separate point.
explain why the losses from trade do not disappear when the economy adjusts.
Correct: The example shows that mobility is limited, so displaced workers do not simply move to new jobs.
qs.x: The example shows that mobility is limited, so displaced workers do not simply move to new jobs. Trap: Missing that the example supports the point about persistent concentrated losses.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that protecting an industry often fails to help its workers over the long run?
o: Workers in protected industries have generally kept stable employment and wages for decades after protection was imposed.
Correct: Stable employment and wages for decades under protection would contradict the claim that decline continues anyway.

qs.q: The author's explanation for why compensation has rarely been paid is primarily that:
o: economists have never proposed a workable method of compensating the losers.
The author names compensation methods such as retraining and wage insurance.
losers organize while the diffuse winners stay silent.
Correct: The author says beneficiaries are numerous and diffuse and have little reason to lobby for transfers.
the gains from trade are too small to compensate anyone.
The theorem says the gains are large enough to compensate losers in principle.

The author says the theorem does not say that compensation will occur.
qs.x: The author says beneficiaries are numerous and diffuse and have little reason to lobby for transfers. Trap: Reading 'could compensate' as 'will compensate'.

qs.q: The author's phrase 'a promissory note that societies have too often failed to honor' implies that:
o: the benefits of trade are merely promises that have not yet been realized for the consumers who were supposed to gain.
The author says the benefits of trade are real.

The author argues against protection as a solution.

Correct: The figure describes the theory's potential for compensation as a commitment that has not been met.
