passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 8
text: In 1774, Edmund Burke, newly elected to Parliament for the city of Bristol, told his constituents that he would not take his instructions from them. A representative, he said, owes his constituents his judgment, and he betrays rather than serves them if he sacrifices it to their opinion. Parliament, in his view, was not a congress of ambassadors from hostile interests, each bound to argue for the party that sent him, but a deliberative assembly of one nation with one interest, that of the whole. The Bristol voters, who valued the commercial interests of their port, did not return him at the next election. Burke's speech has nonetheless been treated ever since as the classic statement of one side of an old debate: should a representative act as a delegate, carrying out the expressed wishes of those who elected him, or as a trustee, using his own judgment of what is best?

The delegate view has the evident attraction of democracy. If citizens are to govern themselves, it seems that their representatives must follow them, and a legislator who overrides his constituents on the ground that he knows better looks like a tutor who has replaced his pupils. The trustee view, however, has a respectable reply. Representatives have time, information, and the opportunity to hear all sides, which the average voter, occupied with work and family, lacks. A decision that depends on the details of a complex budget or treaty is one the voters cannot judge directly, and it is the representative's job to do for them what they would do for themselves if they had the leisure.

Both positions, stated in this way, face a difficulty. The delegate model assumes that constituents have definite opinions that the representative can discover. On many questions, they do not. Public opinion about a proposed trade agreement or a revision of the tax code is often thin, unstable, and responsive to how a question is worded. To follow it faithfully may be to follow nothing. The trustee model, for its part, assumes that the representative's judgment is trustworthy, yet it provides no assurance of this beyond the occasional election. A trustee who is accountable only after the fact may be indistinguishable from a politician who pursues his own advantage and calls it conscience.

Contemporary theorists have therefore suggested that the dichotomy is misleading. On one influential account, representation is better understood as a continuing relationship of communication than as a transfer of authority at a single moment. The representative explains his decisions, listens to the reactions, and revises his positions in light of what he hears. Voters, in turn, judge him not simply by whether he did what they asked but by whether he gave reasons they could accept. By this standard, a legislator who departs from his constituents' preferences is not necessarily a betrayer of democracy, provided that he is willing to defend the departure in public and to be corrected if the defense fails. Conversely, a legislator who follows polls without explanation may be less representative than one who occasionally defies them with candor.

This view does not dissolve the tension between responsiveness and judgment, but it moves it. The question is no longer which of the two should prevail but how the process of explanation and response can be kept alive, and that depends on conditions, such as a free press, active local organizations, and voters who care enough to listen, which neither Burke nor his critics could create by argument alone.

qs.q: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with:
o: examining the delegate and trustee views of representation and presenting an alternative that treats representation as an ongoing exchange.
Correct: After presenting both views and their weaknesses, the author turns to contemporary theorists' account of continuing communication.
defending Burke's position that representatives should ignore the preferences of voters.
The author criticizes the trustee model as well as the delegate model.
showing that voters hold definite and stable opinions on most legislative questions.
The author says public opinion is often thin and unstable.
explaining why Bristol voters chose not to reelect Burke in the next election.
The Bristol outcome is a brief detail, not the subject.
qs.x: After presenting both views and their weaknesses, the author turns to contemporary theorists' account of continuing communication. Trap: Choosing the first figure introduced rather than the passage's overall structure.

qs.q: According to the passage, the trustee view assumes that:
o: the representative's judgment can be relied upon, although voters have little assurance of this beyond elections.
Correct: The author says the trustee model assumes trustworthy judgment but offers no assurance except the occasional election.
voters are well informed and hold firm opinions that representatives can discover.
The assumption about firm opinions belongs to the delegate model.
representatives should act as ambassadors who argue for the interests of their own regions.
Burke explicitly rejected the ambassador conception.
a representative's decisions should be settled by polls on each question, with the representative serving only as a messenger for the electorate's latest preferences.
Polling is related to the delegate model.
qs.x: The author says the trustee model assumes trustworthy judgment but offers no assurance except the occasional election. Trap: Attributing the delegate model's assumption to the trustee model.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author most likely say about a legislator who votes against the preferences of his constituents?
o: He has betrayed his voters and should not be reelected under any circumstances.
The author states he is not necessarily a betrayer.
He is not necessarily failing democratically if he explains his vote publicly and accepts correction.
Correct: The author says such a legislator is not necessarily a betrayer of democracy provided he is willing to defend the departure and be corrected.

He can be judged only by the outcomes of the policy he chose.

qs.x: The author says such a legislator is not necessarily a betrayer of democracy provided he is willing to defend the departure and be corrected. Trap: Falling back on the trustee view without the author's condition.

qs.q: The author most likely includes the observation that public opinion is 'responsive to how a question is worded' to:
o: cast doubt on the delegate model's assumption that constituents have definite opinions to follow.
Correct: If opinion shifts with wording, following it faithfully may be following nothing.
support Burke's claim that the interests of Parliament are those of a single nation.
The point is made against delegate representation, not in support of national interest.
argue that wording of questions should be regulated by law.
The author does not propose regulating wording.
show that voters are less intelligent than their representatives and so ought to defer to them on technical questions.
The passage says voters lack leisure and information, not intelligence.
qs.x: If opinion shifts with wording, following it faithfully may be following nothing. Trap: Reading a limit on opinion as an insult to voters.

qs.q: Which of the following developments would, according to the passage, most help the continuing-relationship model of representation to work?
o: A rule that requires legislators to vote as polls indicate on every issue.
Mandatory poll-following is the delegate model that the author finds inadequate.
A longer term of office, so legislators face voters less frequently.
Less frequent accountability would make the trustee problem worse.
A ban on legislators' communicating directly with their constituents.
The model depends on communication.
A free press and active local groups for hearing explanations.
Correct: The author names a free press, active local organizations, and attentive voters as conditions for keeping explanation and response alive.
qs.x: The author names a free press, active local organizations, and attentive voters as conditions for keeping explanation and response alive. Trap: Choosing a mechanism from the old dichotomy.

qs.q: Burke's speech to the Bristol voters is mentioned in the first paragraph primarily as:
o: an example of a speech that persuaded most of his voters.
The voters did not return him at the next election.
evidence that Parliament was composed of ambassadors from competing regions.
Burke rejected the ambassador conception.
proof that the delegate position is incorrect.
The passage does not claim to settle the dispute at this point.
a well-known illustration of one side of a long-standing dispute.
Correct: The passage says the speech has been treated as the classic statement of one side of an old debate.
qs.x: The passage says the speech has been treated as the classic statement of one side of an old debate. Trap: Reading the outcome of an election as a verdict on the theory.

passages.title: Mini09 · CARS · Passage 9
text: Insurance markets rest on a simple idea: a large group of people pool the risk of an event that would be ruinous for any one of them, each paying a modest premium so that the few who suffer a loss are compensated. For this to work, the insurer must set premiums high enough to cover the expected claims of the group. This is where the difficulty begins, because the people who buy insurance are not a random sample of the population. They know more about their own prospects than the insurer does, and that gap in information can unravel the arrangement.

Economists distinguish two problems that arise from the gap. The first, adverse selection, occurs before a policy is sold. Suppose an insurer offers health coverage at a price calculated for the average person. Those who know themselves to be healthy find the price too high and decline; those who know of a chronic condition find it a bargain and accept. The insurer's pool is now sicker than the population, its claims exceed expectations, and it must raise the premium. The higher price drives out the next-healthiest customers, and the pool deteriorates further. In the extreme case, the market collapses, and the people who most need coverage cannot buy it at any price they could afford. The famous illustration is the market for used cars, where a buyer who cannot distinguish good cars from bad is willing to pay only an average price, so that the owners of good cars withdraw and only poor ones are left.

The second problem, moral hazard, occurs after the policy is sold. A person who is fully protected against the cost of an accident may take less care to avoid one, or may use more services than he otherwise would because he does not bear the price. The word hazard here describes a change in behavior, not a moral defect; the response is a rational one to altered incentives. Insurers have developed familiar tools in response. Deductibles and copayments ensure that the insured keeps a stake in the outcome; premiums that fall for a record of safe driving reward careful behavior; and screening, such as a medical examination, narrows the information gap before a policy is issued.

Each remedy has a cost, however. A high deductible reduces moral hazard but also exposes people to the very financial risk they sought to escape, and there is evidence that it discourages them from seeking beneficial care along with unnecessary care. Screening can protect the insurer, but it may leave the people with the greatest needs uninsured, defeating the purpose of the arrangement. For this reason, many governments have chosen to mandate coverage for everyone. A compulsory scheme eliminates adverse selection, since the healthy cannot leave, but it requires a political willingness to compel participation and subsidize those who cannot afford the premium, and it leaves moral hazard to be addressed by other means.

The two problems are often discussed as if they were separate defects of insurance, but they share a source: the person insured knows something, whether about his health or about his intentions, that the insurer cannot observe. Both are reminders that a market is more than a meeting of buyers and sellers with settled preferences. It is also a system for conveying information, and where information cannot be conveyed the market does not simply perform poorly; it may fail to exist. The design of institutions that do the conveying, through contracts, regulations, or compulsory pooling, is among the central tasks of applied economics.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Gaps in information between insurers and buyers create problems that can undermine insurance markets and require institutional solutions.
Correct: The final paragraph traces both problems to an information gap and describes institutions as the remedy.
Insurance markets function best when buyers and sellers have identical information and settled preferences.
The passage says information is what a market must convey, but not that equality of information is always achieved.
Mandatory insurance is the only remedy for the problems created by moral hazard.
Mandates address adverse selection, and the passage says they leave moral hazard to be handled otherwise.
Moral hazard arises because people who purchase insurance are morally defective.
The author explicitly says that hazard refers to behavior, not a defect.
qs.x: The final paragraph traces both problems to an information gap and describes institutions as the remedy. Trap: Taking one remedy (mandates) as the central subject.

qs.q: The used-car example is included in the passage in order to:
o: show that insurers should avoid selling coverage to owners of used cars.
The example is an analogy, not advice to insurers.
illustrate that adverse selection can occur in markets other than insurance.
Correct: Buyers who cannot tell good from bad pay an average price, which drives out sellers of good cars, as healthy people leave an insurance pool.
demonstrate that moral hazard is the reason that good cars disappear from the market.
The example concerns adverse selection, which happens before the sale.
argue that buyers should never purchase used goods.
The author gives no advice on purchasing used goods.
qs.x: Buyers who cannot tell good from bad pay an average price, which drives out sellers of good cars, as healthy people leave an insurance pool. Trap: Missing the analogy and confusing the two problems.

qs.q: A car owner who has full coverage begins parking in unsafe areas because he will not pay for any theft. This best illustrates:
o: adverse selection, because the owner knew more about his risks than the insurer did.
Adverse selection occurs before a policy is sold.
screening, because the insurer has narrowed the information gap.
Screening occurs before issuing the policy and he did not cause it.
a deductible, because the insured keeps a stake in the outcome.
A deductible would give him a stake; he has none.
moral hazard, because the insured changes his behavior after being protected.
Correct: Moral hazard is a change in behavior after a policy is sold in response to altered incentives.
qs.x: Moral hazard is a change in behavior after a policy is sold in response to altered incentives. Trap: Confusing the pre-sale and post-sale problems.

qs.q: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that mandatory coverage eliminates adverse selection?
o: Governments that mandate coverage must subsidize premiums for people who cannot afford them.
Subsidies are a cost of the scheme the author already notes, not a challenge to the mechanism.
Mandatory coverage leaves moral hazard to be addressed by other means.
The author already acknowledges this limit, and it concerns moral hazard.
High deductibles discourage people from seeking beneficial as well as unnecessary care.
This concerns deductibles, not mandates.
Many healthy people can remain uninsured under the mandate without penalty.
Correct: The claim depends on the healthy being unable to leave the pool; if they can remain uninsured, the pool would still skew toward the sick.
qs.x: The claim depends on the healthy being unable to leave the pool; if they can remain uninsured, the pool would still skew toward the sick. Trap: Selecting costs the author already admits.

qs.q: The author's statement that where information cannot be conveyed a market 'may fail to exist' is most directly supported by which example in the passage?
o: The use of deductibles to keep the insured invested in outcomes.
Deductibles are a remedy for moral hazard.
The collapse of the pool as healthy customers leave and premiums rise.
Correct: The extreme case of adverse selection is a collapsed market in which the needy cannot buy coverage at any affordable price.
Reduced premiums for a record of safe driving.
Safe-driving discounts reward behavior after sale.
The requirement that governments subsidize premiums for people who cannot afford coverage on their own.
Subsidies are part of a mandate, which solves the problem.
qs.x: The extreme case of adverse selection is a collapsed market in which the needy cannot buy coverage at any affordable price. Trap: Choosing a remedy rather than the failure the statement describes.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Until the early nineteenth century, orchestras in Europe commonly played without anyone standing in front of them. Time was kept by the concertmaster, who nodded or swept a bow from the first desk, or by a keyboardist who played continuo and signaled changes of pace with the hands. The ensemble worked because its members shared a repertoire, a style, and often a town. A symphony was usually new, performed once or twice, and rehearsed little; the players' task was to stay together, not to interpret. When a dedicated beater of time did appear, contemporaries were not sure what to make of him. Some thought him a kind of human metronome, and in the opera house he was sometimes nearly that: Jean-Baptiste Lully, in 1687, is said to have marked the beat by pounding the floor with a heavy staff, and to have died after the staff pierced his foot.

The standard account treats the conductor's rise as a response to scores that had outgrown the old methods. Orchestras expanded, harmony grew more adventurous, and rhythms began to shift in ways that a violinist's nod could not manage. There is truth in this. But it explains the conductor's necessity better than his authority. A time-beater needs no particular genius, and the nineteenth century soon decided that its conductors had a great deal. By mid-century the figure on the podium was credited with something beyond coordination: the power to reveal what a composition meant. Wagner argued that the conductor must grasp the melos of a work, its inner line of feeling, and then impose it on the players by sheer presence; tempo, in his view, was not a number but an expressive decision that changed from phrase to phrase. Berlioz, who led his own enormous works, wrote a treatise on the art, and Hans von Bulow made a career of standing for scrupulous fidelity to what he took to be the composer's intentions.

These two ideals, the interpreter who discloses a work's spirit and the servant who obeys its letter, were rarely compatible, and the tension has never been resolved. It sharpened in the twentieth century, when recording allowed a conductor's decisions to be compared across decades. Listeners discovered that the same symphony could last forty minutes under one baton and fifty under another, and that each performance claimed to be the authentic one. Toscanini was praised for severity toward the score, yet his readings were as personal as anyone's, his famous literalism consisting largely of a particular and rigorously maintained view of the music. Furtwangler, by contrast, was admired for a flexibility so extreme that critics wondered whether the composer still had a say.

It would be tempting to conclude that the conductor's authority is therefore an illusion, an inflated claim propped up by ceremony. Yet this overlooks a quieter fact about what a conductor actually does. Much of his influence is exerted through ordinary choices: which passage to repeat in rehearsal, which player to single out, how long to wait before the downbeat. These are small decisions, but in an ensemble of eighty people with no other center of judgment, they accumulate into a recognizable sound. The conductor's power, on this view, is neither the mystical access to the composer's mind that Wagner claimed nor the empty pomp his skeptics allege. It is the power of a person whom many others have agreed, for practical reasons, to follow, and the agreement is what makes the rest possible. Interpretation emerges from this arrangement rather than preceding it.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: The conductor arose because modern scores grew too complex for a concertmaster's nod to coordinate the players.
This is the standard account, which the author qualifies as explaining necessity but not authority.
Recordings have shown that conductors who claim fidelity to a score are merely imposing personal taste upon it, so that the claim of fidelity is only a pose adopted to impress audiences.
Recordings exposed the tension between ideals, but the author does not reduce all fidelity to personal taste, and the passage ends elsewhere.
The conductor's authority, though defended by rival ideals of interpretation, rests mainly on a practical agreement among players to follow one person.

Correct: The final paragraph concludes that authority arises from the arrangement of players and conductor, after the second and third paragraphs show that neither ideal of interpretation can ground it.
The belief that a conductor can reveal a composer's meaning has been refuted by differences in performance length.
The author calls the mystical claim overstated but never says differences in length refute it, and the main point concerns the source of authority.
qs.x: The final paragraph concludes that authority arises from the arrangement of players and conductor, after the second and third paragraphs show that neither ideal of interpretation can ground it. Trap: Picking the standard historical account because it opens the passage, rather than the author's own thesis at the end.

qs.q: The author most likely mentions Lully's staff in order to:
o: demonstrate that conductors were dangerous colleagues because of the crude implements they used to command orchestras.
The injury is incidental; the author is not making a point about danger to players.
support the claim that the first conductors were admired for expressive interpretation rather than for keeping time.
The anecdote concerns pounding out the beat, which is the opposite of interpretation.
show that the earliest time-beaters were humble figures.
Correct: The anecdote shows a beater of time pounding the floor, supporting the point that early leaders merely marked the pulse.
illustrate that opera orchestras were more disciplined than concert orchestras in the period before the nineteenth century.
Nothing in the passage compares the discipline of opera and concert orchestras.
qs.x: The anecdote shows a beater of time pounding the floor, supporting the point that early leaders merely marked the pulse. Trap: Treating a vivid detail as evidence for a claim the passage never makes, such as danger or discipline.

qs.q: The author's statement that the standard account "explains the conductor's necessity better than his authority" most nearly means that:
o: growing complexity shows why someone had to coordinate the players, but not why that person came to be seen as the revealer of a work's meaning.
Correct: The next sentences contrast a time-beater needing no genius with nineteenth-century credit given to the conductor's insight.
complex scores made conductors indispensable, but players resented the power that this indispensability gave them.
Player resentment is never mentioned.
the standard account misdates the point at which orchestras grew large and their harmonies more adventurous.
The author accepts the account's facts and says there is truth in it.
the need for coordination was real but was in practice met by the concertmaster instead of a separate conductor.
The concertmaster served in the earlier period; the passage says the conductor later became the coordinator.
qs.x: The next sentences contrast a time-beater needing no genius with nineteenth-century credit given to the conductor's insight. Trap: Reading a claim about explanatory scope as a claim that the facts are wrong.

qs.q: Which of the following is most consistent with the passage's description of Toscanini?
o: His readings were looser than Furtwangler's, whom critics regarded as severe toward the score.
The passage reverses these reputations: Toscanini was severe and Furtwangler flexible.
His claim to literal fidelity itself reflected a personal conception of the work.
Correct: The passage says his literalism consisted largely of a particular and rigorously maintained view of the music.
His performances were indistinguishable in length and character from those of his contemporaries.
The passage says only that performances of the same symphony varied widely in length.
He rejected the view that a conductor should serve the composer's intentions in favor of freely expressive readings.
He was praised for severity toward the score, so he did not reject fidelity.
qs.x: The passage says his literalism consisted largely of a particular and rigorously maintained view of the music. Trap: Assuming that a reputation for literalism means the performances were impersonal.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most undermine the author's account of how conductors exert their influence?
o: Audiences rate concerts more highly when they can see the conductor than when they cannot.
Audience ratings say nothing about how influence is exerted in rehearsal.
Conductors who rehearse for longer periods produce performances that critics judge more faithful to the score.
This concerns fidelity, and could be consistent with influence through rehearsal choices.
In recorded rehearsals of large orchestras, players disregard the conductor's choices about repetition and timing and follow the concertmaster instead.
Correct: If players ignore these ordinary choices, the accumulation of small decisions into a recognizable sound is no longer explained.
Recordings of one symphony by different conductors differ in length by as much as ten minutes.
Differences in length are consistent with the author's account of conductors' choices.
qs.x: If players ignore these ordinary choices, the accumulation of small decisions into a recognizable sound is no longer explained. Trap: Choosing evidence about audiences or critics when the claim concerns influence inside the orchestra.

qs.q: The authority of the conductor described in the final paragraph is most like the authority of:
o: a monarch who claims the right to rule through divine appointment and personal access to a higher truth.
This resembles Wagner's mystical claim, which the author rejects.
a referee who enforces rules written by an outside body and has no discretion in applying them.
This resembles the servant who obeys the letter and is not based on consent.
a team captain whose standing rests on teammates' agreement and on many small decisions.
Correct: Both depend on voluntary agreement to follow and on accumulated routine choices.
a timekeeper whose only task is to signal the end of each interval and who exercises no judgment.
This resembles the early time-beater, whom the author contrasts with the later conductor.
qs.x: Both depend on voluntary agreement to follow and on accumulated routine choices. Trap: Matching the analogy to the most dramatic image of authority rather than the one the author endorses.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 2
text: In the industrial towns of northern England in the nineteenth century, a mill or colliery of any size was likely to have a brass band. Employers bought the instruments, paid for the uniforms, and hired a professional teacher; in return the band carried the firm's name to festivals and contests, and its members, who were drawn from the workforce, were expected to embody the habits an employer prized: punctuality, sobriety, and discipline. Historians who read these arrangements as paternalism have a strong case. The band was an advertisement, a means of binding skilled workers to the firm, and an alternative to the public house, which employers regarded as the chief enemy of a reliable labor force.

The difficulty is that the same evidence supports a very different story. Valved brass instruments became cheap through mass production in the middle of the century, and players did not need to read music fluently to join, because teachers drilled parts by ear and by rote. A man who could not afford a piano or a violin could belong to a band for a few shillings a week. Rehearsals took place several evenings a week, and the players, not the owners, decided who was good enough to sit in the front row. The contest movement, which grew around annual competitions near Manchester from the 1850s, rewarded precision and musical ambition, and bands began to compete by hiring famous conductors, commissioning arrangements of operatic and choral works, and traveling by railway to meet rivals. Some historians therefore describe the bands as an expression of working-class pride, a cultural world that workers built for themselves with borrowed money.

Neither description survives contact with the details of particular bands. Employers who sponsored bands often discovered that sponsorship did not purchase loyalty. During strikes, bands sometimes played on the picket line or refused to perform at the owner's gala, and a band whose firm failed could simply change its name and carry on under a new patron, its instruments and repertoire intact. Conversely, bands that began as the independent projects of a chapel or a neighborhood frequently accepted gifts from local manufacturers, since uniforms and professional tuition were costly and the contest circuit was unforgiving to the poor. The supposed contrast between control from above and expression from below depends on picturing the band as a single object with a single function. In practice it was a bundle of resources: instruments, rehearsal space, status, a calendar of public appearances.

The same resource could serve different interests at different times. A patron who funded a band acquired a visible symbol of his generosity, but he also gave the players an organization, a treasury, and a public voice that they could use as they wished. What patrons could not control was the musical standard itself. Because contests were judged by outsiders, a band's reputation depended on its quality, not on its owner's wishes, and ambitious players soon discovered that excellence gave them bargaining power. A sponsor who withdrew support risked losing a famous band to a rival firm. The bands thus illustrate a more general feature of cultural patronage: money can create an institution, but once the institution has its own measures of success, those who paid for it may find that they have bought something they only partly own.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the author's view of nineteenth-century brass bands?
o: They resist classification as either employer control or worker self-expression, since patronage produced resources that served several interests.
Correct: The author argues the supposed contrast depends on picturing the band as having a single function.
They were mainly instruments of employer paternalism, since sponsors supplied instruments, uniforms, and teachers and in return expected punctuality, sobriety, and deference from every player.
This is one reading the author accepts only in part and then challenges.
They were independent working-class creations that employers tried and failed to take over.
The author notes that independent bands also accepted gifts from manufacturers.
They were transformed by the contest movement into professional organizations responsive only to outside judges.
The judges set the standard, but the author does not say bands answered only to them.
qs.x: The author argues the supposed contrast depends on picturing the band as having a single function. Trap: Choosing one of the two competing historical readings instead of the author's rejection of the contrast.

qs.q: According to the passage, a worker of modest means could join a band because:
o: employers gave free instruments to any employee willing to rehearse several evenings every week.
The passage says employers bought instruments for the band but not that any employee received one free.
instruments were cheap and parts could be learned by ear.
Correct: The passage says valved brass instruments became cheap and teachers drilled parts by ear and rote.
contest organizers subsidized fees for players from firms that could not afford professional teachers.
Contest subsidies are not mentioned.
bands admitted only those who already read music well, which kept the cost of instruction low.
The passage says players did not need to read music fluently.
qs.x: The passage says valved brass instruments became cheap and teachers drilled parts by ear and rote. Trap: Picking a plausible-sounding subsidy that the passage never mentions.

qs.q: The author mentions bands that played on picket lines or changed patrons in order to show that:
o: brass bands were political organizations seeking the overthrow of the factory system.
Playing on a picket line shows sympathy with strikers, not a revolutionary program.
the contest circuit forced bands to move constantly from one firm to another.
Changing patrons is mentioned as a survival tactic when a firm failed, not as a constant pattern.
employers consistently underestimated the cost of maintaining a band.
Cost is raised later in connection with poor bands, not here.
sponsorship did not buy the loyalty that employers expected.
Correct: These episodes are offered as evidence that employers' investment did not secure deference.
qs.x: These episodes are offered as evidence that employers' investment did not secure deference. Trap: Taking a single illustration as a statement of a broader political claim.

qs.q: The passage suggests that the "social control" reading and the "working-class expression" reading share which assumption?
o: That the contest movement was the most important force shaping band life.
Contests are discussed in only one reading.
That employers had no reason to sponsor bands.
The first reading depends on employers having reasons.
That bands were found only in mining communities.
Mills and collieries are both mentioned, and no such assumption is attributed.
That a band can be understood in terms of one function serving a single group.
Correct: The author says the contrast depends on picturing the band as a single object with a single function.
qs.x: The author says the contrast depends on picturing the band as a single object with a single function. Trap: Selecting a detail that appears in one reading instead of the premise common to both.

qs.q: Which of the following observations would most strengthen the author's concluding claim about cultural patronage?
o: A sponsored orchestra, judged by outside critics, uses its fame to bargain with its sponsor.
Correct: This mirrors bands whose outside-judged excellence gave them bargaining power over patrons.
A museum donor requires that a collection be displayed under the donor's name for fifty years.
This shows a donor exercising control, which does not support the claim.
A company choir disbands as soon as the firm withdraws the funding that sustained it.
This shows dependence, the opposite of the partial independence the author describes.
A foundation's scholars produce work that earns public praise for the donor who financed the project.
This shows patronage serving the patron, with no loss of control.
qs.x: This mirrors bands whose outside-judged excellence gave them bargaining power over patrons. Trap: Choosing an example of patronage in general rather than one in which the patron loses control.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that outside judging gave players bargaining power?
o: Bands that won contests received larger gifts from local manufacturers than bands that did not, and the largest gifts tended to go to bands led by the most famous conductors.
This suggests that excellence was rewarded, consistent with leverage.
Judges at contests were drawn from outside the band's own town and firm.
The claim already assumes judges were outsiders.
Many players practiced several evenings per week, sometimes after long shifts in the mill.
The effort of players is irrelevant to bargaining power.
Rival firms showed no interest in hiring away famous bands, and sponsors who withdrew support suffered no loss of prestige.
Correct: If rivals did not want the bands and withdrawal cost nothing, excellence would not translate into leverage.
qs.x: If rivals did not want the bands and withdrawal cost nothing, excellence would not translate into leverage. Trap: Choosing a finding that restates the premise instead of cutting the link from excellence to leverage.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 3
text: In the 1770s the French philosopher Denis Diderot wrote a dialogue on acting that overturned what most theatergoers believed. The audience, he observed, wants to think that a great performer is carried away by feeling, weeping real tears over the death of a fictional daughter. Diderot argued the opposite. The actor who is swept up in emotion is at the mercy of mood, health, and the weather; he is magnificent on Tuesday and wooden on Thursday. The truly great actor, by contrast, feels little during the performance and produces the same sublime effect every night, because he has studied the outward signs of passion, rehearsed them until they are exact, and deploys them with a cool and observant mind. Sensibility, in other words, is the mark of the mediocre; the great performer's gift is judgment.

The thesis, which Diderot called a paradox, was not published until well after his death, but it has shaped every later argument about the craft. In the early twentieth century Konstantin Stanislavski built a method of training that appeared to say the reverse: the actor should draw on memories of his own experience in order to bring real feeling to the stage, so that the character's grief is rooted in something the performer has known. Bertolt Brecht, in turn, objected to both traditions. He wanted the audience to be kept at a critical distance from the story, and he asked his actors to demonstrate a character rather than become one, so that spectators would think about social conditions rather than weep over fate. Each school claims a theory of what actors really do, and each is supported by testimony from celebrated performers.

That testimony, however, is the weak point. Actors who report on their own states during a performance are asked to observe an activity while performing it, and the evidence of psychology suggests that such reports are poor guides to what is actually happening. Some performers who swear they feel nothing show racing hearts and tears; others who describe total absorption are plainly in command of timing and voice down to the second. Indeed the most common report from experienced actors is that both are true at once: they are moved, and they are watching themselves be moved, and they adjust their weeping to the size of the theater. If so, the opposition between feeling and control may be an artifact of the way the question was framed.

What the quarrel really concerns, I would argue, is a question about value rather than a question about fact. To prefer Diderot's actor is to prize craft: the reliable production of an effect, admirable in the way a violinist's technique is admirable. To prefer Stanislavski's is to prize authenticity: the sense that a human being is truly present before us, taking a risk. These are different goods, and a performance can have one without the other. An audience that is moved by a flawless demonstration of grief has been given something real, and an audience that watches a tearful but clumsy performance has been given something real too. Asking what is going on inside the actor will not tell us which good to value more, and the persistence of the debate for two and a half centuries suggests that nothing could.

qs.q: The main point of the passage is that the dispute over whether actors feel or control emotion:
o: shows that Diderot was correct that great actors feel nothing, and that later schools have only obscured his insight.
The author doubts any account of the actor's inner state can be established.
has been settled by psychology in favor of Stanislavski's method of drawing on personal memory.
Psychology is cited only to cast doubt on introspective reports.
can be settled by what experienced performers report about themselves.
The author calls such testimony the weak point of the debate.
is better read as a disagreement about whether craft or authenticity is more valuable.
Correct: The final paragraph recasts the quarrel as one about value rather than fact.
qs.x: The final paragraph recasts the quarrel as one about value rather than fact. Trap: Picking an option that sounds like a resolution when the author argues that none is available.

qs.q: According to Diderot, the actor swept up by emotion performs poorly because:
o: he lacks the sensibility needed to understand the suffering of the character he plays.
Diderot treats sensibility as the mark of the mediocre, not as a lack.
he studies the outward signs of passion too closely to produce a spontaneous effect.
This is the habit of the great actor in Diderot's view.
the quality of his work varies with his moods.
Correct: Diderot says he is magnificent one night and wooden the next, at the mercy of mood, health, and weather.
he fails to keep the attention of an audience that wants real tears from a performer.
Diderot says audiences want real tears, but this is not why the swept-up actor is weak.
qs.x: Diderot says he is magnificent one night and wooden the next, at the mercy of mood, health, and weather. Trap: Confusing the traits Diderot attributes to the great actor with those of the mediocre one.

qs.q: The author regards the testimony of celebrated performers about their stage experience as:
o: decisive evidence for Stanislavski's view over Diderot's.
The author says each school is backed by testimony and therefore none is decisive.
unreliable evidence, since people are poor observers of their own states while they are performing.
Correct: The third paragraph calls it the weak point and cites psychology showing such reports are poor guides.
flawed evidence because performers conceal their methods from rival actors.
Concealment is never raised.
valuable evidence that is biased toward Brecht's view.
Brecht's view is described only as an objection to both traditions.
qs.x: The third paragraph calls it the weak point and cites psychology showing such reports are poor guides. Trap: Treating the testimony the schools rely on as dependable because of its vividness.

qs.q: Which of the following is the most reasonable inference about Brecht's view of acting?
o: He agreed with Diderot that actors should feel nothing and with Stanislavski that audiences should weep.
The passage says he objected to both traditions.
He believed that audiences cannot be moved by performances that demonstrate rather than embody a character, and he therefore urged actors to embody their roles more fully.
His aim was critical thought, not emotional response, so he had no such belief.
He thought actors should draw on personal memories so that the audience is distanced from the story.
Drawing on memory is Stanislavski's method, and it is not tied to distancing.
He considered emotional absorption in a character an obstacle to the social understanding he wanted theater to produce.
Correct: Brecht wanted critical distance so that spectators think about social conditions instead of weeping.
qs.x: Brecht wanted critical distance so that spectators think about social conditions instead of weeping. Trap: Mixing the three schools' positions together and attributing parts of one to another.

qs.q: Suppose actors who report strong emotion on stage and actors who report none produce performances that audiences rate as equally moving. The author would most likely take this to show that:
o: Stanislavski's method is more effective than Diderot's for producing emotion in an audience.
Equal ratings give no advantage to either method.
great actors must feel nothing in order to keep their performances steady from night to night.
Equal ratings do not show that feeling harms steadiness.
audiences are unable to distinguish genuine feeling from demonstrated feeling under any circumstances.
The finding concerns two particular groups and cannot establish an inability under all circumstances.
reports of an actor's inner state are a poor guide to the effect produced.
Correct: This fits the author's claim that asking what goes on inside actors will not settle the question.
qs.x: This fits the author's claim that asking what goes on inside actors will not settle the question. Trap: Overgeneralizing a single finding into a sweeping claim about all audiences or all actors.

qs.q: Which of the following disputes is most similar to the one the author describes in the final paragraph?
o: A dispute over whether a bridge failed from corrosion or overload, which engineers can settle by inspecting the wreckage.
This is a factual dispute settled by evidence.
A disagreement about a pianist's age, which can be settled by consulting birth records.
This is also factual.
A debate about whether a pianist should be judged on flawless technique or on risk-taking spirit, which no study of the pianist's nerves could settle.
Correct: Like the acting debate, it turns on which good to value, so facts about inner states cannot decide it.
A quarrel over which of two pianists practiced longer, which their diaries could resolve.
This is factual and resolvable with records.
qs.x: Like the acting debate, it turns on which good to value, so facts about inner states cannot decide it. Trap: Choosing the example that merely involves performers rather than the one that shares the dispute's structure.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 4
text: A familiar story about astronomy holds that for fourteen centuries Europeans clung to a clumsy theory in which the planets rode on wheels upon wheels, until Copernicus swept the clutter away by placing the sun at the center. The story makes the Ptolemaic system a monument to stubbornness and the Copernican a triumph of simplicity. It is neat, and it is wrong in almost every particular.

Consider first what the Ptolemaic system was for. Its purpose was to predict where each planet would appear against the stars, and by that standard it was remarkably good. Using circles whose centers could be shifted and smaller circles, or epicycles, carried along larger ones, astronomers could calculate positions accurately enough to compile almanacs, fix the date of Easter, and guide navigators. A theory that worked so well for so long was not an obvious candidate for abandonment. The device of the epicycle was also not an ad hoc patch. It was a flexible mathematical tool that, like a Fourier series, could represent almost any periodic motion to whatever accuracy one demanded, which is exactly why its failures were hard to detect.

Nor did Copernicus's system win by being simpler or more accurate. Committed to the ancient principle that celestial motions must be uniform and circular, Copernicus kept circles, and to match the observations he needed epicycles of his own; his system contained about as many circles as his predecessors', and in its first versions it predicted positions no better than theirs. What it offered was of a different kind. In the Ptolemaic scheme, the backward loops of the planets required a separate epicycle for each planet, whose size had to be fixed by observation, and nothing in the theory explained why the loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn always occurred when those planets were opposite the sun. In the Copernican scheme the loops arose automatically from the earth's own motion, and the order of the planets and the relative sizes of their orbits followed from the observations without further assumptions. This was an advance in explanation: one hypothesis accounting for facts that the older theory had to treat as unrelated coincidences.

The advance was not decisive, because explanation had to be weighed against other commitments. A moving earth contradicted the physics of the day, in which heavy bodies fell toward the center of the universe and a spinning earth should have flung loose objects into the sky. Anyone who judged theories by their consistency with accepted physics could reasonably prefer the older system. Only gradually did the balance shift. Tycho Brahe's precise observations, Kepler's discovery that planetary orbits are ellipses, Galileo's telescope observations, and finally a physics of inertia and gravitation, which made the earth's motion intelligible, together turned a controversial hypothesis into settled knowledge.

The moral is not that the old theory was secretly as good as the new. It is that theory choice rarely pits a bad theory against a good one. It weighs several virtues, among them accuracy, explanatory unity, and harmony with the rest of what is known, which seldom point in the same direction at the same time. Historians who judge past scientists by the outcome alone mistake the end of an argument for its beginning.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: The shift from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy involved competing theoretical virtues, not a contest between a bad theory and a good one.
Correct: The closing paragraph says theory choice weighs several virtues that seldom point in the same direction.
The Ptolemaic system lasted because astronomers deferred to ancient authority despite its obvious complexity, and it was abandoned as soon as simpler alternatives were proposed.
The author argues the system was predictively successful, not merely authoritative.
Copernicus's system prevailed because it used fewer circles and predicted planetary positions more accurately.
The passage says it had about as many circles and was no more accurate at first.
Kepler's ellipses and Galileo's telescope observations were sufficient to establish the motion of the earth.
The passage says a physics of inertia and gravitation was also needed.
qs.x: The closing paragraph says theory choice weighs several virtues that seldom point in the same direction. Trap: Accepting the familiar story the passage sets out to correct.

qs.q: According to the passage, what initial advantage did the Copernican system have over the Ptolemaic system?
o: It predicted the positions of the planets more precisely than the Ptolemaic system could.
The passage says its first versions were no better in prediction.
It explained retrograde loops and planetary order without extra assumptions.
Correct: The passage says loops arose from the earth's motion and the order of planets followed from observation.
It dispensed with epicycles by substituting elliptical orbits for circles.
Ellipses came from Kepler, after Copernicus.
It agreed more closely with the accepted physics of falling bodies and a stationary center.
The passage says a moving earth contradicted the physics of the day.
qs.x: The passage says loops arose from the earth's motion and the order of planets followed from observation. Trap: Crediting Copernicus with Kepler's later improvements or with an accuracy advantage he lacked.

qs.q: The comparison of the epicycle to a Fourier series suggests that epicycles:
o: could be adjusted to fit almost any periodic motion, which concealed their shortcomings.
Correct: The author says this flexibility is why its failures were hard to detect.
were mathematically unsound and survived only because of tradition.
The author calls them a flexible tool, not an unsound one.
were introduced by Ptolemy to correct specific failures in earlier theories, and were added one at a time to rescue the system from refutation.
Origins are not discussed.
were an unsophisticated device soon replaced by more precise methods.
The author describes epicycles as lasting a very long time and being sophisticated.
qs.x: The author says this flexibility is why its failures were hard to detect. Trap: Reading a mathematical analogy as a criticism of the device.

qs.q: Which of the following does the author cite as a reason a reasonable astronomer might have preferred the Ptolemaic system?
o: The Copernican system could not account for the backward loops of the planets.
The Copernican system explained them automatically.
A moving earth conflicted with prevailing physics, in which heavy bodies fell toward the center of the universe.
Correct: The fourth paragraph states this directly.
Tycho Brahe's observations contradicted the order of the planets proposed by Copernicus.
Brahe's observations are cited as helping the eventual shift.
Epicycles gave more accurate predictions than ellipses.
The passage does not compare epicycles with ellipses in accuracy.
qs.x: The fourth paragraph states this directly. Trap: Confusing evidence that eventually favored Copernicus with reasons for resistance to it.

qs.q: Which of the following situations best parallels that of an astronomer considering Copernicus's system in the early sixteenth century?
o: A mathematician who drops a method after learning it gives wrong answers to standard problems.
This involves a clear failure and no conflicting virtues.
A physician weighing a model of disease that explains many symptoms by one cause but predicts no better and clashes with accepted chemistry.
Correct: Like Copernicus, the new model gains explanatory unity but lacks predictive advantage and conflicts with other accepted knowledge.
An engineer who keeps an old design even though a new one proves cheaper and safer in every test, so that the choice involves no real tradeoff at all.
The new option wins on every measure, so there is no tradeoff.
A historian who accepts a theory because it was proposed by the most famous scholar of his time.
This turns on authority, not on weighing theoretical virtues.
qs.x: Like Copernicus, the new model gains explanatory unity but lacks predictive advantage and conflicts with other accepted knowledge. Trap: Choosing a case with a plain winner when the parallel requires conflicting virtues.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine the author's claim about early Copernican predictions?
o: Copernicus's system contained about as many circles as Ptolemy's when all epicycles were counted.
This agrees with the passage.
Navigators using Ptolemaic tables rarely lost their way on sea voyages in the same period.
This is consistent with the Ptolemaic system's practical accuracy.
Almanacs based on Copernicus's tables proved clearly more accurate than Ptolemaic ones.
Correct: This directly contradicts the claim that early predictions were no better.
Most astronomers who studied the Copernican system after its publication rejected its claim of a moving earth.
This concerns acceptance and does not bear on accuracy.
qs.x: This directly contradicts the claim that early predictions were no better. Trap: Selecting evidence about acceptance or practice instead of evidence about predictive accuracy.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 5
text: It has often been said that science owes more to the steam engine than the steam engine owes to science. The remark is an exaggeration, but it points at an inconvenient fact for anyone who pictures technology as applied science, a process in which discoveries made in laboratories are carried out into the world and turned into machines. The sequence in the case of steam runs the other way. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine was pumping water out of English mines in 1712, and James Watt's improvement, the separate condenser, came in the 1760s, some sixty years before anyone produced a satisfactory theory of how heat produces motive power. The engineers who built these machines worked by trial, by craft knowledge, and by careful measurement of what made one engine burn less coal than another.

When theory arrived, it arrived in response to the machines. In 1824 the French engineer Sadi Carnot published a short book asking a question no one had posed: is there a limit to the work that can be obtained from a given quantity of heat, and does it depend on the working substance, whether steam, air, or alcohol? He argued that the maximum depends only on the temperatures between which the engine operates, and he reached this conclusion by comparing the engine to a waterwheel, in which the power obtained depends on the height through which water falls. The analogy rested on the caloric theory, according to which heat was a fluid conserved in the process, and that theory was soon discredited. Yet Carnot's central result survived. When Clausius and Kelvin, in the following decades, reconciled his argument with the conservation of energy, they produced the first and second laws of thermodynamics, in which a limit on efficiency is a consequence of the nature of heat itself.

It would be as mistaken to reverse the old story as to retain it. The engine did not simply give birth to a theory that then sat idly in textbooks. Thermodynamics fed back into engineering, though more slowly than legend suggests. It supplied designers with a measure against which any engine could be judged, and it showed which improvements were worth pursuing and which, like the search for a better working fluid, were not. Engineers such as Rankine adapted the theory to steam practice, and later developments, such as compound expansion and the steam turbine, drew on it to set targets. The steam engine had also supplied science with something more than a puzzle. The indicator diagram, a device invented to monitor the performance of engines, gave physicists a way of plotting pressure against volume that became an indispensable tool of thermodynamics itself.

A more accurate picture, then, is of two traditions with separate origins that gradually learned to use each other's products. Craftsmen produced working devices and instruments; natural philosophers produced concepts and principles that explained, constrained, and sometimes redirected the devices. Neither tradition was subordinate to the other. The lesson for the present is that policies which assume innovation flows only from basic research to application misread the history, and that those which dismiss theory as a luxury misread it as badly.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?
o: Thermodynamics arose entirely from the study of steam engines and had little effect on later engineering.
The passage describes thermodynamic theory feeding back into engineering.
Carnot's reliance on caloric theory was so flawed that his conclusions on engine efficiency had no lasting value for later engineers or physicists, who started over.
The passage says his central result survived.
Technology and science developed through mutual influence, with the steam engine preceding thermodynamic theory and later being guided by it.
Correct: The final paragraph describes two traditions that learned to use each other's products.
Technology depends on basic research, since engines improved only after theories of heat were developed.
The engine preceded theory by decades.
qs.x: The final paragraph describes two traditions that learned to use each other's products. Trap: Preferring a one-directional story even though the passage rejects both directions.

qs.q: The author mentions the indicator diagram in order to show that:
o: Watt's separate condenser was based on an understanding of the theory of heat.
The passage says the condenser preceded theory by decades.
engineering practice supplied science with a useful tool.
Correct: The diagram was invented to monitor engines and became a tool of thermodynamics.
Rankine adapted thermodynamic principles to the design of steam turbines.
Rankine is mentioned elsewhere and the diagram is not linked to him.
experimental instruments are more valuable to physics than are theoretical principles.
The author makes no such ranking.
qs.x: The diagram was invented to monitor engines and became a tool of thermodynamics. Trap: Linking the diagram to the theory-to-practice direction instead of the practice-to-theory direction it illustrates.

qs.q: The passage suggests that Carnot's central result survived the discrediting of the caloric theory because:
o: the caloric theory was later shown to be correct in the case of steam.
The passage says the theory was soon discredited.
its claim that efficiency depends on temperatures could be reconciled with energy conservation once the caloric assumption was dropped.
Correct: Clausius and Kelvin reconciled his argument with conservation of energy, producing the laws of thermodynamics.
Clausius and Kelvin had proposed the same result before Carnot published.
They came in the decades after Carnot.
experiments on steam confirmed the waterwheel analogy that Carnot had used.
The analogy rested on caloric and is not said to have been confirmed.
qs.x: Clausius and Kelvin reconciled his argument with conservation of energy, producing the laws of thermodynamics. Trap: Assuming a result survives only if the reasoning behind it was correct.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the remark that science owes more to the steam engine than the engine owes to science is best described as:
o: approving: it states the true relation between science and technology, and the author endorses it as an accurate summary of the history.
The author calls it an exaggeration and later rejects reversing the old story.
dismissive: it is a slogan with no basis in the history of engines.
The author grants that it points at an inconvenient fact.
qualified: it overstates the case but points to a fact that the applied-science model ignores.
Correct: The author calls it an exaggeration that points at an inconvenient fact.
neutral: it is reported without evaluation as the view of historians.
The author evaluates it directly in the first paragraph.
qs.x: The author calls it an exaggeration that points at an inconvenient fact. Trap: Reading a mild criticism as outright rejection or endorsement.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most weaken the author's claim that thermodynamics fed back into engineering?
o: Records show that the designers of compound engines and turbines were unaware of thermodynamic theory and worked entirely by trial and error.
Correct: This removes the channel through which theory is said to have guided later designs.
Historians find that Rankine published widely on steam practice and corresponded with working engineers about the design of boilers, cylinders, and engine performance.
This supports the link.
Carnot's book remained little known for a decade after it was published.
The delay does not show that later engineers failed to use the theory.
Watt's condenser reduced fuel consumption substantially compared with Newcomen's engine.
This concerns the earlier period before theory.
qs.x: This removes the channel through which theory is said to have guided later designs. Trap: Picking evidence about the early period when the claim concerns later feedback.

qs.q: The author's discussion implies that a policy of funding only basic research, in the expectation that useful applications will follow, would be:
o: sound, because technology depends on theoretical discoveries made first in laboratories and only afterward carried out into machines.
This is the applied-science model the author rejects.
sound, provided that the basic research is directed toward problems posed by industry.
The author does not endorse any version of the one-way policy.
mistaken, because theory has contributed little to the improvement of machines.
The author says dismissing theory is as mistaken as ignoring practice.
mistaken, because in the case of steam innovation came from practice to theory as well as the reverse.
Correct: The author says policies assuming one-way flow from research to application misread history.
qs.x: The author says policies assuming one-way flow from research to application misread history. Trap: Overcorrecting to the opposite extreme and rejecting theory altogether.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 6
text: According to a long tradition, Aristotle held that heavier bodies fall faster than light ones, and for centuries no one thought to doubt it. Galileo, in his Discourses on Two New Sciences, is reputed to have disposed of the view without dropping anything from a tower. Suppose, he said, that a heavy stone falls faster than a light one. Now tie the two together. The light stone, being slower, should hold back the heavy one, so that the combination falls more slowly than the heavy stone alone. But the combination is heavier than either stone, so it should fall faster than the heavy stone alone. The assumption therefore yields two incompatible predictions. Since both cannot be true, the assumption must be false, and the natural conclusion is that all bodies fall at the same rate.

What is striking about this argument is that it requires no new observations. Its conclusion concerns the physical world, yet it seems to have been reached from an armchair, and philosophers have found this puzzling. If experience is the only source of knowledge about nature, how can a mental exercise teach anything about it? One response is that thought experiments are a species of Platonic insight, in which the mind grasps the laws of nature directly, the way it grasps a mathematical truth. The opposing response is deflationary. On this view a thought experiment is simply an argument in picturesque dress. Its premises are things we already know from experience or assume as part of a theory, and its conclusion follows by ordinary logic, so that anything it teaches could have been taught by stating the premises and the inference in plain prose. The vividness of the scenario is a rhetorical flourish, and the appearance of a special route to knowledge an illusion.

The deflationary account has the advantage of sobriety, and it correctly observes that Galileo's argument can be set out as a logical derivation. But I think that it underestimates what the reconstruction leaves out. A reconstruction shows that the conclusion follows, and it does not show how anyone could have seen that it follows. The steps in Galileo's argument are not obvious until the two stones are imagined bound together, and the scenario does something that a list of premises cannot: it makes us notice that two commitments we held at once, that weight determines speed and that a compound body is the sum of its parts, cannot both be maintained. The value of the experiment lies in organizing what we already know in such a way that a hidden inconsistency becomes visible.

This is a modest power, but it is a real one. Thought experiments do not conjure facts out of nothing, so the Platonist claims too much. Neither are they mere decoration, so the deflationist claims too little. They resemble a well-drawn diagram in geometry: the diagram contains nothing that was not already implied by the axioms, yet without it the proof might never be found. And like a diagram, a thought experiment can mislead, since a vivid scenario may lead the imagination to supply assumptions that the reasoner has not noticed adding. The right attitude toward them is therefore the one we take toward other instruments of inquiry: appreciation of their usefulness, and vigilance about the ways they fail.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the author's view of thought experiments?
o: They show that conclusions about nature can sometimes be reached without any experience of the world, so that pure thought can replace observation in science.
The author says the premises come from prior experience.
They can be reduced to logical arguments, so their vivid scenarios serve only rhetorical purposes.
This is the deflationary view the author finds too limited.
They are unreliable because they can mislead, so scientists should depend on observation alone.
The author warns about misleading but still values them.
They are neither a mysterious source of knowledge nor mere rhetoric but tools that expose inconsistencies among beliefs already held.
Correct: The fourth paragraph says they do not conjure facts and are not decoration.
qs.x: The fourth paragraph says they do not conjure facts and are not decoration. Trap: Choosing one of the two views the author rejects as too strong or too weak.

qs.q: The comparison to a geometric diagram suggests that a thought experiment:
o: adds no new content but may make a proof discoverable.
Correct: The diagram contains nothing not already implied by the axioms, yet the proof might never be found without it.
provides evidence that independent reasoning cannot supply, and so substitutes for the axioms.
This overstates the role of the diagram.
is more reliable than a verbal argument because it rests on visual perception.
Reliability is not claimed, and the author notes diagrams can mislead.
is mere decoration that can be removed with no loss because the proof is already complete.
The author denies they are mere decoration.
qs.x: The diagram contains nothing not already implied by the axioms, yet the proof might never be found without it. Trap: Taking the phrase 'adds nothing new' to mean that it is useless.

qs.q: In Galileo's argument, the combination of the two stones is first predicted to fall more slowly because:
o: the combined object is lighter than the heavy stone alone.
The combination is heavier, which is used for the second prediction.
air resistance acts more strongly on bound objects than on single objects of the same total weight.
Air resistance is not mentioned.
the slower light stone would be expected to hold back the faster heavy stone.
Correct: The passage states this directly.
tying the stones together reduces the weight of each.
Weight is not changed by tying.
qs.x: The passage states this directly. Trap: Confusing the first prediction with the second, which relies on the combined weight.

qs.q: The author would most likely say that the weakness of the deflationary account is that it:
o: shows that a conclusion follows but not how anyone could have noticed that it does.
Correct: The author says a reconstruction shows the conclusion follows but not how one could have seen that.
denies that Galileo's argument can be set out as a logical derivation.
The author grants that it can be.
holds that thought experiments give direct insight into nature's laws.
That is the Platonist view.
ignores that the premises of thought experiments must come from experience.
The deflationist emphasizes this point.
qs.x: The author says a reconstruction shows the conclusion follows but not how one could have seen that. Trap: Attributing the Platonist position to the deflationist.

qs.q: Suppose a thought experiment leads to a conclusion later contradicted by careful observation. The author would most likely say that:
o: thought experiments were never a legitimate instrument of scientific inquiry.
The author says they are useful and should be used with vigilance.
the contradiction proves that the premises were never based on any prior experience of the world.
A false conclusion does not show that the premises lacked experiential basis.
Platonic insight is fallible, so thought experiments cannot reveal anything about the laws of nature.
The author does not hold the Platonic view, and fallibility does not imply uselessness.
the scenario probably led the imagination to supply an unnoticed assumption.
Correct: The author warns that vivid scenarios can lead the imagination to add assumptions.
qs.x: The author warns that vivid scenarios can lead the imagination to add assumptions. Trap: Treating one failure as proof that the whole method is worthless.

qs.q: Which of the following is most analogous to the way the author says a thought experiment works?
o: A chemist discovers a new element by heating an unknown ore.
This produces new facts through experiment.
A mathematician accepts a theorem on faith because of its elegance.
This is neither reorganization nor reasoning.
A mathematician accepts a theorem on faith because of its elegance and never examines the argument that is supposed to support it.
This produces new content for enjoyment, not an exposure of inconsistency.
A lawyer arranges familiar facts in a sequence that makes the contradiction in a witness's testimony visible.
Correct: Both reorganize what is already known so that a hidden inconsistency becomes visible.
qs.x: Both reorganize what is already known so that a hidden inconsistency becomes visible. Trap: Choosing an example about discovery in general rather than the exposure of inconsistency.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 7
text: Most legal systems limit the time within which a lawsuit or prosecution may be brought. Wait too long to sue over a broken contract, and the claim is barred, whatever its merit. The rule can look perverse. A wrong does not become less wrong because years have passed, and a court that refuses to hear a legitimate grievance for the sake of a calendar seems to put administrative convenience above justice. Yet statutes of limitations are among the oldest and most widespread features of law, which suggests that they answer to something more than convenience.

The traditional defense offers three reasons. The first is evidentiary: memories fade, documents disappear, and witnesses die, so that a trial held long after the events is likelier to reach an erroneous verdict. The second is repose: people should be able to arrange their affairs, sell property, and plan their lives without the lingering threat of an old claim. The third is diligence: a claimant who sleeps on his rights forfeits them, and the prospect of a bar encourages those who have been wronged to act while the facts are fresh. Each reason has force, but each also has an obvious limit. Evidence may be preserved in recordings and in laboratories, so a rule keyed to the calendar is both too rough and too crude a proxy for the quality of the proof. And the diligence rationale presumes that the claimant could have acted earlier, which is not always so.

The exceptions to the rule are instructive. Most jurisdictions place no time limit on prosecutions for murder, and many have extended or suspended the period for crimes against children, on the ground that a child victim may not understand, or be able to report, what was done for many years. The law of civil claims has developed a discovery rule under which the clock does not begin to run until the injured person knew, or reasonably should have known, of the harm; a patient who learns of a surgical instrument left inside her body decades later is not treated as having slept on her rights. Some legislatures have gone further and opened temporary windows during which claims otherwise barred may be filed. These revival laws are controversial. Critics say they upset settled expectations, since defendants who were entitled to consider the matter closed are suddenly exposed, and that the loss of evidence may make a fair defense impossible. Supporters respond that the very harm alleged may be the reason for the delay, since many victims of abuse are silenced by shame, fear, or dependence on the wrongdoer.

These disputes suggest that the best way to understand limitation periods is not as a verdict that old wrongs do not matter, nor as a mere convenience, but as a way of allocating the risk of uncertainty. Every legal system has to decide who will bear the cost of not knowing what happened long ago, and a fixed deadline places that cost on the claimant who could have acted and did not. The justification collapses in those cases where the delay is attributable to the wrong itself, because a rule that rewards the wrongdoer for the success of his concealment or the severity of his victim's injury turns the protection of repose into a reward for the offense. What looks like a conflict between justice and convenience is therefore better seen as a difficulty in deciding whose silence the law should treat as a choice.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Limitation periods are best understood as a way of allocating the risk of uncertainty, with exceptions where the delay results from the wrong itself.
Correct: The final paragraph states this directly.
Statutes of limitations place administrative convenience above justice and should be abolished for serious wrongs.
The author does not call for abolition.
Revival windows are justified because modern recordkeeping has undermined the evidentiary rationale for limitation periods, so old claims can now be tried fairly.
The author notes evidence may be preserved but does not use this to justify revival.
The diligence rationale is the strongest of the traditional justifications for barring old claims.
The author finds it weak where claimants could not have acted earlier.
qs.x: The final paragraph states this directly. Trap: Choosing a claim about one rationale instead of the author's overall reinterpretation.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT among the traditional rationales for limitation periods described in the passage?
o: Old wrongs become less serious as time passes.
Correct: The first paragraph says a wrong does not become less wrong with time; this is not a rationale.
Evidence deteriorates as memories fade and witnesses die.
This is the evidentiary rationale.
People should be able to plan their affairs free of old claims.
This is the repose rationale.
Claimants should be encouraged to act while the facts are fresh.
This is the diligence rationale.
qs.x: The first paragraph says a wrong does not become less wrong with time; this is not a rationale. Trap: Missing the word NOT and choosing the first rationale that matches the passage.

qs.q: The author describes the patient who discovers a retained surgical instrument decades later in order to illustrate:
o: the discovery rule, under which the period begins when the harm is or should be known.
Correct: The passage introduces the example with the discovery rule.
a revival window opened by a legislature for claims that are otherwise barred by the ordinary deadline.
Revival windows are described separately.
the absence of any time limit on prosecutions for the gravest crimes.
This is the murder example.
the repose rationale as applied to medical professionals.
The example favors the claimant, not repose.
qs.x: The passage introduces the example with the discovery rule. Trap: Connecting the example to the wrong exception among several described in the same paragraph.

qs.q: The author says the diligence rationale "presumes that the claimant could have acted earlier" in order to:
o: argue that claimants who delay deserve no protection from the courts.
This is the rationale the author is limiting.
