show that the rationale fails where the claimant had no real opportunity to sue.
Correct: The author notes this presumption is not always true.
suggest that preserved evidence makes diligence unnecessary in modern cases.
This is the point of the preceding sentence about the evidentiary rationale.
establish that most claimants delay deliberately in order to gain a tactical edge.
The author makes no claim about deliberate delay.
qs.x: The author notes this presumption is not always true. Trap: Confusing the author's point about diligence with the earlier point about evidence.

qs.q: Which of the following would the author's final argument most likely treat as justifying suspension of a limitation period?
o: A plaintiff delays suing for years because she is occupied with her career.
This is delay the claimant could have avoided.
A claimant forgets that a debt was owed to her until after the period expires.
Forgetting is the claimant's own lapse.
A defendant moves to a distant city after the deadline and becomes hard to locate.
The wrong did not cause the delay, and the move comes after the deadline.
An employer conceals records of a safety defect until after the usual period expires.
Correct: Here the delay is caused by the wrongdoer's concealment.
qs.x: Here the delay is caused by the wrongdoer's concealment. Trap: Choosing a sympathetic delay not caused by the wrong itself.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the critics' objection to revival laws?
o: Many claimants in revived cases said fear of the wrongdoer was the reason for their delay.
This supports the supporters.
Revival windows led to a large increase in the number of claims filed.
Volume alone does not show unfairness.
Defendants in revived cases were frequently unable to present evidence that had existed when the claims arose.
Correct: This supports the concern that a fair defense becomes impossible.
Legislatures that opened revival windows later lengthened the ordinary limitation periods.
This does not bear on fairness to defendants.
qs.x: This supports the concern that a fair defense becomes impossible. Trap: Choosing evidence that favors the supporters or that is irrelevant to the critics' specific concern.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 8
text: The lecture has been declared obsolete so often that its survival requires explanation. In the medieval university, where the practice took shape, the explanation was obvious: books were copied by hand, and a manuscript of a major text was worth the price of a farm. A master read the text aloud, the students copied it down, and the master added glosses. The very word lecture derives from the Latin for reading. The invention of printing removed the original reason, since a student who could buy the book no longer needed to hear it recited, and critics from the sixteenth century onward have asked why professors continued to read aloud what the students could read for themselves.

The modern criticism is usually phrased in the language of learning science. Students listening to a lecture are passive, the critics say, and passivity is the enemy of understanding. Experiments in which classes are randomly assigned to lecture or to active formats, such as small-group problem solving, tend to find that students in the latter do better on examinations and are less likely to fail. Some universities have responded by replacing lecture halls with studios in which students work in teams, and a few have flatly urged the abolition of the lecture. Defenders usually reply by pointing to the brilliance of the great lecturers or by appealing to tradition, and neither answer is satisfying.

The strongest defense begins by questioning what the critics assume a lecture is for. If its purpose is to transmit information, then printing, and now the internet, made it redundant, and the experiments show that other methods transmit information more efficiently. But a good lecture does something different. It lets students watch an expert think in real time: choosing an approach, hitting a difficulty, backing up, and recovering. A textbook presents the finished argument, polished to hide its false starts, and a student who reads only textbooks may conclude that understanding arrives without effort and in a straight line. A lecture can model the stumbling by which understanding is actually reached, and it can respond to the audience's expressions of confusion, adjusting its pace and its examples as it goes. The argument is therefore that the lecture's value lies in a skill, reasoning in public, that examinations of recall do not measure.

This reply has weaknesses, and its proponents should concede them. The great majority of lectures do not show anyone thinking; they present notes that have not changed in a decade, and in that case the critics are right that a recording would serve as well. The comparisons that favor active formats are also not simply the artifacts of bad measurement, since many of them do assess problem solving as well as recall. Still, the defense shifts the burden of proof in a useful way. It shows that comparing the lecture with its alternatives on a single outcome tells us little until we say which outcome the form exists to produce. The right conclusion is neither that the lecture is obsolete nor that it is sacred, but that its worth depends on whether the person at the lectern is using it for the one thing it can still do better than print.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main argument of the passage?
o: The lecture is obsolete because print and the internet transmit information more efficiently than a speaker can, so students should simply read the material themselves.
The author says this is true only if transmitting information is its purpose.
The worth of the lecture depends on whether it is used to model expert reasoning, which print cannot do, rather than to transmit information.
Correct: The fourth paragraph says the lecture's worth depends on the outcome the form exists to produce.
Active-learning experiments show that lecturing is a poor method that should be replaced by studio formats.
The author says the defense shifts the burden of proof.
The lecture persists because of tradition and the brilliance of its best practitioners.
The author calls those defenses unsatisfying.
qs.x: The fourth paragraph says the lecture's worth depends on the outcome the form exists to produce. Trap: Choosing the position of one side of the dispute rather than the author's qualified conclusion.

qs.q: According to the passage, the original reason for the lecture was:
o: the belief that students learn better from hearing a text than from reading it.
The passage gives no such belief.
the scarcity and cost of handwritten books.
Correct: Manuscripts were costly, so a master read the text aloud.
the need for masters to add commentary that no manuscript could contain.
Glosses were added but the reason for reading aloud was scarcity.
the expectation that students would answer the master's questions during the reading.
Student questions are not mentioned.
qs.x: Manuscripts were costly, so a master read the text aloud. Trap: Choosing a pedagogical motive when the passage gives a material one.

qs.q: The author finds the defenders' appeals to great lecturers and to tradition unsatisfying because:
o: both concede that most lectures are rarely brilliant.
No such concession is made.
both assume the lecture is more valuable than student success, however much students may learn elsewhere.
This is not stated.
neither is supported by any experimental evidence at all.
The author does not make this claim.
neither answers the charge that lectures promote learning less well than other methods.
Correct: The author calls the replies unsatisfying after describing the experimental criticism.
qs.x: The author calls the replies unsatisfying after describing the experimental criticism. Trap: Reading a general complaint about relevance as a complaint about evidence.

qs.q: Which of the following is a limitation of the author's defense that the passage itself acknowledges?
o: Textbooks present arguments in a way that conceals the false starts of discovery, which is why students need lectures.
This is part of the defense.
Most lectures do not display reasoning in progress, so a recording would serve as well.
Correct: The final paragraph concedes this.
Experiments favoring active formats measure only recall and not problem solving.
The author says many of them assess problem solving too.
Lectures cannot respond to students' confusion in real time.
The author claims lectures can respond to confusion.
qs.x: The final paragraph concedes this. Trap: Choosing a statement drawn from the defense instead of the concessions.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the author's claim about what a good lecture does?
o: Students who attended lectures scored higher on recall tests than students who read the textbook.
This concerns recall, not the modeling of reasoning.
Students who watched an expert solve unfamiliar problems aloud later solved new problems better than students given only the finished solutions.
Correct: This supports the value of watching reasoning in progress.
Students in team-based studios reported greater satisfaction than students in lecture halls.
This concerns satisfaction in the competing format.
Lecturers who reused identical notes for a decade received strong ratings from students.
This does not show the effect of modeled reasoning.
qs.x: This supports the value of watching reasoning in progress. Trap: Choosing evidence about recall or satisfaction when the claim concerns modeling reasoning.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best analogy for the author's argument about the lecture?
o: Watching a chef teaches recovery from mistakes in a way recipe books cannot.
Correct: Both defend a live demonstration of process that a finished text conceals.
A detailed map has been replaced by satellite navigation because both give directions to the same destination.
This resembles the transmission view the author rejects.
A professional sports league uses videos of past games to attract spectators who cannot attend in person.
This is about broadcasting rather than showing process.
A bank uses an automated teller for routine transactions to reduce the time spent with staff.
This is about efficiency, not about showing how skill works.
qs.x: Both defend a live demonstration of process that a finished text conceals. Trap: Choosing an analogy about efficient delivery of the same product.

passages.title: Mini10 · CARS · Passage 9
text: Few moral ideas are praised as warmly as forgiveness, and few are as poorly understood. Religious traditions commend it, therapists recommend it, and popular wisdom promises that the one who forgives will be freed from the burden of bitterness. The very warmth of this consensus conceals several quarrels. Is forgiveness something that wronged persons owe? Does it require the wrongdoer to repent? And what exactly is being given up when someone forgives?

To answer the last question, it helps to say what forgiveness is not. It is not excusing, which holds that the wrongdoer was not responsible, and it is not condoning, which treats the wrong as acceptable. A person who forgives a betrayal still regards it as a betrayal; that is why there is something to forgive. Nor is forgiveness the same as reconciliation, which restores a relationship and requires the other party's cooperation. A woman may forgive the man who injured her and decline ever to see him again. What forgiveness gives up, on the most plausible account, is a particular set of responses to the wrong: resentment, the wish to see the wrongdoer suffer, and the settled tendency to treat him as defined by what he did.

Philosophers in the tradition of Bishop Butler have pointed out that resentment is not merely a painful feeling. It is a form of moral protest, an expression of the conviction that one deserved better and that the wrong mattered. A person who feels no resentment at being abused may be showing not generosity but a lack of self-respect. This observation explains why forgiveness cannot be demanded. If the wronged person owed forgiveness, then withholding it would be a fault, and many victims would be doubly burdened: first by the injury, then by the charge that they were failing to move on. Insisting that victims forgive, particularly when the wrongdoer shows no regret, risks turning a gift into a debt and allowing the offender to collect on it.

At the same time, forgiveness is not arbitrary, and it is not only a matter of private feeling. Most of us believe that forgiveness is more fitting when the wrongdoer has acknowledged the wrong, apologized, and tried to repair the damage, since these acts change what he is saying about the victim: where the offense implied that she did not count, the apology says that she does. Without such acts, forgiving may look like a kind of surrender. Yet this raises a puzzle about the cases of people who forgive unrepentant wrongdoers, sometimes publicly and in spite of every provocation, and are admired for it. One response is that such people are doing something different, which might better be called letting go: refusing to let the offender's act continue to organize their own lives. That is a real good, and it is within the power of the victim alone. But it is not the same good as forgiveness proper, which is addressed to the wrongdoer and answers to something he has done. Keeping the two apart lets us honor the generosity of the one without pretending that the other has been owed or earned.

qs.q: Which of the following best summarizes the author's position?
o: Forgiveness cannot be owed and is most fitting after repentance, though a victim may separately let go of the wrong without forgiving.
Correct: The passage argues that forgiveness cannot be demanded, fits repentance, and differs from letting go.
Forgiveness is a duty of the wronged, since resentment harms those who keep it.
The author says forgiveness cannot be demanded.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are identical, since both restore the relationship between wrongdoer and victim and require both parties to take part.
The author distinguishes them.
Unrepentant wrongdoers should be forgiven, since forgiveness depends only on the victim's feelings.
The author says forgiveness answers to what the wrongdoer has done.
qs.x: The passage argues that forgiveness cannot be demanded, fits repentance, and differs from letting go. Trap: Choosing the popular view the passage begins by questioning.

qs.q: According to the passage, resentment is:
o: a painful feeling that forgiveness is meant to eliminate in every case.
The author says feeling none at abuse may reflect a lack of self-respect.
an emotion indicating that the wrongdoer ought to be punished in some way.
The wish to see the wrongdoer suffer is one response forgiveness gives up, but this is not the passage's account.
a form of moral protest that may reflect self-respect.
Correct: The third paragraph describes it this way.
a reaction that is excusable in victims who have been unable to move on from an injury.
The author does not treat resentment as an excuse.
qs.x: The third paragraph describes it this way. Trap: Seeing resentment only as a harmful feeling to be overcome.

qs.q: The author argues that forgiveness cannot be demanded because:
o: it would require victims to excuse wrongs that were not wrong.
Excusing is a different concept the author distinguishes.
it would imply that the offender need not apologize.
The author says nothing of this kind.
it would conflict with the rule that reconciliation requires mutual agreement.
Reconciliation is distinguished from forgiveness.
demanding it would burden victims a second time and let offenders collect on a gift as though it were a debt.
Correct: The third paragraph states this.
qs.x: The third paragraph states this. Trap: Importing the distinction among excusing, condoning, and forgiving into the demand argument.

qs.q: A woman publicly forgives a man who has shown no remorse for injuring her. The author would most likely say that she:
o: has failed to show self-respect, since resentment was the only fitting response to a man who showed no remorse.
The author says forgiving unrepentant wrongdoers can be admirable.
has excused the man by denying that his act was wrong.
Forgiveness does not deny the wrong.
has done something admirable that is better described as letting go than as forgiveness proper.
Correct: The final paragraph proposes this description of such cases.
has reconciled with the man, since forgiveness requires restoring the relationship.
The author separates forgiveness from reconciliation.
qs.x: The final paragraph proposes this description of such cases. Trap: Reading admiration for the act as agreement that it is forgiveness proper.

qs.q: Which of the following findings would most challenge the author's claim that apology makes forgiveness more fitting?
o: Most people judge forgiveness of unrepentant wrongdoers to be more fitting than forgiveness of repentant ones.
Correct: This would contradict the intuition on which the claim rests.
Most people judge that victims should not be required to forgive wrongdoers who are remorseful, since forgiveness is a gift.
This agrees with the argument that forgiveness is not owed.
Wrongdoers who apologize are more likely to be reconciled with their victims than those who do not.
This concerns reconciliation, not fittingness.
Victims who forgive unrepentant wrongdoers report feeling less bitterness than victims who do not.
This concerns benefit to victims, which the author separates from fittingness.
qs.x: This would contradict the intuition on which the claim rests. Trap: Choosing a finding about outcomes when the claim concerns what is fitting.

questions.q: Which amino acid is most likely to disrupt an alpha helix when it appears in the middle of the helix?
o: Alanine
Alanine has a small methyl side chain and is a strong helix-former.
Leucine
Leucine is a common residue in helices and fits easily.
Proline
Correct: Proline's side chain is bonded to its backbone nitrogen, which has no amide hydrogen for hydrogen bonding and restricts rotation, kinking the helix.
Glutamate
Glutamate readily occurs in helices, although its charge can interact with neighboring side chains.
questions.x: Proline's side chain is bonded to its backbone nitrogen, which has no amide hydrogen for hydrogen bonding and restricts rotation, kinking the helix. Trap: Picking the largest or most polar side chain instead of the one that disrupts backbone hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: Which feature of a eukaryotic mRNA primarily protects its 5' end from degradation by exonucleases?
o: A Shine-Dalgarno sequence
This ribosome binding site occurs in prokaryotic mRNA.
A 7-methylguanosine cap
Correct: The 5' cap, added co-transcriptionally, blocks 5'-to-3' exonuclease attack and helps ribosome binding.
Removal of introns by spliceosomes
Splicing removes introns but does not shield the 5' end from exonuclease digestion.
A poly-A tail
The poly-A tail protects the 3' end, not the 5' end.
questions.x: The 5' cap, added co-transcriptionally, blocks 5'-to-3' exonuclease attack and helps ribosome binding. Trap: Selecting the poly-A tail, which protects the opposite end of the transcript.

questions.q: A woman who carries one copy of the X-linked recessive allele for red-green color blindness has children with a man with normal color vision. What is the probability that a daughter of this couple will be color blind?
o: This applies the autosomal recessive ratio to an X-linked trait with a normal father.
This would require the father to be affected as well.
This is the probability that a son is affected, not a daughter.
Correct: The father gives every daughter a normal X, so a daughter is at most a carrier and cannot be affected.
questions.x: The father gives every daughter a normal X, so a daughter is at most a carrier and cannot be affected. Trap: Using the probability for sons for daughters.

questions.q: In the citric acid cycle, which step produces a nucleoside triphosphate by substrate-level phosphorylation?
o: Isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate
This step is an oxidative decarboxylation that reduces NAD+ to NADH.
Succinate to fumarate
This step reduces FAD to FADH2 and is catalyzed by a membrane-bound enzyme.
Succinyl-CoA to succinate
Correct: Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples cleavage of the thioester bond to formation of GTP (or ATP) from GDP and Pi.
Malate to oxaloacetate
This step reduces NAD+ to NADH and does not directly make a nucleoside triphosphate.
questions.x: Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples cleavage of the thioester bond to formation of GTP (or ATP) from GDP and Pi. Trap: Choosing a step that makes NADH or FADH2, which are not direct phosphorylation reactions.

questions.q: Hepatocytes of a patient taking a drug for many months show a marked expansion of an organelle that contains cytochrome P450 enzymes. Which organelle has expanded?
o: Peroxisome, a single-membrane organelle for oxidation
Peroxisomes handle fatty acid oxidation and hydrogen peroxide, not cytochrome P450 drug oxidation.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum studded with ribosomes
This organelle is specialized for the synthesis of secreted and membrane proteins.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
Correct: The smooth ER hosts P450 detoxification enzymes and proliferates when drug exposure is chronic.
Golgi apparatus, the cisternal stack near the nucleus
The Golgi modifies and sorts proteins and lipids, not drug metabolism.
questions.x: The smooth ER hosts P450 detoxification enzymes and proliferates when drug exposure is chronic. Trap: Selecting the rough ER because it is the most familiar ER type.

questions.q: In bacterial conjugation between an F+ donor and an F- recipient, what is transferred, and what is the usual outcome?
o: One strand of the F plasmid passes through a pilus-formed bridge, and the recipient becomes F+
Correct: Transfer of a single plasmid strand is replicated in both cells, so the recipient gains the F plasmid.
The entire donor chromosome passes, and the recipient becomes an Hfr cell
Only Hfr cells with an integrated F factor transfer chromosomal genes, and usually only part of the chromosome.
Phage particles carry donor DNA, and the recipient becomes lysogenic
This describes transduction.
Free DNA is taken up from the medium, and the recipient becomes antibiotic resistant
This describes transformation, not conjugation.
questions.x: Transfer of a single plasmid strand is replicated in both cells, so the recipient gains the F plasmid. Trap: Confusing conjugation with transformation or transduction.

questions.q: A human cell has 46 chromosomes in G1. Which description applies to the same cell in G2?
o: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids
Correct: DNA replicates in S phase, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids while the chromosome number stays 46.
92 chromosomes, 92 chromatids
Chromosome count does not double until sister chromatids separate in anaphase.
23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids
The cell remains diploid with 46 chromosomes; halving occurs after meiosis I.
46 chromosomes, 46 chromatids
This would be the G1 state, before replication.
questions.x: DNA replicates in S phase, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids while the chromosome number stays 46. Trap: Counting chromatids as chromosomes after replication.

questions.q: A toxin blocks voltage-gated potassium channels in a neuron but leaves voltage-gated sodium channels functional. Compared with a normal action potential, the action potential in the treated neuron will most likely:
o: have a larger hyperpolarization afterward
Hyperpolarization depends on K+ efflux and would be reduced.
have an increased resting membrane potential because K+ leaves faster
The toxin reduces K+ permeability, so K+ leaves more slowly.
fail to depolarize
Depolarization depends on sodium influx through channels that still work.
have a prolonged repolarization phase
Correct: Outward K+ current drives repolarization; without it, the membrane remains depolarized longer.
questions.x: Outward K+ current drives repolarization; without it, the membrane remains depolarized longer. Trap: Reversing the roles of sodium and potassium channels in the phases of the action potential.

questions.q: In which segment of the nephron is the largest fraction of filtered water reabsorbed?
o: Collecting duct
Water reabsorption here varies with ADH and totals far less than the proximal amount.
Proximal convoluted tubule
Correct: About two-thirds of filtrate water follows active solute reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
Descending limb of the loop of Henle
This segment reabsorbs a smaller amount, roughly 15% of the filtered water.
Distal convoluted tubule
The distal tubule reabsorbs a small fraction, adjusted by hormones.
questions.x: About two-thirds of filtrate water follows active solute reabsorption in the proximal tubule. Trap: Choosing the collecting duct because ADH regulates it, rather than the segment with the largest volume.

questions.q: Which hormone acts by diffusing across the plasma membrane and binding to an intracellular receptor that regulates gene transcription?
o: Glucagon
Glucagon acts through a cell-surface G protein-coupled receptor and cAMP.
Cortisol
Correct: Steroid hormones are lipid soluble and bind cytoplasmic receptors that act as transcription factors.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine binds G protein-coupled receptors on the surface of target cells.
Insulin
Insulin binds a receptor tyrosine kinase at the cell surface.
questions.x: Steroid hormones are lipid soluble and bind cytoplasmic receptors that act as transcription factors. Trap: Choosing a peptide or amine hormone that signals from the cell surface.

questions.q: A decrease in blood pH, as occurs in exercising muscle, affects the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in which way?
o: It does not shift, because hemoglobin responds only to PO2
Hemoglobin affinity is modulated by pH, CO2, temperature, and 2,3-BPG.
It shifts to the right, lowering hemoglobin affinity for O2 and promoting unloading of O2 in tissues
Correct: The Bohr effect: protons and CO2 stabilize the T state, so more oxygen is released at a given PO2.
It shifts to the left, increasing hemoglobin affinity for O2
A leftward shift is produced by alkalosis or decreased temperature.
It becomes hyperbolic, because acid disrupts cooperativity
The curve remains sigmoidal; acidity only shifts it.
questions.x: The Bohr effect: protons and CO2 stabilize the T state, so more oxygen is released at a given PO2. Trap: Shifting the curve left because lower pH seems like it should increase binding.

questions.q: Which statement describes facilitated diffusion of glucose through a GLUT transporter?
o: It is saturable and moves glucose down its concentration gradient without direct ATP use
Correct: Carrier-mediated transport is limited by the number of transporters (saturable) but is passive.
It is not saturable, because it depends on the lipid solubility of glucose
Glucose is not lipid soluble, and carrier-mediated transport shows saturation.
It requires a sodium gradient to couple glucose entry to sodium movement
That describes secondary active transport by SGLT proteins.
It moves glucose against its gradient using ATP hydrolysis
That describes primary active transport.
questions.x: Carrier-mediated transport is limited by the number of transporters (saturable) but is passive. Trap: Mixing up carrier-mediated passive transport with active transport.

questions.q: A car traveling at 20 m/s brakes to a stop with all wheels locked on a level road. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.80. Using g = 10 m/s², what is the stopping distance?
o: This omits the factor of 2 in the denominator.
Correct: a = μg = 8.0 m/s², and d = v²/(2a) = 400/16 = 25 m.
This divides by 4μg, doubling the factor in the denominator.
This is off by a factor of ten.
questions.x: a = μg = 8.0 m/s², and d = v²/(2a) = 400/16 = 25 m. Trap: Dropping the factor of 2 in v² = 2ad.

questions.q: Blood flows at 0.25 m/s through the aorta, whose cross-sectional area is 4.0 cm². The total cross-sectional area of the capillaries is 2000 cm². Assuming incompressible steady flow, what is the average speed in the capillaries?
o: This multiplies by the area ratio instead of dividing; flow slows as total area increases.
Correct: By the continuity equation, v₂ = v₁A₁/A₂ = 0.25 × 4.0/2000 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s = 0.50 mm/s.
5.0 mm/s
This is off by a factor of ten.
This assumes the speed stays constant, which contradicts conservation of volume flow.
questions.x: By the continuity equation, v₂ = v₁A₁/A₂ = 0.25 × 4.0/2000 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s = 0.50 mm/s. Trap: Applying continuity with the area ratio inverted.

questions.q: A 6.0 μF capacitor and a 3.0 μF capacitor are connected in series across a 12 V battery. What is the potential difference across the 3.0 μF capacitor?
o: Correct: C(series) = 2.0 μF, so Q = 24 μC on each, and V = Q/C = 24/3.0 = 8.0 V.
This is the voltage across the 6.0 μF capacitor.
This applies to capacitors in parallel, not in series.
This splits the voltage equally, ignoring the different capacitances.
questions.x: C(series) = 2.0 μF, so Q = 24 μC on each, and V = Q/C = 24/3.0 = 8.0 V. Trap: Treating series capacitors as if they shared voltage equally.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Which description fits the image?
o: Virtual, upright, and enlarged
This applies to an object inside the focal length.
Real, inverted, and the same size as the object
Correct: 1/di = 1/15 - 1/30 = 1/30, so di = 30 cm and m = -1.
Real, inverted, and smaller than the object
This describes an object beyond twice the focal length.
No image forms
An image forms at infinity only when the object is at the focal point.
questions.x: 1/di = 1/15 - 1/30 = 1/30, so di = 30 cm and m = -1. Trap: Misplacing the object relative to the center of curvature.

questions.q: Uranium-238 decays by alpha emission. Which nucleus is the immediate product?
o: Protactinium-234
This has Z = 91, the product of beta decay of thorium-234.
Thorium-238
This removes protons but not nucleons.
Thorium-234
Correct: An alpha particle carries 2 protons and 4 nucleons, so Z = 90 and A = 234.
Radium-230
This would require loss of an alpha particle from thorium-234.
questions.x: An alpha particle carries 2 protons and 4 nucleons, so Z = 90 and A = 234. Trap: Confusing which nuclear particle changes Z and A.

questions.q: What is the pH of a 1.0 × 10⁻³ M aqueous solution of Ba(OH)₂ at 25 °C?
o: This counts only one OH⁻ per formula unit.
This is the pOH, not the pH.
This treats the solution as an acid of the same concentration.
questions.x: [OH⁻] = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M, pOH = 2.7, pH = 14 - 2.7 = 11.3. Trap: Counting one hydroxide per formula unit of a dibasic base.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules has no net dipole moment despite having polar bonds?
o: XeF₄
Correct: XeF₄ is square planar, so its four Xe-F bond dipoles cancel.
SO₂
It is bent, so its two bond dipoles add.
PCl₃
It is trigonal pyramidal, and the dipoles add.
CH₂Cl₂
It is tetrahedral but with two different substituent types, so the dipoles do not cancel.
questions.x: XeF₄ is square planar, so its four Xe-F bond dipoles cancel. Trap: Assuming that polar bonds always produce a polar molecule.

questions.q: A compound has a partition coefficient K = [ether]/[water] = 4.0. A 100 mL aqueous solution containing 1.0 g of the compound is shaken once with 100 mL of ether. What mass of the compound is in the ether layer after equilibrium?
o: This would result if K were 1.0.
This is the mass remaining in the water layer.
This results from using K = 2.0.
Correct: Fraction in ether = K·Vₑ/(K·Vₑ + V_w) = 4/(4 + 1) = 0.80, so 0.80 g.
questions.x: Fraction in ether = K·Vₑ/(K·Vₑ + V_w) = 4/(4 + 1) = 0.80, so 0.80 g. Trap: Mixing up the mass remaining in water with the mass extracted into ether.

questions.q: How many stereoisomers exist for 2,3-dibromobutane?
o: Correct: It has two stereocenters but is symmetric, so there is a meso compound plus one pair of enantiomers.
This counts 2ⁿ without allowing for the meso form.
This counts only the enantiomeric pair.
This counts only the meso form.
questions.x: It has two stereocenters but is symmetric, so there is a meso compound plus one pair of enantiomers. Trap: Applying 2ⁿ to molecules with internal symmetry.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ/mol and ΔS = +120 J/(mol·K). Above which temperature does it become spontaneous?
o: This fails to convert kilojoules to joules.
Correct: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS < 0 when T > 40,000/120 = 333 K.
This inverts the ratio and also mishandles the units.
This equates the temperature with ΔS.
questions.x: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS < 0 when T > 40,000/120 = 333 K. Trap: Mixing kJ and J when comparing ΔH and TΔS.

questions.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion?
o: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴
This removes two 3d electrons first.
[Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵
This removes one 4s and one 3d electron.
[Ar] 3d⁶
Correct: Iron is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶; the 4s electrons are removed first.
[Ar] 3d⁸
This adds electrons rather than removing them.
questions.x: Iron is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶; the 4s electrons are removed first. Trap: Removing 3d electrons before 4s electrons when forming cations.

questions.q: A sound has an intensity of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ W/m². A second sound has an intensity of 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ W/m². By how many decibels does the second sound's level exceed the first?
o: 20 dB
Correct: ΔL = 10 log(10⁻⁶/10⁻⁸) = 10 × 2 = 20 dB.
2.0 dB
This reports the logarithm without the factor of 10.
100 dB
This reports the intensity ratio itself.
200 dB
This multiplies the ratio by 2.
questions.x: ΔL = 10 log(10⁻⁶/10⁻⁸) = 10 × 2 = 20 dB. Trap: Reporting the intensity ratio or the logarithm instead of 10 log of the ratio.

questions.q: A group of friends who each mildly favor a somewhat risky investment meet to discuss it, and after the meeting they all favor a much riskier option than any member preferred beforehand. Which concept best describes this outcome?
o: Group polarization, in which discussion strengthens the average initial leaning of the group
Correct: Discussion exposes members to persuasive arguments and social comparison, which pushes the group further in the direction it already leaned.
Social loafing, in which individuals exert less effort when working in a group
Social loafing concerns reduced effort, not extremity of opinions.
Deindividuation, in which anonymity reduces self-awareness and increases impulsive acts
The friends were not anonymous, and the outcome is a shift in attitude, not loss of identity.
The mere exposure effect, in which repeated contact increases liking
Repeated contact would affect liking for people or objects, not the extremity of a choice.
questions.x: Discussion exposes members to persuasive arguments and social comparison, which pushes the group further in the direction it already leaned. Trap: Choosing a group process that reduces effort or identity rather than one that amplifies opinions.

questions.q: In a jury, one member consistently and confidently argues for acquittal while ten others favor conviction. Over time, several jurors privately change their views. Which mechanism most likely explains the private change?
o: Normative influence from a majority that leads members to comply to avoid rejection
Conformity to a majority yields public compliance but not the change toward the minority position.
Informational influence from a consistent minority that leads members to reconsider the evidence
Correct: Consistent minorities cause people to think more deeply and sometimes actually change their private beliefs.
Obedience to an authority figure who has legitimate power over the jurors
The dissenting juror has no authority over the others.
Social facilitation from the presence of others, which improves performance on well-learned tasks
Facilitation concerns task performance and not opinion change toward a dissenting position.
questions.x: Consistent minorities cause people to think more deeply and sometimes actually change their private beliefs. Trap: Assuming that influence in groups always flows from the majority to the minority.

questions.q: A man who has never thought about his attitude toward running notices that he runs several mornings every week. He then concludes that he must enjoy running. This inference best illustrates which theory?
o: Self-perception theory, in which people infer their attitudes by observing their own behavior
Correct: The man infers a preference from his own behavior, with no prior attitude to compare.
Cognitive dissonance theory, in which inconsistency between beliefs and behavior creates discomfort
The scenario describes no conflict or discomfort that he resolves.
The elaboration likelihood model, in which attitudes change through central or peripheral routes
This involves a persuasive message, which is not present here.
Classical conditioning, in which a neutral stimulus acquires emotional value by pairing
No pairing of stimuli is described.
questions.x: The man infers a preference from his own behavior, with no prior attitude to compare. Trap: Choosing dissonance whenever behavior and attitude are discussed together.

questions.q: A casino patron keeps pulling a slot machine that pays out after an unpredictable number of pulls and continues long after a losing streak begins. Which schedule of reinforcement does the machine use, and what does it predict?
o: Fixed-ratio, which produces a pause after each reinforcement and rapid extinction
A fixed ratio would pay off after a set number of pulls, not an unpredictable number.
Variable-ratio, which produces a high, steady rate of responding that is highly resistant to extinction
Correct: Unpredictable payoffs after varying numbers of responses sustain responding even during long dry spells.
Variable-interval, which produces a slow, steady rate of responding based on time elapsed
Payoffs here depend on the number of pulls, not on the passage of time.
Fixed-interval, which produces a scalloped pattern with responding rising before each reinforcement
Fixed-interval schedules depend on time and predictable intervals, which do not describe a slot machine.
questions.x: Unpredictable payoffs after varying numbers of responses sustain responding even during long dry spells. Trap: Mixing up the ratio and interval schedules or the fixed and variable patterns.

questions.q: A teenager who is repeatedly described as shy by family members and teachers begins to see herself as shy and avoids new social settings. Which sociological concept best describes the process by which her self-concept was shaped?
o: The looking-glass self, in which people form a self-concept from how they imagine others perceive them
Correct: She internalizes the views of family and teachers as a mirror for her own identity.
The generalized other, in which a person takes on the standards of society as a whole
This concept concerns internalized societal norms in role-taking, not responses to labels from particular people.
Anomie, in which social norms break down and individuals feel disconnected
Anomie describes normlessness in society, not the formation of an individual's self-concept.
Role strain, in which demands within a single role conflict with each other
No conflicting demands within one role are described.
questions.x: She internalizes the views of family and teachers as a mirror for her own identity. Trap: Selecting a broader social concept rather than the specific idea of reflected appraisal.

questions.q: Teachers are told that a randomly chosen group of students will show a late growth spurt in ability. At the end of the year, those students show larger gains than their classmates. Which mechanism best explains the finding?
o: The fundamental attribution error, in which dispositions are overestimated and situations underestimated
This concerns explanations of others' behavior and not the effect of expectations on outcomes.
The halo effect, in which one positive trait colors judgments of all other traits
The students were selected randomly, and no particular positive trait influenced the judgments.
A self-fulfilling prophecy, in which expectations lead to behaviors that make the expectation come true
Correct: Teacher expectations alter attention and feedback, which in turn help students achieve more.
Stereotype threat, in which fear of confirming a negative stereotype impairs performance
Positive expectations rather than fear of a negative stereotype are described.
questions.x: Teacher expectations alter attention and feedback, which in turn help students achieve more. Trap: Choosing a perception bias rather than a mechanism that changes actual behavior.

questions.q: A person hears that a stranger was robbed and thinks, "She must have been careless; things like that do not happen to people who are careful." Which belief does this reasoning most clearly reflect?
o: The self-serving bias, in which people credit successes to themselves and failures to situations
This bias concerns one's own outcomes, and the judgment here concerns a stranger.
The actor-observer effect, in which actors blame situations and observers blame dispositions
This describes differences in explaining one's own and others' actions, not the need to see outcomes as deserved.
The just-world hypothesis, in which people assume that outcomes are deserved
Correct: The person blames the victim to preserve the belief that the world is fair.
The out-group homogeneity effect, in which members of other groups seem more alike
Nothing in the scenario refers to group membership or perceived similarity.
questions.x: The person blames the victim to preserve the belief that the world is fair. Trap: Picking the attribution effect that sounds close without matching the need for fairness.

questions.q: A server who is polite and smiling at tables but complains and jokes openly with coworkers in the kitchen is best described by which concept?
o: Symbolic interaction, which holds that society consists of shared meanings that arise in social interaction
This is a broad perspective, whereas the scenario illustrates a specific presentation of self.
The Thomas theorem, which says that situations defined as real are real in their consequences
This concerns how definitions of situations produce effects, not the management of presentation.
Role conflict, in which two statuses held by the same person make incompatible demands
A server and coworker are a single role set without a conflict between demands.
Impression management using front-stage and back-stage behavior in the dramaturgical approach
Correct: Different performances for different audiences are the core of dramaturgy.
questions.x: Different performances for different audiences are the core of dramaturgy. Trap: Choosing the broad theoretical label instead of the specific dramaturgical concept.

questions.q: Two people who are assigned to adjacent seats in a class become friends, and both discover they hold similar views on many topics. Which two factors most directly contribute to their attraction?
o: Proximity and similarity
Correct: Frequent contact and shared attitudes are two of the strongest predictors of attraction.
Reciprocity and complementarity
Complementarity (opposites attract) is weak, and the scenario describes similarity.
Physical attractiveness and scarcity
Neither the person's looks nor limited availability is mentioned.
Anonymity and diffusion of responsibility
These apply to behavior in groups or emergencies and not to attraction.
questions.x: Frequent contact and shared attitudes are two of the strongest predictors of attraction. Trap: Assuming that opposites attract in forming friendships.

questions.q: A public school offers a lunch program to feed children and, as an unintended result, gives parents a chance to meet other parents and form social networks. Which sociological terms describe these two outcomes?
o: A latent function (feeding children) and a manifest function (building networks)
This reverses the labels, since feeding children is the intended purpose.
A dysfunction (feeding children) and a manifest function (building networks)
Feeding children is not harmful, and networks were not the intended purpose.
A manifest function (feeding children) and a latent function (building networks)
Correct: Manifest functions are intended and recognized, while latent functions are unintended consequences.
A primary group (feeding children) and a secondary group (building networks)
These terms classify social groups, not the purposes of a program.
questions.x: Manifest functions are intended and recognized, while latent functions are unintended consequences. Trap: Reversing intended and unintended functions.

questions.q: A country has 1,000 people: 180 are aged 0 to 14, 620 are aged 15 to 64, and 200 are aged 65 or older. What is the total dependency ratio per 100 working-age people?
o: About 32 per 100
This is 200/620, the old-age dependency ratio alone.
About 61
Correct: (180 + 200)/620 = 0.613, or about 61 dependents per 100 working-age people.
About 38 per 100
This divides the dependent population by the total population (380/1,000), which has a different denominator.
About 29 per 100
This is 180/620, the child dependency ratio alone.
questions.x: (180 + 200)/620 = 0.613, or about 61 dependents per 100 working-age people. Trap: Using only one dependent group or the total population as the denominator.

questions.q: A researcher finds that Black women in a society earn less than both Black men and white women, an amount that exceeds what either race or gender alone would predict. Which concept best describes this pattern?
o: The glass ceiling, in which invisible barriers prevent advancement to top positions
This concerns advancement into leadership positions, not the combined effect of two social categories.
Residential segregation, in which groups are separated across neighborhoods
The scenario concerns income, not the spatial distribution of groups.
Social reproduction, in which class position is passed on across generations
This concerns the transmission of class status, not the combination of race and gender.
Intersectionality, in which overlapping social categories combine to create distinct forms of disadvantage
Correct: The compounded effects of race and gender together produce a distinct experience.
questions.x: The compounded effects of race and gender together produce a distinct experience. Trap: Describing a combined effect as simply the sum of two independent disadvantages.

questions.q: Which interaction stabilizes an alpha helix?
o: Hydrophobic interactions between the peptide backbone atoms and the surrounding water
The backbone is polar; hydrophobic interactions involve side chains and tend to bury them, not the backbone.
Disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains of residues that are four positions apart in the sequence
Disulfide bonds are tertiary structure and need not recur every four residues.
Ionic bonds between the side chains of every pair of adjacent residues along the helix
Side chain ionic interactions can contribute but do not define the helix, and adjacent residues point in different directions.
Hydrogen bonds between a backbone carbonyl oxygen and the amide hydrogen four residues along the chain
Correct: The helix is held by regular i to i+4 backbone hydrogen bonds, which repeat along its length.
questions.x: The helix is held by regular i to i+4 backbone hydrogen bonds, which repeat along its length. Trap: Attributing secondary structure to side chain interactions rather than to backbone hydrogen bonding.

questions.q: A double-reciprocal plot of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction shows two lines, with and without an inhibitor, that intersect on the y-axis. The inhibitor is most likely
o: an activator, because the slope of the line is decreased
A decreased slope means faster catalysis, but an inhibitor increases the slope on this plot.
noncompetitive, because Vmax is decreased while Km is unchanged
Noncompetitive inhibition lines intersect on the x-axis, since Vmax falls while Km stays the same.
competitive, because Vmax is unchanged while the apparent Km is increased
Correct: The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, so a common intercept means unchanged Vmax; a greater slope reveals an increased apparent Km.
uncompetitive, because both Vmax and Km are decreased
Uncompetitive inhibition produces parallel lines.
questions.x: The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, so a common intercept means unchanged Vmax; a greater slope reveals an increased apparent Km. Trap: Mixing up the intercepts of a Lineweaver-Burk plot.

questions.q: Which of the following is a function of the 5' cap and poly-A tail of a eukaryotic mRNA?
o: Base pairing with the anticodon of the initiator tRNA
The start codon, not the cap or tail, pairs with the initiator tRNA anticodon.
Stabilization of the mRNA against degradation
Correct: The cap and tail increase mRNA stability and promote translation initiation.
Binding of RNA polymerase II to the promoter, which starts transcription
Transcription initiation depends on promoter sequences in the DNA.
Recognition of the mRNA by a snRNP complex to catalyze removal of introns
Splicing is directed by sequences at intron boundaries, not by the cap or tail.
questions.x: The cap and tail increase mRNA stability and promote translation initiation. Trap: Assigning the cap and tail to splicing or transcription rather than to stability.

questions.q: An autosomal recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 people in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. The frequency of carriers is closest to
o: 1 in 26
Correct: q^2 = 1/2500, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98; carriers are 2pq = 2 x 0.98 x 0.02, about 0.039, or about 1 in 26.
1 in 50
1 in 50 is q, the allele frequency (0.02), not the carrier frequency.
1 in 100 is q/2, a quantity that has no meaning for carrier frequency.
1 in 2,500 is the frequency of affected individuals.
questions.x: q^2 = 1/2500, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98; carriers are 2pq = 2 x 0.98 x 0.02, about 0.039, or about 1 in 26. Trap: Reporting the allele frequency q as if it were the carrier frequency 2pq.

questions.q: How many molecules of FADH2 are produced during complete beta-oxidation of one molecule of palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons)?
o: 14 is the total of FADH2 and NADH, not FADH2 alone.
Correct: A 16-carbon fatty acyl-CoA needs 7 cycles of beta-oxidation, each producing one FADH2 and one NADH, along with 8 acetyl-CoA.
16 is the number of carbons.
8 is the number of acetyl-CoA produced, which is one more than the number of cycles.
questions.x: A 16-carbon fatty acyl-CoA needs 7 cycles of beta-oxidation, each producing one FADH2 and one NADH, along with 8 acetyl-CoA. Trap: Counting cycles as equal to the number of acetyl-CoA produced.

questions.q: Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV). Compared with before addition of cyanide, isolated, well-supplied mitochondria would show
o: a lower NADH/NAD+ ratio in the matrix, since NADH oxidation is stimulated by the electron backup
NADH cannot be reoxidized when electron flow stops, so the ratio rises.
a higher NADH/NAD+ ratio in the matrix and a collapse of the proton gradient
Correct: Blocking the final electron transfer stops electron flow, so reduced carriers accumulate and proton pumping ceases.
an increased oxygen consumption rate, since cytochrome c accumulates in the reduced state
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor; without Complex IV activity, oxygen consumption falls.
an increased rate of ATP synthesis, since protons accumulate in the intermembrane space
Without electron transport there is no proton pumping, so the gradient falls and ATP synthesis stops.
questions.x: Blocking the final electron transfer stops electron flow, so reduced carriers accumulate and proton pumping ceases. Trap: Predicting that a blocked pathway makes upstream carriers more oxidized.

questions.q: Patients with I-cell disease lack the Golgi enzyme that adds mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes. In these cells, newly made lysosomal hydrolases would most likely
o: be degraded by the proteasome immediately after translation
The enzymes are properly folded and enter the secretory pathway, not the proteasome.
be delivered to peroxisomes, which have similar acid hydrolases
Peroxisomes import proteins by a different signal and have different enzymes.
be secreted instead of reaching lysosomes
Correct: Mannose-6-phosphate is the signal for sorting to lysosomes; without it the enzymes follow the default pathway to the cell surface.
accumulate in the nucleus, since they cannot be exported
Hydrolases are made in the rough ER and pass through the secretory pathway; they do not go to the nucleus.
questions.x: Mannose-6-phosphate is the signal for sorting to lysosomes; without it the enzymes follow the default pathway to the cell surface. Trap: Expecting a mis-sorted protein to be degraded rather than to follow the default secretory route.

questions.q: Two strains of bacteria are separated by a membrane filter whose pores let viruses pass but block cells. DNase is added to the medium. Strain A acquires a gene from strain B. This transfer most likely occurred by
o: binary fission, in which the gene is copied into the daughter cell
Binary fission is asexual reproduction and transfers genes only from a parent cell to its daughters.
transduction, in which a bacteriophage carries donor DNA to the recipient
Correct: Phage particles can pass the filter and protect DNA from DNase within the capsid.
transformation, in which the recipient takes up free DNA from the medium
Free DNA would be destroyed by DNase.
conjugation, in which a sex pilus brings the two cells into contact
Conjugation requires direct cell contact, which the filter prevents.
questions.x: Phage particles can pass the filter and protect DNA from DNase within the capsid. Trap: Forgetting that DNA in a phage capsid is protected from DNase.

questions.q: If a pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in meiosis II in one of the two secondary cells, which gametes result from that division?
o: Two gametes with an extra chromosome and two missing a chromosome
That outcome occurs with nondisjunction of homologs in meiosis I, where both cells are affected.
Four normal gametes, since meiosis I already separated the homologs
A failure in meiosis II causes an error despite normal meiosis I.
Two normal gametes, one with an extra chromosome, and one missing a chromosome
Correct: The unaffected secondary cell makes two normal gametes; the affected one makes one n+1 and one n-1 gamete.
Four gametes each with an extra chromosome
Only one of the secondary cells is affected, so not all gametes are abnormal.
questions.x: The unaffected secondary cell makes two normal gametes; the affected one makes one n+1 and one n-1 gamete. Trap: Confusing the outcomes of nondisjunction in meiosis I and meiosis II.

questions.q: Why do steroid hormones such as cortisol circulate in the blood bound to carrier proteins?
o: They are rapidly degraded by plasma proteases unless protected
Protease sensitivity applies to peptide hormones, not to steroids.
They bind membrane receptors that require them to be in a bound form
Steroids act through intracellular receptors after diffusing across the membrane.
They are hydrophobic and have low solubility in plasma
Correct: Steroids derive from cholesterol and are nonpolar, so carrier proteins increase their transport in aqueous plasma.
They are large polypeptides that would otherwise be filtered by the glomerulus
Steroids are small lipid molecules, not polypeptides.
questions.x: Steroids derive from cholesterol and are nonpolar, so carrier proteins increase their transport in aqueous plasma. Trap: Treating steroid hormones as peptides.

questions.q: An increase in venous return to the heart increases stroke volume by the Frank-Starling mechanism. This occurs because
o: greater filling raises the heart rate, which reduces diastolic filling time
Heart rate is not the cause of the increase in stroke volume.
greater filling activates the baroreceptors, which immediately increase the sympathetic stimulation of the SA node
The mechanism is intrinsic and does not need baroreceptor reflexes.
greater filling reduces the afterload, which increases ejection from the ventricle
Filling does not reduce afterload; afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome.
greater filling stretches the ventricular myocardium, which increases the force of contraction
Correct: A longer sarcomere length at end diastole yields a greater force of contraction for the same neural input.
questions.x: A longer sarcomere length at end diastole yields a greater force of contraction for the same neural input. Trap: Attributing an intrinsic length-tension effect to a neural reflex.

questions.q: Furosemide inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Which effect is expected?
o: A larger urine volume of higher osmolarity, since water reabsorption is increased
Water reabsorption is reduced, not increased, when the medullary gradient is lower.
A smaller urine volume of higher osmolarity, since sodium is retained in the tubule
Inhibiting reabsorption of Na+ keeps it in the tubule and holds water there, which increases volume.
No change in urine volume, since the collecting duct compensates fully
Compensation by the collecting duct is incomplete, and diuretic use lowers the capacity to concentrate urine.
A larger urine volume of lower osmolarity, since the medullary gradient is reduced
Correct: Blocked NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb decreases the interstitial osmotic gradient, so less water can be reabsorbed, producing more dilute urine in larger volume.
questions.x: Blocked NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb decreases the interstitial osmotic gradient, so less water can be reabsorbed, producing more dilute urine in larger volume. Trap: Overlooking the role of the loop in establishing the medullary gradient.

questions.q: A 60 kg student climbs a flight of stairs that rises 5.0 m in 10 s at constant speed. Using g = 10 m/s², what is the average power the student expends against gravity?
o: This divides by 100 instead of 10 s, or divides the work by an extra factor of 10.
This doubles the work, as if the student had to lift the body weight twice.
This reports the work in joules (60 × 10 × 5) without dividing by the time.
Correct: Work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 5.0 = 3000 J. Power = 3000 J ÷ 10 s = 300 W.
questions.x: Work = mgh = 60 × 10 × 5.0 = 3000 J. Power = 3000 J ÷ 10 s = 300 W. Trap: Reporting the work in joules as the power.

questions.q: A uniform seesaw is balanced on a central pivot. A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from the pivot on one side. How far from the pivot must a 20 kg child sit on the other side for the seesaw to balance?
o: This inverts the ratio of the masses (30/20 and 20/30 confused), giving a distance too small.
Correct: Torques must balance: 30 × 2.0 = 20 × d, so d = 60/20 = 3.00 m.
This assumes the second child sits at the same distance regardless of mass.
This multiplies the distance by the mass ratio squared.
questions.x: Torques must balance: 30 × 2.0 = 20 × d, so d = 60/20 = 3.00 m. Trap: Inverting the mass ratio when balancing torques.

questions.q: Blood flows steadily through an artery whose radius is reduced by half at a stenosis. Assuming an ideal, incompressible fluid, by what factor does the blood speed at the stenosis change compared to the speed in the normal region?
o: It increases by a factor of 2.
This applies continuity using the radius ratio rather than the area ratio, which depends on the square of the radius.
It increases by a factor of 4, since area falls by 4.
Correct: Continuity gives A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Halving the radius quarters the area, so the speed rises fourfold. Bernoulli's equation then predicts a drop in pressure at the stenosis.
It decreases by a factor of 4.
The speed increases when the area decreases for a fixed flow rate.
It is unchanged, because the flow rate is the same.
The flow rate is the same, but speed times area is what is constant, so the speed changes.
questions.x: Continuity gives A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Halving the radius quarters the area, so the speed rises fourfold. Bernoulli's equation then predicts a drop in pressure at the stenosis. Trap: Using the ratio of radii instead of the ratio of areas in the continuity equation.

questions.q: A 12 V battery with negligible internal resistance is connected to a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor in parallel. What is the current in the 6.0 Ω resistor?
o: This is the current in the 3.0 Ω resistor, not the 6.0 Ω one.
Correct: Each parallel resistor has the full 12 V across it, so I = V/R = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A. (The 3.0 Ω resistor carries 4.0 A, and the total is 6.0 A.)
This is the total current drawn from the battery.
This divides the voltage by the sum of the resistances (12/9), as for a series circuit.
questions.x: Each parallel resistor has the full 12 V across it, so I = V/R = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A. (The 3.0 Ω resistor carries 4.0 A, and the total is 6.0 A.) Trap: Applying the series-circuit current formula to resistors in parallel.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters a glass with a refractive index of 1.50. What is its wavelength in the glass?
o: 900 nm
This multiplies the wavelength by the refractive index instead of dividing.
400 nm
Correct: The frequency is unchanged, and the speed becomes c/n, so λ(glass) = λ(air)/n = 600/1.50 = 400 nm.
600 nm
This confuses the wavelength with the frequency, which does not change at the boundary.
300 nm
This divides by 2 rather than by the refractive index of 1.50.
questions.x: The frequency is unchanged, and the speed becomes c/n, so λ(glass) = λ(air)/n = 600/1.50 = 400 nm. Trap: Multiplying rather than dividing the wavelength by the refractive index.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons are in the ground state of Fe³⁺ (atomic number 26)?
o: Correct: Neutral Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s². Fe³⁺ loses the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron, leaving 3d⁵, with one electron in each of the five d orbitals.
This is the number of unpaired electrons in Fe²⁺ (3d⁶), not Fe³⁺.
This results from removing electrons from the 3d orbitals rather than the 4s orbital first.
This assumes all the electrons are paired, as would occur in a noble-gas core only.
questions.x: Neutral Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s². Fe³⁺ loses the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron, leaving 3d⁵, with one electron in each of the five d orbitals. Trap: Removing 3d electrons before the 4s electrons when forming a cation.

questions.q: The Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What is the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water?
o: Correct: For AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = s². Therefore s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M.
This takes the Ksp itself as the solubility.
This divides Ksp by two, an incorrect treatment for a 1:1 salt.
This doubles the Ksp, which is also unrelated to the equilibrium expression.
questions.x: For AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = s². Therefore s = √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M. Trap: Using Ksp directly as the solubility instead of taking its square root.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules has a nonzero net dipole moment?
o: CO₂
The two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions in a linear molecule and cancel.
BF₃
The three B–F dipoles in a trigonal planar arrangement cancel by symmetry.
SO₂
Correct: SO₂ is bent because of a lone pair on sulfur, so its two S=O bond dipoles add to a net dipole. The other three molecules are symmetric.
CCl₄
The four C–Cl dipoles in a tetrahedral arrangement cancel by symmetry.
questions.x: SO₂ is bent because of a lone pair on sulfur, so its two S=O bond dipoles add to a net dipole. The other three molecules are symmetric. Trap: Judging polarity from bond polarity alone, without considering geometry.

questions.q: In a thin-layer chromatography experiment, a compound travels 2.4 cm from the origin while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. What is the Rf value of the compound?
o: This is the inverse ratio, front distance over spot distance, which is greater than 1.
This is the fraction of the path the spot did not travel (1 − 0.30).
Correct: Rf = distance traveled by compound ÷ distance traveled by solvent front = 2.4 ÷ 8.0 = 0.30.
This is the difference between the front and spot distances in centimeters.
questions.x: Rf = distance traveled by compound ÷ distance traveled by solvent front = 2.4 ÷ 8.0 = 0.30. Trap: Inverting the Rf ratio so that it exceeds one.

questions.q: D-Glucose and D-galactose differ only in the configuration at carbon 4. What is the stereochemical relationship between them?
o: They are enantiomers.
Enantiomers differ at every stereocenter, so they would be D and L forms of the same sugar.
They are anomers.
Anomers differ only at the new stereocenter of the cyclic hemiacetal, carbon 1.
They are constitutional isomers.
They have the same connectivity and differ only in spatial arrangement.
They are epimers.
Correct: Diastereomers that differ at exactly one stereocenter are epimers. Glucose and galactose are C4 epimers.
questions.x: Diastereomers that differ at exactly one stereocenter are epimers. Glucose and galactose are C4 epimers. Trap: Confusing epimers with anomers or enantiomers.

questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = +60 kJ/mol and ΔS = +150 J/(mol·K). Above approximately what temperature is the reaction spontaneous?
o: Correct: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 when T > ΔH/ΔS = 60,000 J/mol ÷ 150 J/(mol·K) = 400 K.
This omits the conversion of kJ to J, giving a value 1000 times too small.
This divides ΔS by ΔH, inverting the ratio and using the same unit error.
This multiplies ΔH and ΔS rather than dividing them.
questions.x: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 when T > ΔH/ΔS = 60,000 J/mol ÷ 150 J/(mol·K) = 400 K. Trap: Mixing kJ and J when computing the crossover temperature.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 20 minutes. What percentage of the reactant remains after 60 minutes?
o: This treats the reaction as linear, losing one third per half-life instead of half.
This counts only two half-lives.
This counts four half-lives, corresponding to 80 minutes.
Correct: 60 min is three half-lives. The fraction remaining is (½)³ = 1/8 = 12.5%.
questions.x: 60 min is three half-lives. The fraction remaining is (½)³ = 1/8 = 12.5%. Trap: Miscounting the number of half-lives in a given time.

questions.q: A participant can just barely tell the difference between a 100 g weight and a 102 g weight. If Weber's law holds, what is the smallest difference likely to be noticed when the standard is 300 g?
o: 6 g
Correct: The Weber fraction is 2 / 100 = 0.02, so for a 300 g standard the just noticeable difference is 0.02 x 300 = 6 g.
2 g
2 g would hold the absolute difference constant, which Weber's law does not predict.
3 g
3 g is not obtained from a constant proportion of the larger standard.
12 g doubles the correct value.
questions.x: The Weber fraction is 2 / 100 = 0.02, so for a 300 g standard the just noticeable difference is 0.02 x 300 = 6 g. Trap: Keeping the absolute difference (2 g) constant instead of the proportion.

questions.q: A listener hears a high-pitched tone. According to place theory, which part of the basilar membrane is maximally displaced?
o: The region near the apex, at the far end of the cochlea
The apex is tuned to low frequencies.
The middle region, which responds equally to all frequencies
No region responds equally to all frequencies; tuning is tonotopic.
The region near the base, close to the oval window
Correct: In the cochlea, the base is narrow and stiff and responds to high frequencies, while the apex responds to low frequencies.
The tympanic membrane, which vibrates at the frequency of the tone
The tympanic membrane is in the middle ear and is not part of the basilar membrane.
questions.x: In the cochlea, the base is narrow and stiff and responds to high frequencies, while the apex responds to low frequencies. Trap: Reversing the frequency map of the cochlea.

questions.q: A person remembers the ten-digit number 5558675309 more easily by thinking of it as 555, 867, and 5309. This strategy is an example of:
o: maintenance rehearsal
Maintenance rehearsal is repeating items without reorganizing them.
chunking
Correct: Chunking groups items into larger meaningful units, increasing how much working memory can hold.
the serial position effect
The serial position effect is better recall of items at the start and end of a list.
the method of loci
The method of loci links items to places along a mental route.
questions.x: Chunking groups items into larger meaningful units, increasing how much working memory can hold. Trap: Choosing a memory strategy by name recognition rather than by what the person actually did to the digits.

questions.q: A patient speaks slowly and with great effort, using mostly content words, but understands spoken questions and follows commands well. Damage to which area is most likely?
o: Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
Correct: Nonfluent speech with relatively intact comprehension is characteristic of damage to Broca's area, which is involved in speech production.
Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe
Wernicke's damage causes fluent, meaningless speech with poor comprehension.
The arcuate fasciculus connecting the language areas
Arcuate damage mainly impairs repetition while leaving comprehension and fluency intact.
The primary auditory cortex in both hemispheres
Bilateral auditory damage would impair comprehension, not just production.
questions.x: Nonfluent speech with relatively intact comprehension is characteristic of damage to Broca's area, which is involved in speech production. Trap: Associating any language deficit with Wernicke's area.

questions.q: After a week of news coverage of a rare disease, a woman estimates that the disease is far more common than statistics indicate. This is best explained by:
o: the representativeness heuristic
Representativeness involves judging by similarity to a prototype, not ease of recall.
functional fixedness
Functional fixedness is a limit on using objects in new ways.
the availability heuristic
Correct: People judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind, and heavy coverage makes examples vivid and accessible.
belief perseverance
Belief perseverance is holding a belief despite disconfirming evidence.
questions.x: People judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind, and heavy coverage makes examples vivid and accessible. Trap: Mistaking a frequency judgment based on ease of recall for a judgment based on similarity.

questions.q: A man's heart begins pounding when he sees a snake on the trail. He concludes that he is afraid because his heart is pounding. Which theory does this sequence best illustrate?
o: Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion occur simultaneously and independently.
Schachter-Singer two-factor theory
Two-factor theory requires cognitive labeling of arousal using situational cues.
James-Lange theory
Correct: James-Lange holds that the experience of emotion follows from perceiving bodily arousal.
Opponent-process theory
Opponent-process theory concerns the hedonic aftereffects of emotional or drug states.
questions.x: James-Lange holds that the experience of emotion follows from perceiving bodily arousal. Trap: Picking the better-known two-factor theory without checking whether the cognitive labeling step is described.

questions.q: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, which level of arousal is most likely to produce the best performance on a very complex, unfamiliar task?
o: High arousal
High arousal helps simple tasks but tends to impair complex ones.
Arousal that is as high as possible on every task
More arousal does not always improve performance, since the relation is an inverted U.
No arousal at all
Some arousal is needed for alertness; zero arousal would impair performance.
Low to moderate arousal
Correct: The optimal arousal level is lower for difficult tasks and higher for simple or well-learned tasks.
questions.x: The optimal arousal level is lower for difficult tasks and higher for simple or well-learned tasks. Trap: Assuming more motivation always improves performance.

questions.q: In a study of twins, the correlation for a trait is 0.80 for monozygotic pairs and 0.45 for dizygotic pairs. Using Falconer's formula, the estimated heritability is:
o: 0.35 is the difference in correlations without doubling.
0.45 is the DZ correlation, not an estimate of heritability.
Correct: Heritability is estimated as 2 x (rMZ - rDZ) = 2 x 0.35 = 0.70.
0.80 is the MZ correlation, which includes shared environment as well as genes.
questions.x: Heritability is estimated as 2 x (rMZ - rDZ) = 2 x 0.35 = 0.70. Trap: Using the difference in correlations without doubling it.

questions.q: A man who harbors intense, unacceptable hostility toward his coworker becomes unusually warm and solicitous toward that coworker. Which Freudian defense mechanism best explains this behavior?
o: Projection, attributing his own hostility to the coworker
Projection would lead him to believe the coworker is hostile toward him, not to act warmly.
Reaction formation, acting opposite to the impulse
Correct: Reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse into its opposite, so hostility appears as exaggerated friendliness.
Displacement, redirecting the hostility toward a safer target
Displacement would direct the hostility toward a less threatening person or object, but here it is not expressed at all.
Sublimation, channeling the hostility into a socially valued activity
Sublimation would channel the impulse into a constructive outlet such as sport or art, not into its opposite emotion.
questions.x: Reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse into its opposite, so hostility appears as exaggerated friendliness. Trap: Choosing displacement or sublimation because the hostility is being redirected, when the behavior is the direct opposite of the impulse.

questions.q: A researcher runs 20 independent hypothesis tests at alpha = 0.05 when all null hypotheses are true. About how many statistically significant results should be expected by chance alone?
o: Zero would require no Type I errors at all, which alpha = 0.05 does not guarantee.
Five would correspond to a 25% error rate per test.
Twenty would mean every test came out significant.
Correct: The expected number of false positives is 20 x 0.05 = 1, which is why multiple comparisons require correction.
questions.x: The expected number of false positives is 20 x 0.05 = 1, which is why multiple comparisons require correction. Trap: Ignoring that the Type I error rate applies to each test independently.

questions.q: A random sample of 100 adults has a mean systolic blood pressure of 120 mm Hg with a standard deviation of 10 mm Hg. Which interval is the best approximation of the 95% confidence interval for the population mean?
o: 118 to 122 mm Hg
Correct: SE = 10 / 10 = 1, and the interval is roughly the mean plus or minus 2 SE, 118 to 122.
100 to 140 mm Hg
100 to 140 is the mean plus or minus 2 SD, which describes the spread of individuals.
110 to 130 mm Hg
110 to 130 is plus or minus 1 SD.
119 to 121 mm Hg
119 to 121 is plus or minus 1 SE, a roughly 68% interval.
questions.x: SE = 10 / 10 = 1, and the interval is roughly the mean plus or minus 2 SE, 118 to 122. Trap: Using the standard deviation instead of the standard error.

questions.q: A hospital study finds that patients taking vitamin D supplements have more bone fractures than those who do not. Which explanation is most plausible?
o: Vitamin D supplements directly weaken bones in all patients who take them.
A direct harm cannot be concluded from observational association alone.
The result must be due to chance, because observational studies cannot detect real associations.
Observational studies can detect real associations; they just cannot establish causation.
Patients who do not take supplements are less likely to be admitted to the hospital.
Nothing in the stem suggests unequal admission rates.
Patients at higher risk of fractures, such as those with weak bones, were more likely to be prescribed the supplement.
Correct: Reverse causation or confounding by indication: the outcome risk may have led to the treatment.
questions.x: Reverse causation or confounding by indication: the outcome risk may have led to the treatment. Trap: Reading an association in observational data as evidence that the treatment caused the outcome.

questions.q: A tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Ala is placed in an electric field at pH 7.4. Which statement best describes its net charge and migration?
o: Net charge of +1, migrating toward the cathode
The side chains of Glu and Asp are deprotonated at pH 7.4, so the peptide is not positive.
Net charge of 0, with no migration in the field
Only a zwitterion with balanced charges would be neutral, and the two acidic side chains prevent that.
Net charge of -2, toward the anode
Correct: At pH 7.4 the N-terminal amine is +1, the C-terminal carboxylate -1, and the Glu and Asp side chains -1 each, for a net of -2; negative species move toward the anode.
Net charge of -3, migrating toward the anode
The N-terminal amine contributes +1, so the net charge is -2 rather than -3.
questions.x: At pH 7.4 the N-terminal amine is +1, the C-terminal carboxylate -1, and the Glu and Asp side chains -1 each, for a net of -2; negative species move toward the anode. Trap: Counting only the three carboxylate groups and forgetting the positive N-terminus.

questions.q: A protein migrates as a single band of 60 kDa on a nonreducing SDS-PAGE gel but as two bands of 35 kDa and 25 kDa after treatment with beta-mercaptoethanol. The protein is most likely
o: a homodimer held together by noncovalent hydrophobic interactions between two identical subunits
SDS disrupts noncovalent interactions, so a noncovalent homodimer would not run as 60 kDa and would give equal bands.
a heterodimer whose two different subunits are linked by an interchain disulfide bond
Correct: A reducing agent breaks disulfide bonds; two unequal bands that sum to the intact size show two different chains joined by a disulfide.
a single polypeptide with an intrachain disulfide bond
An intrachain disulfide would give one band on both gels.
a monomer cleaved by the reducing agent at peptide bonds
Reducing agents cleave disulfide bonds, not peptide bonds.
questions.x: A reducing agent breaks disulfide bonds; two unequal bands that sum to the intact size show two different chains joined by a disulfide. Trap: Forgetting that SDS dissociates noncovalent assemblies, so a persistent larger band implies covalent linkage.

questions.q: A drug inhibits DNA ligase in dividing cells. Which result is most expected immediately after treatment?
o: Accumulation of RNA primers on the leading strand
The leading strand is made continuously with a single primer and does not rely on ligase for continuity.
Failure of helicase to unwind the origin of replication
Helicase acts before ligase and is not dependent on it.
Loss of the 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading of DNA polymerase III
Proofreading is a polymerase function and is unaffected by ligase inhibition.
Accumulation of short Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand
Correct: DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments after primer removal, so inhibiting it leaves unjoined fragments on the lagging strand.
