questions.x: DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments after primer removal, so inhibiting it leaves unjoined fragments on the lagging strand. Trap: Applying a ligase block to the leading strand, which is synthesized continuously.

questions.q: An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 2,500 newborns in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the approximate frequency of carriers?
o: 0.0004 is the frequency of affected individuals (q squared), not carriers.
0.020 is the allele frequency q, not the carrier frequency.
Correct: q squared = 1/2,500 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98; carriers are 2pq = 2(0.98)(0.02) = 0.039.
0.980 is the frequency of the normal allele p.
questions.x: q squared = 1/2,500 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98; carriers are 2pq = 2(0.98)(0.02) = 0.039. Trap: Reporting the allele frequency q instead of calculating 2pq.

questions.q: Complete beta-oxidation of one molecule of myristic acid (14 carbons, saturated) yields which products?
o: 7 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH2, and 7 NADH
The final round releases two acetyl-CoA, so only 6 FADH2 and NADH are made.
14 acetyl-CoA, 6 FADH2, and 6 NADH
Each acetyl-CoA contains two carbons, so 14 carbons yield 7 acetyl-CoA rather than 14.
7 acetyl-CoA, 6 FADH2, 6 NADH
Correct: A 14-carbon fatty acid gives 14/2 = 7 acetyl-CoA, and it requires 7 - 1 = 6 rounds of oxidation, each producing one FADH2 and one NADH.
6 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH2, and 7 NADH
Six rounds of oxidation yield 7 acetyl-CoA, not 6, and 6 FADH2 and NADH.
questions.x: A 14-carbon fatty acid gives 14/2 = 7 acetyl-CoA, and it requires 7 - 1 = 6 rounds of oxidation, each producing one FADH2 and one NADH. Trap: Setting the number of cycles equal to the number of acetyl-CoA molecules.

questions.q: In I-cell disease, lysosomal enzymes are found in the extracellular fluid instead of in lysosomes. Which defect best explains this finding?
o: Failure to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi apparatus, which prevents sorting to lysosomes
Correct: Lysosomal enzymes are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi and recognized by receptors that carry them to lysosomes; without the tag, they default to secretion.
Failure to add a signal sequence to enzymes, which prevents entry into the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the secretory pathway
Without a signal sequence, the enzymes would not be made in the rough ER and would not be secreted.
Failure to acidify lysosomes, which prevents the activity of hydrolases
Poor acidification would reduce enzyme activity but would not move enzymes outside the cell.
Failure of the peroxisome to import enzymes containing a PTS1 sequence
Peroxisomal import defects affect peroxisomal enzymes, not lysosomal ones.
questions.x: Lysosomal enzymes are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi and recognized by receptors that carry them to lysosomes; without the tag, they default to secretion. Trap: Choosing a defect in ER entry for a problem with Golgi sorting.

questions.q: A donor Hfr E. coli cell is mixed with an F- recipient. After brief mixing, the recipient most likely
o: receives part of the donor chromosome but remains F- because the F factor is transferred last

Correct: In an Hfr cell the F factor is integrated into the chromosome; transfer starts within the integrated factor and the rest of F enters last, so mating usually breaks before it reaches the recipient.
becomes F+ because the F factor is the first segment of DNA to be transferred during the mating
F+ conversion occurs with F+ donors, not Hfr, because the F genes are at the end of the transferred DNA.
receives the whole donor chromosome and becomes Hfr
Complete chromosome transfer would need about 100 minutes of undisturbed contact and is rare.
acquires only the F plasmid and no chromosomal genes
Transfer of the chromosome, not of an F plasmid, is what characterizes Hfr matings.
questions.x: In an Hfr cell the F factor is integrated into the chromosome; transfer starts within the integrated factor and the rest of F enters last, so mating usually breaks before it reaches the recipient. Trap: Confusing Hfr matings with F+ by F plasmid transfer.

questions.q: Which of the following tissues is derived from embryonic endoderm?
o: The epidermis of the skin
The epidermis is formed from ectoderm.
The smooth muscle of the intestinal wall
Smooth muscle is derived from mesoderm.
The adrenal medulla
The adrenal medulla comes from neural crest cells, which are of ectodermal origin.
The epithelial lining of the trachea and lungs
Correct: The epithelium of the respiratory tract and the gut forms from endoderm, whereas muscle, blood, and bone come from mesoderm.
questions.x: The epithelium of the respiratory tract and the gut forms from endoderm, whereas muscle, blood, and bone come from mesoderm. Trap: Assigning organs by the location of the tissue rather than by embryonic germ layer.

questions.q: A patient takes atropine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist. Compared with the resting state before the drug, which change is most likely?
o: A decrease in resting heart rate, because sympathetic input is blocked
Atropine does not block adrenergic receptors; sympathetic input is unchanged.
An increase in resting heart rate, because vagal slowing of the SA node is blocked
Correct: At rest the vagus nerve releases acetylcholine on M2 receptors, which slows the SA node; blocking this removes vagal tone and raises the rate.
No change in heart rate, because the SA node is regulated by hormones only
The SA node is under dominant parasympathetic tone at rest, so blocking it changes the rate.
A decrease in resting heart rate, because parasympathetic input is enhanced
Atropine antagonizes the receptor and does not enhance parasympathetic action.
questions.x: At rest the vagus nerve releases acetylcholine on M2 receptors, which slows the SA node; blocking this removes vagal tone and raises the rate. Trap: Assuming that a muscarinic antagonist should slow the heart because it is called an autonomic drug.

questions.q: A woman with a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma has amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Treatment with a dopamine agonist is effective because dopamine
o: stimulates prolactin release from the hypothalamus, which lowers LH
The hypothalamus does not release prolactin, and dopamine does not stimulate it.
inhibits prolactin release from lactotrophs, which lowers prolactin and restores GnRH secretion
Correct: Hypothalamic dopamine is the prolactin-inhibiting factor; high prolactin suppresses GnRH, so lowering it restores menstruation.
inhibits oxytocin release, which prevents milk letdown
Oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary and is not the target.
stimulates GnRH, which directly shrinks the tumor
Dopamine does not shrink tumors through GnRH.
questions.x: Hypothalamic dopamine is the prolactin-inhibiting factor; high prolactin suppresses GnRH, so lowering it restores menstruation. Trap: Remembering that dopamine inhibits most pituitary hormones but missing that, for prolactin, tonic hypothalamic input is inhibitory.

questions.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis breathes deeply and rapidly. This pattern is best explained as
o: respiratory compensation that raises arterial PCO2 and thereby lowers blood pH
Raising PCO2 would worsen the acidosis.
respiratory compensation that lowers arterial PCO2 and thereby raises blood pH toward normal
Correct: Metabolic acidosis lowers pH and stimulates chemoreceptors, so hyperventilation blows off CO2 and shifts pH back up.
a renal response that increases the excretion of bicarbonate
Excreting bicarbonate would worsen the acidosis; the kidney would conserve it.
a primary respiratory alkalosis caused by a pulmonary disease
The ventilation pattern is a response to acidosis, not a primary lung disorder.
questions.x: Metabolic acidosis lowers pH and stimulates chemoreceptors, so hyperventilation blows off CO2 and shifts pH back up. Trap: Calling the hyperventilation a primary disorder instead of a compensation for metabolic acidosis.

questions.q: In the small intestine, which enzyme activates trypsinogen to trypsin and thereby starts the cascade of pancreatic zymogen activation?
o: Enteropeptidase, from the duodenal brush border
Correct: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) cleaves trypsinogen at the duodenal surface; trypsin then activates other zymogens, including chymotrypsinogen.
Pepsin, secreted by the chief cells of the stomach
Pepsin works in the acidic stomach and does not activate trypsinogen.
Chymotrypsin, secreted by the acinar cells of the pancreas
Chymotrypsin is itself activated by trypsin and does not activate trypsinogen.
Amylase, secreted by the salivary glands and pancreas
Amylase digests starch and does not cleave proteins.
questions.x: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) cleaves trypsinogen at the duodenal surface; trypsin then activates other zymogens, including chymotrypsinogen. Trap: Picking a pancreatic protease rather than the brush-border enzyme that initiates the cascade.
